I bought this game on sale for around £3 (might be $5-6 dollars for non-Brits). After playing it for four hours I am entirely convinced that I will never play it again. I even feel a little bad about spending this small sum of money on it. What caused this strong negative reaction?
I don't think I can define Torchlight II as a game. The central facet of a game, for me, is that my mental skill (knowledge and understanding, including memorisation) and/or physical skill (think fast-fingered arcade fare) improve, thereby improving my achievement. The player should be able to get better. *I* want to achieve. That's what I enjoy. I don't play games for the same reason I read a book or watch a film: games need to be, for me, an interactive experience in which I play a central part.
So I get my female Beserker with a badger as a pet. I'm already excited. The options available are clearly huge. What will I do? Who will I be?
I quickly divine that most of the skills are useless. I focus on dexterity and the Beserker skills around critting.
Four hours later I have a character who mostly specialises in auto-attack. Having given up already I check out Gamefaqs and note that more experienced players agree that a lot of the active skills are garbage. Why have I given up?
1) Exploration is pointless. Do you know what you will find? I do, and I've only played for four hours. The game has not shown me that there will be any capacity for it to surprise me.
2) Improving is illusory. So many skills are so pointless, and the game is so generous with loot that it's just numbers going up. I hit harder but the enemies have more HP. To me nothing has really changed.
3) I don't feel like the character or care about the pet. The storyline is boring and the writing is genre-fiction at its most unexceptional. I was already uninterested with the Alchemist while watching the first cutscene.
You might be thinking "you played it on Easy, it will be better with a challenge". Do you know what that challenge is? The numbers go up. That's it.
This game is not for people who think that games are something which involve the player. However, if you want to click on stuff and watch numbers happen then this experience is undeniably cheap, and it works well enough that the numbers keep coming.

Ok, full release is out. Here's my two cents on the full game.
If I consider buying this game a tribute to the creators of the show, it's barely worth $10 price tag during sale. I believe $10 is a fair price for this game. But at $25 full price? I cannot recommend it.
I notice they added an extra hit to Yang's uppercut combo but the overall chain combo mechanics is still short and inflexible. There's still no overkill mechanics and creeps still die when their HP gauge is depleted making it difficult to maintain chain combo. Invisible walls are still everywhere. There's a small pole in the middle of the yard in chapter 4 that has huge collision box. I lost combo and got slashed because of that pole.
And now after the update, the camera keeps zooming in the enemies in close combat causing unwanted disorientation. To add salt to the wound, the final boss is harmless, uncreative and yet extremely time-consuming. The reuse of the elevator voice line and the new hunter's rank system just screams how repetitive this game is.
I guess it does have some replayability with friends, except that after 3-4 rounds, no one wants to go the same places, beat the same mobs and spam the same skills over and over again. So the game is worth around 12 hours of gameplay if you're at lucky. If you're willing to spend $2 per hour of gameplay, go ahead and buy it. Me? I prefer titles that yield "cents in hour" rate.
TL;DR:
Is it a good game despite the short coming? I'm leaning to "yes".
Is it worth the price tag of $25? It's a big fat "HELL NO!"

An emotionally charged coming of age puzzle adventure.  If it doesn't bring tears of happiness / frustration / sorrow / joy to your eyes, I don't know what will!  It's not particularly challenging but buy it when it's on special for the play style, as a unique "single player co-op" (esp. if you have a controller with two sticks), or enjoy it as a simple interactive 2-player story on the same keyboard, as I did with my kids.  Just be aware, it does get quite dark and surreal / scary for kids, with drowning, family member loss and even suicide being very minor themes that might affect people sensitive to that sort of thing.  It is entirely linear, but many incidental obects and people can be interacted with by both brothers in different ways, and there are 12 side achievements you can work towards.  If for no other reason, the visual aesthetics and certain cut scenes are magnificent, making it a most enjoyable 4-6 hour journey.  I thoroughly recommend it!

Trine is a series that is so good you forget it's still indie. In AAA commercial games the sequel usually takes itself too seriously and 'fixes the broken elements', removing all the things that made it fun to begin with. Which is why I'm glad to say the wizard is every bit as OP as he was in Trine 1! Well okay maybe not quite as OP. They removed the floating platforms BUT in a fun trade off they also removed the MP system! Yes that's right you can keep spawning boxes until each level is beaten and never run out of MP! It's downright silly how often balancing boxes and planks beats each level. In one situation I had to pull a lever that extends a platform then race up a path and cross a gap before the timer runs out and the platform falls. After a couple tries I gave up on the lever, spawned 4 boxes under the exit then climbed up and walked out. Another victory for the wizard! All in all I love Trine 2 and not just cause there's a Linux build but also because it's fun and SO BEAUTIFUL!

I've been pleasantly surprised by this game. I bought this to keep busy during a quiet winter holiday season. It is an under-rated game that nearly compares to Skyrim. There is plenty to do. By no means is this a perfect game. Character customization is lacking; the constant running into invisible walls is infuriating. And the side quests tend to get repetitive at times. However, the story makes up for the flaws in the game. This is definitely a must-have game that should be picked up on a Steam sale. Kingdoms of Amalur was, in my personal opinion, a good purchase.

Modding the online multiplayer portion of any game should always be met with heavy penalty, and all proactive efforts should be taken to remediate such actions. This type of modding is often toxic and usually has a negative impact other players' online experience.
Modding the offline/singleplayer portion of games makes gaming what it is today. It allows players to express their creativity by taking a game and putting their own unique spin on it, generally enhancing the experience. There should absolutely never be a situation where a game developer should punish those seeking to mod this portion of the game. It restricts creativity and is a slap in the face to anyone who wants to get the most out of their gaming experience.
The recent news regarding Take Two Interactive's cease and desist letter to OpenIV is a blatent overstep of their authority. Unless their decision is reversed, and they take no other actions in the future that punishes ethical modding, players will unite and make a difference.

This game is one of the weaker Artifex Mundi games. It's a hidden object game taking up the story of Petar Plagojević a farmer of the backwater community Kisilova and the Kameralprovisor Frombald, who allowed the folk belief cure of cleansing the community from vampires, although he did it with a lot of resentment for the superstitious folk beliefs that were held by the people. The Case is well known and aside Vampires the people called it back then Consumption, and later tuberculosis, a disease that killed ten thousands of people around the world and was still a very dangerous disease back in the early 20th century. Some of the scariest ghost stories revolve around this disease and the hospitals in which the sick were treated under sometimes inhumane conditions.

However the Story of Petar Plagojević would have earned a more suspenseful storytelling, the voiceacting is at times abysmal, as are some twists and turns of the story - aside of that the game wouldn't have gotten past quality control under normal conditions, some hidden objects are placed so bad, that they trigger a "hint" - best example for this is the eggplant in one of the later hidden object pictures, and the duck in one of the very first ones... (Olga's Bedroom). The Riddles are recycled at least most of them, and some are also badly executed - others are well made, but too weak to be a challenge.
This game might be a musthave for Vampire-Cosplay diehards, at least the historical setting albeit not correctly transposed (1725 and already a Steam-driven ferry?) is an interesting backdrop - if the devs only had put more love into the voiceacting, the story itself and put a lot more into the folk tales of that time and the horror of the villagers, the game would have been a really decent choice. With this it's just an average port of a well known story, barely enough to scare little kids out of their pants, not enough to be a jewel, but also not bad enough to totally tear it down.

So, it is Friday the 13th (well, it will be for another hour here). I figured I'd play and review one of the myriad of spooky games I bought for this month. (The intention being since Halloween was coming up, to fit the theme.)
This particular game is a fun, short, Hidden-Object Game. It is loosely based on an incident that happened in Kisilova, in the Hapsburg (later Austro-Hungarian) Empire. There were a series of mysterious deaths, they blamed a recently deceased man, exhumed him, discovered what they thought were indications of him being a vampire, staked and burned the body.
This takes that incident (which was one of the first vampire tales to reach the western audience) and adds a bit of fluff to it. The games are interesting, and the plot intriguing. There is also a bonus chapter that only matters for its own feat (meaning you will already have gotten the no-clues/skips achievements, if you had not used them). It has a single choice at the end, which determines your fate...
I would recommend this game, though perhaps in a bundle or on discount would be best.

Whoa the reviews exploded after the release o.o First of all, please mind the ones that give negative reviews after under 2 hrs of play. There is so much potential in this game, but it won`t hit you untill you pass the first "what does this button do" hour. I was a bit disappointed too at first when i bought this game (in early access), but after getting the hang of things...it gets addictive ^.^
PROS:
- the music. It is amazingly catchy. Be sure to unlock the vinyl thingy, which will allow you to listen to all the soundtrack
- the super fast response time and availability of the developer team. They indeed seem present and interested to communicate
- the barbarians system (some kind of hoolingans that will start attacking your shoppe just cuz they can) Not only their numbers increase over time, but there are some funny types of bosses spawning around
- the thieves system. Honestly, being able to fry/chop/slash into tiny bits a pesky little thief that dares to steal your hard-earned merchandise? 11/10
- the time management/shop management/dungeon hunting/fantasy-medieval idea - the only other game on steam that fits these shoes (that i am aware of) is Recettear, so if you are a fan of this type of games, this is a huge plus
- the price. It is well worth it. If you expect to receive some super top polished game for 7 $ then... you aren`t living in the real world, i can tell you that. Only the soundtrack is worth almost that much ;)
- (this one can also be a minus, depending on preference) tin-man type of characters
CONS
- maybe the leaving early access was a little rushed, minor bugs here and there
- no true tutorial phase
- no access to the key bindings from the playing interface (Edit: fixed with a recent patch)
- limited hints and tips. If you don`t check the wikia before starting to actually play, you will find yourself starting a new game over and over, as you uncover what this and that button do. (Edit: partially fixed with a recent patch)
- adventuring takes awfully long, so if you intend to grind for specific reagents in order to craft some fancy equipment, brace yourself for a loooong journey (Edit: time required diminishes drastically after your champ reaches higher levels)
- very limited options for customizing your char
- no "rush time" option
- no way to identify a customer by class unless you hover over him (which is very tricky during rush hours, when the customers are roaming the streets)
All things considered, I would say a solid 8/10, with a lot of room for improvement and a lot of potential. If the devs continue to constantly keep in touch with the community and working to add new features, I am sure this game will get better and better.
I would advise to give this game a chance and keep in mind that the dev team is very small.

Sims 3, for all it's faults and troubles is probably the best Sims game to date.
The open world provides a sense of immersion not achieved by earlier games.  This is a feature that was missing in previous games.
There are a wide variety of expansion packs to provide additional functionality for just about anyone.
You can pretty much play the game however you want, you can make your sim an upstanding citizen, a socialite, an excentric recluse, a crook or anything inbetween.  You can have your sims befriend everyone and be known for being nice, use them to express your darkest desires to ruin all your neighbor's lives, or even ruin their own lives if you so chose.
That is not to say the game doesn't have it's problems.   It is probably the buggiest game ever released by EA, and that includes Sim Copter and Streats of Sim City.   It is using an archaic branch of Mono which makes the Mono releases chosen by Unity3D look new, and has a severely garbage collector that leaves unnecessary cruft everywhere and instead vacates other objects from memory as soon as you leave the lot they are on.   It seems either the core programmers didn't know how to mark something as a cached asset, or just didn't bother.   Despite the size of the game, there is no attempt to use either a disk heap, or a secondary virtual memory segment to store cached assets, and until recently it didn't even support over 2GB of game memory space.
Tech support is nearly non-existant, but fortunately the game has finally stopped being update to support expansion packs, which would commonly break the game completely for older expansion packs, so there are fewer issues.
To put it simply, the game itself I give a wonderfully positive rating as a near perfect game for it's category.  It is everything a Sims game should be.  However, the backend is flawed at best, and often downright broken, while tech support is downright non-existant.   Frankly, I think EA could care less about technical support or keeping their older games functioning on newer technology, and I think recent reports of having the worst customer support in the video game industry are not only accurate, but an understatement.
Still, if you can put up with these faults, The Sims 3 is certainly worth your time and frustrations.

Made by the guys that made Diablo 2, since most of the senior staff at Blizzard have left over the years.
-Immensely satisfying combat. The developers understand what makes these games good, it's the screen shaking, enemy-exploding combat coupled with loot hoarding. This is something that I really noticed with competing games like Path of Exile and Marvel Heroes, is that they lack the combat emphasis that Torchlight has. Hits don't feel heavy, and they don't cause enemies to die in satisfying ways.
-Pets. They help with combat, can cast spells to support you, and run errands to town to sell your excess loot so you can keep going (and make them buy items on the way back if you want). And hey, who wouldn't love a ferret gnawing on goblins by your side?
-Loot management is simplified, so no inventory tetris is necessary. Of course, if you enjoy inventory tetris, this is not a merit, but each to their own.
-Mods. UI, custom quests, custom classes, more maps, you name it, it's got it.
-LAN (yeah I'm looking at you Diablo 3.
-Can be played offline or online. Again, looking at you Diablo 3. You don't need to worry about some server on the other side of the world dying, or your ISP hiccuping, which does happen unless you live in a perfect universe.
-Hilariously simple story with no real plot. A bad dude is doing bad things, you must stop him. That's basically it.
-Not very difficult, especially for ARPG veterans, unless you crank the difficulty up. I rarely die on Standard, so it's casual friendly, for good or ill.
-Loot can be a bit bland, as you tend to get a lot of useless tier 'common' loot while levelling up, and it doesn't really serve a purpose besides being vendor fodder. There's also no loot quality filter like some games (Grim Dawn), but it's not a big deal.
-Multiplayer. One problem about modding is that other people online will not show up on your search list unless they have the
, which has led to much discussed fragmentation of the online community. While I almost never play online, other players have expressed frustration at this, and it's a valid point.
Seriously, buy it, unless you absolutely loathe action RPG's. It goes on sale frequently, though I believe it's worth the full price (obviously).

Onto the weapons, these themselves are quite fun but to use any weapon aside from the defaults you must craft them with a generation system, by which you use ores gained from completing achievements in game in the Tesla Shop, unlike a normal system you cannot craft the weapons that you specifically want you must input the ores into a machine which then pops out a random wep.

If you like RWBY and hack-and-slash gaming, this one is for you. It's surprisingly fun to smash a bunch of Grimm over and over again, and there is a pretty decent variety of attacks for each character.
There are several frustrating problems I have with this game, such as the inability to gain all the upgrades, the inability to counter an attack unless prompted (very inconvenient when being mobbed), and the repetetive nature of the story mode. Also, I still haven't been able to figure out what attack the second skill (called Reap for Ruby, Frostbite for Weiss, etc.) is. There is no tutorial and the game never tells you the name of each attack, except the special attack.
Aside from these problems, the game is quite fun to play, both online and offline. It's really great that the game auto-adjusts the difficulty as players connect and disconnect from the party, and that if the host leaves, another host is chosen; this way, the other players don't get booted from the game if the host leaves.
I would like to see the solo mode provide the rest of team RWBY as AI and possibly allow the player to switch between them during gameplay.
The replay value is questionable at the moment, but I am hoping that the full version coming this week will change this for the better.

EDITED DUE TO GAME'S EXIT FROM EARLY ACCESS
Pretty much the same as it was in early access, except it costs more (for the addition of about 2 maps/missions). Menus and character portraits look nicer though, so that's cool. Other than that it's the exact same really. Boring.
The environments are straight walks to the objective, scattered with small amounts of XP granting relics (which respawn when you die, meaning that you can farm within the first level in order to reach the maximum level). While interesting on the first runthrough, the environments quickly begin to become a blur of walled off areas and the journey from location to location becomes tedious and you soon realize that the sound of enemies materialzing out of thin air is obnoxious.
Littering these environments are enemies, leading to the game's boring as hell combat. Tou can literally beat just by kiting and pressing the ranged attack button to interupt an enemy's attack animation (seriously, it takes a bit of time but you can cheese practically the entire game minus the minibosses). The game, in it's entirety, consists of the the same repetitive objectives in different environments.
This is the entirety of the game. There is nothing else: "Kill all enemies here. Now run over here. Now kill some more enemies. Now run some more. Defend this object! Run a bit more. Now push this button. Surprise! More enemies! Go kill them! Having fun yet? No? Would more enemies help? How about a miniboss! No? Getting tired of fighting the same 3 enemy types? Too bad! Have some more!"
RWBY: Grimm Eclipse lacks anything to break up the action (If you can call the combat "action"), and the skill system, while interesting in it's requirements of kiling enemies in specific ways, lacks the form of progression that really makes you eager to level up (the hunter rank prestige system really doesn't help either). The skills feel noninfluential and only make fighting slightly quicker, which I guess I should be thankful for given it's dull nature.
Lastly, the mere discussion of the inclusion of DLC into the game in it's current state is an absurd notion and I strongly hope that the developers realize that the game needs a significant increase in polish and redesign of fundamental gameplay before additional paid content is added. RWBY: Grimm Eclipse is an egg that definitely should have been left to simmer on the metaphorical frying pan for a while longer before becoming a full title. It is now an undercooked and unappetizing mess, but one that could be salvaged into an at least bearable breakfast burrito, but only if the developers choose to do so.

I have a few HOGs under my belt now and Kisilova is quite different from other offerings by Artifex Mundi.  The graphics are more subdued but still lovely, erring on the side of realism compared to more brightly palletted games.
I found the puzzles quite challenging, but far from requiring a walkthrough.  I didn't manage to finish a hidden object scene in under a minute until the bonus section.  The mini-games are also more challenging than HOGs I have played.
A couple of times it was unclear why I was collecting certain items, but a thorough exploration of the area revealed the intent.  Most of the scenes remain unlocked for the whole game, rather than the usual 3 or 4 scene restriction that designers use to hand-hold players through the story.  It actually recalled to mind the wanderings of old-school adventure games.
I see some people commented on the character's accents ... I think this is nit-picking.  I found the voice acting quite pleasing.
All told, Kisilova was wonderful and made me use my brain (a bit) for a change.  The plot is obvious, but many of the puzzles are not.

Compared to other artifex games it is one of the weakest. The story is nothing to get excited about, except that it's based on a true legend. Amazing. Tekken - finally on PC and done extremely well.
I pre-ordered this game to show my support to Namco expecting it probably wouldn't even start up on my low-end hardware (Intel Compute Stick - Core m3 with 4 GB Ram and Intel HD 515 graphics). Having been a Tekken fan from Tekken 1 onwards - I just had to buy it at full price to show my support and expected to be able to play it in the future at some point.
BUT - IT'S ACTUALLY PLAYABLE ON A CORE M3 COMPUTE STICK! Of course with everything dialed down to minimum settings etc, but still - actually playable. Amazing.
Even Mortal Kombat X dialed down to the lowest of the low doesn't play as well as Tekken on this hardware. Yay Namco - awesome job! (Even online play and local VS matches run smooth!!! The same can NOT be said for MK X on this hardware...not at all...)
As for the game itself? What can I say - it's Tekken. Tekken updated with fantastic graphics, engaging story mode etc.
For those that don't know Tekken very well: In my opinion Tekken is the most intuitive fighting game out there; techniques begin to flow together quite naturally after only a few tries and it even features a 'take-over' mechanic (where a punch or a kick of an opponent can be caught and he / she will either be thrown or forced into a submissive locking technique). Virtua Fighter also features this but it is too complicated by comparison. (Plus there hasn't been a new Virtua Fighter in a long while... especially on PC...)
Unlike Mortal Kombat for exampe where playing quickly becomes "button mashing" trying to remember and execute a large number of moves without any subtle grappling / take-over mechanics whatsoever. In my experience it mainly amounts to who can mash the other to bits the fastest. Tekken is simply way more nuanced. One can play it simple or one can turn it into a "combat chess" game of sorts. Tekken also beats Street Fighter in my opinion as SF is a 2D based fighting mechanic with 3D graphics, whereas Tekken is true 3D and again - Tekken features the beautiful "take-over" mechanic. (Only DOA features this as well (other than the 'dead' Virtua Fighter franchise), but that's a story for another time).

I'm just completing the main game now and I have to say, this is one of my favorite open world RPGs. It shows its age in some of the systems (inventory, quest management) but has otherwise aged well.
What's to like about this game? The initial allure is sparked by the allstar team creating the world and game. This flame is kept burning by the charming world, the really fun combat system, and extremely flexible character development. I played a Chakram-wielding mage but I definitely respecced a good deal throughout the ~80 hours of my first playthrough. The story is good. Not Witcher good, but still good enough to suspend disbelief. If you're a lore buff, there's a lot to chew on in this game, so take a break at a tavern and read.
Where did I get frustrated? It's very obvious there's an Oblivion influence on this game. The questing system shares some of that era's awkward management style. There's a few quests that I got messed up and couldn't abandon. My only gripe about the combat system is the interrruptions with every hit. That can be a bit tiring when you're facing a bloodthirsty mod of Niskaru. Additionally, I tried the crafting system and I honestly only found Alchemy to be of some use. I found the quest rewards and found loot to be sufficient.
All in all, great game. So if you're lapsed back into Skyrim, gives this guy a shot. Certainly one of those games I'd take with me on a desert island.

I'm writing a review with only 11 minutes of playtime. I don't have much to say about the gameplay itself. It started off super boring, I'm sure it gets better over time. The issue I had is that the tutorial is impossibly bad. This game was stone unplayable without a list of controls on the second monitor.
While playing in 1080p the tutorial messages were so small on my screen that I didn't even notice them at first. Once I did notice them, I was incredibly disappointed by them. They did not tell you what buttons did what. The first prompt was "Press the action button to travel between your personal house and the back of your shop." What it didn't tell me is what the keybind for the action button WAS, or that I had to press that button while selecting a trapdoor on the ground.
After I figured that one out I walked into my shop and it said "Place a display in build mode before you open your shop." I promptly had to google how to enter build mode. The next prompt it gave me was to open my shop. I understood this one, but immediately went "Waaaait, don't I need to put ITEMS on these displays first?" Fortunately, my earlier random key smashing had brought up an order form, and I recalled that the keybind for that was Q. I ordered some health potions and placed them on my tables! Hooray! Success!
"Time to open my shop!" I said. Then I hovered over the potions to realize with horror that I was selling them at cost! My extensive time in terrible retail jobs told me that was a bad idea. I promptly returned to my second-screen wiki control page and found the controls for increasing and decreasing the prices. When I pushed the button to increase the price, nothing seemed to happen. I was confused. But wait! Something is happening! It's increasing the price of my health potion. . 1% at a time.
Now, you might be thinking that there's nothing wrong with that. . But when your health potion costs 10 gold, having to press the button to increase its price 10 times in order to raise the price by 1 gold is pretty damn annoying. It was a death by 1000 cuts. Those 11 minutes did it for me. I'm out. I wanted to like this game. I have failed.

Disclaimer: I will begin by saying that I love the Deus Ex universe, so it will make my review more biased than others (i think). I also don't care much for DLC or in-game purchases. I only opened the storage once and I didn't pre-order the game for it's "special content" so I've tried not to let it affect my personal experience with the game. Anyways, let's get the review out of the way shall we?
Gameplay: The gameplay mechanics is very solid. The augmentation systems is improved with better over-all design and some new augmentations, they feel better designed than the previous Deus Ex title. Dragging a body after incapacitating it is much faster and the cover system is improved. The gameplay is not without bugs, however, with some of them funny and some of them quite irritating. For example, the rag-doll mechanics that occur while dragging a body makes it stuck to corners.
Sound and Music: The sound effects are very solid and I don't have anything negative about them. Perhaps that's the problem - it's just "okay" and not "great". The music is excellent as always and is very similar to "Deus Ex: Human Revolution", but with a more "rock"-like tune to it. It's an improvement in my opinion.
Graphics: It's not next-gen, but the graphics are okay. The textures have a much higher resolution than before and the visual effects, such as particle effects are very good. The animations, however, are bad. For example, the characters look like lamp-posts with only their heads and hands moving during a conversation.
Story: Very good, as expected of a Deus Ex game. It's hard to compare it with "Deus Ex: Human Revolution" and make it justice. That's because it feels like the storytelling is different somehow. The character development with all the new characters is told in a solid fashion and I can't really think of anything bad how they where designed. Also, the game contains a lot of well written side mission and the side- missions affect some, but not a lot, of the end-game of the game.
Summary: For me, Dues Ex: Mankind Divided was almost everything I was expecting. The story and characters are well written and the sound is very good - almost hypnotic at times. While the graphics are good, it's not great, so don't go into this game and expect to get your mind blown. The gameplay feels like a large improvement of the previous Deus Ex title, but it's not without it's glitches and yes - glitches exists in the game (mostly UI-related glitches).
I would give this a 7.5 / 10 with a "must-buy" stamp on it, at least for people who love Deus Ex games. You will not be disappointed.

I was considering waiting for the full release to post this, but there's plenty to review right now.
When I first got this game, I didn't think I was going to give it a negative review. Upon release, it showed a great deal of promise while very accurately replicating the feel of the RWBY show. It was rather lacking in content  and some polish, but those were clearly signs of an early access game. By the devs own admission, it was something like 8-10 months from release when it entered early access. With the devs rapidly updating,  I figured that it would be plenty of time for development.
I was wrong.
The combat itself is good, with the combat revision being a great improvement upon the original style, the overall difficulty is good, and the level designs themselves are passable. Forever Fall's layout stands out in particular. All the voice actors are back and give faithful performances.
But some of the design choices have been disastrous and quickly gotten lukewarm reception or  even backlash. The biggest one, by far, has to be the models. Initially, the models were ripped straight from the show and looked completely accurate. Then, without any warning, the devs changed all the models into something completely different, it looked like a claymation nightmare. Backlash was intense, so the devs changed some of the effects to look more like the show. Except.... The models, while better, still do not give me the same feeling as the old ones do. I understand they were less efficient from a technical level, so I expected them to get changed, but the new models just do not look proper for RWBY's general look. It  also  clashes with the overall aesthetic of the new UI and talksprites during game. Grimm Eclipse lost a sizable amount of its positive reviews due to this.
Now, the devs are rushing the release by pumping out the other 2, of 4 total, campaigns in a single update and making a ton of other sudden revisions without EA testing. Considering the update history, I am concerned about how these sudden revisions will be in practice and if they'll be as bad as the model update.
Releasing this early also seems to defeat the point of early access. If memory serves, the game was in 0.28 or so on EA release, December 1st. It took till June to hit 0.60. That's a time of 6 months. Yet, not even one month later, we're going from 0.60 to 1.0, and there's not EA testing of the new amount of content. Why go into EA to get feedback and the like, if you're not going to let the player base test almost 50% of the game?
Essentially, the game started off strong, but begin to spiral downhill and took a nosedive around the model update. And if the new campaigns are only 2 stages, like Forever Fall is, it is going to have a serious lack of content. I do not recommend getting this game until the  devs put out more content and the changes coming in full release have been properly reviewed.

Fans of western RPG's need not look any further. A narrative from a NY-Times best seller that features many entertaining deviations from the standard high-fantasy tale. A whimsical soundtrack from the beloved composer of many classic Rareware games, Grant Kirkhope; and visuals that will both charm and astound you without being too demanding on your GPU.
Comparable to Witcher 3 in size, Reckoning will keep you engaged for dozens or even hundreds hours depending on your completionist tastes. The game runs flawlessly, never crashed, froze, stuttered and maintained a solid 60 fps throughout.
Simply put, Kingdoms of Amalur: Reckoning is the total package and stands tall amongst Bethesda's and Bioware's RPG juggernauts and is worthy of your time and money.

Kingdoms of Amalur: Reckoning (KoA) is probably one of the best games I've ever played and ever will. Soon after you fall down into a pile of bodies and miraculously come back to life your pitted in a war against the people of Amalur and the Tuatha. The Tuatha are a race of the Fae that have been corrupted. You start with one area gathering armor, weapons, supplies, allies, ingredients, crystals, and other different nouns and items. There is a great leveling up system that gives you unique and different abilities. I never got the hang of dispelling or lock-picking so I'd recommend upgrading those early so you can force them. Let's also talk about how there are lore stones that give you background information on the land around you. You'll enjoy your time in KOA from becoming a witches husband or the hero of the Warsworn. There's also a achievement if you talk to someone with nothing equipped so that's cool. If you'd like to discuss more about the game feel free to friend me. It's worth whatever amount of money you pay for it. Rate 10/10 Rank The Best

my first game:
I spawn as a carpenter on a large ship, with maybe twenty other people on it, in the middle of the ocean. We approach a fleet of British ships ready for a bloody fight. The boom of cannons and the ring of muskets deafen us as swarms of projectiles fly in our direction, smashing into our ship.
We fire back, and watch with joy as the large metal balls from our cannons smash into the enemy. After about another minute of fighting, our ship is stuck between several of the enemy's. We are barraged until our ship slowly begins to sink into the water. The last few remaining crewmates boarded a nearby British ship, attempting to take control, but are quickly mowed down by musket-fire.
I pushed a rowboat off of the ship, attempting to get away from the massive amount of bullets being shot in our direction. I watched as the rest of my crewmates were all easily killed. I hid in the water until the enemy boats had moved on to their next target, narrowly evaing death. I pulled myself up onto a lifeboat, looking for any other survivors in the debris. One man swam out of the wooden rubble and came aboard. I began to steer the boat toward a friendly ship. Suddenly, the man pulled out a violen and began to play the most beautiful songs, filling my ringing ears with wonderful tunes. We slowly made our way back towards the battle, all the way listening to his beautiful music. As we approached an enemy ship on out lifeboat, we drew our weapons, but were unable to get out of the way of the massive boat and were run over and killed.
10/10 would die in a lifeboat listenting to music again

Well here we are. Thief is♥♥♥♥♥♥ Thats the truth it might have been good in the 90's but know it doesn't hold up for many reasons to numerous to name so here a few cons and pros of the game:
Cons
Graphics: The graphics are old thats the best way to say it but to be honest graphics quality doesn't really bother me but i know a lot of people are quite into their graphics so thats why its here.
Map: I have nothing wrong with map screens if they have some sort of sanity put in them but Garrett god bless him decided to draw them by hand badly so the fun of a non-linear world is ruined by having no way of navigating it.
Combat mechanics: Unlike most stealth games nowadays where there is a focus on action over stealth which is good because it gives variety and change to the genre but what makes a stealth game great for me personally is choosing how you would like to carry out your task. Basically whether you want to go in guns blazing or be more sneaky in your execution, Thief doesn't give you this option as the combat mechanics are really bad and trying to fight the guards is like trying to beat a dark souls boss while armed with a wooden stick.
Pros:
Non-linear map: With reference with my map problems this is feature is sort of ruined but i am still going to add it because maybe you can decrypt Garretts map and get enjoyment out of the exploration of these massive maps.
Stealth mechanics: Brilliant, top of the range, amazing.. All words you could use to describe the stealth mechanics: Different materials make varied sounds either loud or soft forcing you to be more careful and thoughtful when you are sneaking through an area, The detail thats gone into the lighting and shadow casting is amazing for such an old game and it really adds to the dark grimy feel of the game but also makes for great stealth moments.
In conclusion. I do not recomend Thief as compared to the stealth games we have now a days (Dishonored and Hitman for example) and i know a lot of people are going to disagree with me but know they are doing it because they are filled with nostalgia and nostalgia can only be felt in people that played the orginal thief so if you are looking for a expansion on the orginial game with the same mechanics and atmosphere then go nuts but, if you are like me and have not played it then i would avoid this game as it doesn't hold up to games like Dishonored (my personal favourite stealth game) and Hitman.

As a Tekken player on console, was very skeptical about the PC release, so I grabbed it during sale and wished I had bought it sooner. This is probably the top fighting game on Steam right now, and runs like a dream compared to others (SF/MKX for example).
This series is forever evolving, and when you think the current game tops it off the next will completely smash it and take the crown. Each game in the series adds NEW mechanics to learn, and they are implemented perfectly. In 7's case, each character have their own 'specials' which adds even more dynamic play to the already overwhelming combo list.
Here are some reasons to grab this on PC over console, or even if you're looking to switch over from other fighters:
+ 60FPS
+ Well-polished, virtually bug/glitch free
+ Beautiful visuals and design
+ Fantastic port, as if it were made for PC
+ Simple, easy on the eyes UI
+ Online connectivity is fairly good, with low disconnects (UK-Europe-US)
+ Online: NEW Tournament mode gives you the competitive feel with huge in-game rewards
+ Very active PC playerbase, despite being a
+ TONS of content to unlock
+ Character customization top of it's league, hundreds of items to change your appearance from head to toe, not just whole costumes (although lacking compared to Tag2)
+ Gigantic roster, with guest characters (SF, and soon FFXIV)
+ Easy to pick up and learn
+ Incredibly fluid movement and combos
+ Each character has 100+ moves
+ Specials, 2 types per fighter, can be used on their own or tie in with current combos, well balanced
+ Stages well designed and the music gets you pumped like no other game
+ Story mode is far more improved than T6's 'scenario' campaign
+ Fairly priced DLC (first season pass in the series)
- Feels a bit 'barebones' compared to TAG2
- Time Attack and Survival modes gone, Arcade remains but downgraded
- Some people are suffering bad online connection/disconnects
- Currently one pre-order bonus fighter locked behind paywall, £4
- They removed our favourite drunken master, Lei who had been in the series since no.2!
- Online guides are a must since the game does not cover mechanics/combos in-depth
- Guest characters are a little off-putting since their animations and move sets are near identical to other games
- AKUMA LEVEL
- Tekken Bowling, first actual mode introduced in the DLC. I feel they could have spent better time and effort on bringing in new characters and stages

it is a fantastic new development in the series, and for a PC release, the series 1st, it has shocked me at how good the quality is. High recommend grabbing this while the sale is on, in all fairness you do not need the season pass right now, so for a fighter this good £20 is a steal.

Played Tekken for a long time and most of its iterations so this is a somewhat biased review.
It's easily one of the best fighting games out there. Tekken 7 is the best version of the Tekken franchise in regards to overall game mechanics. The system is balanced and it has a lot of intricacies that it retained from older Tekken games. It's a fighter with 3D movement which adds a layer of complexity compared to standard 2D fighters. Great roster of characters which most are based on real life martial arts for better or worse. Some have unique playstyles and you feel they're different when you play them. Characters easily have over 50+ moves which sounds a lot to remember but it adds another layer of complexity to the game. There are armor moves, a crush system, parries, reversals, throws, etc. Really great fighting game system overall.
Sadly other than the actual game mechanics itself there isn't a lot going on in regards to other content. Theres a currency system to buy items to customize your characters or buy movies for the gallery but the currency is useless as you can easily unlock all content by just playing 2000 matches. The arcade mode doesn't even feel like an actual arcade mode due to how short it is and treasure battle is just a chore for unlocking items you can't buy via chests with random loot. It's better to just play the 2000 matches and unlock everything that way rather than rely on RNG. The story mode could've been a little better but it was okay for the most part. There are also character episodes for some of the cast to where they have their own ending movie. Tekken was known for its funny and/or awesome ending movies but on this one most of them feel unsatisfactory. So if you're playing this game solo for the offline content I feel players will be disappointed.
Is this game worth the full price? Just for the fighting system and using it to play with people I would say yes. This game was meant for a person to play against another person (duh). So if you don't like playing against real people then do not purchase this game. But if you like fighting games I highly recommend this game. The game is easy to pick-up but hard to master. Once you dive in and invest yourself in this game and learning the mechanics, this game does not disappoint.

"Finally Made It To PC" was my Steam Awards Selection Comitee (SASC) write-in nomination for Tekken 7. Sure, I could have picked the "Even Better Than I Expected" award, since I really did pre order it immediately upon seeing the epic reveal trailer and investing so many precious hours into this single game when it released, almost neglecting everything else I've played before this ***Coughs*** Paladins ***Coughs***.
But let's address the elephant in the room, Tekken was always a Playstation exclusive. I was introduced to the Tekken Universe through Tekken 5 (Yes, I know, there are many that aren't too fond of 5) but it was all I had, which kept me really entertained with its quirky characters and hilarious humour from some of those cut scenes (Paul and Law, or Asuka and Jin to name a few) and I've always hoped this amazing game would one day make its way to the PC. But of course, everyone knew that if you wanted to play the next Tekken game, you'd have to fork out the money to buy the next generation of consoles which isn't necessarily a viable option for everyone. But then BOOM! They announce at E3 that this game will be coming to steam - shut up and take my money
Maybe the game didn't have as much comedy as 5 and took a much more serious, story driven approach - which is in no way bad because there were quite a few things that didn't make sense in the previous games, but the important thing was that it strengthened the community by leaps and bounds, because never before could so many people have access to a Tekken game and I'm sure the PC version has invited alot of newcomers to the Tekken Universe which is absolutely stellar
The game would be so much better if Sony and Microsoft would just do away with their silly politics and think about the players for once. If all Tekken fans could unite seamlessly, regardless of whether they are on PC, PS4 or XBOX ONE - Possibly even the Nintendo Switch - this game would have nothing but a bright future ahead of it
But nevertheless, bringing it to PC was a wise decision, and hopefully just the beginning. Hope to see sequals on PC as well.
Final thoughts, it's a great 3D fighting game and everyone should at least give it a chance, I'm sure they'll come to love it.

Mankind Divided is the kind of game where if you liked the last game, you'll probably like this one too. For the most part, it takes Human Revolution's framework and builds on it. The graphics are much better, the characters don't animate like marionette puppets in cutscenes anymore, you get XP for using passwords now, and the game adds a lot more use to the augs that were pretty much a waste of praxis in the last game, like the toxic gas breathing aug or pretty much any of the eye augs. There are a handful of new augs added in, but most of them do the same thing and involve shooting things from your arm, ranging from lethal to nonlethal, though there are some interesting ones like a remote hacking aug too. The game only has one hub, Prague, but they seem to have taken notes from 2014's Thief (which, no matter what you might think of the game as a whole, had an amazing city hub), and there's dozens of hours of content in the city, with plenty of things to do and see and steal, and its design really encourages you to get the most out of the navigation-based augs. It is a bit disappointing that it's the only hub, but each time you come back to it it feels a lot different than the revisits to Detroit and Heng Sha from HR.
The only part that doesn't really hold its weight is the main storyline, unfortunately. There are little bits and pieces of a conspiracy, and the game brings Janus and Vega (though even the two other people who played The Fall would be forgiven for not recognizing her, since they changed her design to the point that she's black now for some reason) into the main series, but the overall storyline feels fairly insignificant, and by the time it ended I thought it was just starting. I already felt like Human Revolution was a bit light on the overall conspiracy aspect that the series is known for, but in Mankind Divided it's not really there at all except in the intro and outro. That isn't to say that the story is bad by any means, and the main missions are still great and plenty of fun, but fairly often I felt more drawn to the side content than the actual main story because it tended to be more interesting. I also felt like the whole racism thing was seriously overplayed; it's interesting to see, but at the same time it's also really unbelievable at times, and feels a bit cartoonish in some cases.
But with all that being said, you can't review this game without also addressing the elephant in the room. Mankind Divided features microtransactions, allowing you to purchase praxis kits with real money. The Season Pass also includes "free" praxis, and so does the paid side-game Deus Ex Go. Personally, I didn't have any trouble having too much praxis to know what to use it on by the end of the game, and though it is a bit telling that the only person who sells praxis kits in-game has doubled the price since HR, I don't personally think it's a problem, but your opinions may vary. The microtransactions are very subtle, and aside from the Shop option in the main menu you won't even know they're there if you don't want to see them. It's also worth noting that the preorder DLC items seem to be a one-use thing, and if you bring them into your game you can only use them in one save file. Thankfully, the game features New Game+.
Overall, Mankind Divided is a fantastic game, and probably my favorite game from Square's Eidos. If you're the kind of person who likes to explore and do things on your own (and if you're a Deus Ex fan, you probably are), you can easily get around 40 hours out of the game; I spent 15 just doing side quests and exploring the city before I even started the first real main mission. I have heard of others finishing in around 20, but I can't imagine that unless you rush through the game. There's plenty of detail packed into every level of MD, and it really encourages you to take your time and look at everything. The main storyline is probably the weakest of the series so far, but it wasn't bad, and definitely not bad enough for me to not recommend the game. Overall, MD isn't the perfect modern Deus Ex we've been waiting for, but you can see it from here.

The game is somewhat short, and offers little replay value, maybe revisiting it once quite some time later. There is no branching path, it's a very linear story and game, the only alternative endings being a choice you make at the end of the bonus chapter.

This game is the perfect compliment to any fans of RWBY, while still delivering on some unique innovations to the hack 'n' slash genre. Each character has enough variety to feel unique from each other and to justify multple play throughs as all members of team RWBY.
Here's a short list of some of the pro's and con's in case you don't want to read all the way through...this is pretty long.
- Combat is easy to pick up, while fun to master
- Once you do master combat more, you'll lose yourself in the zen of battle (this is a good thing)
- Animations are well done, and this adds to the flow of combat
- Sound design is nothing too special, but the effects do add to each punch, stab, and slash
- Each character has a distinct look and feel
- The levels are beautifuly decorated, albeit, bland outside of combat
- Multiplayer is fast to find lobbies and to get a full team going
- It supports a dynamic drop-in drop-out multiplayer system
- Even though it's co-op, the scoreboard makes sure there's a competetive feel for those who want it
- Plenty of RWBY charm with the main characters' dialogue
- There's a diverse range of enemies to fight through out the missions
- Challenges and achievements give plenty of replay value
- Having a full 4 player team gives a great deal more fun in combat (and it's easy to find a full team)
- Takes almost no time at all to start a game or even join a friend's game
- The music is straight from Jeff Williams and Steve Goldshein themselves -- in other words, it's amazing!
- Although there aren't many graphics settings, the game looks great at any detail level (potato to Ultra)
- The game can be very easy, and it really is only hard on single player (though maybe that's because I've sunk 20 hours and probably have a good amount of skill now)
- Single player can be a bit of a drag at times (the characters do better as a team)
- The story is nothing special and feels a little cheesy (mostly the villian)
- There aren't too many graphical options and no way to set key-bindings
- There isn't a tutorial, but you do pick up on the game fast. Still, it would've been nice to see it.

I think the negative reaction is from people who expected this game to be a much bigger project than it ever was intended to be. They created a vision for this game, which the team never could achieve.

The combat system is desceptively simple, and you'll find you'll be learning some of the deeper ins and outs of each character hidden beneath what would seem to be button mashing. It's like any fighting game then; you can just button mash at random to get by, but learning to use your combos wisely will help you chew through waves of enemies much faster (thus giving you a better score). The main point is combat supports a n00b style, while still rewarding players who can master the mechanics.
That being said, some of the levels feel a little empty. Beautiful detail and fine craftsmenship to appreciate, yes, but outside of combat, the levels don't previde much to do. This isn't really a large issue because combat is extremely fun, and the time in between encounters helps with pacing. Searching for the hidden artifacts is perhaps the only interesting thing to do, but aside from a 100xp reward, they don't do much. There are some interesting jumping puzzels with artifacts at the end, but I never found too many sadly.
The main campaign does feel a little short, but it was never expected to be that long in the beginning anyways, so this is a minor annoyance. The point is to play through these missions multiple times, so perhaps it would be bad for the games design if the campaign took forever. It's much like Titanfall in this regard; if that's a good thing is completely up to you, however. The story isn't very great, and the main villian seems a bit cheesy if you ask me, but hey, it's an E for Everyone title. The story can only do so much to fit an E rating; though, it could have been better.

The few jump puzzles I encountered were fun and gave a nice change of pace. I would consider placing more of those to test the player's agility (jumping, climbing, etc.) outside of combat. Have a jumping puzzle be the only way to progress further, rather than just a way to a hidden extra. It's *butter than just sprinting through these otherwise beautifully colored levels full of atmosphere (Forever Fall is amazing!)
Forever Fall the the Island (day and night) seemed to be the best designed. The poisonous pits that you have to avoid work well with the gameplay, as a lot of it involves careful positioning of your character. So it would be nice to see something like that in more of the levels. Lastly, the invisible walls are far to great in quantity. If there was more mobility in the characters (double jump, ledge grab, etc.) then I could see how these walls could be removed in many places.
The story has a whole feels a bit brief, but again I feel that works well with the style of gameplay (though two more missions wouldn't hurt). Dr. Merlot is a very over-the-top kind of character, which helps keep the mood light, but if his lines had more subtlety to them, he would come off as more genuine. During the final boss fight, he uses one line with a ton of aliteration, which if he had done more of this throughout, it wouldn't feel so out of place. If he was portrayed more as insane to the point where his whole speech is dominated by aliteration and rhymes, that would've made Dr. Merlot feel a lot more in place with his over-the-top style.
The final boss is basically just waiting until he strikes the ground. He doesn't react to the player much at all, and there's no real point in even moving until his stinger is exposed. It would be better if there was some way to proc his stinger attack, such at hitting him with a close up attack (seeing as how a lot of his attacks are close range), or maybe by interacting with the environment: destroy a piece of pipe to spew hot steam over him. As it stands, the best way is to just wait -- waiting isn't difficult, but it does create the illusion of difficulty, so all this boss really does is drag on and feels exhausting. The boss needs to better react to the player's behaviors at the very least.
In short, this game is an amazing treat for fans of the show, while still giving plenty for newcomers to enjoy! The characters combat styles are very true to their depictions from the series and are very full of RWBY flavor: Ruby and her Syth weilding spins in the blink of an eye, Weiss with glyphs galour - freezing foes where they stand, Blake shadow jumping into the frey - letting her enemies fall in a flash, and Yang going full rage with unrelenting strikes to anyone foolish enough to stand in her way. The story could be better, and the ending to the campaign feels a little lack luster at best. This game is best enjoyed with a party of 4 (which is very easy to find)
With the addition of Horde mode to come in a free update, I can easily see myself playing this game for many more hours in the future, and with the promise of more content on the way after release (JNPR has been teased greatly!) there's going to be plenty of growth after the game's release.

Guncraft is a voxel-based shooter, but it's not just Minecraft with guns.
The standard FPS Deathmatch/Team Deathmatch is reminiscent of the Call of Duty franchise, albeit with a much more light-hearted and playful vibe. Combat is fast-paced and unpredictable, as players are free to destroy and rebuild the environment on the fly. The mining mechanic has been simplified from Minecraft because it's no longer the focus of the game. Mined blocks are traded for Resources, which are measured in dollars and correlate with the mined block's durability; resources can also be earned by scoring kills or achieving objectives. Resources can then be traded for new blocks, Killstreaks (a la COD), or prefabricated structures, which cost as much as their constituent blocks but spawn much more quickly.
In addition to maps and prefabs, players can also craft their own weapons. Players build their weapons using the same controls as in map and prefab editing, then select an archetype (assault rifle, shotgun, etc.) and assign points to different categories (hipfire accuracy, shoulder accuracy, damage, etc.). Players can make anything they want as long as it's not obscene or trademarked, and share it with the community on Steam Workshop.
Guncraft gives players plenty of opportunity to enjoy their new maps, prefabs and weapons. In addition to the stadard DM/TDM, Guncraft also offers plenty of unique game modes:
-In Spleef, players have only a drill and are trying to dig the floor out from under other players so they fall into the lava.
-In Paranoia, one or two players are randomly selected as zombie queens, who try to infect normal players and turn them into zombies. Normal players can't chat and don't know who's a queen, ratcheting up the tension.
-In Lava survival, players try to push each other into rising lava. The similar Meteor survival mode has them trying to survive a meteor barrage. In both modes, players only die from contact with the environmental hazard; weapons only freeze the target for 12 seconds.
-Race is just what it sounds like.
-Onslaught pits a team of up to four players against ever-increasing hordes of enemy bots. Very difficult, and very exciting.
Overall, the game balance is surprisingly good. It definitely feels like an Indie game, but not in a bad way. The developers are very responsive to community feedback and concerns, and the game is always improving. The community is small at the moment, but loyal. We could always use you if you want to join.

When purchasing something, there is a belief that the consumer is buying a fully functional product. This however was not the case with Mortal Kombat X. Upon launch, as I am sure you are well aware, the PC port was prone to a wildly inconsistent frame rate, unpredictable crashes, data wipes and, an unusable netcode for online play among other issues. I resisted the urge to immediately demand a refund as I had fallen to the sunk cost fallacy (having bought the game and the kombat pack) as well as having faith in Netherealm's announcement that they would fix the game. Fast forward a few weeks, the game received two massive patches in one day. The first one crashed the game and wiped user's local save data. The second one was implemented to fix the first patch. Neither of these two patches fixed the other problems the game had. Netherrealm made numerous promises to their consumers to fix the game. It took nearly 6 months to finally have a stable build of the game for offline play. The netcode was still abysmal and the community was nearly dead. Fast forward to today, I learned that not only will PC users not have access to the new characters coming out in the next few weeks but I will also not have access to the improved netcode that will be implimented in the future. As a fan of Netherrealm's games, I that instead of being rewarded for having faith in the company and their product, I feel as if I am being punished for not demanding refund sooner.

After months of terrible support from Netherrealm and HVS, the former decides to stop support and future updates for MK X. No KP2 or the GGPO netcode. I wasted money on this game and this is the last time I'll ever purchase a Netherrealm game.

Edited to include more details as requested:
I do applaud the devs for their work and their responses to the issue. I am sure a lot of work has gone into this, but it's not ready to leave early access. To answer the dev's question:
The tutorials should be built into the actual gameplay. For example, you do have a message flashing over the door of the shop to put down some displays and items before opening the shop, which was good. So I tried to figure out how to do that - I pulled up tutorials, read a little, and it kept repeating things like "use [action] button" or "use [imprint] button", but wouldn't tell you the actual keys to use. I then tried to look in options to find the keys, but they weren't listed - I had to save my game, close it, quit the game, and then from the settings menu look at what key the action key was. I shouldn't have to quit the game to figure out I need to use the "f" key.
Then I purchased some health potions to put on the displays, but I couldn't figure out how to change the price so I could actually sell for more than I had paid. I tried quitting the game again and pulling up key bindings, but it wasn't listed there either. I finally searched and found the same question on the forums - but the answer told me I needed to use numpad + or -. I'm playing on a laptop. I don't have a numpad, and regular + and - didn't change the item price. I tried pressing almost every button on my keyboard but saw no change in item price.
At that point I quit the game and asked for a refund. There may eventually be a great game there but I don't feel like fighting the UI to try and find it. I will likely look this game up again in a few months and see how it's doing. I wish the developers all the best.

This game has been on my wishlist for a long time. I was just waiting for it to emerge from Early Access to pick it up. Well today is that day and I have to say - it still feels like an Early Access game. I read a number of the other reviews and they just don't feel genuine to me, based on my experience in the game.
The user interface is clunky at best. For instance, they have a text based Tutorial in game that you can call up at any time, as well as some hints when playing. The hints say use the 'Action Button' to perform an action. Fair enough - but what's the Action Button mapped to? Ok, pull up the Options menu and look for keybindings...nope! You have to save your game and back out to the main menu just to look at the keybindings. Not a deal breaker but pretty annoying when you are first learning the game.
Next up - they have mini-quests you can complete (like sell 5 health potions) for experience. Great! I chose an easy quest and was on my way. But there are other quests you can choose too. So I pick a second one to optimize my time. Except when you select it you replace the original, without any prompt warning you that you lose all progress on the existing quest. Ugh.
Some pretty clear bugs in the UI, like looking at the skills. A hint says to select a skill to see its description and cost. Except it doesn't work. You click on the icon and it just asks you if you want to buy the skill without telling you the cost or the description.
Then there's the gameplay. Let's be fair I only played an hour so I didn't see very much. But that first hour was dreadfully boring. Purchase a display, purchase an item to put on the display, open the shop and literally watch the shop to see if any customers (or thieves) come in to do business. For 15 minutes you just stand there waiting to see if any customers come in. I'm sure there's much more to the game after this, but after an hour of just staring at the screen waiting for customers to buy I couldn't take it. This is only a $10 game, but it just isn't fun in the current state.

Continuing along with some older games and series that I've wanted to play for years, I now play the original Thief game (without having played any of the others, so I am going in order) after just playing System Shock 2, which I loved. Unfortunately, I did not love Thief, nor did I really like it, though I came in with high hopes as I knew that the same developers made System Shock 2.
Firstly, I don't mean that the game is inherently bad in many ways. In fact, the majority of the game's design aspects are actually very well done, except for one, which killed the game for me: the level design. Before I get there though, I will first go through everything else I thought about the game, on the positive side:
+ The story of the game was very interesting, even just starting with the first cinematic, which got me excited about the game actually going somewhere.
+ Garrett is a very likable character and had his own unique attitude, unlike a good amount of protagonists (e.g., the one in System Shock 2 had no character to himself).
+ The graphics of the game were decent and didn't bother me, though some things were badly distorted and the mansion in The Sword was ugly.
+ The mechanical design of the game is great. I love all of the different items you can use, including intriguing things like the Moss Arrows. The fact that game properly organizes the stealth depending on the material you are walking upon is good, as some current games don't do such a thing. Simple things like directional combat when swinging the sword is good, which again most games don't do nowadays. And changing the difficulty and indirectly changing the objectives of levels is a great idea to add replayability, extending the levels.
But sadly, none of the above things helped me get over the level design, which was abysmal. The first level was a generic mansion with nothing special about it, but I was like "Okay, just a way to get you into the stealth." The second level was just as generic, as I didn't find the zombies or caves interesting, and the prison was boring. The third level started making me really dislike the design.
At that point, I realized that the levels were mostly generic, giant mazes. Labyrinths, basically! Really, the third level was "unrealistic" in terms of size and really killed my mood. You're walking through the same-looking caves and crypts over and over, in circles. Even though I got through eventually, it was just random waddling and being bored. Most of the levels turned out to be this way. The levels are generally split up into different areas, but all of the rooms or places in a given area usually look the exact same in design. The only levels I ended up enjoying even remotely were the Haunted Cathedral and Strange Bedfellows because of atmosphere.
I enjoy stealth games greatly, and I didn't get impatient with the levels because you should take things slow. I'm fine creeping around as needed in such a game. I just got terribly bored and annoyed because most places took forever to find out how to actually get around simply because they were artificial expanses that had no character to them. Occasionally finding notes added some of that, but for the most part, it was all just so boring finding your way through. I know some people will ask if I was bored because I wandered around repeatedly knocking people out, but that was not the case. I was fine with the gameplay and I tried ghosting some levels anyway. It is just the design and layouts that I disliked and ruined everything for me.
I mean really, they are just expanses of nothingness... the crypts, the thieves guild, the mansion in The Sword, so on. I loved System Shock 2, and I love other stealth games like the Deus Ex, Metal Gear Solid, and Hitman series, and Dishonored as the most recent example, in which I went through the entire first playthrough not hurting anybody or being seen. But this game's world design made it so boring to play, even though I really was interested (and still am) with the story.
And you have the exact opposite with the last level in terms of approach. You go from incredibly open places to the most linear level ever... and just as boring. Fighting the enemies didn't interest me anymore at this point, and in fact, I ended up beating the level in less than 8 minutes (not counting waiting for the ritual at the end) because I simply just jumped along the way, evading all enemies. The only reason it even took that long was because of the water stream.
But after the final level, the final cutscene was still very interesting... So I'm hopeful that the next games get better in their levels. I guess I will find out.

Only a little ways in and I already love this game- finally, a multiplayer game that makes the "over 160 players in one game, wow!!!" statement actually -mean- something.
Games in this feel like real battles, and not just a meat grinder. Captains gather soliders for charges, battalions stage impressive defensives with cannons and mortars, and there are heroic last stands.
The battles are slow paced, but that works very much in the game's favour. Onus is put on carefully choosing your position, waiting to fire, and knowing when to get into a melee. Cautious fighters tend to get more kills and it's not just about how fast your reactions are. It's about picking the right time and distance to shoot or if the better course is to retreat. Shooting makes you vulnerable while you reload so you must pick your time right and depend on your team to cover you.
The feeling in game is generally irreverant and good-natured and a loss feels almost as satisfying as a win.
The class based system helps bolster the strategic element to the battles- the voice chat of captains is louder and marked in red for attention, allowing them to gather and direct troops.
Surgeons can provide healing, Carpenters can break or make siege works, and musicians... play delightful music! (good for if you like playing a more passive role in battle).
I only have a few caveats so far-
First, swapping weapons or melee feels a little awkward right now. It's easy to not know when you're in melee mode or not- a visual cue with the player's stance would be much appreciated.
Second- when playing as the french, the french voice stabs that you can activate, unless you are a native speaker, aren't easy to pick out. A visual cue over a shouting player's head to indicate what they're calling out may be a good addition.

I have three complaints:
1) The microtransaction thing is dumb, so just ignore it. I finished the game with a significant surplus of credits and praxis; you could buy more from the store if you are lazy, but the game gives you plenty if you take the time to explore and finish the side stories.
2) The end of the game is clearly a setup for the next game and/or the DLC. Kind of annoying but pretty typical of games, movies, novels, etc so I don't see why people get so worked up over it.
3) Has some optimization/stability issues for some people. Make sure to pick video settings that will actually work on your system.
Beyond those issues, there's a lot to like about this game. The environments are diverse and interesting. The atmosphere is really great. There's a ton of depth to the story and setting if you're willing to dig into the various emails, eBooks, newspapers, and so on. You're forced to make legitimately difficult decisions at various points in the game.
I could go on at length, but basically: If you like stealth action, exploration, and cyberpunk this is a good game. Play it, enjoy it, and don't let the little things ruin it for you.

RWBY: Grimm Eclipse is a Hack-N-Slash, Multiplayer, Coperative game. And today, I will be giving out pros, cons and verdict:

However, if you are to play the game with a processor like mine, I recommend having the settings on either Potato (Low) or Standard (Medium). Plus, the game actually has a very fast loading time, so I'm impressed on how Rooter Teeth pulled that off.
2)Game mechanics: The mechanics for the game are simple after a couple minutes of playing it, and they really fit with the flow of the game. The Grimm may appear to have low health, but they do take quite a while to kill, which I kind of like about Hack-N-Slash games.
3)Level System: The level system a key part of RWBY:GE. And boy, oh boy, did Rooster Teeth do a good job. The system in my opinion is very balanced and you can get upgrades for three things:
a)General Attacking
b)Special Attack
c)The character themselves
Each RWBY character has their own unique upgrades which are not only useful to them, but can also have a benefit on others. When a weak player is in peril, you with good upgrades can help them get back on their feet. You are part of the team, so make a good contribution to it.
4)Game Design: Now, some people may disagree with me but I like how the game looks in it's current form. Ever since the "Forever Fall" update, the models and textures were re-designed to look more like the show. And personally, I think that RT did brilliantly with the designing for the characters. They look really smooth and detailed and I really like it.
CONS:
1)Aura: To be honest, I like the aura system, but I think that it should have some adjustments in the final release. When a Beowolf hits you, nearly all of your aura is depleated and you have to run quickly to get it recovered. So I think that Rooster Teeth should make the Aura system a little bit more balanced.
2)Upgrade station: I like the station as a whol but there is one thing I would like to point out about using it in SinglePlayer. Now, I know that the Singleplayer in it's current form is in BETA, but the game should stop while you upgrade because most of the time, my deaths are from upgrading my weapons.
3)Level System: I like the system for leveling up and I think it's very fair and fairly balanced. But, the problem is, it only goes up to level 10 and that results in not being able to buy all the upgrades. Also when you level up, it doesn't get stored so you can't keep your upgrades and use them in another chapter/level. I hope that this come into effect on July 5th.
4)Death screen: When you play SinglePlayer or Multiplayer and you or all die, the screen showing the scores, stays ther for like half-a-minute, instead of only like 7 seconds. This can really bug me but i understand why RT put that in. Just in case there are any slow readers playing the game.
VERDICT:Even though there are a few things that need improving such as: pausing, leveling up, and aura. I believe that this is a fantastic game for those looking for Hack-N-Slash games and want to enjoy playing by themselves and with friends.
I would give this game overall: 9/10
