It's about time I've written a proper review for this game. I've played it since its standalone beta well before it came out on Steam. I had a different account back then of course.
Pros:
-It is fairly historically accurate with some very nasty exceptions like USSS fighting the U.S.
-There is a massive weapon/plane/tank variety.
-There is a combination of RTS and FPS that is not often seen.
-There is a variety of highly specialized classes.
-The FPS side has more strategy/skill involved than your typical Red vs. Blue FPS would.
-WW2 (There is not exactly an abundance of GOOD WW2 games that are still played these days.)
-There is bullet drop/travel time. (Hitscan is awful)
-It is not pure arcade like CoD but it is not a sim either.
-The game has combined arms between classes.
-It has a fairly decent community. It is no where near as toxic as the ones for games such as CS:GO.
-While clunky, the combat can be extremely fun.
-There is not USUALLY any 1 man army bs, it takes more than 1 guy to win a match.
-It has fairly large/varied maps.
Cons:
-There is an insane grind, I'm not even done grinding at my hours.
-It is very hard on new players.
-There are massive server/ping issues.
-The game is not optimized very well so even higher end pc's can lag.
-The asymetrical balance system between factions adds character but it causes more balance problems than it is worth imo.
-The armor in this game does not behave like armor, it behaves like artillery for the most part.
-There is horrible anti-tank balance. Tanks easily get obliterated by infantry carrying anti-tank grenades. (Almost all inf do)
-The movement system for both vehicles and soldiers feels rather clunky.
-There are rng mechanics for things just as hipfire, accuracy, and recoil for some weapons. This often results in random headshots which always instakill in this game.
-There are relatively few maps (and they constantly crash for me.)
-The average teammate tends to be foreign/hard to understand or braindead and won't play objectives/assist you.
-There are relatively few gamemodes so it can get quite stale, especially at my hours.
-There are cases of extreme spawncamping every so often, especially by planes and tanks.
-You will want a friend to play with as you will often face teams of friends or clans that will roll you as numbers matter in this game.
Tldr: It's a great game but it requires a hefty time investment or a lot of irl money. It is much better with friends. In addition to that, the game is in decline and this review may change to reflect that.

Grotesque Tactics, developed by an indie German studio by the name of Silent Dreams in a joint venture with Headup Games, is a turn-based strategy game in the same vein as Final Fantasy Tactics, Tactics Ogre, or any of the other hundreds of games with "Tactics" tacked on to the title. But let me clear the air here: unlike the aforementioned games, Grotesque Tactics is bad. Not "bad" as in Big Rigs: Over The Road Racing bad, but more like "all I wanted for Christmas was a Nintendo 3DS but all I got was a Nokia N-Gage" type of bad. You know, the type of disappointment you get when you are hyped up on all the good things, but are let down on every level.

The plot is nothing to write home about. There are no plot twists, no overly-emotional scenes, nothing. Just you and your party against an evil empire. You play Drake, a drop-out from the Glory Military Academy. By a stroke of luck, the very fact that you were the only dropout in the history of the academy has saved you from death in battle at the hands of the Dark Church (the aforementioned evil empire). Being mopey and emo (and yes, the game makes use of "emo" way too much), Drake finds the courage to fight back against the Dark Church with the help of the Semidivine Holy Avatar, the stereotypical "I'm better than you, and women love me" beefcake of the game. Together, you and Holy scour the world rescuing maidens, recruiting party members, and completing side-quests. Like I said before, it's nothing to write home about.

On that note, I should mention the writing. I'm guessing Silent Dreams hired a 16-year old high-school dropout to translate the game for them, because even though the game has had an extensive grammar overhaul for the English version, the writing would make even a first-year college student cringe in terror. Grammar and spelling mistakes abound, and any hint of humor the game wanted to convey has been lost due to the horrid translation. For example, Candy, one of the three maidens you rescue and recruit, constantly says "Hihihihihi" instead of "Hehehehehe" or *giggles*. The only thing that would make that worse is if Navi from The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time was put in the game and constantly said "HEY! LISTEN!" every ten seconds. But even then I would have fond flashbacks to my time playing an infinitely-better game. Grotesque Tactics just makes me want to punch babies.

And then there's the humor. I'd like it to be known that humor is NOT universal; it is purely subjective. Unfortunately, the game is billed as a parody of other great games. If anything, Grotesque Tactics is a parody of computer game designing. There is a difference between parodying a game and simply referencing a game, and Grotesque Tactics references the hell out of other games. The humor is extremely in-your-face, much like playing an interactive version of the Meet The Spartans movie. While it's not as ham-fisted as UnEpic, at least UnEpic is a good game.

The entire cast is a tragedy upon game design. The main character is an emo who isn't really emo all that much except in certain combat situations, the supporting character is the stereotypical knight-in-shining-armor with sunglasses, the rogue is a goblin who joins you because you killed his buddies, and various other travesties. Oh, and if any reader of this review is black and you want to see how German game developers portray black people, play this game. The only way the token black dude could get more stereotypical is if he had fried chicken in one hand and purple drank in the other. Yes, this is what Silent Dreams considers a parody. Sad, is it not?

From the moment you boot up the game, you can already tell you're in for a world of hurt. The pre-game loading screen features Holy Avatar and the three maidens, but the whole thing looks like it was made in Poser. Then the game starts and the Poser-like art is replaced by anime character portraits. Holy is pretty much the♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥of the group, while the three maidens and other female characters are in various states of undress. Let's not forget that while you are rescuing said maidens to recruit them, they are screaming about getting their clothes torn off. The character interaction, combined with the almost-ecchi artwork makes me believe that this game is the lead designer's attempt at a VERY bad self-insert fanfiction rather than a clever satire of RPGs.

And finally we come to the meat and potatos of the game: the gameplay. As I've said before, it's a clone of the various Tactics games you see or have seen on the market. Turned-based strategy on a battlefield with positioning. Nothing new, so let's move into what makes Grotesque Tactics stand out from the crowd (other than the sad attempt at German humor).

The really big thing about the game is the Obsession system. The game flat-out tells you in the tutorial that this is a limit break (I'm guessing Silent Dreams' thought process was "LOLOLOLOL! I MADE A FINAL FANTASY 7 REFERENCE! LAUGH, PEONS! LOLOLOLOL!"). Each character has their own way of increasing their Obsession, from hitting stuff (Drake) to getting hit (EVERY SINGLE PARTY MEMBER). Each Obsession does their own unique thing, but more often than not it involves the obsessed party member attacking another party member. West goes berserk, attacking anything in range (friendly or not), the maidens and the angel simply attack a party member, the goblin rogue blinds everyone in a radius (again, no thoughts to friendly fire) and warps to Holy, and Drake buffs nearby party members' attack rating but at the cost of halving his attack rating a few turns afterwards. Drake is obviously the most benefitial of the party, but that's not saying much considering everyone else is geared toward screwing you over.

Inside combat, you control all characters in order based on their agility. Outside of combat, however, you can only control Drake while the others automatically follow him. This works out fine, except for one major game-breaking bug that was the straw that broke the camel's back for me: Afflictions aren't removed once combat is over. In the battle leading up to getting the mage party member, West went berserk due to his Obsession. I ended combat right next to a treasure chest in a narrow 1x1 area in the forest with West blocking the only exit in or out. Since he was technically still berserk, he refused to move, and I cant move through party members. Needless to say, I was stuck and had to reload the entire damn mission. Have I told you yet how much I hate this game?

And lastly, I come to the deal breaker: the camera. Or, rather, the automatic camera panning. Any time there is dialogue or a character is moving, the camera will pan to that character. This isn't such a big deal if the damn thing would actually CENTER on said character. Instead, it trails behind a moving character. Trying to manually compensate for this means your camera goes out of whack and ends up 50 feet in some random direction. Again, this wouldn't be such a big deal if we could turn automatic camera panning off, or if movement outside of combat wasn't in real time. Alas, no on both accounts. This will, more often than not, lead to clicking the wrong square or giving you a fit of nauseua.

There aren't many grid-style movement, tactical, turn-based RPGs like this.  There is a good handful, but by no means are there many compared to other similar genres.  This is a pretty great game if you are a huge fan of the genre in search of new games to try.  If you aren't that big of a fan of the genre, then this may not be a good game for you.  The thing is: this game is technically a parody RPG, and lacks depth in many areas.  However, ironically, it still winds up being a pretty good game in the genre it is trying to parody, even though it is simple and minimalistic.
You need to go into the game understanding it's supposed to be simple and whimsical, and then you can enjoy it for what it is.
doesn't have very much depth in the departments of tactics or RPG elements, which many other games in the genre do have.  Each character is a set "class" and only learns 2 "spells."  And there is only really one set of weapons/armor for each character that you acquire through the game.  The story is linear and there are no choices. And since all the characters have a set class with set abilities, it takes a lot of the tactical aspects of party formation out of the game; but you still have to plan your actions on the battle-grid accordingly. So there are still some tactical decisions to be made, just far less than is typical in the genre. But even with this lack of depth, the game is still charming in its own right.
The characters and narrative progression are purposefully cliché and it works out in a charming way.  And the graphics and soundscape are fitting with the game; nothing jaw dropping but nothing jarring. The result is an overall presentation that is sarcastically atmospheric and endearingly casual.
So even though this game is just a "parody," and therefor is simplistic compared to others in the genre— it is a welcome addition to a small list of games to a true fan of an amazing genre. The game is just fun, simply, especially to a fan of the genre itching for a novel experience.

Man it sucks to throw a negative review on Shoppe Keep; after playing for 30+ hours, however, I feel like I've seen more than enough of the game to be informed enough to discuss it's merits.
Quick pro's and con's:
Shoppe Keep follows suit of games like Recettear, allowing the player to manage a shop for adventurers to get some items (potions, weapons, and armor). The premise of it, and initial outlook, are a lot of fun! Setting up your furniture to display your wares, scrounging around in trash cans, launching thieves into the air with your lightening. You slowly accumulate wealth, which allows you to purchase more furniture, display more items for sale, and expand your shop size.  It isn't a bad premise.
The first issue that absolutely destroys the game is busy work. This involves picking up items that customers remove from your shelves (for no reason other than to force you to pick it up, and give you a task while it's open). Once your shop is displaying 50+ items, and your customers throw 20 items everywhere in the first three minutes, it becomes a headache. It's been proposed to further drop the prices: at 130%, it still happens to frequently to be worth dealing with.
There was what appears to be a proposed fix, in the form of allowing robots to pick up the items for you (among other menial tasks these robots can accomplish); however, the robots cannot understand your floor layout, so you can throw your inventory quotas to♥♥♥♥♥♥ or you can not use them. Even with using them, you still ave to remove each piece of gear from the robots and place it back on the shelf.
The second busy work is sweeping. Yeah, you get a little broom, and every customer that comes through your shop, on top of throwing your♥♥♥♥♥♥all over the place, track mud everywhere. So you sweep all day. This has seen an attempted fix, however, in the form of highly expensive floor mats that are destroyed after about 60% of the day passes. Which can give you a leg up in picking up all of the♥♥♥♥♥♥everywhere, but you'll go back to sweeping before the day is done. And after the day is done. And sweep up all of the corpses.
After receiving some advice from the forums, I reattempted to get back into Shoppe Keep, but did so with a stop watch so I could measure the amount of time spent doing "busy work" and the amount of time spent actually managing inventory, upgrades, and the shoddy questing/champion system (more on that later). Of an hour and a half of play time, I spent 78 minutes doing busy work. It becomes tedious, to say the absolute least.
So then we have the singular dimension I've mentioned. You never see anything
the store. You never do anything but increase your wealth and buy more things. Then sell the things you've bought. On top of sweeping and picking up the damn items. They have something called a
that you can unlock, and send him on "adventures" (which consists of you clicking a GUI to send him to a location, and then reading the quest log). You can try your hand at gardening, which consists of clicking at dirt and waiting ~5 minutes.
I'm not mentioning the bugs because it's still in development, and it's pretty ♥♥♥♥♥♥ to call out a developing game for those. They could sweep me off my feet and change a LOT before release. As of now, just go play Recettear.

Short, beautiful, and surprisingly dark. Brothers – A Tale of Two Sons is a twin stick indie adventure game from Starbreeze Studios AB. Let’s get rocking.
The Good
I have nothing but good things to say about Brothers. Seriously though. This game is amazing from start to finish.
The world in this game was completely stunning. Every environment you’ll go through is gorgeous, plain and simple. This game has the sort of places you’d want to go on a vacation or, at the very least, on an epic quest of your own.
Brothers didn’t need intelligible dialogue to have characters that you feel attached to and have empathy for. You’ll quickly grow fond of the two brothers that you are in control of and of several of the characters that you’ll meet along the way. In addition to the fantastic characters, the story of Brothers (while simple) was touching, devastating, and wonderful all at once.
The puzzles were easy enough to get through as this game focuses much more on it’s story than it’s gameplay. Gameplay itself was also uncomplicated and easy to pick up, although, it was difficult to master. Each brother is controlled by a separate joystick of your controller (this game requires a controller or gamepad, by the way) and, at times, you’re going to get mixed up as to which joystick is controlling which brother.
The Bad
Okay, I thought of one bad thing about the game. It ended and, if you’re like me, you won’t have wanted it to. It was too short a time to spend in such a magical world, no matter how sad the tale.
The Meh
I’ve got nothing for you here, sorry.

Brothers - A Tale of Two Sons is about two brothers embarking on a dangerous quest in search of an elixir for their gravely ill father.
It is a single-player co-op game: you control both brothers using either the keyboard (as I have) or controller. The game itself consists of linear exploring, puzzles you have to solve using both brothers, some boss fights and a very powerful narrative. The game will last you approximately 2.5-3 hours.
For me the story takes the cake. Although the game is without a single (understandable) spoken word, I felt connected to the brothers and shared in their emotions as they came to pass. No game has ever done that with me to this extent.
The mechanics - controlling both brothers - tie in beautifully with the narrative and feels intuitive. They have their own strengths and weaknesses and during the course of the game frequently lend each other a helping hand. Controlling them can be quite tricky in the beginning though.
As you journey and explore the beautiful, varied landscapes you come across puzzles and boss fights. These tend to be on the easy side, but are very satisfying nevertheless given the mechanics. And they are varied enough to make sure they don't outstay their welcome.
The only two negatives I can think of is that the story is rather linear and that in order for some actions to work, the brothers sometimes need to stand in a very specific area. However, these issues are so minor compared to the gem that is Brothers - A Tale of Two Sons that I recommend the game even to non-gamers. Play/experience this game: you will not regret it.

This is a really good Fantasy RPG.
The character progression, both in equipment and in skills, is very well designed, you constantly have a significant goal in sight that motivates you. One feature worth explaining is your chosen destiny card, depicted as similar to tarot cards ("The Warrior", "The Seer" etc.), that do not only give you specific stat bonusses, but also help you identify with your role for the time being. I put it like this because after every level-up, you can choose a new destiny card. Those are unlocked with higher levels and perk points in one of the three classical RPG playstyles (Might, Finesse and Sorcery), and as you can respec at any time (by visitting a Fateweaver), one and the same character can be a soldier, a magician, a thief or even a hybrid class during his playthrough. As far as I know, this version of a flexible class system is unique to Kingdoms of Amalur, and I find it to be very creative.
Main questline(s), faction questlines, sidequests, exploration are all written and scripted according to high standards of quality and never feel like a dull grind. Some are a bit stereotypical, some voice actors sound a little boring (e.g. the final enemy in the Warsworn questline), your dialogue options are typically quite limited - but this only takes away very little from the epicness and entertainment potential of your adventures.
The world is enormous and colourful, many natural sights are real beauties. People and structures look a little too cartoonish for my taste, reminding you that this game is half a decade old - but you get used to it. Magical objects and plants glow and sparkle, which creates the vibe of a fairy tale. Immortal Faes (Elves) left ruins in the "enchanted forest" (that's not its name, but it feels like it) that impress by their style and their size, castles and dungeons are very spacious as well. If I am not mistaken, this world is much larger than Skyrim.
The combat system is definitely better than Skyrim's. It is very fluent and tactically varied, due to dodging, parrying, swift standard attacks, special moves and abilities you learn by spending skill points (which means that your fighting technique, as opposed to mere stats, developes while levelling up). Even my heavily armoured warrior rolled and killed like a Ninja swordsman, it just felt awesome. A very small annoying thing are the constant reminders of the option to "fateshift" (a special killing ability), something that was OK in the tutorial, but becomes really unnecessary after you have done it a few dozen times - and it covers an important part of the screen while the combat continues. I believe that this could have been fixed very easily, but then, nothing is perfect.
A weak point of this game is the lore. I  am not able to put my finger on a certain reason, but it does not appeal to me. Perhaps it is the way in which the lore is presented: "Lorestones" are inexplicably distributed throughout the land, and after you activate them, a part of a myth is narrated in voices that tend to be as weird as the worst of the NPC voice actors. After you activated all Lorestones in a region, you receive a stat bonus...very technical and quite unimmersive in my opinion.
Nevertheless, this game was absolutely worth the full price, and now that you can have it on sale, it is definitely a must-buy. It receives a solid 8/10 from me!

There seem to be a lot of negative reviews of this game, so let me put in my two cents.
When I first saw this game in the steam store it looked like a wallrunning ninja tps hybrid. And when I downloaded and played it, that is exactly what I received.
I was also pleasantly surprised by the 4player Co-op option and the the campaign doesn't start off fantastic I hear it gets fairly good, and playing with three friends always makes things more fun.
The game also has pay to win and MMO elements;
MMO elements like friends lists, PMs, and the option to make a clan, add something nice to the game.
I found the "pay to win"esque nature of the game wasn't a deal breaker for me, because it's more like "pay to advance faster". Without paying a single cent you can exceed at the game by skill alone easily.
The other thing is game progression, meaning players who have spent longer on the game will have better gear than you, and a few extra abilities.
However, this does not put them at an extreme advantage, and is balanced nicely.
On my first game I was able to get a nice amount of frags even though I was a beginner.
In terms of gear, the best gear is only slightly better than the defalut stuff, with upgrades being slight. This means that no matter what, you still need skill to win, not money. A player with the best gear will still easily be poned by a more skilled player.
I think this game s a lot of fun because of the ninja like elements to it with the wall running, the variance in the classes, and because of a lot of the unique gameplay aspects in it. Being able to switch weapons quickly means that a lot of the time you will be most efficient in using your entire aresenal agains an opponent, like switching from close range to mid range quickly to retreat from a flamethrower, or as a sniper dashing back quickly from an approaching assailant with a sword, to then quickly pull out your own sword and dash forward to catch them off guard. I like that you can use weapons while dashing and wallrunning, meaning I can dash sideways to avoid a sniper, and then quickly run across the wall towards him firing my SMG while jumping from wall to wall to avoid his fire, then dash to the side onto a pillar, then change to my sword while running in a spiral around that pillar so he can't keep track of me, then dash behind him and finish him off with the sword.
There are breast physics as some have so crudely fixated on, but unless you are swinging around character models in the lobby, they don't distract from gameplay. Also when characters with skirts die sometimes, they ragdoll into some compromising positions, but again, it's easy to either ingore or fixate on, depending on your attittude.
So in short, I really love the gameplay.
I love the way it blends long, mid, and closerange.
I love how fast paced it is.
I love the ability to form my own clan or get tegether a team line up with my friends and together wreak havoc online.
I love fealing like a ninja when I drop off a chandelier to take down an unsuspecting enemy.
I love the split second reactions in just the sword play alone, and I love that there is a whole gamemode dedicated to this.
Personally, I recomend this game, it's fun and it's free.

I'm a Pretty Big RWBY fan, but even so, it is just a FUN game. The New stuff that has been coming out is great, and the game runs pretty smoothly on my computer.
Online:
The RT and RWBY community is an amazing place. It doesn't happen often (because we get too involved with the game), but I have, in many of my game sessions, started typing in chat. And I get a really great response most of the time. For instance, I'll message when we come across Dr. Ooblek in game and I'll say something along the lines of "Hey Joel!" or "Hows it going Caboose?", and more often than not, you get into a game with someone who will laugh along and then you will be chatting and joking around in between hordes of grimm. Almost all if not every single person in game has something in common with you, something you both love. Its a great way to meet friends, even temporarily while in game.
Gameplay:
The attacks are really smooth and the leveling works really well. I was amazed when first playing the game when someone would drop out or a person would join in and the difficulty of the monsters would match it perfectly. It would change the difficulty on the spot and I found that to be really enjoyable. The Grimm are not overall too challenging but when you get into Hordes of enemies, you can't be surprised when you or a teammate gets overwhelmed and gets downed. Otherwise, it is an amazingly enjoyable time to pund your way through tons of enemies at a time.
New Stuff:
The game is really enjoyable as is, and is extrememly replayable (considering the campaign takes maybe an hour to complete and I have... holy crap... 16 hours into it as of me typing this), but it would be enjoyable to have just a little more "stuff" in the game. Recently they released Forever Fall which was an amazing update to the campaign and a whole new beautiful map to go through, plus the new type of grimm which is extremely fun and challenging to come across. I know the people over at Roosterteeth games are planning on introducing more maps, more campaigns, more gamemodes, and... more characters I believe. Until then, everything is being perfected as much as it can be.
Staff:
The people over at RT Games really listen to the feedback from the community, and it feels like we are having a conversation with them more than anything else. They tell us what they are working on, why they are working on it, and are open to suggestions and comments more so than any other community game maker I've seen.
Playing with Friends:
The ability to invite friends into the game session, and even make your own private lobby, is a real bonus to this game. None of my direct friend yet own this game, but I am pressuring them into getting it sooo hard. Until they do, I go online. The online people make it seem like I am playing with friends (if my friends were a lot nicer and actually helped each other out :) ), they go out of their way (most of them) to make each other's gameplay enjoyable. If someone is in a pinch, others will bail them out. If someone is down, others will risk their own lives to get them back up as quickly as possible.
Overall, Yes. You should get it if u are a rwby fan and have the money to do so.

In recent years follow-ons have had the unfortunate habit to under deliver and over promise. However When I played Deus Ex: Mankind Divided I was pleasently suprised. It manages to offer more gameplay elements and features while still retaining the feel of Deus Ex: Human Revolution.
Deus Ex has always been about story. Well crafted, well executed story; but more than that it has been about your story, offering multiple paths and outcomes. Are you the covert agent, the soldier, the negotiator. It rewards you for completing the game your own way, in overt and sutble ways. Choosing to persuade someone is an obvious choice in the dialogue and augment menu, however choosing to only use non-lethal weapons and avoid unecessary slauther through out the game not so much.
Similarly it lets you make choices devoid of moral implication, it's not telling you what the 'good' choices is or the 'bad' choice it treats the player with enough intelligence to let them come to their own decision, without embedding the developers bias, a trait far too rare in modern games.
The gameplay and combat is very much the same as the previous installment, Deus Ex: Human Revolution, but includes a host of new augments which bring new ways to tackle a level.
The area in which this game falls dramatically short however is in the publishing. With overpriced DLC, microtransactions and a host of day one bugs on PC it feels like the usual grievences the gaming and developer community has with publishers runs true here. However without the financial backing of a publisher this game could not have been as well made as it was.
Overall overlooking the technical issues, as hopefully they'll eventually be fixed, Deus Ex: Mankind Divided is a very well thought out and constructed game with interesting gameplay that rewards the player for exploration and doing things their way. The lack of developer bias in the enevitable moral choices the player faces in the story is refreshing and something in which more games should follow. I would wholly recommend this game to people, however I would wait for a Steam sale or discount to purchase the DLC that accompanies this game.

Overal - 9/10
Over 30 hours in so far, and I am still discovering things. Side quests, hidden loot, interesting stories and lore. People who say it is only 10 hours long just followed the main story and didn't do any exploration. You have to actually discover side quests (listening in on conversations and paying attention to details in the world), the game doesn't just throw them in your face (with a few exceptions), which makes finding them fun and rewarding.
There is even plot to uncover that the game doesn't give you waypoints for. You might find an email here that points you to a location over there, and when you get there you find what was obviously some kind of ritual, and exploring further will let you learn more about what you just saw. Just as an example.
My first run lasted 23 hours, and I didn't even uncover more than half of the sidequests.
I actually prefer a shorter main story with more side quests like this, so it is a positive for me. It rewards exploration, and the length is nice for doing multiple playthroughs (for example a lethal run or a non-stealth run) to experience what the game has to offer. Also nice for trying out different choices to see what outcomes you can get. If you prefer a longer story and less exploration, this would be a negative.
The port has been decent in my experience. There are a few quirks, but overal it was positive. For example, not being able to drag my mouse on the hacking screen to move the view bugged me. My GTX770 got 60fps on medium settings, and the game still looked great. I've seen a lot of people complain about performance with 8xMSAA turned on, should be common sense that you would have terrible performance with that on.
It took all the good from HR and built on it. There are very few things I would change to make it better. The only things that come to mind are being able to bind augments to keys closer to my hand, rather than the f keys, and a more punishing "overclock" system. without spoiling it, there is a choice you can make to make yourself stronger but with negative effects. In my opinion, those effects should be stronger.
There were some odd choices made by the publisher. Microtransactions and you can only access your pre-order loot on one save. Honestly, I wouldn't have even noticed the microtransactions if someone hadn't pointed them out to me. They are THAT unintrusive. They don't bring down the game at all imo. I don't get the hate personally. If the microtransactions were required to progress or something, I'd understand, but that isn't the case. I thought the preorder loot going away on a new save would be frustrating, but after starting a new game to get some achievements I missed on the first run, I didn't miss it. It is very easily replaceable in-game. In fact I'd almost say the game was better without it. It gave me too much power too early, ruined progression.

Grotesque Tactics is a turn-based strategy parody, that pokes fun
of other standard RPG games.  The music is done very well, and keeps the
pace and atmosphere of the game.  Each character represents some form
of a classic hero; be it the warrior, archer, or mage, but does an
excellent job of augmenting the comedic aspects of each one.
The controls and interface are sleek and well done, and I found
the gear progresses with the player in a very balanced way.  Tactically,
the game is good for a novice turn based strategist, but the story
appeals to everyone.
One unique twist is the obsession meter, which when filled, the
hero reacts in an unexpected way that may cause damage to anyone.  The
combat is simple, but the dialogue is entertaining and intriguing.
The characters and story parody other RPG's in an entertaining
manner, and I enjoyed playing this game.  I never felt my time was wasted,
and I can easily recommend this game.

The premise seems simple, poking fun at tired RPG/fantasy tropes, but in practice this game feels like a checklist of how NOT to make a game.
Steam says I played this for ~5 hours, my only playthrough clocks at ~1.5 h. The extras are repeating parts of the game because of random crashes, horrible slowdowns (my computer meets the requirements comfortably and yet the game slows down to 3-5 FPS (!) in explore mode, even with lowest video settings.
The camera is sometimes non-responsive and often annoying in its movement and positioning. The character movement is terrible as well, on multiple occasions I've had problem pathing from like 5 squares to an NPC I had to talk to (during 1.5 h of playtime!).
The interface is designed in a weird and non-intuitive way. LMB for attack? Nah it's for selection, RMB for execution. Esc to exit an inventory/option menu? Naaah, let's limit that to the [X] closing button, Esc just slaps the main menu over it. Oh, and if you try to start a new game then, the old menu persists on the screen. I couldn't check if it happens when you load a game with a menu open, because the only time I could load a game was after a fresh start, otherwise it crashed.
I wanted to like the game for being something different, but the end result will probably go into my "garbage" category, never to see the light of day again.
Oh, and if you want a good fantasy/RPG parody, try Unepic, that one's actually well-made.

Ok so here is my review for Samorost 2.
Like the other Samorost games Samorost 2 has some amazing art. It is a little more hand drawn looking than 3 whether this is a pro or a con is up to you but I personally enjoy it and it has a nice feel all around. The art is very consistent and really flows from one place to another. Everything has a nice mix of the look of a picture, an abstract world and random items in the everyday world. The only gripe I have about the art is the lack of screen shots. I really wish you could take screen shots in this game and I would really like it if they added that (don’t expect them to because of the platform its running on and the fact that it’s an older game). Although it is really a con I would still totally recommend the game.
The story in this game like in the others is very simple and nice. I doesn’t make you think too hard and there are really no decisions to make. This might not be for some people but it makes the game wonderful to play when you just wana check out and enjoy some free time. There are 2 main objectives of the story or game and each brings you some fun times and is decorated with amazing art and sound not to mention some great puzzles. The game took me around 4 hours to complete with some help and really feels like a treat instead of a grind.
The sound is really an excellent feature of this game. It incorporates great and odd voicing and smooth music/sounds. The environment is constantly being noisy and involves and draws you in with interesting and fun sound cues. I highly recommend playing this game with a headset and if you don’t I don’t think you will get the true feel of the game.
The puzzles are very nice and unlike samorost 3 and have a clear answer based on the environment or plot of the story. This makes the experience much more enjoyable and you will not need a guide to finish the game if you really wana do it by your own wits and cunning :P. I used a guide that I will link in the description. Most of the puzzles are not too easy and not too hard and can take from 5 to 10 minutes depending on the use of a guide. If a guide is used then you can quickly 2 to 3 minutes. I used a guide on most of the harder puzzles and it took me roughly 4 hours to complete.
You can tell that this is an older and homemade game. It’s not to polished and is a little bit clunky at times. This is where Samorost 3 and Samorost 2 really differ. You can’t free roam as much in this game. This make the world just a little less inviting but doesn’t really effect the gameplay in a negative way. Sometimes you will get stuck in a puzzle and will have to complete it before you can move or back track again. This is somewhat of a double-edged sword and made it easier to complete the game in a quick run. The other edge is that it also makes it less of a joy to free roam in and just enjoying the environment. In all I would prefer the ability to free roam and be able to walk in various places instead of a semi small area. The last thing is that sometimes your lil gnome or whatever he is will not look natural going or exiting a building and seems to get caught on the walls or doors. Although this games mechanics are not as good as its successors it’s still usually very clean and has a noice feel to it.
The characters really gave this game its fantastical feel. There are a variety of distinct species and subsets of characters to interact with. Most of them have a purpose and they really give the game its amazing fun and different feel.
This is a great game and a must have if you enjoy fun little games with amazing art and a good old calming feel. The puzzles are great for a relaxing time and generate just enough difficulty to make them feel interesting. The music and sounds are crisp and real and it doesn’t feel like any other game (besides the other Amanita Design games). It’s a steal for $5 USD and you can find it for $2.50 USD or under on sale most of the time. I would highly recommend this game before buying Samorost 3 because if you like this then you will also like 3. Below are a few links to videos and guides I found usefully in the game.

The stealth game that all other stealth games should be compared to Thief: The Dark project (later titled Thief: Gold) is one of the most difficult, most balanced, and most well represented stealth action games that I have ever played. Perhaps nostalgia is partially to blame for my love as I purchased the game when it was originally released as well as it's followup Thief 2: The Metal Age and Thief: Deadly Shadows. Thief introduced some of the most well known stealth mechanics still found today such as light/dark with indicators, leaning to avoid detection, smart AI that listen and search for you, and tools to incapacitate and confuse rather than kill your enemies. Add on top of this a three teired diffculty system that not only increases the number of enemies on the map, but also the objectives you must complete, and the AI's intelligence and ability to detect you and Thief shows us what a true stealth game can be if enough effort is put into design rather than art.

Thief: The Dark Project is the first game of the Thief series and basically the mother of first person stealth games. The gold version on Steam is the base game plus the expansion levels. This review contains minor spoilers but they are kept at the absolute minimum.
Garrett is a street child who survived by stealing. One day he gets caught by one member of a secret organization called the Keepers. The man, noticing Garrett's natural talent offers him the opportunity to join the Keepers instead of calling the city watch. Garrett agrees to join the Keepers and undergoes several years of training in covert operations. But eventually he grows tired of the Keepers who are only about keeping secrets and reciting prophecies, so he decides to leave to live by himself again. The Keepers are not keen of his decision but let him go. Garrett wants nothing more than not getting involved with other people's problems and eventually getting enough money for him to quit stealing altogether. However, things don't go as planned. Eventually Garrett gets involved with the wrong people and finds himself within a major conflict that he cannot ignore any more.
Thief's setting is a weird but interesting mix of middle ages, fantasy and industrialization. Due to not knowing a better word for it I'd call it fantasypunk. While swords and bows are common weapons electric lights and sophisticated machinery are often seen. Also does magic exist as well as undead and other monsters. The city is controlled by an extremely wealthy elite on one hand and a religious group called the Hammerites on the other. The Hammerites believe in absolute technological progress and also have a zero-tolerance policy against all criminals and non-believers. They are responsible for most of the technological wonders of the city. They have so much influence that they even run their own prisons. The Pagans, the other major religion in the city, have nearly no influence any more. If they are caught by the Hammerites they are likely to be executed since their beliefs are the polar opposite of the Hammerite doctrine.  They believe that humanity is already too advanced and needs to embrace nature again.
Garrett is neither a fighter nor is he able to cast magic spells. He is however extremely good at hiding in the dark and sneaking past people without getting noticed. He also is able to use some gadgets to aid him the most important ones being his arrows. In addition to his sword and his blackjack Garrett is carrying a bow for which he possesses various arrow types. The ability to use those arrows might actually be minor magic but that isn't clarified anywhere. Garrett can for example use water arrows to extinguish light sources from a safe distance. He also has rope arrows which can be shot into any wooden surface and provide a rope to climb up. Garrett also has access to noisemaker arrows come in very handy if he wants to distract enemies from his current hiding spot. Even though Garrett is able to kill with his sword or his broadhead arrows stealth is highly emphasized in Thief. On the highest difficulty setting it is not even allowed to kill any person. Killing someone always makes some noise unlike knocking them unconscious or avoiding them altogether. Even a one on one fight is dangerous for Garrett since his fighting skills are not comparable to those of the guards. If you knock somebody unconscious it is highly advised to hide the body somewhere in the dark so people don't find it. In addition to stealth the gameplay naturally revolves around stealing things. In most missions you have one main object to  steal and many other valuables that you can sell for cash after the mission to get more equipment or hot tips that may help with that next mission.
The level design focuses on big, sprawling and open levels. Most of the time there are several paths to approach your target. It is always beneficial to search every corner because you might find valuables, documents or even secret doors. The levels look and feel like actualy places, not just like a path for the player to walk. The game's sound design is top notch and still cannot be matched by many modern games. The graphics are obviously a little dated but there is a community patch that not only makes everything look a little crispier but also fixes all compatibility issues with widescreen monitors and multicore processors.
Thief features a quite unusual approach on difficulty settings. A higher difficulty does not make the enemies stronger and also does not place more enemies in the level. Instead it just adds more mission objectives. On the lowest difficulty it is often enough to just get your main target. On the highest setting it is not enough to just put the treasure in your pockets. You also need to get out afterwards. In addition to that there are more objectives like finding more special items or stealing a certain amount in gold value. There are many parts of the game that you can only experience on the highest difficulty setting, therefore I recommend playing it on that.
Thief: The Dark Project is still one of the best and most atmospheric stealth games out there and I think everybody who is in the least interested in stealth games, games that are heavy on atmosphere or games with good level design should give it a try.

This game is incredibly fun, and is really (I think) the best shooter/minecraft hybrid out there. It has auto-build features in-game for what are called prefabs, this way you can be building, and defending at the same time which is very useful. It is true, the game has a small (really small) player base, sometimes to the point where 4 people are playing in visible servers and that's it. However, this is why you should buy this game and spread the word about it. It has everything to be a very well populated game, it just doesn't have the advertising strength.
Some people may argue the game isn't balanced because Sniper Rifles are OP, however, they only kill in one shot with a head shot (if the rifle is max power which results in one shot per clip) and characters move at about 1% of their normal speed when reloading a sniper rifle balancing out the power well, because they become a sitting duck when reloading. Each weapon type has a certain level of skill needed to be used effectively, and each gun certainly does work differently from the next, so everyone will have a gun they can excel with.
Vehicle play in this game makes it very unique when compared to games such as Ace of Spades, I mean, who wouldn't want to fly a helicopter over a football stadium and blow a hole through a wall for your team mates to rush the enemy flag through?
Pros:
- Unique Maps and reflect varying Gameplay
- Vehicles
- custom guns you can make or download
- Good Balance, even with custom guns
- Kill Streak Perks
- Construction block by block, or automated pre-fabs
Cons:
- Small player base
- Poor advertisement resulting in a very very slowly growing player base
- Some maps can be too large for idealistic game play
- The active servers often have a high ping (90-130), but they are still playable.

Many other reviews have talked about the humor and technical issues you will experience with this game.  Based on those reviews you've either decided this game interests you or it doesn't.  For anyone still considering
, let my tell you why I would recommend it.
What I appreciate about this game is it's casual nature.  Sure, I like games that provide a challenge, but every now and then I want something a bit more simple and less challenging, for example, something to play during lunch break.  The turn based aspect of this game, by its nature, means I can take my time to plan out my moves without penalty.  In normal difficulty the combat is just difficult enough to require that I think about what I am doing, but not so difficult that my party is constantly wiped.  Additionally, the game's generous resurrection mechanic means I don't have to be concerned if any of my party (except for one or two key members) are "killed" in battle.  While not super challenging, this does keep the story progressing and I find that important when my time is limited and I don't want to be fighting the same battle over and over again just to get to the next stage of the game.
Equipment is also simplified.  There is only one type of weapon or armor for each class and whenever you buy/find a new piece, it is obvious if it is better, equivalent or worse than what you already own.  This may sound boring to min/max'ers, but is a welcome feature for those of us who want a nice, casual experience without a lot of complicated formulas.  Overall,
is a fun, entertaining game if you are looking for something that doesn't require a lot of deep, concentrated thought and doesn't expect to be taken too seriously.

There are many old school (sounds corny) shooters out there but Rise of the Triad is one of the best. Here's why.
First there is a points system so you can set yourself up higher. You can also do this with the achievements. You get points based on the coins you find, how well you kill enemies, and the difficulty you are playing on.
Second it's challenging. This mostly comes from the traps at first (Leon S Kennedy probably played this game before rescuing Ashley in Europe) but later on you find yourself facing tougher enemies. You WILL feel satisfied when you beat the final boss.
Third you are encouraged to use powerful weapons. Frequently you will find a powerful weapon that has about 8 shots. So you will these shots immedieatly instead of saving it because you will more than likely find another powerful weapon a minute later. Theres also plenty of fun powerups and powerdowns
Fourth it has autosaves so you don't have to predict how the level is gonna be and use a quicksave in a bad spot (quicksaves give a penalty)
This game is different because it requires you to dodge traps. Once you get used to it you will have the reflexes of a quicktime event.
So if you are looking for an old school shooter try this one out. You will only be dissapointed if you don't like a challenge (you can always try easy)

Monday After school, I finally got to play the full game, on my slower computer, with the screen shrunk down to 80%, and It was amazing.  I played through the game long enough to get bored of gaming on PC... which now that I think back... this is the game that killed PC gaming for me.
Not realizing the last statement, I bought the game on the cheap on Steam, mapped the controls to a 360 controller, and gave it a whirl.
Nostalgia.
The only driving force in playing this game was nostalgia.
It has the effect of Pancakes, with extra butter, syrup, vanilla ice cream and cherry compote.  Those first 3 or 4 bites are amazing.  But tastebud overload subsided, you realize, you don't really want this any more.
By the time I made it to the 3rd level, I was bored.  I had the strange feeling that the first few levels were ripped from the original game design.  Up until this point, I felt my interest in the game waning pretty fast... and then it happened.  I died.
The exact same thing happens to me, like a stored trigger point, every time I play a game for Nostalgia.  What ever caused me to press quit game the very last time I played the game, seems to do it all over.
This happens every time I play anything old.  SMB, DK, Street Fighter, it doesn't matter.  Game over means... Hey I'm playing something else.
Over all,
if you are playing the game for a budget entertainment standpoint: Buy it.
if you are looking to revitalize a memory from years gone by: Buy it... but don't expect Pinnacle of gaming, like it was.

It doesn't have the greatest story in the world but that's kind of the point. Its meant to be a parody on the Fantasy RPG setting using a retro Tactics style gameplay.
It lacks the depth of anything like Final Fantasy tactics. All the armor and weapons you come across will be direct upgrades. And the various items you get were mostly unnessessary.
Every character on your team is a double edged sword. Each is a timebomb. Once a specific requirement is filled for each of them they go off and hurt anyone nearby. The key is to be aware of this waiting until their fuse has almost ended and position them so that they'll help you and hurt your enemies.
It's very similar to Vandal Hearts of the PSX in that every character has a unique function and you always have your entire group with you at all times, All the equipment will always be direct upgrades, and there are no skill points or classes to allocate. It also lacks Vandal Hearts triangle combat system no weapon type has any advantage over any other.
If you enjoy tactical RPG's and Vandal Hearts especially you may enjoy this aswell. It won't be the best Tactical RPG you've ever played but it's still a decent game in it's own right.

The original Rise of the Triad was a minor mid-90s FPS which pales in comparison to the true classics of that era: the likes of Doom II, Duke Nukem 3D, and Shadow Warrior. It was built on the already-elderly Wolfenstein 3D engine and represented an abortive sequel to that game.
This remake was clearly made with a genuine love of the original game which is odd, given how thoroughly mediocre the '94 version was and remains. What it was not made with is a commitment to quality control or a clear design focus. While a huge amount of effort is evident in the visuals, the AI is truly atrocious, the weapon selection is unvaried and dull, and the gameplay carbon-copies the very worst of 1990s FPS design. Worse still, the game is unstable, poorly optimised and buggy: levels full of spinning blades are boring, but they also aren't even a challenge when the hit detection is so broken that you can frequently just glide right by or through them.
If Rise of the Triad looks fun to you and if you haven't already, then do yourself a favour and seek out the real classics of '90s shooting. Buy Doom II, fire up a source port and play some of the incredible maps that have emerged in recent years; or, grab yourself a copy of Flying Wild Hog's infinitely superior Shadow Warrior reboot. A great game remade well is a far better investment than a mediocre one remade lazily.

It's not a bad game, but it's also not good.
This game fails in it's main objective and reason to be: a nostalgic trip through the FPS of the 90's.
Jesus, this game doesn't even makes you remember the original Rise of the Triad!
Pros:
- Ocasionaly (rarely) makes you remember Wolf3D and Doom.
- Has its funny moments
Cons:
- Mediocre graphics and bad optimization
- Gameplay is broken
- Mostly, it gets boring and frustrating
- Fails to bring nostagic moments
Score:
5/10

After finishing the game I am ready to give my final opinion on the game. The first and second paragraph is gonna be addressing the controversy on the game right now on Steam and the PC port in general. If you are just wanting to know if the game is good or not skip to the third paragraph.
First off lemme say this to anyone thinking of purchasing the game, make sure your PC can handle it, this is one of the most demanding games I have ever seen in recent memory and the requirements dont lie. Hell I had to put my game on the lowest settings possible just so I am able to run this game in a smooth framerate. Other than that it seems to help, loading times for me were short and rarely went above one minute for me. I never had a CTD ever and framerate dips were rare. So my advice for now, play the game on low settings until the game is fully optimized.
As the microtransaction fiasco thats going on. Ignore those people giving this game a no reccomendation just for it, it is simply avoidable. I never used my free goodies that I got from purchasing the game early and the season pass. By not purchasing the game you are not giving the chance for more Deus Ex game sin the future as they wont get your money. The micortransactions however, JUST DONT BUY ANYTHING FROM THE MICROTRANSACTIONS, ENOUGH SAID!! Square will get the message then that we dont like this♥♥♥♥♥♥in our single player games.
Now, onto the game. Is it any good? Coming from someone who was hyped form the start cause he bought Human Revolution at the perfect timing just as the game was announced? Simply put, yes the game is a good one. Is it a great one? Thats a little more debatable.
In terms of gameplay, this is Human Revolution done with more bells and whistles, so if you are familiar with the gameplay in that one, you should be fine, there are a few new additions to the gameplay that make it better, such as a new cover system tahts more fluid and takedowns can be now done from cover. In terms of something new there is a crafting system in place here and its pretty simplistic and really easy to understand. Hacking has a few new twists in place that keeps you thinking on which path to take and you can encounter firewalls on the way that can throw you off so keep that in mind.
Adam Jensen has new augs to play with in this one, they are nice and some do help you but most imo are pretty gimmicky. I did get good use out of some of them but really this game is choosing how you wanna approach it so you may not have the same opinion as me. Speaking of which the level design in this game is absolutely great just ike in Human Revolution, multiple paths to take whether you are going loud or stealthy there are many ways to complete your objective.
Now in terms of story, its kinda weak. It does have its moments at times, especially during the side missions which have the best stories woven in them, one of them even tying between Human Revolution in a big way which I wont spoil but to those curious its Side Mission 6. However the overall package is pretty weak as in there is a subplot makes you feel like you are getting into the huge internal struggle Adam is dealing with when it comes to the Illuinati and everything and while it does go there for a while the sub plot gets dropped entirely for the rest of the game and doesnt get brough up until the game is over. Simply put the game presents a story that its payoff is nothing like what we were led to believe and for that the game suffers for it.
Speaking of the story the game does throw a few curveballs at  you in terms of choices and there was one where you had to pick between 2 missions and you could only do one. In that moment I wracked my head on which choice to pick and it was almost impossible for me to choose. The game loves to throw these types of choices at you but some are more impactful than others. This gives me some hype for future playthroughs I may do on this game.
All in all the game is a good one and gets my reccomendation. I am slighly dissapointed by how it turned out but overall Im happy and hope to see more Deus Ex in the future.

Before I write anything, anyone who is suffering from crashes or freezing in a specific location, TRY WINDOWED MODE, for some reason it works if you are stuck in a certain section due to crashing/freezing. ALSO, DO NOT SAVE WHEN IN COVER (more details in crashing/freezing section).
I never thought I would give a Deus Ex game a bad review... but here I am.
I'll start with the
- Side quests have been vastly improved compared to Human Revolution (HR); they actually serve a purpose now.
- Gameplay has also improved compared to the previous games, combat option feels significantly better compared to HR and doesn't feel like you are being penalized for choosing combat.
- Very good balance between weapons, praxis kit locations, and item availability.
- Higher difficulty levels actually make enemies smarter and bolder versus just being bullet sponges.
- Graphics (disregarding performance issues) has improved greatly and looks excellent.
- Level design is top notch. There will always be at least four different ways to complete an objective or infiltrate a location (combat, sneak through the front door, do some puzzling and find a path through vents, or talk to someone in a nearby for an access card or information on how to infiltrate).
- Extremely detailed levels. There's trash in trash cans, washed up leaves and garbage near drains, people's homes are actually unique, etc...
- Decent selection of graphics and display options.
- Very good use of multi-threading and hyperthreading. I see that Core 0, used for the main program thread, is at ~40% load and the rest of the cores, including the "virtual hyper-threaded" cores are all evenly used at ~10%-28%.
- Decent Multi-/Triple-/3D-/Monitor support with an actually respectable FOV slider.
- Temporal AA is implemented very efficently, costs almost nothing.
- Cover system has been vastly improved and is a pleasure to use.
Now here is the
- Graphics performance... is... just bad, mainly due to memory issues. Running on High texture resolution all 4GB of VRAM are used, and it looks like the textures are not even that high resolution at that setting, maybe 1024x1024..? My only guess is they are not using instanced materials and have unique texture files for each little "clutter" object in the world, instead of using just one big texture atlas with all clutter objects mapped onto it. Additionally, they are using a deferred rendering pipeline and have only TAA and MSAA options... why not include FXAA as the middle ground? Speaking of MSAA, it is most likely broken/written wrong as setting 2xMSAA SHOULD NOT MORE THAN HALVE MY PERFORMANCE WITHOUT ANY NOTICEABLE EFFECT ON ALIASING!
- Crashes and freezes. I did not experience any start-up crashes, but I experienced a crash or a freeze ~1 every hour. Throw in the occasional memory leak that chews up 31GB of memory and you get a very buggy game. Speaking of freezes, there is a location where I got stuck in a game-breaking glitch, look at the top of this review for how I got around it. Also, I had two instances where the game froze solid when quicksaving, THIS IS WHY PEOPLE SAVE THEIR GAME! While on the topic of saves, saving while in cover and loading the save results in you either jumping over the cover or running out of the cover because for some reason the game registers both the action and *To continue press [SPACE]* in the same frame, this sometimes ends in hilarity as you jump over cover and fall into the middle of the room while surrounded by enemies and get immediately swiss cheesed. If the save system is unreliable, then all hope is lost.
- Game is roughly the same length as HR, but most of the time is side quests. The main story is probably only 10 hours long and not very well written.
- No option to turn off mouse acceleration.
- Animations have taken a step back compared to the previous game, especially the facial animations. I do not think that the facial animations are just not synced up right with the voice, but actually just plain WRONG. Additionally, when someone is rabidly voicing their opinion, there is no change is facial expression... voice just gets louder and weirder.
- There is only one location. Prague, with a short detour to Golem City. If you saw the gameplay videos/trailers pre-launch, you already saw Golem City. This makes me sad; there is plenty of conversation in the game about Paris, Berlin, and London to make you think that you will end up in those cities eventually, but that does not happen.
- Story: SPOILER:
- Now to put the final nail into the coffin of this review, the game seems like it was directed by the marketing team. They added extra weapons, two of which, devastator and battle rifle have as much ammo and mods as they have animations, making them completely useless blocks in inventory tetris. The said marketing team also added SINGLE USE DLC's AND PAY TO WIN MICROTRANSACTIONS IN A SINGLEPLAYER GAME>>>>>...???? I guess they figured... more features (regardless of quality) = more sales.
EDIT: This is running with nvidia's game ready drivers for Mankind Divided.

When The Sims 3 came out, that was a different story, I didn't like it at first, no matter how much I tried to like it with all the expansions I bought, I couldn't. Sims 3, like the Sims 2, is a massive improvement to the previous 2, regardless of the ridiculous microtransaction. The game is meant to simulate... Well, life! They even added a open-world aspect to the game! Oh, skills now varies from what you learn, it's not just a general thing like Creativity for arts and music, it's now skills like Guitar, Drums, Piano, Painting, so much more! Even exploring the neighborhood collecting items and finding interesting things for your skills. In some expansions, there is a new Life State I taken a liking to, such as Imaginary friends, a great way to build my family tree since you could make a Imaginary friend of the opposite gender of the owner. Even Aliens make a return in Seasons, and oh~ my~, they're even cuter than Sims 2 with that synthesize voice!
Overall, like Sims 2, a massive improvement to the previous Sims. Get it and save your money for the expansions!

I recommend this game with a major caveat.
Firstly, the positives. This is a beautiful game. The music is absolutely gorgeous and up there with some of the all-time classic gaming soundtracks. The character classes are diverse and there is a great deal of customisation available and the modding community - oh my. Synergies takes this game to a whole new level and is an almost essential download for those who have installed it for the first time.
But here's the rub. Having spent literally hundreds of hours combined on other ARPGs (Path of Exile, Diablo 1, 2 & 3, Van Helsing and TItan Quest etc.) Torchlight is the one I cannot get into. There's a feeling you get playing an ARPG, lets call it 'fatigue', when you realise you've been pounding the left mouse button for hours and taking out horde after horde of enemies starts to get boring.It tends to happen after a very long play session, or once you've sunk hundreds of hours into a game and you feel a bit like you are grinding aimlessly in hope of a rare loot drop. Once I feel fatigued by an ARPG I tend to give up and move on (or at least take an extended break). The trouble is, I get fatigued by Torchlight II within a couple of hours. I've tried to work out why, but I think it comes down to one thing: there is no respite from monster killing
It sounds a bit counter-intutitive to criticise this in a game about monster killng, but you need moments of respite, you need peaks and troughs, you need quiet to root through your inventory and skills, then bursts of conflict. Think about Titan Quest how you bounce from cluster of enemies to cluster of enemies; or how Diablo 3 forces you to return to base regularly to progress through the story. You move ever forward at a balanced pace. In Torchlight II you are attacked relentlessly and it is exhausting and you have to teleport back to the base to do the basic character and inventory management you can normally do on the fly. Monsters seem to be able to sense you from beyond your view distance and will come for you, relentless. Its exhausting. When it become irritating to have to kill monsters, something isn't quite right. A game needs to be like the old adage about Pixies tunes - loud, quiet, loud.
So my main caveat is that I felt like the pacing was off. Perhaps its the way the randomisation of enemies and environments have been programmed... perhaps its the size of the maps... perhaps its an AI aggression issue. Either way, I have never been able to get through the main storyline of Torchlight II and after another failed effort to get into it again I'm not sure I ever will.

Skills feels useless in this game. If I recall, using damage abilities as an example, almost none of the skills in the game do 100% of your damage or more. All of your abilities do one other thing plus some small percentage of your damage. This isn't in and of itself a problem, except the other thing they do tends to be pretty irrelevent, and the damage it does tends to make it even out to just doing normal attacks anyway. Like on the Berserker, I believe he had an ability that did like 30% of your damage and let jump through enemies, and it healed you for each enemy hit with the ability by like 5% of your health (with a cap on how many times it heals).
The problem comes in that, not only is the damage or heal insignificant for the most part, but upgrading the ability does almost nothing. Every point you put in the said ability above increases the damage it deals by like 2% and the healing by like .5%.
This is honestly the main reason I dislike this game. Each class feels like the same class, in effect, because their abilities have no impact or have no differentiating factors. Maybe it's just me, but almost all of the fun in playing an RPG like this is getting cool new abilities that change the way you play the game in some sense. But for Torchlight 2, there is no such thing.
I'd say just get Torchlight 1. It might not have multiplayer, but the singleplayer experience is a lot more enjoyable. Each class is distinct, their abilities are significantly different in their use, and every single one of them has a significant impact on you. You don't need 20 points in an ability for it to become better than just right clicking.

I will start off by saying that I really, genuinely enjoyed Torchlight 1. I put 4x as many hours into it as I did this game (And I've put 25 hours into this game, they were just mostly offline so Steam doesn't count them.)
However, this game is boring. I derived no enjoyment from it. Playing with mods was amusing (Navi follower, anyone?) but didn't improve the game for me.
1. Enchantment system is boring in this game. There's a hard limit of about 5 enchantments you can put on any item, likely to preserve"balance" and that's it.That's the most you can get on an item. Torchlight 1 had no such limitation. You could literally enchant items until the enchantments rolled off the screen, then complete the game and pass your item on to your successor, and add more after that! The enchantment system in this game is just terrible, in my opinion.
2. The skill trees are boring. Every X levels, you get a new chunk of skills available, and while I can appreciate what the developers were going for by not requiring pre-requisite skills, it just means the useless skills won't be used and the good skills will. Why would I want to pick a crappy skill from the three new skills I just unlocked when these other two skills are CLEARLY better?
3. When you have multiple activation skills... it's just goddamn tedious to use them. Itjust really is. I found myself just getting as many passives as possible and spamming a single activation skill as much as possible instead of trying to vary it up, making combat boring like you would not believe. TL1 was better, because skills and abilities and spells weren't focused on too heavily, they were mainly for support. Here, they're everywhere and they're not much better than the regular attack.
4. The levels are boooooring. Soooooo boring. Just walking around, killing things, no story to lead you anywhere except for Boring Generic NPC 167 who is a load of boring. I remember playing Diablo 2 and every new area was dripping with atmosphere, story, and places to go. This game has confinced me that open world ARPG's are inferior to linear ARPG's.
5. Speaking of which, there is literally no goddamn main story in this game. You just go places, do things, and that's it. I couldn't even beat the game because I was so bored to tears. I have not played Diablo 3, but I bet it has more story and atmosphere than this game. In fact, even TL1 had a better main story than this game. It wasn't good by any stretch of the word, but at least you knew you had to kill The Alchemist. Even FATE had a better story than this game!
Overall, this game has garnered positive reviews and I have no goddamn clue why. I rate it 3/10 stars, only because I tried to play it enough to get my $20 worth. If you must buy this game, wait until it's 75% off :V

Thief is not a stealth game for the light of heart.  For starters, you may be used to backstabbing enemies in other games, such as Dishonored, which was inspired by this game.
You would be better off unlearning that instinct, as this is a game that emphasizes the fact that you are a thief.  Not a "Rogue" from D&D, and not an Assassin from Assassin's Creed.  Garrett is no swordsman, carrying his sword more for self-defense than necessity.
The swordplay is intentionally awkward, as they originally developed the engine for another game they had planned, but discovered it was too difficult to use.  Then they realized they could apply it to a game where the player character isn't expected to be a good swordsman.
As far as stealth mechanics go, you will learn to love the shadows.  Garrett is practically invisible while in the darkest shadows, and thus you will find yourself flitting from shadow to shadow, like a true thief, while fearing the light that exposes you to your enemies.  You will also learn to pay careful attention to the sound you make, as guards have ears and will pay attention to sounds you make.
Being a thief, however, Garrett is squishy.  And on the highest difficulties, he considers himself a professional - that means no murdering.  This is what sets Thief apart from other games - it discourages simple murder, and encourages you to get around obstacles instead of cutting your way through them.  This is a simple thing that Deadly Shadows and Thief 4 have neglected.
The graphics are dated, but this can be mended by the HD mod, which improves the quality of the textures.  However, if you can overcome the graphics, you will find a rich and rewarding experience.
As far as the plot goes, well,, it is slow to start off with - Garrett takes the first chance he gets to escape from the Keepers, and tries to make his own fate outside of their influence.  The plot of the game doesn't kick in until part of the way in.  More impressive than the plot, however, is the atmosphere.  You are in the !@#$iest steampunk city in the entire fictional universe.  The rich are corrupt, the poor are sick and hungry, one religion's word is law, and another religion is trying to kill everyone.  Even the bears suffer (if you eavesdrop on a conversation in the first proper mission of the game).
Even if you are a new player, I would recommend playing the game on Expert.  Expert is where Thief truly shines, as it requires the most gameplay out of you.  It isn't just a flat upgrade in stats, you have more objectives you are required to complete, objectives you might not have ever known about on any other difficulty.
What are the bad parts of this game, you might ask?  For starters, the controls are outdated.  You can remap them, but you have different keys for "walk forward" and "run forward", and you WILL be using both.  Thankfully, the game doesn't use TOO many keys, so just remap them to your comfort level.
All in all, if you're a fan of stealth games, I would DEFINITELY recommend Thief.  If you are interested in starting a stealth game, I would recommend giving this a try, too.  If you hate Stealth games, why are you reading this?
If you want a Thief game where you play as a Thief and not a kleptomaniac Assassin, this is the game for you.

First up: The game itself is amazing so far, I don't have any performance issues and the controls are a tad different from Human Revolution, but you get used to it pretty quickly. Nevertheless I can't recommend anyone to buy this game. At least not at the moment. It is simply ridiculous to offer microtransactions for a single player game.
You may ask: Why not? Everybody can decide if they want to spend money on it to make it easier if they can't cope with the difficulty. In principle you are right, but the big problem is, that this results in no effort to balance out the game itself. On the long run, it basically means that companies make their games so hard, that you have to buy additional help via microtransactions. If it wasn't a full price game in itself this would be a dubious but legitimate business model. But on a full pcie 50 € game (70 € with pre order and season pass, which I unfortunately spent) this is simply not acceptable.
Additionally to the microtransactions the pre-order DLCs are a joke and seriously regret buying it. I hope that the missions, which are yet to come make it worthwhile. At the moment you get some weapons (which are reusable for each rerun) and some credits, parts and Praxis Kits (Skill Points) which are one-time use only. And this is a no-go in my opinion and I am seriously disappointed of the publisher.
In summary: The game is awesome and a really worthy successor to Human Revolusion (as far as I can tell, roughly 8 hours in to the game), but the business model set by the publisher is a disgrace and an insult to the whole gaming community. If there was a possibility to support the studio without giving money to the publisher, I would recommend you to do that. But as it is at the moment: DON'T buy the game, and especially not the DLCs!

This is one of those games that I'm hesitant to recommend--not because it's a bad game (in fact, quite the opposite), but because it's plagued with a few unfortunate setbacks, the likes of which aren't going to be fixed any time soon.
The biggest of these setbacks is the fact that the AI pathing in this game is absolutely horrible. Whenever a Sim gets stuck (and they WILL get stuck), the entire game will freeze as it tries to fix the sim's path. What this means for you is sitting at a frozen screen incessantly for minutes at a time. Luckily, there is a mod that can help mitigate this problem--Nraas's Overwatch--but it won't completely solve the issue, so be aware of this problem before you decide to buy.
With the mod, the game becomes much more bearable, to the point where you can actually enjoy it! The Sims is considered one of the best "life simulators" for a reason. When it comes to beauty both musically and visually, look no further than Frozenbyte's Trine franchise. Trine 2 remains largely unchanged from its predecessor. For some, this may be a good thing but a little innovation usually wouldn't hurt.
The original Trine is a fantastic looking game. The environments were not only colorful, but more importantly, they were varied. Trine 2 improves upon this by adding even more detailed landscapes and a new physics engine that bring the world to life.
Gameplay has not changed. The player can switch between three characters: a box and platform conjuring and levitating mage, an agile and deadly-at-range rogue, and a fierce and protective knight. Despite the varied play styles, the game can still get repetitive.
Online multiplayer is a welcomed addition but does little to add replay value. The story is weak, predictable, and forgettable. Aside from its artistic value, collectibles are the only other incentive to replay Trine 2.
Grade: B-
