It is now 2017. The Weiss character short was released, and the animation has improved dramatically. Funny thing, the characater models got better too. Yet RWBY GE still has the horrid models that replaced the original character models. Why? Why is this still a thing? If the models were causing performance issues for some then simply keep the decent models under the highest graphical setting and use the meh models for the other settings. This wouldn't even be that big of an issue IF THEY HADNT USED THE SUPERIOR MODELS FROM THE START.  A step back when they were already two steps ahead. Real shame.
But what of the actual gameplay for those of you who never say  the glorious models we once had. Its fun, but its not the sort of thing to have a lasting feeling for you, unless you're a fan of the series in general. Its a fun game when you just want to hack and slash some grimm, but the story is no masterpiece and the enemies are for the most part easily dispatched. The difficulty is altered not by harder ai but simply adding more enemies. As a result the game can be easily completed solo, until you get to the island. As I mentioned, MOST enemies are easily dispatched, but the robots you start seeing on the island onward are not so easily dealt with. I've only ever played the game on eclipse since it was added so perhaps they are easy when dealing with one, but they spawn in 3-5 at a time in eclipse and hoo boi are they a pain then. Combat is simple, but I think thats fine as it makes it easier to pick up during free time to just play for a while and relax.
So what of the characters? Honestly I don't see why people play anyone besides Blake or Weiss aside from being a fan of whatever character since both Blake and Weiss can easily breeze through the game. Blakes range can be upgraded to have a stun effect that  is rather wide and goes through enemies. This means you can just stun a whole horde, heavy attack, and then those that didnt die can be killed off with team attacks. Weiss has a freeze that essentially has the same benefits. The other characters are fun to play, but as far as efficiency they just dont have it when compared to Blake and Weiss.
All in all, I say the game earns a 8/10 for a rwby fan, and a 6/10 for your typical consumer.
But for real, please fix the character model issue its WELL overdue to be corrected.

Pros:
-Fun to play
-Controls are intuitive and logical
-Challenges are low risk, high reward
-Story and characters are amazingly fleshed out and you will cry tears of joy
-Beautiful environments to explore set to a stunning soundtrack
-Characters communicate entirely in a synthetic language, which actually enhances the emotional connection with the player
Cons:
-Very short--I honestly could have played a game like this for a straight day, but the game lasts only about 3 hours, 4 if you count achievements
-The achievements are really easy and require little thought to accomplish
-Some of the details in the story could have been fleshed out better (why send two unarmed kids to get the water when you have an entire village of able-bodied adults, for example--there's got to be a reason for this, and I just wish this were elaborated on)
-The few times when the game takes control and you're forced to just sit back and watch make it feel somewhat incoherent, especially considering you're playing the brothers' roles, and yet during the cutscenes, they play themselves
I highly recommend this game as an experience, and a lot of these cons show that I really just want to see more of this world, these characters, and this gameplay. The younger brother, especially, exhibits so many deep and almost prophetic psychological states in the first few chapters alone. PTSD, the five stages of grief, self-loathing, rebellion...all shown only through body language and facial expressions, and it's beautiful. You will tear up along the way.

An open world RPG that rewards patience featuring satisfying combat.
50 some odd hours and at least 10 characters and I still haven't even scratched the surface of Warband. And I still hardly even know what I'm doing! There is no hand holding or instruction that breaks character. You are in the world of Calradia and its on you to make the most of it. In an age of gaming featuring arrows and highlights its really quite nice. Even third party guides and wikis are better ignored in my opinion. No need to learn the 'best' soldier or 'best' way to start or 'best' way to do this or that. Just get lost in the world. There's nothing more satisfying than discovering a new wrinkle organically in this unforgiving world.
While not a looker, the game plays great. Gameplay ALWAYS trumps looks. And for the willing, this is some of the best you'll find. The much ballyhooed melee combat lives up to the hype. Its fully satisfying to wield once learned. And will be the emphasis if multiplayer is your thing. But if you're a singleplayer like me there's a lot more to talk about. The living open world of Warband is immersive like I mentioned above. You're making your own way in this rough world of Calradia. The factions have different styles. Companions have their own stories and personalities. War is constantly raging as there is a power struggle with countless outcomes. Political intrigue, love, loss, business opportunities, tournaments and more await you to stumble upon them. Its spectacular fun but punishing. Patience and forethought are paramount in surviving this world.
All that and DLC and mods? A demo to try? This is PC gaming personified. Regularly on sale and bundled too! Easy recommendation for anybody remotely interested.

I am deeply saddened to see the game at 64% positive reviews. This is, I believe, the symptom of a much deeper problem, namely that any AAA game is bashed, shamed, and unreasonably criticized by hordes of entitled gamers. If the game has loads of options to tweak and customize, they just want their all-ultra preset to run at 144 fps on a 4k setup, because they have spend 10.000 dollars on a quad-sli rig, they are entitled to it. If the game lacks options, it's a crappy console port. There is no pleasing the masses. Hopefully, in a few weeks, the initial upsurge will die down, and people will actually start reviewing the game based on its merits, rather than some hazily defined expectations and entitlement.
The game itself is solid. It plays well, caters to any style, be it running and gunning, or ghosting through the levels without enemies catching even a glimpse of the player. The graphics are great, and the optimization is entirely serviceable, no matter what enraged teens may think. On a 2 year old GTX 980, I am able to run the game at a locked 60fps (with about two locations dropping it to 50, big deal) at a mixture of very high, high, and ultra settings (texture very high, shadows on high, MSAA and specular lightning off, all else on very high and ultra). If this game was crysis 4, it would be praised and sainted for being futureproof and progressive, because it includes settings no current-gen PC can handle properly. Now, it is shamed and ridiculed for supposedly being a bad port, even though the console versions are nowhere near the PC version in terms of detail. People should start accepting that having the latest hardware does not, in any way, mean that they can run every single product on all ultra. My settings are beautiful, and I'm perfectly satisfied. (As a sidenote, Fallout 4's Boston area produces 20-ish FPS on the same GPU, regardless of any settings. Interestingly, that game was not reprimanded half as seriously by the community as Mankind Divided)
The story is fairly good, but as others have pointed out, ends in a cliffhanger, and I admit, the last hour of the game leaves a lot to be desired, with all the backtracking, and dragging on. Nonetheless, the rest of the game is extremely well thought-out, and the pacing is entirely decent. There are, however, some minor bugs that would probably prevent me from giving the game 10/10 if I had to score it, these including:
-You have to press 'space' to start the game after a loading screen, and you also use 'space' to exit cover. For some reason, the game registers it twice, so if you save in cover, you automatically jump out and get shot to death.
-Some terminals and computers have the tendency to crash the interface, necessitating a reload.
-Newspapers and ebooks have weird controls, and half the time, I'm not sure which article I'm reading, and where the text continues
-Face animations and textures are relatively subpar compared to the rest of the models and the environment
-I have seen many complaints from native speakers of czech, that the czech texts in the game are translated unprecisely, or make no sense. I do not speak czech, but with a background in linguistics, it broke my immersion to even know about it.
-Length. Where I live, the price of the game (60 dollars) nets me and my girlfriend a visit to IMAX 3D, and snakcs for both of us to go with it, followed by a dinner at a chinese fast food place on the way home, clocking at about 4 hours of entertainment alltogether. The game is about 25-30 hours in length if one explores everything, does every sidequest, and enjoys the atmosphere, so comparatively, it is still a good buy, especially in an age where 4 hour long shooters are the norm. Still, I am somewhat disappointed that it is less epic in scope than , for instance, Witcher 3, one of my all-time favorites. Such a comparison would be unjust though, but I still can't help feeling that I wanted more.
-The XP-system also needs some tweaking. Human Revolution also suffered from the selfsame issue, whereby finding door codes are not at all rewarding, as you end up hacking the panel nonetheless, for the XP reward.
All in all, I am somewhat torn between a 9/10 and a 10/10 rating. I enjoyed the game immensely, but some bugs (that will probably be fixed in upcoming patches) frustrated me quite a bit, so I wouldn't call the experience perfect. It was still better than most games I've played recently though. If you are put down by all the negative reviews, and whining, and not sure whether to buy, rejoice, they are mostly without basis. A word of caution is in order though. The game really DOES need a powerful PC to run, there is absolutely no chance on running it on the minimum requirements.

Grotesque Tactics: Evil Heroes is a turn based 'strategy' game featuring specific characters, a linear storyline, and no random encounters.  I love turn based strategy games (Cute ones like Disgaea, serious ones like X-Com, easy ones like Final Fantasy Tactics, and unforgiving ones like Jagged Alliance).  I thought this one would be right up my alley.  Here is why it wasn't.
The gameplay lacks real strategy.  There isn't any units you control outside of what they issue you in the story.  Each unit is unique in character, has semi-unique abilities (all three archers have little variation), and is limited to how they level up (limited, set number of possible encounters).  Keeping low levels up to speed becomes exceedingly difficult as the stronger characters tend to have to bail out the weaker.  The characters have unique abilities (similar to the Final Fantasy Limit Break system), but they tend to be counter-intuitive to how they are used.  When the characters see enough action, their special ability happens automatically, which can affect both your enemy and friendlies the same way.  If that wasn't frustrating enough, there are also neutral monsters that will sometimes attack your enemies for you.  That sounds fun and exciting at first, but then you realize they only take away xp from your own units.  Due to the lack of balance between weak and strong units, and the limited amount of xp to be gained, battlegrounds can turn in to a game of luck more than strategy.
The lack of camera controls, playable area (boundaries), and fixed (unchangable) game controls also make for frustration as well.  They don't break the game entirely, but still will probably be noticed enough to slow down the flow of gameplay.
I would like to play a polished version of this game, with some random encounters added to train up my low characters, but that simply will never happen.

Pretty fun game, with plenty of replayability, especially with the new Steam Workshop recently added in. There is an immense variety of maps, innovative gamemodes, interesting vehicles, and nice character models. It does lack ambient sound effects, so you might feel alone in the game even though there are 7 players competing against each other to turn them into snowmen. Other than that, it's worth the money and is better than spending endless hours modding Minecraft itself.

If you like customization with some sort of hybrid of CS/COD hybrid, then this is for you. You can make your own guns with your own unique, balanced (Keyword, BALANCED) weapons, and your own skins for your player. The editor is basic enough for new guys to make weapons, while the Minecraftian artists will still have plenty of fun making detailed, fine crafted ones.
While the killstreak list is tiny, aiming can be difficult, and the controls can be frustrating, gameplay is still okay.
It plays like a normal shooter, with grenades, two guns, and a melee. The keyboard controls are spread out everywhere, so finding what button does what can be a challenge.
One of the funnest game modes to play is the lava survival, provided you can avoid everyone else. Most of the time, however, you'll find yourself inside a pit with a half naked man standing above you lobbying grenades down to make sure you stay there. All in all, it's really good for customizing, but not worth 15 bucks juuuust yet. However, if it's on sale, go ahead and try it.

It is now 2017. The Weiss character short was released, and the animation has improved dramatically. Funny thing, the characater models got better too. Yet RWBY GE still has the horrid models that replaced the original character models. Why? Why is this still a thing? If the models were causing performance issues for some then simply keep the decent models under the highest graphical setting and use the meh models for the other settings. This wouldn't even be that big of an issue IF THEY HADNT USED THE SUPERIOR MODELS FROM THE START.  A step back when they were already two steps ahead. Real shame.
But what of the actual gameplay for those of you who never say  the glorious models we once had. Its fun, but its not the sort of thing to have a lasting feeling for you, unless you're a fan of the series in general. Its a fun game when you just want to hack and slash some grimm, but the story is no masterpiece and the enemies are for the most part easily dispatched. The difficulty is altered not by harder ai but simply adding more enemies. As a result the game can be easily completed solo, until you get to the island. As I mentioned, MOST enemies are easily dispatched, but the robots you start seeing on the island onward are not so easily dealt with. I've only ever played the game on eclipse since it was added so perhaps they are easy when dealing with one, but they spawn in 3-5 at a time in eclipse and hoo boi are they a pain then. Combat is simple, but I think thats fine as it makes it easier to pick up during free time to just play for a while and relax.
So what of the characters? Honestly I don't see why people play anyone besides Blake or Weiss aside from being a fan of whatever character since both Blake and Weiss can easily breeze through the game. Blakes range can be upgraded to have a stun effect that  is rather wide and goes through enemies. This means you can just stun a whole horde, heavy attack, and then those that didnt die can be killed off with team attacks. Weiss has a freeze that essentially has the same benefits. The other characters are fun to play, but as far as efficiency they just dont have it when compared to Blake and Weiss.
All in all, I say the game earns a 8/10 for a rwby fan, and a 6/10 for your typical consumer.
But for real, please fix the character model issue its WELL overdue to be corrected.

A quick rundown on character roles, so you can be aware of what you're going into, and who to pick:
• Ruby (Jack of all Stats): A good balance of range and power, a decent ground and air game over all.
• Weiss (Support): Weiss' linear upgrade trees and melee game leave a lot to be desired, but her long-ranged ice spells are wonderful for supporting your team. A good spell-sniper can make everyone else's job tenfold easier.
• Blake (The variable): Blake is interesting, as having one of the widest skill trees allows her to play  either as a teammate-rescuing support of a super-offensive smashfest. A favorite of veteran players.
• Yang (The Beatdown): Yang is all about short range, fast, intense action. Whether on the ground or in the air, she's always moving on a horizontal plane. Her attacks are fast and powerful, but  unfortunately she has a neigh non-existant range game, relying soley on her ranged special to hit anything more than a few feet away. Also, due to her short range and the fact that, unlike others, her combos are unlikely to launch her out of harms way, the Yang on your team will typically have the most downs by a long shot.
But yeah, it's purty good.

A couple days ago I started to play DE:HR for a third playthrough to prepare myself for DE:MD, but after I finished and I wanted to get the game I read all those negative reviews which got me a bit worried. After a short contemplation I thought "the heck" and just went with it as I was pretty sure the actual game would not disappoint me - and I was right.
First of all, I have a rig like many other people here, nothing really impressive or anything. (GF 970, 3770k, 16 GB Ram) Before I bought the game I read through all the reviews, but also the tips how to optimize the game the right way to get a stable and satisfactory framerate and I have to say that it runs absolute smooth for me. No lags, no crashes (except an early one when I watched the intro movie) and the graphics are still good even though I have everything only on high settings. I got to say though that the graphics are not as great as expected and the game's demands are quite high indeed. Especially when I compare it to the Witcher 3 where I had everything on Ultra and it runs with higher fps as well. But, like I said, graphics are still satisfactory.
The microtransactions are also a cause for major negative feedback and I can and support the backlash. However, as far as the game goes, it doesnt effect me at all and I think it shouldnt be a big dealbreaker, just make sure to not buy anything frome the ingame shop and support that kinda stuff.
Gameplay is great, feels just like DE:HR and everything works smoothly. They implemented a little crafting system to enhance your weapons, but also craft stuff you need for your augmentations or to recharge your energy.
The story I can't really say too much about yet as I am only ~6-ish hours into the game. What I have seen so far is very solid though. Especially the sidequests make a better impression on me than in the previous game. They just seem to be more relevant and more in-depth and detailed. The atmosphere of the game is great. You really feel that the Augs are treated poorly and in a very xenophobic way. Prague is great to explore and there is much to see and listen to, even just listening to common npcs on the street and their conversations is adding to the overall atmosphere.
All in all, I can really recommend the game and urge people who are not completely sure if to get the game or not to give it a try. Cheers!

It's pretty much THE 3D fighting game to play if you're walking into this realm of fighters. Other 3D fighters like Soul Calibur, Virtua Fighter, etc. can't seem to capture charm that Tekken has. And now, for the very first time in history, it's on PC, and the PC version is quite excellent and it is superior version among the others (PS4/XBox). This is probably the best version of Tekken to date.
What's new in Tekken 7?
*Rage Arts (like Supers in Street Fighter)
*Rage Drives (in a sense, a combo extender)
*Power Crush (moves that absorb hits)
*Screw Attacks (re-worked from the "bound" system in the previous entry (Tekken Tag Tournament 2))
Pros
====
+Netcode seems to be better handled than Street Fighter V (not based on rollback netcode). For example, having 4 bars out of 5 in Tekken is playable and very good. Lag is practically not noticable. However, when you have 4 bars in Street Fighter V, you will occassionally see "teleporting".
+Graphics are top notch and the effects are explosive and flashy. Very exciting to watch.
+"Slow/Matrix" effect hypes up the matches
+Being able to choose which side to play on (1P/Left or 2P/Right side). And yes, both players can choose the same side. The screen will essentially be a "mirror" to the other player.
+Training Mode has lots of features and is robust
+Lots of customization for your characters. If you like to pimp out your favorite character, there is a large selection of gear to choose from, and you don't have to pay with real money. In game currency is relatively easy to obtain and the customizations are easy to unlock. Although unlocking them is random like loot boxes, you'll never get the same item twice though, so you'll always be unlocking new items. Eventually you'll unlock them all if you play 1500 matches in total (offline and multiplayer matches).
Cons
====
-Very steep learning curve for new comers
-Lack of tutorial for basic mechanics of the game. In addition, there are "hidden" moves/mechanics that the game simply doesn't even tell you about. You have to find this out from forums/videos/other players.
-No challenges/character trials. It'd be nice to give newer players a way to learn a specific character and I find that doing a challenge/character trial (like Street Fighter) is a good way to start.
-Currently missing some senior characters in the game (like Lei Wulong, Michelle Chang, Anna Williams, etc). Possible that they'll add them in future DLCs, but currently not announced as of writing this review. Please add in Lei Wulong, Harada-san!
-Can't skip turn or go back of queue in Multiplayer lobbies.
-Tekken Bowling is currently not multiplayer. Might be added in the future, who knows.
-Story mode isn't quite that good and fully fleshed out, but if you don't care about that, then disregard.
For the most part, the characters are well balanced and it honestly comes down to player skill and knowledge. They are all very unique and have different playstyles. There's a character for everyone.
If you're coming from 2D fighters, boy, you have a steep hill to climb, but if you keep at it, you'll be able to climb it. It definitely won't be easy but will be satisfying once you reach the peak.
A few things you'll need to learn/get accustomed to:
*3D movement (background and foreground)
*Frame data knowledge is much more important to have
*There are at least 50+ moves for each character (although there's really a handful that you would consider top tier moves). Some characters have 100+ moves.
*Combos need to be accomodated for wall splats and ground breaks if you are fighting on a stage that has them.
*The list can go on...
I recommend this if you like fighting games in general and have a passion for it. However, be prepared to lose a lot if you're new to the game. 3D fighters are a whole different ball game.

One of the best Early Access games on Steam. This game has a ton of promise, and worthy developers.
If you even remotely enjoyed Mount & Blade Napoleonic Wars, pick this up now, it's fantastic!

As an initial disclaimer I will say this: the game feels very much like an Early Access game.
Many aspects are very rough around the edges, such as melee combat which the devs have named as their top priority at the moment. Also full or nearly full servers can cause FPS drops and latency issues which makes core gameplay features, such as the melee combat, nearly impossible.
However, the game already shows great promise. The graphics are pretty and refreshing after M&B Napoleonic Wars, which was definitely showing its age, and are highly configurable with the amount of options offered to you. The HUD also features a lot of togglable options, meaning you can either have all information on display or a completely clean HUD and everything in between depending on your preferences.
The variety of classes is good, providing all the roles you would expect, from line infantry to officers and even surgeons who can heal their comrades. Cavalry is notibly missing but the developers have assured us that they will be added in the future when they feel polished enough. There is also a surprising number of game modes for a game in this setting, including naval battles which involve player-crewed ships and a roster of naval-specific classes. The unique Coastal Seige mode may be my favourite, with small ships ferrying troops towards coastal defences while blasting away at the defender's walls with their cannons.
The voice acting is awesome, allowing you to insult your enemies, encourage your team-mates or just scream as you charge bayonet-first. Adding to the authentic atmosphere are the musician classes which can deliver such 1815 bangers as 'The British Grenadier March" and "La Marseillaise" with fife and drum.
Overall, as long as the developers keep putting in the hard work, this game is clearly going places. However if you expect to dive straight into a polished, deep and well-populated experience, maybe you ought to avoid it for now. Follow the game's social media, steam page and everything else you can find and make the decision to purchase when you think the time is right.
But if you love games like this, you should take the plunge, fund its development and help provide important feedback during this critical Alpha stage.

This game only released a few days ago. It already has a decent sized playerbase and organized clans referred to as regiments.
Lets start with the basics. You load into the game, pick France or Britain. From then you choose your class. There are so many roles, from Officer to Drummer, to flag boy to rifleman to Line.
When you first start your match you'll see some unusual things. Half of the people on your team are wandering in unorganized masses, taking cheap shots against the same group of enemies.
The other half is people standing in flawless lines, with one or two officers, a flag and some musicians. They begin assembling into units. Some of them break formation to march, others are so disciplined that they simply walk to the front, maintaining perfect formation. You can hear the commands of their officers from even a distance, with the piping tunes of patriotic music and the beating of drums.
It strikes you that none of these are bots. They are all people. Eventually you fill in your place in what is called a regiment.
In the regiment, you are taught the basics of formation and what their orders mean. You become a part of the collective force of your regiment.
Eventually as you gain experience, your regiment joins a skirmish, an organized event made by regiments. Everyone is in perfect line, and you imitate Napoleonic era battles in the most accurate way yet imaginable.
Does this sound like a good game? Of course it does. This is one of the most amazing games on Steam, and is worth every last dollar.

Thief Gold is a first person stealth game. Singleplayer only. Released in 1998.
It's quite old but you can believe me: It's nice and worth a try.
Graphics:     8/10
It's an old game. So I can't compare it with Crysis 3. The textures and effects are really ok.
The most important thing here: They created a really nice atmosphere with textures you would describe nowadays with the word awkward.
Leveldesign:     7/10
Let's split this topic. There are good levels and bad levels.
The bad levels are so confusing that I wish I could erase them for good.
For our luck these levels are fairly rare.
Most levels are really well designed. You have to think and search for the best path
in the shadows hoping to not get detected. Sometimes there are more ways to get to the target location. There are plenty of secrets and loot. I admit that sometimes it's extremely hard to find the correct answer to the riddle and the game becomes frustrating.
To sum it up: 7/10.
Sound:     5/10
On one hand you have really annoying enemy sounds, on the other hand you can locate the enemies' footsteps and the rest gives you a fitting sound ambience. Music is virtually not existent and not necessarily needed in this genre but I miss it.
Gameplay/Handling/Equipment:     9/10
You are the thief crawling in the shadows. The game wants you to hide and sneak. And I swear you will do it. Otherwise you will have a really bad time playing the game. The enemies are too strong for you to kill them in combat (most of them). You must use the really innovative equipment to take your enemies down and find the best way to infiltrate. But it takes a long time to get used to the controls and "rules" of the game. For example: Killing people with arrows is nearly impossible except you do it from the shadows (1-shot kill). The same thing with the club. Knock people out with one hit from the back or die after trying to kill your enemy face to face. The most important tool is your bow. Use your rope arrows to climb up, use water arrows to extinguish the torches, use the noise arrow to distract enemies, use moss arrows to silence your steps (etc.).
Enemies/AI:     9/10
Ok - now I have to explain. Nine out of ten is really high.
I have to remind you that this game is really old. And it's really amazing that guards don't just ignore dead or sleeping bodies and keep on searching you until they find you. The AI reacts if you miss the shot and I never experienced a real bug. Sometimes the AI has problems with altitude but it's not gamebreaking or noticeable.
So for this time: Awesome!
BTW.: Most undead are dumb like they are meant to be.
Story:     7/10
It's a nice story with unexpected twists. Some people may have a problem with the fact that the story becomes science fictional and doesn't remain realistic. The voice actors for the characters are really fitting and it will never be boring throughout the game. The best thing is that you can hear Garrett's thoughts which makes the chacacter lively.
Critic summary:     7.5/10
Personal fun rating:     8/10     [very good game]
The game is oldschool and one of the first stealth games. And it deserved the name Thief..
I can recommend the game for genre-fans. One warning: If you don't have patience then this is not your game.

While I enjoyed Machinarium a lot, Samorost 1 and 2 is clearly one of the first games of Amanita Design, where they experimented and learned, and didn't know yet how to make an enjoyable game. It's extremely short and most of the puzzles involve a *lot* of pixel hunting. There's logic in them, but they are completely unobvious you have to constantly mouse-over everything on the screen. If you're stuck, there's no help (like in Machinarium). It's not a bad game, but keep in mind it's one hour long and you'll most probably need to find an online guide. Can't recommend. Play Amanita's later games, they are much better.

The first Samorost game is free, browser-based and available on the Amanita Design website -
- whether you enjoy this or not should be a reasonable (though not watertight) indicator of how you'll feel about 2.
In Samorost 2 you guide a space gnome on an adventure through various environments/scences, solving puzzles, all in hopes of rescuing his dog. And that's more-or-less all there is to it.
Samorost 2 is a short game and I have criticised other games for being too short/simplistic to be worth it.. but I can't bring myself to do that here. Everything about this game is just too damn charming to me. The artwork is gorgeous, the music is relaxing and I enjoy the quirky atmosphere, creatures and puzzles enough to justify it.
Another valid point, though, is that there's very little guidance - this will appeal to some and not to others. For the most part, I quite like working out what it is I have to do in a scene (even if that involves mousing over everything to find out what I can interact with first ;), but I appreciate that not everyone feels the same way - preferring a clear objective.
So while I do definitely recommend Samorost 2, it's worth keeping in mind that it's a short game with little direction in each scene, making it not worth it for some.

IMPORTANT: DO NOT BUY MKX ON PC
WB/NRS has abandoned the development of the PC version of Mortal Kombat X as of January 2016, it will no longer be getting any of the new fixes/DLC that's being released for consoles. The last PC build  still has major performance and balance problems in both single and multiplayer and for that reason and the fact that WB games/NetherRealm seems to have no faith in their products on PC I cannot recommend the game to anyone.
You have been warned.

An open world RPG that rewards patience featuring satisfying combat.
50 some odd hours and at least 10 characters and I still haven't even scratched the surface of Warband. And I still hardly even know what I'm doing! There is no hand holding or instruction that breaks character. You are in the world of Calradia and its on you to make the most of it. In an age of gaming featuring arrows and highlights its really quite nice. Even third party guides and wikis are better ignored in my opinion. No need to learn the 'best' soldier or 'best' way to start or 'best' way to do this or that. Just get lost in the world. There's nothing more satisfying than discovering a new wrinkle organically in this unforgiving world.
While not a looker, the game plays great. Gameplay ALWAYS trumps looks. And for the willing, this is some of the best you'll find. The much ballyhooed melee combat lives up to the hype. Its fully satisfying to wield once learned. And will be the emphasis if multiplayer is your thing. But if you're a singleplayer like me there's a lot more to talk about. The living open world of Warband is immersive like I mentioned above. You're making your own way in this rough world of Calradia. The factions have different styles. Companions have their own stories and personalities. War is constantly raging as there is a power struggle with countless outcomes. Political intrigue, love, loss, business opportunities, tournaments and more await you to stumble upon them. Its spectacular fun but punishing. Patience and forethought are paramount in surviving this world.
All that and DLC and mods? A demo to try? This is PC gaming personified. Regularly on sale and bundled too! Easy recommendation for anybody remotely interested.

This game is the best parts of Diablo 2 with very few of the drawbacks. The only two real issues I've found that may turn off some gamers, especially those who fondly remember Diablo 2, are the graphics and the skilltrees. I've got no problem with the graphics myself anymore, they do take a little getting used to, but for those who preferred Diablo 2's dark horror-genre appropriate atmospheres, this game could be off-putting and disconcerting with it's bright, sometimes almost cartoony graphics. Don't let that fool you; beneath the exterior, this game is just about as serious as Diablo 2 ever was. Sure, the antagonist isn't quite a demonic force of incredible evil, but he still causes about as much damage despite that.
But the part about Torchlight 2 that disconcerted me so far is the Skilltrees. Keeping in mind that I have a tendency [well, 2 connected tendencies,] to a) grind my characters in both short and long spurts past the recommended level for an area and b) drop and pick up the game on a frequent basis, I've found that skills can be a little easy to misapply, making character builds that are difficult to survive with if you're not careful. You had that problem in Diablo 2 as well, though it tended to be more noticeable later in the game if you'd made the wrong build choices, but it can be especially bad here. You have the abiloity to buy a respec (redistribution,) of your last 3 most recently gained skills, too often however my build problems went farther back than that. Still, an option that wasn't available in earlier games like Diablo 2.
But those 2 problems aside, this game has a lot going for it. Official Mod support makes it possible to expand the scope game incredibly, there's several mods currently in the works that are being billed as entirely new Modder-Made Acts, which is something I'm honestly excited about and intend to try when they're finished. Even without counting the option of playing game again on a higher difficulty, the game doesn't end once you've beaten the main boss, even without mods; not giving any spoilers, but there are several ways to continue adventuring post-game even without mods (SPOILER - For newcomers as veterans would already know; Mapworks, a carryover from Torchlight 1 that's available Postgame, basically randomly generated dungeons appropriate for your level.) There's also hidden things to look for all over the game, like the robot parts. There's the multiplayer aspect of the game as well, but I have to admit, I don't play games for the multiplayer stuff so I can't say much about it other than I've heard nothing but praise for it.
In conclusion, there's a lot to do in Torchlight 2 so long as you're careful with gear and skill choices. If you love Action RPGs (like Diablo 2,) go ahead and buy Torchlight 2 if you haven't already.

This is a PC port quick analysis for the ones interested
-I've initially wrote a negative review for Deus Ex Mankind Divided as i was having some extreme stuttering while roaming the first City Hub making it unplayable. Seems like buying an extra RAM stick fixed the problem quite amazingly. So as long as you have RAM to spare and keep your graphic settings in a state that matches your GPU specs you should enjoy this game with a stutter free experience.
-The options MSAA and Volumetric Lighting are framerate killers, so adjust those settings accordingly. The only thing still bugging me is the 100% CPU usage while in the city hub. I know city hubs are open area/busy places in Deus Ex games but developers surely could optimize these areas a bit more. 100% CPU usage is abnormal for any recent core i7/i5 while gaming.
-There is a mouse acceleration feature in this port that can't be turned off. It's quite noticeable even when you tune down Mouse Sensivity. This might be a problem if you can't accept nothing less than perfect mouse aiming.
As for the game i'll write a full review later but so far it is everything Human Revolution was but improved.

the pathing when using right-click-to-attack prioritizes stepping in the highest defensive terrain than maximizing a character's range or staying away from enemies. of course, moving and attack can be done seperately, but it's not as obvious as click to attack. click to attack will inevitably get a character killed. logically, it should move to the closest space and attack, not walk out and around to a bush. logic isn't this game's strong point.
the obsession meter might be the worst mechanic to ever be featured in a game period. as characters are attacked - or for a few preform attacks - a red meter fills up. when it fills, characters do something, ah, unique. this might be putting friend and foe to sleep, but it's probably hitting one of your allies. actually for over half of your small army, it's hitting your own allies. having your beserker or healer hit - not even killed - might force you to lose the whole map because dice roll decided that they'd kill your main character. obsession is not fun. it's supposed to be funny and keeping tabs on it is apparently another layer of strategy, but there's nothing good about it. it doesn't enhance the experience, it screws it all up. nearly all of the times I lost, I lost because my own ally killed me, and there was little control I had. to avoid obsession, you're forced to bench characters, effectively limiting strategy instead of enhancing it
that's implying this game gives you any moments of strategy. using items have no repurcussions. you could win a whole map with one character and potions. I think that's supposed to be a joke, but after redoing so much of the same crap then given the same crappy character again, I took it personal. small stat increases greatly overpower characters and there is no linear balance from one map to the next

Grotesque Tactics is a story driven, satirical RPG with a strategic combat system. A party of 10 anti-heroes are fighting in a grotesque world that combines the features and clichés of Western and Asian Strategy RPGs like Final Fantasy Tactics, Heroes of Might & Magic and Fire Emblem.
Grotesque Tactics weaves a humorous storyline and plenty of amusing dialogue, poking fun at some of the most successful RPGs, such as Oblivion, Gothic and Lord of the Rings.
To protect the kingdom from the merciless cult "The Dark Church" which has murdered all of the kingdom’s heroes and knights, you will have to hire dubious soldiers and rescue jealous maidens who will follow you into combat as your groupies.

I'll recommend this, but with a caveat. This game is really gorgeous and is well put together. Barring a couple of little flukes, like the saw portion seeming to be weird with USB keyboards, this is very much a playable game. That being said, the storyline is pretty simple with a few twists here and there, making it pretty engaging.
With all that being said, this game feels like a game engine demo. The thin plotline, lack of character complexity and language, and pretty heavy-handed game mechanics make it feel like a guided tour through the possibilities with the game engine. The simple controls make for pretty simple puzzle solving, and the game is pretty short; I played through in 3 hours.
I wouldn't recommend this game for seasoned gamers looking for a pretty long-haul RPG trek. However, this game would be a pretty solid, low-cost buy for a younger gamer. The challenges for a younger gamer would be more appropriate and accurate, the storyline wouldn't go over their heads, and it is honestly a good game in terms of visuals and feel.

This game can for the most part be a fun multiplayer fps with intense gameplay action, but it seems like the whole building aspect of the game is a bit lacking. Yes, it's called Guncraft, which emphasizes the guns and shooting part, but this game was promoted as being open to building things as well and the choices are not that much. In build mode you get a simple list of blocks you are able to insert into the map, and if you are crafty enough you can build your own structures with the blocks. But for all the promoting and advertising done on this game it's obvious playing it long enough that it is mainly an fps shooter game and secondarily a block building game.
The multiplayer aspect though can be fun, with a wide range of weapons classes to use, as well as the option for anybody to build a custom gun and submit it for later use. Killstreaks add benefits to the game if you do well enough in a match to get them. The default map list is large, with various types of maps to choose from that are quite creative. Overall, this game is a fine fps multiplayer game but it does not do so well on the building part. If you can deal with building blocky plain structures, and blowing people's square heads off, this game is for you.

TL;DR:
It's a short and fun PCA (Point and Click Adventure) with a fascinating art style and great music. Has a few actual puzzles beyond just clicking the right spots.
Graphics: 7/10 (Sub-HD resolution, no scaling. The art and the style are amazing; I wish it were scalable! Everything feels so alive!)
Sound: 10/10 (The music matches the art style; extremely well done!)
Interface: 5/10 (Simple minimalistic menus. Password level/"save" system.)
Story: 7/10 (Entertaining but superficaial. Acceptable for a short game, though!)
Characters: 6/10 (Samorost is playful and fun, all the others are well drawn/animated, but just didn't have any depth beyond their utility.)
Toughness: 5/10 (Security through Obscurity. Nothing too difficult here, though, you may find yourself wondering what to do, at times. Discworld = 10/10, for reference).
Length: 3/10 (I know, it wasn't meant to be a long game, just a fun and light-spirited story that sparked a design studio to create some of the most beautiful games in the PCA genre.)
Overall: 6/10 (A short and fun adventure with some very amazing artwork and soundtrack. Give it a play; you'll enjoy it!)
Thanks for a PCA that wasn't affraid to break conventions, displayed amazing artistic talents, and is fun without requiring a serious time commitment.

I've had bad luck when it comes to getting hyped for a game. But, having been very exciting to play this since it was announced, I'm very happy to say I haven't been disappointed. I have had over a year of experience within the Mount and Blade: Napoleonic Wars mod community before moving my group there to this game, and we're all pretty pleased with how things are going here. I'll take the unoriginal path here now and give a pros/cons list.
Pros:
+So far, a very nice community. The Napoleonic Wars scene was infamous for its "bushpirates" (people who would be leaked the password to an event so they could come in and disrupt it) and troll regiments, but the vast majority of regiments I've met and seen in this game seen to take things pretty seriously and they all want to keep the community here to be a repeat from NW's.
+Very cool and dedicated developers. This whole game was made by just 3 guys, and if that isn't impressive I don't know what is. They're all working closely with the major regiments leaders to fix issues that are going on to bring the game out of Early Access and constantly approve it.
+Excellent graphics, very large improvement from NW.
+Shooting mechanics greatly improved from NW. There's still an element of randomness due to the base inaccuracy of a musket, but now there is some defined bullet drop, making shooting MUCH more skills based, which I like.
+Lots of shouts. For people that don't own a microphone, there's so many voice clips they can use in game to communicate.
+Speaking of communication, there's in game VOIP, making it possible to talk with anyone on the battlefield. As a side effect of this, on all the official battle servers I've been on recently there has been actually structure, it's kinda like the Napoleonic Roleplay server on NW but with voice chat. The people who go the Officer unit will gather up a group of men at spawn and they'll all go out to fight the other side together. It's pretty cool to see this happening on public servers, and it's led to some pretty funny and great experiences for myself.
+Maps are pretty good.
+Naval stuff is sweet.
+The Surgeon class is a great addition.
+The fact that you can move a bit while you're reloading is really helpful. Being able to address gaps in the line during events without having to break reloads is a godsend.
+No cav yet! I can't say I hated anything much more than getting demolished by a cav unit in NW.
Cons
-Melee combat still needs to be improved. Comparing the game again to NW, there's been a trade off, shooting has been upgraded to be skill based and melee has been downgraded to spam a lot and hope your stab connects. Hitboxes are pretty weird and the way the flow of combat works it's almost impossible to block as a reaction. Swords are SUPER OP compared to muskets at the moment.
-Cannon reloading is waaaay too quick. Also, I don't quite like the fact that no matter what class you are you can operate a cannon. I prefer NW's artillery setup.
-Server admining is tough right now. You have to use console commands rather than an easy to use admin panel like in NW. Not having a slay command, and no free camera spectating makes it nearly impossible to punish anyone for rule breaking. Also there's no holy hand grenades :(
-Just two factions at the moment, France and Britain. I hope when the time comes to introduce a new one there'll be some kind of poll for it, because I want to get the Ottomans up in here. Something we haven't seen in base NW that has a bunch of cool, unique units. Thought at the moment I am also mourning the loss of the Russian Partizani.
-Just one look for Line Infantry units. I liked how in NW there were multiple Line Infantry units with different uniforms. I don't know if this is something they're planning to implement, but I hope it is.
-No cav yet! I can't say there's anything that felt better than demolishing an enemy as cav in NW.
Overall I'd give this game a solid 9/10. As an Early Access game the flaws are pretty much excusable for right now, and the fact that the dev team is so small AND I trust that they'll be working their hardest on them. I'd recommened this game to anybody REMOTELY interested in it, I promise you won't be disappointed unless the melee combat is a deal breaker for you. I'm very much looking forward to what the future holds for Holdfast and I hope I'll still be enjoying it just as much a year from now.

I continually refer to this game as the best $20 I have ever spent.  I bought it at full price and would buy it again.  I really, really like this game. Read on if you want to know why.
You will probably get around 50 hours of gameplay out of this title, and that's if you only play through it once.  The modding community for this title is VERY active and offers an extreme number of ways to customize your game.  Even without mods this game offers amazing replayability due to the procedurally generated levels the game has. I mean the 95 hours I have logged with this title were before the editor was even released.  It also has Online Co-op too.
The game offers great character customization too.  The game offers three different sets of skills for each class.  Active skills range from Fire Pillars to summons that heal you and your friends.  You also have access to passive skills which boost damage or your defenses.  The skills are flashy and the game has no shortage of explosions.  It looks and feels great to play.
Each of the game's acts takes place in a radically different environment.  Each map has a completely different tileset and enemies.
It's also worth noting that the game offers multiple difficulty levels that you can change on the fly to make the game suit how you want to play.
If you're a fan of Hack'n'Slash ARPGs with tons of loot to collect and lots of deep character tweaking, buy this game, it's the best one on PC.

Not to fight and be an unrealistic dual weapon wielding juggernaut, but to negotiate your way stealthily through levels, as a true Thief would. Thief is undoubtedly the father to many excellent stealth games such as Splinter Cell, and does not merit the fame or praise it rightly deserves from many.
Also noteworthy is our narrator and protagonist, Garrett - easily one of my favourite protagonists for his little monologues now and again.

Thief along with Metal Gear shaped the stealth genre and to this day still nothing can rival this first person stealth game... You are placed in huge mission areas and its up to you to use your wits and problem solving skills to over come each and every obstacle Garrett(MasterThief) faces. Impressive. I love all the various interactions that you can do within the game. The ending is acceptable to me since not everything should go the way you expect it to. SPOILERS ahead, read on if you don't mind.
PROS
1. Fantastic Novel Way of Playing
Controlling 2 characters at once is tricky yet possible with the keyboard. Most impressive use of the hardware. Note that the keyboard is only able to register 2 keys pressed at once, not 4.
2. Incredible Story
I love how touching the story is at the beginning, although I do begin to doubt the wisdom of the physician. Sending 2 young kids to search for a magic water while putting their lives at risk does sound a bit irresponsible.
3. Imaginative and Immersive World
Trolls, Giants, Giant Orcas, Ice Sea Turtles, Invisible Ice Monsters, Spider Woman, Blood of Giant Tribes, Hippogryphs, Hang Gliders, Monster Roots/Trees, these are just some of my favourite things.
4. Interactions
It's amazing how you can interact with so many things e.g. Spitting into a well, each additional well you spit into adds another spit droplet. Picking up balls and playing basketball. Not only that, each brother has his own unique interaction with an object.
5. Puzzles
Easy for kids and fun to pick apart. E.g. Trapping the troll in the cage while hiding behind walls.
CONS
1. Slight repetition
Some of wall puzzles show some similarity to previous puzzles. It does not make sense that so many locations conveniently have a broken ladder for you to climb.

Sooo... First of all - microtransactions in this game are... well... idiotic. I get the idea that everyone need a quick buck, but they are not needed in the core mechanics - you wouldn't spend your money if you play your cards right and you don't need Praxis because you can basically get a build for your playthrough after literally second quest. No, there are a lot of good augs there that you may want, but game itself gives you more than enough XP for that. Ant i did not even mention NG+ in which you are basically starting the game with all your hardearned gear.
I generally don't dwell on microtransactions too much because... well, it's your choice to buy or not to buy, but here they are just so pointless, that i just don't get why would anyone bother buying them...
The game itself... well, it's good. Like - very good. Story is interesting (and not about saving the princess and then the world), characters are well-written, dialogues are on point. Gameplay mechanics hit almost every time - you can play it like shooter, or you can go through a game without a single shot fired, it's your choice. Artwork and overall designs are just fantastic. Perfomance is questionable at times, but bugs not very tiresome (although i own a decent PC with good SSD for games, so maybe not everyone would be happy). In my playthrough game crashed two times in about 40-50 hours of playing, so it's not a big deal. Gameworld is not very big, but the tone of the game kind of leans toward small ctories, so it seems natural.
So yeah, it's basically another good Deus Ex game. If you liked the series as a whole, you would probably like Mankind Divided. If you are an RPG-fan, this game gives you something different from usual for the genre fantasy setting. If you like shooters... well, you could find a better one for this price tag (although, it's still better than Call of Duty experiments with this themes), new Doom for example. But overall it is a good role-playing game, with a great replay value.

The graphics in this game are exceptional, really beautiful. The content, the number of items and enemies is sufficient. Brothers - A Tale of Two Sons manages to accomplish something few games attempt to achieve; it tells an emotional and compelling story. The basic premise of the game is that of two brothers who have set out on a quest through a fantasy world to find a mystical cure for their ailing father.
To be reductive, the game is a simple puzzle-driven adventure game in which you control each brother with one of the analogue sticks and perform context sensitive actions using the triggers. It's through this control scheme that makes you fully see the Brother's reliance on each other and while the game is by no means hard, you'll find yourself focusing on the emotional context of the puzzles rather than the solution (which is almost always pretty straight forward).
The game has a sort of breezy (no pun intended) dream like quality to it. You'll travel through beautiful fairy tale-esque environments, non of which overstay their welcome, highlighted by gorgeous camera angles. There's an incredible sense of scale, distance and perspective and for a "small" game it's amazingly impressive.
This is the type of game that really showcases just how unique and powerful a video game story can be when gameplay is utilised to help tell that story.

If somebody told me six months ago that I'd ever play a game as beautiful as Trine, I would have scoffed, and yet here I am, playing its sequel - a game that takes its astoundingly high production values and raises the bar to unimaginable new heights.
So, for anybody who is unaware, Trine 2 is the sequel to Finnish developer Frozenbyte's 2009 side-scrolling fantasy puzzle platformer, which refines and continues to build what I suppose I should be calling the "Trine franchise". All the majesty of Trine is present, though there are a few changes that are definitely worth giving attention to.
Read my full review (with screenshots) here:
Multiplayer Trine arrives at last. Great platforming fun. Some quirks and annoyances, but overall recommended - especially if you can get some Multiplayer going!

Trine 2 follows up the original game with everything one could have hoped for in a follow-up: more variety (in combat, enemies and environments), more beautiful graphics (which I did not think was even possible), and last but not least, support for online co-op multiplayer! Simply put - it is the perfect sequel. Everything that was great about the first game (refer to my previous recommendation for details) is still great in Trine 2, if not better. Other notable changes include boss fights and the removal of the limiting "magic meter" mechanic of the original. The story this time around is also pretty neat and the same humorous banter between the three characters is on display. The game is extremely fun to play with a friend or two online, but it is definitely also worth playing solo, if that's all you can manage. In summary, Trine 2 is an all-around amazing game, and the price is right too. Highly recommended!

Deus Ex: Mankind Divided is a worthy sequel to Human Revolution, and improves on it's predecessor in almost every way imaginable.
In regard to
implementing micro-transactions for praxis and credits:
None of these items are required to play the game. There is no content locked behind pay-walls, and by the end of the game, even playing on hardest* difficulty, I had 30k credits with nothing to spend them on and about 85% of the augmentation tree unlocked - the same percentage as a similar run through HR would have got you. I am not going to give
a bad review for something they likely had no control over. That said, I do not think it is acceptable to put micro-transactions in a $60 game.
With a FX-8320 and 980Ti (albeit both overclocked), I was able to max out the game at 60fps with the exception of contact hardening shadows and volumetric lighting. I also did not experience any of the crashes others have reported, and the mouse acceleration issue was not present. The game is very beautiful; particularily the screen-space reflections, I often found myself pausing to take in the scene of Prague at night.
MD improves upon HR's already great gameplay. Changes to the energy system, revamped shooting mechanics, and experience balancing for both stealth and combat playstyles all combine to make the perfect "play how you want" experience. The new augmentation additions such as the Titan Shield or the remote hacking are also welcome additions, adding further depth to combat and exploration.
Some say Mankind Divided's story is too short, like the game was split in two. You will not find a more immersive game...
Thief Gold is an expanded version of Thief: The Dark Project.  It contains 3 more missions than the original 12 in the first game, new enemy types, some revisions to some of the maps/loot and expanded on the story and the universe the game takes place in.
Thief: The Dark Project came out more than 15 years ago, Thief Gold coming out a year later.  It was the first ever first-person 3D game where stealth, not fighting was the emphasis.  In fact, trying to play it like it was any other first-person game up to that point would result in a very quick and unceremonious death.  You aren't a strong warrior skilled with a sword, you are a Thief, adept at lockpicking, pickpocketing and burglary.  When it comes to combat you will often find you are weaker, slower, and deal less damage than your opponent.  You do, of course, carry a sword and you can parry blows from enemies.  However, a blackjack to the back of the skull when they don't know you are even there is much more effective, and satisfying.  An arrow shot from afar, though cowardly, is always better than more direct confrontation.  Heck, you can play through most missions without even engaging the enemy, so long as you are careful, clever and patient.  Regarding enemy takedowns:  you need to hide unconscious bodies (and corpses) because if other enemies stumble upon it they will go into full alert mode.  This could also mean having to use a water arrow to wash away the blood you've spilled, you murderer.
Thief: The Dark Project was, and still is, one of the most immersive games you will ever play (the others being Thief 2: The Metal Age, and Thief: Deadly Shadows).  Even the 2014 THIEF (reboot) game cannot compare to the original(s).  Not in immersion, mechanics, scope or story.  The game required you, as a master Thief, to creep along in the shadows, avoid detection by enemies, steal some nice loot, and meet the mission objectives, because dammit - you have bills to pay.
The levels are huge, complex and sprawling.  They take you through the streets of a dark city, mansions, caverns, crypts...  it wouldn't be unfair to say that the game is part 'Tomb Raider', in that you sometimes find yourself trying to figure out how to avoid clever traps in tombs far underground where undead and burrowing beasts make their home.  You have to climb ropes, leap from ledge to ledge, and swim, among other things, to meet your objectives.
One of the greatest things this game and it's 2 immediate successors had was the mythology of the game's universe.  There are interesting factions with opposing ideologies and myriad layers of philosophical inferences made by all of them.  The Hammerites are devout followers of an orderly religion that worships a "diety" they call "The Builder".  The Builder is revered for casting down the "Trickster" and leading the way for progress, particularly in building and forging.  The Trickster was a chaotic pagan god of the wild forests of the old world.  He's a Puckish character; part Pan and part Green Man.  There are "The Keepers" who watch from the shadows all the happenings of the world, intervening only to maintain a balance between opposing forces, and keeping scholarly records of all that occurs.  There also exist the "Mages", who are akin to Nietzsche's Super Man, in that they have excelled beyond their human abilities, but in turn have lost some of their human moral sensibilities, isolating themselves away from society to study deeper mysteries.
Regarding gameplay mechanics:  You have a light gem on the HUD that brightens and darkens signifying how exosed you are.  When it is black you are in pitch blackness and therefore completely invisible to the enemy.  You also have health shields to signify what your physical status is.  Your arsenal can include a sword, blackjack, arrow, water arrow, noise arrow, fire arrow, rope arrow, moss arrow, and gas arrow.  The sword will be the least used of your weapons.  The blackjack will knock an enemy out.  An arrow can kill most enemies on the first shot so long as they have no idea you are there and you have the arrow fully cocked.  Water arrows extinguish torches and fires, and can even kill fire elementals and fire shadows.  The noise arrow will distract enemies.  The fire arrow can kill, light torches, and explode explosive barrels and other such.  The rope arrow allows you to climb to otherwise unreachable places.  The moss arrow makes loud and noisy surface soft and quiet.  The gas arrow knocks an enemy unconscious.
Items include various food items that can increase health, health potions, breath potions, flash bombs to blind the enemies, mines, gas mines, keys, lockpicks, and other useable items.
Unlike games of today, there are no in-game cutscenes.  The game is broken up into missions and there are cutscenes inbetween that expand upon the story, though much of the story unfolds in readables and overheard conversations during gameplay.  Overhearing an important conversation, finding a key item, or stumbling into a room full of guards and dealing with it's consequences ALL takes place within the game.  You are ALWAYS in control.  How any situation is dealt with is entirely up to you.  Do you shoot a noise arrow down that hall to distract the enemies so you can run by?  Or maybe you could douse all the torches and make it dark enough to creep past.  You could fire a gas arrow at their feet and put them all asleep.  Maybe you could toss a flashbomb at them temporarily blinding them.  Or you could just try looking for another way in.  There's always another way in to be found.
One of the most immersive aspects of the game is it's sound propogation.  Sound carries and it gives you an indication of how near or far an enemy is, from which direction, and it informs how you proceed in the game.  You can lean your ear against closed doors to listen for footsteps or conversations happening on the other side - opening doors willy-nilly is not the best approach in this game.  In this respect, it's very much a strategy game:  when to move, when to take, when to engage,...  Another factor that determines how the game is played is in the difficulty settings.  On Normal difficulty you have generally less restrictive objectives.  You can kill "enemy" ai, if you want.  On Hard difficulty your loot quota goes up, more objectives are added, and you have fewer health shields.  On Expert difficulty your loot quota goes up higher, even more objectives are added, you have even less health shields, and on most missions you cannot kill anyone.  I could be wrong, but I believe the difficulty settings also affect starting equipment and where some items are to be found.  I know of one mission in particular where a secret door is inaccessible on higher difficulty levels.  No matter what the difficulty level, finding as much loot as possible is strongly advised, because you spend the loot you find before the start of the next mission buying the equipment you will need for it.

If you can get over the odd terrain, some blindingly painful to look at maps, glitches, and some wonderful but not appropriate map designs, then Guncraft is for you. If you don't get the whole building, crafting and voxel style game then this probably won't win you over. That said, for the price, there's some good value here although could have prolonged the life a bit more with some single player content.  Guncraft is a Fun but flawed game which hopefully will address the problems in the future.

is a splendidly innovative, little game with pleasing aesthetics and a touching narrative that is sure to amuse nearly any gamer.  This game is a quintessential example of the avant-garde in gaming.  Perfectly crafted
is now a reality as
will have you controlling two characters simultaneously (by using the dual joysticks of modern controllers) as you embark on a short, but heartfelt, adventure.
The game plays as an adventure-puzzler game.  You will have to control both of your characters simultaneously and use their different strengths and abilities in tandem to solve the various puzzles you encounter on your adventure.  It really is quite an experience and there were several times where I could actually feel my brain get crossed-up as I tried to control both characters at once.  This is definitely the kind of game that exercises your brain.  I would say this mechanic alone would make the game worth playing, even if the other aspects were poor.  Fortunately, pretty much all the other aspects of the game are first-rate as well.
Supplementing the innovative mechanics at the core of the game are the elegant graphics, pleasing soundscape, and overall charming atmosphere.  There are some really varied and well-crafted areas to traverse as you play through the story.  More than just
different, the various areas of the game
different—  and each add their own twist to the gameplay.
The game is ultimately a story-driven experience.  That story is simple, but told well— evoking empathy.  The levels, while gorgeous, are quite linear; and the puzzles, while innovative, are quite simple.  And those factors only serve to contribute to the brevity of the game.  Most people should be able to complete the game in 3 to 4 hours; it is the kind of thing that can (and probably should) be done in one immersive sitting.  It is the definition of “short-and-sweet.”

Before i start the review, I'll explain a little bit about my experience playing this game:
I first played the first few minutes of this game at a friend's house. He got me interested in the game and a few days later i bought it when it was on sale. Because this game is about 2 brothers, i took the oppertunity to play this game with my little brother (10 years younger than me). We ended up finishing the entire game together, playing at the same time or occasionally taking turns when one of us was about to die of sleep deprivation. This game is meant to be single player, but you can technically make it a co-op if you share the controller. So grab your brother (or better yet, 2 misbehaving siblings you want to teach a lesson about taking turns and co-operating with one another) and start the game up!
Regarding myself and the little brother i played it with, we're 10 years apart. I'm nearing my 20's and he's still in elementary school at the time of this review. I wouldn't reccomend playing this game with a younger brother whose uncomfortable with themes of death and darkness. If you decide to play with a younger brother who doesn't understand the concept of death yet or is slowly learning the concept of death, this game may be a good way to introduce them to those themes, but this game CAN GET DARK. The game has many themes of death and it's very much a coming of age story for both brothers. In the game you'll encounter dead bodies, scary graveyards, nature coming to life trying to kill you,
, and an NPC 'tempting his own fate' to put it lightly... So just use your own judgement regarding your experience with your little brother of choice. As for the adorable child i played with, he can tolerate most things and only flat out refused to play the game in one section because he witnessed some gore he wasn't expecting but easily shook that off and played with me again immediately after that section was over. We played the game up until the end, wtinessed the ending together and he is not psychologically scarred by it in any way. We only used a walkthrough ONE time and even after the game was over we jokingly call eachother what the Brothers call eachother in the game.
Ok, now onto the review:
Brothers: A Tale of Two Sons is a puzzle/adventure game similar to the likes of ICO and Shadow of the Collasus for the PS2. The world Brothers takes place in is GORGEOUS to look at and feels incredibly massive but dangerous at the same time.  If you love RPGs and puzzles with huge worlds you'll love the way this one looks and feels. Unlike ICO and Shadow, the controls for brothers are extremely simple. You move with the analog sticks and interact with R2/L2. You can play solo controlling both titular brothers or grab any male sibling you get along with and each of you can share the controller, controlling 1 brother each. Both brothers are also very balanced. Big Brother (Maya?) is strong and tall but he doesn't jump very high or run as fast as Little Brother (Maii?), who is weaker and shorter but can jump higher. They can help eachother around the enviornment by picking eachother up, helping eachother up ladders, solve puzzles together in ways renimicent to ICO and Yorda and they're enjoyable to play as despite speaking a nonsense language (also very similar to the language spoken in ICO).
The story: a simple fetch quest. The boys' father gets sick and they must retrieve an antidote from a tree hidden up in the mountains. And that's it. The story doesn't get more complex than that save for the fact their mother has died by drowning and Little Brother is also trauamtized by that event and unlike Big Brother, he can't swim. The game isn't so much about a story, it's more about a journey. The landscapes are beautiful and while wandering the world i couldn't help but want to know more about the lore of the world they're travelling through. It feels very Scandinavian in nature, what with all the giants, the beautiful snowscape, the water and the beautiful castles. I can't get over how wonderfult he game looks. At first glance, this looks like one of those games that'll look better than it actually is but in the case of Brothers, i say the looks are just a bonus for the journey. As for the journey is self, all the puzzles are solveable. If you play with a friend or a brother of your own, niether of you will get too frustrated.
One thing that prevents me from buying most adventure/puzzle games is if the puzzles will be solveable. It's what makes or breaks a puzzle game. And thankfully despite the occasional camera wonky-ness all of the puzzles are solveable without a walkthrough. For myself and my brother, we only used a walkthrough for one puzzle we were confused on and after 10 minutes of testing theories we gave up and resorted to youtube. But other than that small experience, you could easily get through all the puzzles and they can all be solved without ripping your hair out trying to retrace your steps. Everything you need is always in the right place, where you need to go is always hinted at, you sometimes just need to look from a new perspective or look a little more carefully. For me at least, i enjoyed that the puzzles weren't too complex. If the puzzles are too complex that's usually the point where i give up on the game. And the puzzle layout is especially useful if you plan on playing with your younger brother.

Grotesque Tactics is a satire RPG with tactical combat.  As you progress, you build a party of characters to take on the Dark Church, the generic evil organization in the world of Grotesque.  The game is fairly well written with decent humor and its own set of purposefully cliched characters, but it unfortunately has a lot of problems.
Though the game isn't even 10 hours long, I had quite a few instances where a quest script broke or the AI got stuck in an infinite loop during combat, forcing me to reload my previous game.  One time a quest NPC accidentally got put to sleep during combat and since effects don't wear off while out of combat, I couldn't wake him up to continue.
Combat can be rather unbalanced at times, with some enemies possessing instant kill attacks and others able to hit for nearly half a character's life and hit 3 targets with one shot.  Each character also has a special charge-up behavior that automatically triggers when their bar is full.  One of the characters will turn and randomly attack another party member when this happens and will kill most of them with this attack.
The interface needs a lot of work as well.  Clicking through conversations often results in your character moving after the conversation has finished because the game registered the last click as a movement order.  The camera position keeps your character very low on the screen, so it's difficult to move down without resorting to manual camera control.  The camera also uses very slow panning to follow action, which I probably don't have to tell you is quite annoying.
On top of those problems, the game engine is simply atrocious.  The graphics are pretty simple, yet the game stutters like I'm trying to run a game from 5 years in the future on my computer.  Turning on the "quality renderer" option makes the game look worse with reduced lighting and really nasty flickering shadows under plants.  There are also numerous graphical glitches with water, and flashing triangles across the screen if I zoom the camera out.
I'm having a hard time recommending this game.  While the game itself is compelling, there's too many bugs and design flaws that get in the way of enjoying it.

The Campaign mode is horribly dull when compared with the rest of the series. The characters are awesome, but the story and several missions...Bland. They could have built something beautiful, something far more intricate. Solo, it just feels very limited.
Online.....Yikes. It is a hit and a miss, honestly. Sometimes you'll find a server with some decent folks, group up together and do jobs, be it selling drugs and whatnot from businesses, stealing and selling cars, the works...
But the vast majority will seek you out and hound you every step of the way, making sure you're stopped in your tracks to prevent you from getting money. The worst ones are those nerds that are in jets that fly around doing airstrikes across the city. The messed up part, is no matter how much destruction they cause, the cops never seem to want to take them down.
The game itself is VERY fun, not going to lie. Love the customization, from cars, to guns to clothes. But to make money, it all hinges on who your put with in a server. Lack of money stands in the way of unlocking and customizing.
Kind of wish they had a sort of bodyguard option, not just the Merryweather Support chopper and the merc hitsquad. Would be cool to hire some thugs or whatever to follow you around and help defend you. It is kind of needed when you get chased across Los Santos without any sort of support.
I didn't use mods all that much, however I did use it in solo-player, installed that Bodyguard mod, and it was pretty damn fun. Played out a turf war, with Franklin and a group of Green guys. Wreaked havoc with Michael and a team of security guards. And sowed chaos just about everywhere with Trevor, with a bunch of hobos and addicts. Good times.
Anyway. People are attacking Rockstar and Taketwo about the modding thing, and I totally understand and get that. I would have been pretty♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥too. But they are in fact, running a business and are looking for ways to milk out the cash out of us. Instead of investing in better anti-cheats and whatnot, they decided to say 'no' to all mods in general.
I see their point of veiw, and I see ours. I don't think we ought to judge them too harshly. If it was us running this, we'd probably do the same thing, but I am sure there are better alternatives. I hope they patch things up, and I hope they continue to create great games. Though maybe without as much useless emphasis on the Movies, golf, tennis, when some folks would rather run their own Cartel, Cult, or Government Agency or whatever.
