I was told that the game would last me for 30+ hours however having completed the main story and most of the side missions I made it through the entirety of the game in less then 12 hours.
Many people are complaining about the optimization issues however from the way I see it their expectations are too high when it came to maxing out the graphical settings in their system. I'm running on a GTX 970 with an i7 4790k processor and found that disabling just a few of the most performance hogging graphical settings that I was able to get some buttery smooth performance.
In addition, the storyline for this iteration of the franchise is much weaker then that of its predecessor due to the fact it felt more of an episonic storyline then a full fleshed out one leaving all of its player base with a cliffhanger ending left open to possibly another game coming in some point in the future.
The gameplay feels much improved and if you've played Human Revolution you'll find that you'll adapt to these new mechanics much quicker then those who have never played any of the Deus Ex games. In contrast to the last game you are left with few areas of interest to explore, and by that i mean you are mostly stuck in Prague and only in bits of the storyline will you travel to London and an additional area at some point half of the way there.
As for the microtransactions, I don't believe that it hinders the gameplay at all as I am find with what I have now and don't feel the need to make any additional purchases.. It is however you're choice whether or not you want to put more money into the game. People make it sound as though they are forced to in order to get a better more enjoyable experience and further hinders their judgement in the overall game.
In essence I don't believe it was a bad game at all, it just left me hungering for more answers in the end with what will happen to Adam Jensen, but that may be left for future games to come. It plays better then DXHR however with the weaker plot that game with this years iteration of the game I feel that I should give it a lower rating then the last simply because I've enjoyed the stories told in the Deus Ex universe.

Very good game, plays almost identically to Human Revolution.
Exposition is a bit heavy-handed, but it works itself out quickly. I'm guessing this is primarily because it's a direct sequel off of HR and is meant to inform those who didn't play the last game, but I'd figure the 10 minute optional intro would sort that out.
Interestingly enough, the vibe of the game reminds me a bit more of the original Deus Ex than the third instalment, both in the art and general story.
I haven't had any technical issues, just keep in mind that to run the game on very high or ultra, you will need THIS generation's top hardware, not the last gens: this game is very intensive on video memory inparticular.
There ARE microtransactions -- apperently. I haven't seen them after playing the game completely through and starting a newgame+ however, so you shouldn't encounter them unless you go out of your way to find them.
The story does have some loose ends to the casual player, but those who have played Deus Ex, and Deus Ex: Mankind Divided will quickly recognize important figures such as Bob Page, Morgan Everett, Manderly, and Lucius which can give some insight as to who's pulling the strings and what may happen next. Much like HR, there is a post credit scene (which I won't spoil), that does indicate a sequal or continuation DLC; seeing how well the game is put together and it's length however, I wouldn't worry about a DLC made of cut content or intended for a cash-grab.
TL;DR: Plays like HR, feels like Deus Ex; touches quite heavily on Deus Ex. Video memory hungry, but looks great. Most likely will have a sequal or very large expansion DLC, which I can't complain about. I would very much reccomend to long-term fans of the series. My playthrough took me about 22 hours.

What is there NOT to talk about with a game like Guncraft? Let's get the less convincing things out of the way first and spare you the loss of build up:
- The movement is a little floaty and not like any other FPS I've played. When you slide off a surface, you act like Bubsy the Bobcat and just continue to glide and slip all over the place when you just want to land. Be careful with themz ledges and edges.
- Also there is no stairblocks added so far but you can sprint up the blocks, although that gets tedious really fast. Jumping across them is no faster.
- The concept of throwing out Bouncing Betties are a good feature from more popular FPS series that they tried in this game. But the reason why it worked in those games and not this one is that there was a limit to one per person. Now, what happens when Guncraft allows players to throw out five Bouncies', die, respawn and repeat?
You get a mine field. And that's NOT fun nor strategic.
With the bad side aside, let's move to what Guncraft did right:
+ If you like those FPSs that I just mentioned then you are in for a treat because Guncraft uses some of those better elements in its own favor such as Perks, Killstreaks and Vehicles.
+ While you are equiped with Guncrafts Hookshot, you can fly and parachute all over the map if you have a tall building to cling on to. It's really satisfying!
+ An obstacle in your way? Pull out your Sword/Hammer/Pickaxe/Drill and get to work and show that hinder whos the baws! That's right, you can dig and place blocks in battle using build mode to get through a wall or build a barricade to gain that tactical advantage.
+ Now to the big one: The idea that the game depends at like 70 percent of your creativity! That's right, you can craft anything like, your own guns, skins, prebuilts that you can just plop in in the midst of battle and to build your own maps and levels and use help from the built in filters and generators incase you want the right terrain like mountain, field, taiga, etc. When you're finished you can also add your new made work to your Workshop Page and let your friends have a look even though they don't own the game.
In conclusion, the game does have bad stuff but it quickly makes up for it with its gameplay that's dependant on the player and his commitment.

Before i start the review, I'll explain a little bit about my experience playing this game:
I first played the first few minutes of this game at a friend's house. He got me interested in the game and a few days later i bought it when it was on sale. Because this game is about 2 brothers, i took the oppertunity to play this game with my little brother (10 years younger than me). We ended up finishing the entire game together, playing at the same time or occasionally taking turns when one of us was about to die of sleep deprivation. This game is meant to be single player, but you can technically make it a co-op if you share the controller. So grab your brother (or better yet, 2 misbehaving siblings you want to teach a lesson about taking turns and co-operating with one another) and start the game up!
Regarding myself and the little brother i played it with, we're 10 years apart. I'm nearing my 20's and he's still in elementary school at the time of this review. I wouldn't reccomend playing this game with a younger brother whose uncomfortable with themes of death and darkness. If you decide to play with a younger brother who doesn't understand the concept of death yet or is slowly learning the concept of death, this game may be a good way to introduce them to those themes, but this game CAN GET DARK. The game has many themes of death and it's very much a coming of age story for both brothers. In the game you'll encounter dead bodies, scary graveyards, nature coming to life trying to kill you,
, and an NPC 'tempting his own fate' to put it lightly... So just use your own judgement regarding your experience with your little brother of choice. As for the adorable child i played with, he can tolerate most things and only flat out refused to play the game in one section because he witnessed some gore he wasn't expecting but easily shook that off and played with me again immediately after that section was over. We played the game up until the end, wtinessed the ending together and he is not psychologically scarred by it in any way. We only used a walkthrough ONE time and even after the game was over we jokingly call eachother what the Brothers call eachother in the game.
Ok, now onto the review:
Brothers: A Tale of Two Sons is a puzzle/adventure game similar to the likes of ICO and Shadow of the Collasus for the PS2. The world Brothers takes place in is GORGEOUS to look at and feels incredibly massive but dangerous at the same time.  If you love RPGs and puzzles with huge worlds you'll love the way this one looks and feels. Unlike ICO and Shadow, the controls for brothers are extremely simple. You move with the analog sticks and interact with R2/L2. You can play solo controlling both titular brothers or grab any male sibling you get along with and each of you can share the controller, controlling 1 brother each. Both brothers are also very balanced. Big Brother (Maya?) is strong and tall but he doesn't jump very high or run as fast as Little Brother (Maii?), who is weaker and shorter but can jump higher. They can help eachother around the enviornment by picking eachother up, helping eachother up ladders, solve puzzles together in ways renimicent to ICO and Yorda and they're enjoyable to play as despite speaking a nonsense language (also very similar to the language spoken in ICO).
The story: a simple fetch quest. The boys' father gets sick and they must retrieve an antidote from a tree hidden up in the mountains. And that's it. The story doesn't get more complex than that save for the fact their mother has died by drowning and Little Brother is also trauamtized by that event and unlike Big Brother, he can't swim. The game isn't so much about a story, it's more about a journey. The landscapes are beautiful and while wandering the world i couldn't help but want to know more about the lore of the world they're travelling through. It feels very Scandinavian in nature, what with all the giants, the beautiful snowscape, the water and the beautiful castles. I can't get over how wonderfult he game looks. At first glance, this looks like one of those games that'll look better than it actually is but in the case of Brothers, i say the looks are just a bonus for the journey. As for the journey is self, all the puzzles are solveable. If you play with a friend or a brother of your own, niether of you will get too frustrated.
One thing that prevents me from buying most adventure/puzzle games is if the puzzles will be solveable. It's what makes or breaks a puzzle game. And thankfully despite the occasional camera wonky-ness all of the puzzles are solveable without a walkthrough. For myself and my brother, we only used a walkthrough for one puzzle we were confused on and after 10 minutes of testing theories we gave up and resorted to youtube. But other than that small experience, you could easily get through all the puzzles and they can all be solved without ripping your hair out trying to retrace your steps. Everything you need is always in the right place, where you need to go is always hinted at, you sometimes just need to look from a new perspective or look a little more carefully. For me at least, i enjoyed that the puzzles weren't too complex. If the puzzles are too complex that's usually the point where i give up on the game. And the puzzle layout is especially useful if you plan on playing with your younger brother.

Pros:
-The game doesn't use English (I hope that's correct for the sake of my hearing/intelligence) but it still has a wonderful and captivating story that will not want you to put down your controller even for a minute.
-Speaking of controllers I was able to get the game to work even without a controller although it is very very difficult.
-It is very atmospheric and has beautiful backgrounds throughout the entire game.
-The music, although not common, is very suiting and emotional when it is being played.
-There are many different designs and environments so you can't get bored by the same setting.
Cons
-It is short.  I could play a game like this forever.
-Can't keep the adorable cat, dogs, chickens,  goats, sheep, birds, fish or whales, etc.
-Not all your questions will be answered (for example, why there is mounds of snow shaped like and/or contain people?  One of nature's mysteries I guess...)
Opinionated views (Could be pros or cons depending on you)
-Not much of a challenge at all.  If you buy this for the puzzle tag, don't expect anything even close to something like the Portal series.
-Lots of walking (not for people who like a slower paced game)
-Makes you feel all the emotions
-Controlling both characters at the same time can challenging.
-This is more of an experience than a game.  In the short 3 hours it takes to finish, you will find yourself reminiscing about previous encounters in the game.
-Will make you think about your own life choices and will make you feel bad for playing a computer game instead of being with your family...that is until you start all over again.
Overall 9.5/10.  I just wish it was a little longer.  Try to catch it on sale if you can but it's still worth it if you don't.

Torchlight II is a great action-RPG: you have 4 class with lots of skills to choose from as you build you character. You can replay it through and through to try out different classes without getting bored, since most maps are randomized and will be different. It is also a good game to play with friends: you can start co-op games both on the internet or in LAN netowrks
If you like collecting items, levelling up, killing monsters, and exploring dungeons, then this game is worth a look. A solid diablo 2 clone top-down action RPG game worth many hours of your time.

I've always enjoyed games in the style of Diablo, and Torchlight II is no exception.  Simply playing the game in its vanilla state is a blast, and that's not even talking about the plethora of mods that do everything from tweak the game in small yet important ways to completely taking it to the next level with new characters and items.  There's just something about games with tons of loot, skill trees, and customization options that I find very fulfilling, I guess.  The cool, uniquely stylized art style and epic soundtrack certainly don't hurt, either.
Overall, I personally believe that Torchlight II is a fantastic game and an almost diabolical time sink!  If you're a fan of Diablo style games like me, I seriously doubt you'll be disappointed.  Check it out!

So I’m just gonna start this off by saying while I can’t recommend this game at it’s full price if it ever dips below 30 USD it’s probably worth it.
The game itself is fairly good. The gunplay is decent, augments handle well, NPC pathing has been improved considerably over the first game and the crafting system is tolerable. It’s worth mentioning that while there are micro-transactions in the game it’s not only possible, but still fairly easy to beat the game without making use of them.
It's important to mention that unless you've got a Solid State Drive your gametime will probably be around 30 hours, if you've got an SSD you'll probably finish in about 12ish hours.
The graphics of the game are probably it’s best point, which normally would be a bad sign but in this case they’re truly stunning. Even while my PC won’t run it on maximum settings, it’s pretty beautiful on Very High.If you’ve got a high end rig and like FPS games it might be worth buying on that alone. (Remember the warning from the start however.)
The gunplay handles about on-par for your average big-studio first person shooter. Augments make things interesting and allows for different play style and while Stealth is the most challenging way to play while going guns out is the easiest but death effects the story so it’s an interesting choice.
The story however is where this game falls short, it’s sub-par for an RPG let alone a Deus Ex game, a lot of the characters are predictable and repetitive and their motives are completely transparent at times. But most importantly just when it looks like your at the halfway point of the game, it ends. Almost like they’re trying to make sure they’ve got enough content for another game but the ending hits so quickly you’ll be asking yourself “Wait what?!” when it ends. The game was marketed on how big of an effect your choices on the world will have however it seems none of my actions had any effect and when I thought they would the game turned around and made sure they didn’t.
All in all, if it ever drops down to 30 bucks or so it’s probably worth it, but I’m going to be kicking myself for the foreseeable future for having not only pre-ordered the base game, but for pre-ordering the season pass.

Mankind Divided plays out in a very similar way to Human Revolution. The gameplay is the exact same: You can fight through an area, hack your way through doors, or find a way to sneak through. However, some augments seem TOO good.
Patrolling guards? I can use the cloak to get by them. Laser grid? Can move through it with cloak. Security camera? Cloak.
The high jump augment also seems much more useful than it was in Human Revolution. Gate has a security level 5 keypad? The fence is low and you can just jump over it. You can also jump onto balconies to enter an area easily, or get into a high place accessible only by high jump that bypasses a lot of patrols or security.
Speaking of security, it seems more relaxed in Mankind Divided. Patrols can be easily bypassed, you never have to hack a keypad in sight of a camera or a patrol, forcing you to disable it or knock the patrol out.
The good:
+Gameplay offering multiple choices to solve things
+The final boss can be dealt with non lethally
+Very detailed environments. Not just graphics, but there's a lot of objects unique to certain rooms, giving them a personal touch.
The bad:
-Doesn't improve on Human Revolution in any meaningful way
-Too easy, even on the highest difficulty
-Microtransactions in a singleplayer game
-Game is short, and the story is left on a cliffhanger, probably for the DLC or a sequel.
Verdict: Unless you are a fan of Human Revolution and can't wait for more of the same gameplay, wait for this to go on sale.

Thief Gold puts you in the role of Garrett, a master thief and former member of the Keepers. As a thief, your main concern is stealing, and this game does a magnificent job at making you feel like you're the master rogue himself, slipping from shadow to shadow as you make your way through the 15 exhilarating and sometimes terrifying locations that the game has to offer.
You are dropped into a huge, open ended area, ranging from colossal mansions to a large labyrinth of underground sewers, full to the brim with every kind of imaginable loot. What stands between you and your prize are a wide array of guards and creatures, patrolling the perilous corridors and walkways. How you get to your destination, is up to you, and Garret's wide arsenal of different arrows and gadgets make every playthrough potentially different.
The City is dark, gritty, and immerses the player into an abnormal world, bridled by cults and sects which give the game life, giving it a particularly paranormal feeling not seen in any other game. The gameplay itself is close to being absolutely flawless, making use of the revolutionary "Dark Engine", with great AI and magnificent stealth mechanics.

*Early Access Review* Also sorry for wall of text, I just have a bit to say about this.
Honestly I just adore this game. It caught my eye about a month after being Greenlit and have continued to play it since. The developers are consistently updating with bug fixes and quality content. If you were looking for a good example of how to do a Greenlight on Steam right, look no further. The premise is a simulation/management of a adventuring equipment shop which you have started after "taking an arrow to the knee".
Pros/Things that I enjoyed:
1. Despite that pesky arrow to the knee, you manage the shop pretty well on your own, theives and all.
2. Leveling system with perks for becoming the best provider of goods the town has ever seen. And "selling quests", because selling 80 mana potions is no joke and deserves a little xp reward.
3. Unlockable crafting recipes, items for sale, garden for growing seeds into plants, adjustable profit margins, and an adventurer to adventure for you (give him some proper knee protection, why dontcha).
4, Shoplifters to help keep your righteous smiting powers sharp.
5. Assorted shelves and benches for displaying your goods.
6. Helper bots to help you with certain tasks (though at this point I find them a little more buggy than effective but I am hopeful that this will change as development continues).
Cons/Things I don't like so much:
1. Customers becoming irrate and knocking over goods. Firstly because it's downright rude and secondly because retrieving the items from the floor/etc can be a little buggy/glitchy.
2. Customers tracking so much dirt into the store. Not a big deal but would be nice to have an option to buy a floor mat or have help to clean.  I also think that while it is a nice mechanic to have to repair the displays, they degrade sooo fast :/
3. Still has the occasional (often funny or just buggy) glitch, but still not final release so there is that. I almost did not mention this because the devs are so good and consistent with patching these things in a timely fashion and do actually listen to the community. But it is here because you should expect to see some bugs/glitches.
Honestly I can say this is one of the many Early Access games I have decided to take the plunge with and not once have I regretted it. In my option this game is worth every cent and I cannot wait to see the full release! I've spent a bit of time on the game, and cannot believe how easy it is to I am very pleased with the direction the devs have taken this and look forward to each new update!

(some even move while in that default, civilian-like pose) But if you like first person platforming (many people don't) and oldschool non-subtle commando style gameplay (doom, quake, serious sam), then you'll love ROTT 2013. The pacing is fast and the enemies can be unforgiving even as you're mowing them down in unrealistic numbers at ludicrous speed. It takes a little time to get used to the first person platforming, but once you get a sense of where you're supposed to go, it's pretty fun. The controls are probably the game's strongest point -- I had no problem getting used to the unrealistic 3d platformer physics.

Let me first say I really enjoy this game. But I was both pleased and disappointed at this remake of the classic from 1994. More pleased than disappointed though which is good.
I remember buying the original ROTT back in 1994 at a store and playing it for hours on end.
My first impressions of the new 2013 remake was good. It feels very much like the classic with similar controls, feel, sound effects, right down to the coins you collect and the soldiers that beg for their life. Had they left it at that it would stand alone very well and be a good remake of a great classic game...but...
In my personal opinoin, they went too far by adding F-bombs, bad "Duke Nukem voice and one liners, and other tasteless items sprinkled around such as books on masturbation and photos of almost nude people. There's just no point to add that junk in a remake of a classic like this.
I personally don't have problems with bad words, gore, nudity or other mature content in games, (heck, I play POSTAL 2 for crying out loud,  but it felt out of place with this game and wrecked the classic feel it worked hard to recreate, at least for me. Overall I enjoy the game, but the devs didn't trust in a good game and tried to pander to a new generation of player and against games like Duke Nukem needlessly. Good game though!

The haters are gonna hate on this one, but along with Shadow Warrior and Tomb Raider, it's another awesome addition to the 2013 reboot/remake lineup. It seems like we're way too focused on byzantine plots, dark and brooding characters, and general depressing stuff. Rise of the Triad is actually FUN, and never takes itself too seriously. Pick it up on sale if you're a skeptic, otherwise have at it.

Rise of the Triad, the original, never amounted to much - sure it had some features not found in other FPS games of it's era, but it really didn't garner much more than a niche fan base.  This remake will likely only accomplish the same minimal popularity.
If you were a fan of the original, the devs did a decent job of an update - however, that's about it.  Nothing here really feels new or fresh to the FPS genre.  This is just a simple run and gun FPS - nothing less, nothing more.  There's a decent amount of gore in it - but it grows tiresome.  The game also feels overly difficult for all the wrong reasons - oftentimes I'd get confused which way the game wanted me to go, or I'd be getting shot from a distance and it was difficult to gauge where.  And there is humour in the game.  Actually, let me rephrase that.  And there is "humour" in the game.  You can tell the dev's have about the same level of wit as a college freshman - needless to say, I rarely even cracked a smile.
Some notes:
1) The 360 controller works, but doesn't work very well - and there are no means of adjusting the thumbstick sensitivity or modifying the buttons.  I personally prefer playing games with a controller - so this was a thumbs down for me.
2) I haven't experienced any of the "bugs" mentioned by other players - I don't doubt they exist, but it may not be as common as reported.
3) The games icon (some guys "O" face) is just stupid - you can tell the dev's wanted to find the most absurd image, almost to slap the people purchasing their game in the face.
4) Apogee's Twitter support is a joke - whoever is running it acts like a little kid who has a tantrum if you disagree or make any form of criticism.  If someone at Apogee reads this - fire the idiot, he's not doing your company any good!
Buy this game if:
A) You absolutely adored the original
B) You're a fan of run and gun FPS games with minimal substance
C) You get it bundled in one of the various "Indie Bundles" available (this is how I purchased it).
Otherwise, don't bother.

BROTHERS: A Tale of Two Sons is a fun little puzzle-adventure game that's short and sweet. It is, at its core, a fairy tale about sons going off on a quest to save their father.
The puzzles aren't too complicated; most of the difficulty stems from the unique cotrol scheme, wherein you control both brothers simultaneously and navigate the world, depending on each other to complete each level. The visuals are stunningly good; not ultra-realistic, but they don't have to be. This is detail without realism, like a well-drawn painting. The story is communicated though the imaginary language used by the characters, and their very telling body-acting. The music is great, the fiction is good.
This is a short game; took me only a couple hours to clear, but I enjoyed all of them. The pacing is fantastic. For the price of a movie ticket, you could also sit down with a game that exudes character, personality, and that tells a really gripping story without using a single syllable of English. Very well-made.

So after investing a hefty amount of time into this game, I have some nitpicks that I'll get out of the way now before I get too carried away with it. The world seems open, but it's just a very big hallway, so exploration doesn't matter very much unless you're hunting those collectibles that grant you experience. Character skilltrees are diverse, but not big enough for any kind of actual playstyle builds so I would recommend a bigger skilltree and maybe some team up combos when in co-op play. Invisible walls are everywhere so going off the beaten path to look for hidden goodies is a no no.
I do love how most of the original cast of voice actors are here reprising their respective roles and the maps of certain areas are breathtakingly goregous. The gameplay is pretty fluid and the combat is steady, but the lack of a lock-on system really makes fighting Grimm a hassle especially when you get demolished by the werewolves.
I do recommend you give this a try and see for yourself if you want to stick around for the long haul.

Alright in all honesty, it's not a bad game.  Even though I'm not recommending it, you should at least try it.  I give it this rating because there's too many small things that bug me about it for me to continue investing time into it, but I did get some fun out of my short stint.

Great Gameplay: The gameplay is extremely fun. This game will have you hooked after you learn the ropes. I'll touch more on that later.
Great Graphics: Really awesome graphics. This is one of the things the game excels at. From the start, I found that the game is just really nice to look at.
Great Animations: Top notch animations make it easy to recognize what players are doing.
Phenominal Variety: Each player has their own unique play style. There are currently 5 different characters that each excel in their own fighting style. Not only do they have that going for them, but the way they designed their characters makes silouetting each character really easy. I look forward to the characters they may add in the future.
Bad Tutorial: The tutorial does not at all reflect the actual gameplay of multiplayer, and doesn't even show you your character's special abilities, a very important portion of the game.
Unforgiving Start: Two parts to this one. When you first start the game, you are prompted to enter a username. No problem. After that, you are forced to choose your starting character that you will unlock for free. The only thing you have to go on is a description of the character and some short videos that repeat and show their basic loadout. This is a huge problem, as I started with a character that I didn't end up liking, so I was forced to grind my way to the necessary 10,000 gold to purchase another character (which you still cannot test). The only saving grace to this is that the gameplay is still pretty entertaining, regardless of your character abilities. If you do happen to choose a character you do not like, you have to play an average of about 15-20 matches to get the 10K gold and blindly purchase another character.
Second part. The learning curve is really rough. Your first matches will probably be really un-fun and have you pretty frustrated with your character, no matter who you choose. This can be solved by one, more players in the community, and two, by having some sort of level restricted mode that new players can play in. This should also include a testing ground where you are free to play every character a few times so you can get the right one for you.
Unbalanced "Matchmaking": I get the game is new, and might not have a lot of users, but the matchmaking is pretty bad. My highest level character is level 5, and in the time it took to level him I have played against maybe 10 matches where your team has absolutely no chance to win. If you are one to get really mad at unbalanced matchmaking, maybe give this game a few weeks before you jump in.
Weird Campaign: There is a campaign to the game, so you don't have to play against people right away, however, the campaign has a limit to the number of spawns you have. I haven't gotten completely used to how you get "respawn tokens" but the player has a limited amount of them. Once you are out, you can't spawn anymore, and therefore, have to quit out as soon as you can't spawn again.
Server Errors: The servers go down some times when in the client. I've only had one game lose connection, but the game will fairly often cut you off while browsing the store of queueing for a match. This isn't a really big issue as the game is quick to boot up, so I'm not viewing this as a gigantic problem with the game.

Going back to Thief: The Dark Project after playing its (superior IMO) sequel, The Metal Age, is quite a jarring experience.
The Dark Project is one of those games that, in retrospect, comes off as more of a tech demo showcasing the potential of the licence than a fully-fleshed out gaming experience. While you still get a lot of fun out of it, looking back, you can see the cracks and rudimentary design that would be further polished and refined down the line.
You see it everywhere - guard patrols that stack up four or five deep in a single line, rooms with lots of guards facing away from the player, smaller levels on average, rougher animation, etc.
Yet, for all that, the original Thief is still an engrossing and eminently-playable experience. The bones of the engine are all there, and blackjacking and using rope arrows still feels as good as it did when I first played it back in the late 90's. It's definitely worth picking up both of the games, if only to see how much the engine and gameplay developed between the two original installments.

Mankind Divided plays out in a very similar way to Human Revolution. The gameplay is the exact same: You can fight through an area, hack your way through doors, or find a way to sneak through. However, some augments seem TOO good.
Patrolling guards? I can use the cloak to get by them. Laser grid? Can move through it with cloak. Security camera? Cloak.
The high jump augment also seems much more useful than it was in Human Revolution. Gate has a security level 5 keypad? The fence is low and you can just jump over it. You can also jump onto balconies to enter an area easily, or get into a high place accessible only by high jump that bypasses a lot of patrols or security.
Speaking of security, it seems more relaxed in Mankind Divided. Patrols can be easily bypassed, you never have to hack a keypad in sight of a camera or a patrol, forcing you to disable it or knock the patrol out.
The good:
+Gameplay offering multiple choices to solve things
+The final boss can be dealt with non lethally
+Very detailed environments. Not just graphics, but there's a lot of objects unique to certain rooms, giving them a personal touch.
The bad:
-Doesn't improve on Human Revolution in any meaningful way
-Too easy, even on the highest difficulty
-Microtransactions in a singleplayer game
-Game is short, and the story is left on a cliffhanger, probably for the DLC or a sequel.
Verdict: Unless you are a fan of Human Revolution and can't wait for more of the same gameplay, wait for this to go on sale.

Infiltrations can be approached covertly or aggressively which provides good replay value. And although stealth is limited and deadly force is hard to justify, the freedom of engagements is delightful. All of this is supported by the city of Prague, a wonderful hub that is almost perfectly utilized, and a few other carefully-designed locations. This is a sequel that stands alongside Human Revolution and that makes it essential for series fans itching to get back into those nurturing vents—whichever direction they may lead.

I'm running a 980, and I'm not even on ultra, I'm mostly on just high (aside from one or two options here and there, and there's very high between those two settings, too), and the game refuses to stay at a stable 60 in large swathes of the game. I had Rivia Statistics Tuner running the whole time, and I noticed that it rarely - if ever - used more than 65% of my GPU, but it used loads of my CPU, which, being an i5 3570, is no pushover, either. Why? Couldn't tell you. My guess is they're using the CPU for shadows too much, like Fallout 4 did, but I really couldn't tell you since I didn't really bother to find the offenders. I put up with it because this is a Deus Ex game and I was enjoying it, but it put a very distinct blemish on the whole thing. It never dropped below 30, but that only makes me even more aware that this is a botched console port instead of a PC first title, which pisses me off since this is supposed to be a Deus Ex game. Also, if you were in cover when you saved, you had better have some quick reaction times, because the "space" action is going to happen whenever you finish loading. Oh, and the mouse acceleration thing.
Oh, and did I mention how ♥♥♥♥ing ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ talking about the Illuminati with your partner in a crowded train station covered with police, drones, and scanners that the Illuminati could use to track you is? Oh wait, yes they do, it's called the "infolink," and they kind of make a big deal about how secure the infolink is in Human Revolution, so it's not like they even have to wait to have the conversation, they just need to use the infolink instead of their mouths like smart people, but no, they just talk about it out in the open....
All in all, it's a good game marred by incompetence and it simply being incomplete. Buy it on sale if you don't feel right buying it in its current state.

I really love games by Amanita, with Botanicula currently being by favorite.  They're quirky, they're cute, and they're fun to figure out.
The Samorost games contain my favorite character, the space gnome, but be aware that the first two are very short, and among the first created by the company.  (See the full rundown of release dates on Amanita's wiki
.)  The earliest titles were made to be browser-based flash games, which is why the Samorost 2 playing area takes up a smallish area of the screen (if you have your destop set at 1920x1080, anyway.)
The game will open up full-screen with a black background, but if you hit the Esc button, it will play windowed.  Gameplay itself consists of finding clickable areas, then figuring out the correct sequence -- and sometimes timing -- to allow you to progress.
There are seven levels to complete, and as you start each one, you will be given a level code so that you can return to that area if you need to turn off the game, or just feel like revisiting.  You can find the walkthrough
, and the level codes are the first thing you'll see, so no worries if you don't want spoilers. ;)
In closing, Samorost 2 is a short, fun romp through one of Amanita's earliest games.  I personally would not pay full price for the game unless I was buying directly from the developers in order to support them, and recommend getting it on sale.  Definitely looking forward to Samorost 3!

I love physics-based puzzle games. Why? Because they make me feel smart(er than I really am) and because I find it fun to crack a puzzle using some crazy idea I just got rather than just blast my way through (don't get me wrong, that's fun too..just not always). Trine 2 is a wonderful physics-based puzzle platform game. Like other similar titles, it reincarnates the old murky platform shooter into something brand new and exciting. With three different characters (wizard, warrior and thief) all with their own attributes, you must work together (either alone or co-op with two other other players) to solve the puzzles that the environment and orc/goblins set up. It's fun, beautiful and it seamlessly brings out the best in both single-player and multiplayer gaming experiences.

This is a wonderful game to play with your two closest friends that can also provide quite a laugh when your friends formulate plans that look far too dumb to work and then it actually succeeds.  When you find you or your friends saying, "wow, was I supposed to do that?" you just know a game like this is truly the refresher that the 2D platformer needed, even for people who didn't originally care for the genre.  I would easily recommend this game, especially for the $15 price tag.  Hell, I'd have paid $30!

Unrealistic, buggy, frenetic, pick your complaint; it's all irrelevant. I can't help but think some of the negative reviews are coming from those who weren't reared on 80s and 90s arcade style gaming. There aren't markers leading you around the map, it isn't some grand-scale Zynga/iPad game like much of what modern gaming has become, and there are no pretensions to high art. Games in our age are either based in mindless repetition/accumulation  and/or are attempting to replace books and movies by guiding you benignly through a plot; thankfully, ROTT breaks that mold entirely. ROTT offers a sweet, simple, often forgotten goal: getting the high score. Achieving this is difficult, but the path to doing so is both straightforward and thrilling.
One comment I've seen in forums as a complaint is: "enemies shoot you from far across the map where you can't see them". I implore any readers of this review to understand: that is the point. Games aren't meant to hold your hand or play fair. If you want linear quests and cinematically placed enemies play a different game; otherwise, find and kill the hidden guy shooting you.
Again, no questmarkers. No "spam X to achieve Y". No "walk to the next cutscene". How is it that such a childish game as ROTT asks more of us than the high-budget, high-profile games that, rather, turn us into children?

So after hitting my 100th hour I figured it was time to update my review as I now have a broader opinion.
First of all I'm going to split the review into two. Public play and Regimental play, as I know some people only have interest in one of those and they play quite a lot different than you think.
TLDR at the bottom.
Public Play:
I'll start off by saying Public play is FUN and I mean really fun. The guns are inaccurate (as they should be) and melee still needs some polish. Although you're missing half your shots and you're getting chopped up by some guy with a sword, the sense of satisfaction when you blast some dude, screaming down voip with his bayonet on a collision course with your gut, to oblivion with your musket is like no other.
I'd also like to add that somehow within all this chaos people manage to just naturally work together. Whether it be teammates just sticking together because they know that a 20 second reload time is most likely going to see you stabbed to death by the enemy team. Or some roleplaying officer that's managed to muster half the team into a line firing volleys into the enemy. Then in response someone will lead an enemy line to counter and the dynamics of the match completely change. I find it quite brilliant.
I'm just going to also add that the community in this game as a whole is one of the best I've ever encountered. Everybody is super helpful if you're unsure about controls etc. As mentioned before the roleplaying guys are a blast to play with, especially because they don't take themselves too seriously and tend to turn into some quite hilarious characters.
Now you've also got the guys that play music down voip. This 'part' of the game used to be a bit of a 50/50 for me, it's funny when used right but not when abused. Much of the problem was fixed by adding the ability to easily mute players.
Somebody once played the Cha-Cha Slide down voip at spawn to which the whole team joined in, well we at least did our best as criss crossing was difficult and nobody could clap their hands.
Regimental play:
So there are a few different types of regiments/crews. There are those that heavily roleplay, those that don't take it seriously and are about having a good time, and those that are competitively focused and find the best strategies within the rules they play under.
I find last one to be the best for me, and you should also find what you think you'll enjoy the most and start searching on the regiments section of the forums for something that fits your criteria.
So depending on the regiment, or crew for naval, you'll play in battles of up to 200 players and probably do some kind of training to learn all the orders. These are relatively simple to pick up.
You'll either play a linebattle, siege or coastal siege. Each with a set of rules decided on by the regiments that play in these events.
I've found these rules don't hinder your experience, without them it simply wouldn't work because the game is alpha and there are a few things that need to be restricted. e.g. the rifleman class (basically a sniper at the moment).
These battles are crazy fun. Flanking your enemy and letting off a volley into the rear and watching their line crumble. Or when the lines come in close quarters and you can almost see the whites of their eyes, obliterating each other with a volley or two and charging gloriously to your death.
A few weeks ago I was part of a testing for increased player count on the servers. The last round was melee only, this meant that everyone on the server slammed into each other at once (Two lines of opposing force of 100 people) and I can honestly say i was one of the best sights I've ever seen in a game. And furthermore it reminded me of the potential of this early access game, and where the finished product mind end up.
The only downside of regiments is lies within a little part of the gameplay. At the moment the weapons are near perfect for the public servers. However in linebattles each round is one life and you can get killed from 200+ metres, so it becomes quite frustrating. You'll often find yourself moving closer to your screen to see what you're shooting at because the more people you can kill at that range the less you have to deal with close up when the weapons are super effective as everyone is standing in a big line.
BUT there has been rumours about a seperate 'hardcore' mode tuned towards the gameplay of the linebattles, sieges etc. If/when the implement this it'll improve everyone's experience massively.
Regardless of this I still have a lot of fun and some good laughs with the people in my regiment.
Conclusion / TLDR :
The community is helpful, and has a lot of experience from similar games. Doesn't take itself too seriously which helps with it being very new player friendly,
The gameplay is very fun but has a few problems with melee and what I mentioned in the regiments section about accuracy. But it's in alpha and the next patch brings some good fixes for melee and the accuracy is still to be fine tuned.
In such an early state, the game being fun is what matters most and it very much is.
The future is bright for this game, the 3 devs do an excellent job and put out more content/updates than studios far larger than them.
The game is well worth the standard price of £15.99, but if you can get it on sale that's a bargain.

KoA Reckoning might be one of by favorite games of all time. Its right up their for me along with Morrowind, Skies of Arcadia and FFIX.
Now, Reckoning is facinating not only because of its plot and design choices but because of the history of the game itself. It's probably a miracle that this game was ever made in the first place. It was started by 38 Studios, (owned by Kurt Schilling of all people) who gathered an all star team to develop a World of Warcraft killer MMO.Art Direction by Todd McFarlane, music by Grant Kirkhope, written by R.A. Salvatore...this game had it all. Unfortunatly, (or perhaps fortunatly) the MMO project was scrapped, and was retooled into a single-player RPG with the help of Big Huge Games, then lead by Ken Rolston, the dude who was the lead designer for Morrowind and Oblivion.
I should point out that one of the reasons this game is so great, and feels so large and polished, is because 38 and Big Huge spend so much money developing this game that in order for it to break even it would have had to sell an absolute ♥♥♥♥ ton of copies. According to the Governor of Rhode Island at the time and future unsuccessful democratic primary canidate Lincoln Chaffee, the game would have had to sell 3 million copies in the first 90 days. Why would Lincoln Chaffee care about this game? Well, Big Huge and 38 Studios where located in Rhode Island during development because of a tech stimulus program that was supposed to turn R.I. into the next big tech hub. Basically, if you move your tech company to R.I, you would not only get tax breaks, but R.I. would invest in your company. When 38 Studios when bankrupt because they made a game they couldn't hope to get returns on, R.I. got all rights to the company. So if you buy this game you will be giving money to Rhode Island. Hope your O.K. with that.
Anyway, on to the game itself: You will probably be able to tell that is was supposed to be an MMO. The enviroments are very open and full of randomly scattered enemies, and there are alot of quests that are 'Gather X numbers of Y thing.' The major cities feel...empty. They feel like they were made to acommodate more than one player. That being said they are GORGEOUS. The art direction in general of this game is amazing. the enviroments are large and very pretty...if you can see them. The game has a very annoying MMOish camera angle that is at a steep angle. I know that it would have made sense in an MMO, so you can see you AND all your friends doing stuff. But in a single player game, it makes no sense. I recommend installing a mode to fix it.
Thats the first of my two major complaints with this game; the other being in the plot. The games begins in usual RPG fasion, in that it doesn't tell you♥♥♥♥♥♥about your character's backstory. I assumed that it was hoping we would fill in the blanks, Elder-Scrolls style. But later in the game, in one of the final main quests, THEY TELL YOU YOUR CHARACTER'S BACKSTORY. After 75 hours of letting you make your own. Oh, and the final boss is pretty♥♥♥♥♥♥
Combat is fluid, and the game lets you create your own personal playstyle. You can get traits in one of the three usual areas, stealth, magic or combat. But you can mix up the three playstyles, and get traits that are in two or all three.

Thief GOLD is absolutely incredible! I'm glad I finally played it. When I was younger, I skipped out on the Thief games because they had stealth and seemed hard. Thief GOLD is no walk in the park and is quite challenging. I clocked in about 26 hours and some missions took me 1-2 hours to complete. I had to use a walkthrough and watch youtube videos for some parts because it is easy to get lost! The map system is more like a visual representation of hints and doesn't actually tell you where you are, thus making the levels seem almost maze like. However, the gameplay and atmosphere of Thief totally make up for this. The game is totally immersive and sucks you into it's universe. The gameplay is really simple! You play as a thief, Garrett, and must follow certain objectives to complete a mission like stealing loot for item purchases after the end of each mission. Also, you must sneak around; castles, caves, dungeons, cathedrals, mansions, and med-evil cities without getting caught by guards and monsters. The visuals and controls obviously have shown it's age compared to modern games, but they definitely have charm. I would totally recommend this game! Great atmosphere, great gameplay, great protagonist, and a good challenge.

Samorost 2, released 6 years later, continues the journey of our gnome-like protagonist who sets out to retrieve his stolen dog from aliens.
Although very short, Samorost is a great point-and-click adventure game which has a very unique artwork. The gameplay is very simple - we look for clickable objects on every screen and try to solve the puzzles that represent obstacles before Gnome could proceed any further to reach his goal. I really like the game's surrealistic world with its unique creatures - above all, Gnome itself, who lives on an asteroid full of plants.
The game was designed in flash, hence the use of macromedia player when the game is launched. Also, the game omits any achievements or additional challenges. While the game offers the "play again" option you do not click on it because there are things you haven't seen in the game's roughly 2-hour long journey - you start again to see how very well it is designed (albeit everything in it is minimalistic) and to listen to its great accompanying ambient music.
It is a tad bit expensive for 5 euros, however, if it is on sale it is a great purchase. I look forward to seeing how Amanita continued the adventure in the 3rd episode.

Samorost2 is a point-and-click adventure puzzle game from Amanita Design.  Amanita’s quirky characters, worlds, and stories are truly unique, even in the indie game landscape.  In Samorost2, follow a cute space gnome as he searches for his alien-abducted dog.
Samorost1 is available for free, right on Amanita’s website!  Play that first, and if you like it, invest in Samorost2.  Samorost1 is a Flash-based game, and Samorost2 expands on its ideas and you can really see that the developer learned from the first game and it outpaces the first both technically and gameplay-wise.  In each game, you will guide the little gnome from static screen to screen, clicking objects in the environment and figuring out how to open the path forward.
The gameplay here is simple.  If something looks interesting, click on it.  It will either help you progress, make a cool sound effect, or do nothing at all!  Most of the game you will be squinting at the screen to try and find the one object that turns your cursor into a hand (indicating a clickable object), or trying to determine the correct order to click things in.  Often it is not 100% apparent exactly what you’re supposed to do, but the options are generally limited enough that you can stumble across the solution pretty easily.  This is not an adventure game that makes you feel very clever for having figured it out, but rather one where the atmosphere and the weird surroundings make you curious and inquisitive to see how things fit together.  Real-world knowledge of how things work is not very useful here, where items behave in unexpected ways.  The joy in this game is not figuring it out based on what you already know, but by being inquisitive.
The graphics are one of the outstanding things about this game.  Simple, but evocative.  You’ll see an old oil can used as a spaceship.  You’ll see mossy tree trunks used as massive structures filled with life.  Strange alien landscapes made out of things we see everyday bring a refreshing look to a genre that is often all about either retro pixelation or brown realism.  Also, Samorost2 can be run on almost any old Windows machine, due to its incredibly simple Flash programming.
The audio in Samorost1/2 is really interesting.  Ambient, often soft and eerie, you’ll be displaced by the music and thrust into this odd world.  The sound effects are also incredibly detailed.  Animals will make unique sounds, alien machines will clank and whir strangely, and wind will blow through the “trees”, lending a beautiful atmosphere to the game.
Obtuse puzzle games like this can be frustrating at times, where you see a bunch of clickable objects, but have no idea how to put them together.  Even when you do manage to blindly stumble into the solution, that is often unsatisfying.  However, Samorost drips with such charm and quirky joy that you’ll often find you do not care.  The uniqueness of the alien landscapes, coupled with the cuteness of the gnome and his dog (and the smoking bro), will likely make you enjoy yourself regardless.
Samorost1 and 2 are interesting games for more than just their own sake.  Amanita Design went on to make some of the most highly-praised adventure games of the past few years, including Machinarium and Botanicula.  Some of the features that made those games so great are present here, in Samorost, in their infancy.  Amanita’s first foray into adventure games is well worth your time, if only to see where it all began.

This is an interesting game. Not only does it tell a story through characters that talk in... well... what I THINK is gibberish, it also manages to make a quite weird concept kind of fun.
"Brothers - A Tale of Two Sons" tells a story about two motherless brothers out to save their dying father. They go out on a dangerous adventure to try and find something that'll cure him, traveling through strange environments and encountering strange creatures that will either help them or try to kill them.
The story is pretty good. It's told mostly visually and it's pretty simple. It's very focused on the adventure and nothing shocking happens until close to the end. As for the adventure? It's close to the style of "The Lord of the Rings" in that you walk a very long distance to get to a particular place and fulfil a particular task.
The game-play involves controlling the two brothers (we'll get to the controls in a moment) and walking them through the environment, solving puzzles using the particularities of each. Both brothers can do something that the other cannot and you have to work with this to proceed. Puzzles involve climbing, jumping and walking over fallen trees or around ledges, or just walking, and doing certain actions like pulling switches and throwing down ropes. There are also physics based puzzles involving weight.
Now, the controls are the interesting part. For the camera, you use LB and RB (yes, you NEED a controller to play this. It's not optional) and you control both brothers simultaneously. How? Well, to control the big brother you use the left analog stick to move him and you hold LT to perform actions. For the small brother you move him with the right analog stick and you hold RT to perform actions. You normally use them simultaneously, so it takes some learning to get adjusted to the controls.
There are some negative points. The game is only 2 hours long if you focus on getting through the story, it's very short. I guess that would be a plus due to the controls and the experimental nature of the game, but I feel it could've gone on for longer and I didn't feel satisfied when it ended. This is a very fun game once you get the hang of it and it's a shame that it is so short. It's also a little bit painful to control because you must hold the triggers down to proceed, and, if you have big, sweaty hands like mine, your fingers are going to slip quite a lot. Don't let that throw you down, though, you can get used to it. Also, spider. I wouldn't recommend playing this game if you're arachnophobic. Ok, the spider only appears once, but it's a pretty big spider and you have to fight it by making it go belly-up and ripping its legs out. Watch out for that. On to the the scores!
Scores:
1 - Not recommended;
2 - Only if you're a fan of the series/genre;
3 - Recommended.
Therefore, I give this game a 3/3. It's not perfect and it's pretty short, but it is a pretty fun game and you should definitely give it a try.

Mount&Blade: Warband is a sandbox game where you make your own story. Its a game where you play as a chracter who's origins you can choose that is living in a fictional medieval realm controlled by 6 factions. The factions are the Kingdom of Swadia (Knights), Kingdom of Nords (Vikings), Khergit Khanate (Mongols), Sarranid Sultinate (Saracens), Kingdom of Vaegirs (Eastern Europeans), And Kingdom of Rhodoks (Italian States). In the game you decide which land of these factions you go to after the origin selection but choose wisely since each faction has a different way to be handeled.
The gameplay of Mount&Blade Warband is fun and engaging, the combat is fun and based on how good you are at fighting (Note that how good you are is not the same with as stats) and the archery is based on how good are you at aiming (Note that the damage you deal on archery and combat is based on your stats but the way you play is based on your skill). Horse riding is fine for the most part but can be a bit clunky in combat. However the gameplay can be repetative at some parts like for example the traveling on the main map. The traveling can take a while and can easily cause boredom and when you're chasing routing enemies or herding cattle can cause frustration at times. Combat can also be tiring but you can just send your men to fight without you but if you are gonna fight with them prepare for the amount of enemies you'll face since it can be pretty ridiculous and mind numing.
The game can look pretty bland and just meh since you're mostly spending your time on the main map itself. There isn't really much to look at in cities, towns, and castles other than npcs walking into walls. There are not much glitches on the game and there are only a few bugs so there isn't much to worry about.
There is so much to talk about that I can't cover it all on one single review but I will say this, it is a very fun and immersive experience and it does have a ton of replayability. Overall I recommend this game, a worthwhile game for sandbox players and medieval genre fans.

I would like to begin by stating that Mount & Blade: Warband is a truly marvellous game, Mount & Blade: Warband is a Role-Playing game which has many elements of strategy involved, it is set in the Medieval period in the discordant land of Calradia where six opposing monarchs are striving for the lordship of all of Calradia. Each monarch rules a faction  and have numerous vassals to support their claim to the throne of Calradia.
The names of these factions are as follows: (Nords, Khergit Khanate, Vaegirs, Sarranids Sultanate, Rhodoks and Swadians.) These factions have their own unique units and cultures which took inspiration from certain countries during the medieval period. However as the protaganist of the game you will ultimately become the king of all of Calradia but there are a multitude of paths that you can take before ascending to the throne, for example you could be a merchant, bandit, knight etc. before doing so. You will find that there will be many oppurtunities in the game that can turn out to be profitable for you or could potentially lead to your downfall.
As you can see I have already invested a number of hours into Mount & Blade: Warband due to the vast replayability that this game has to offer, furthermore the DLC developed by Taleworlds such as Viking Conquest and Napoleonic Wars and mods made by the community provides the game with a fresh experience so that you never grow tired of some features that the native module has to offer.
Personally I was dissapointed by some aspects that I felt the base game could improve in, such as the very repetitive nature of the quests given to you, the lack of battle formations, the inability to execute lords (Klargus) and the game lacking some immersion, the game could have had more interactions between the NPC's and your character and you should be able to do more things than raid villages and caravans or slaying bandits on the world map, although as I have already said, the DLC's and mods made by the community can provide fresh experiences and can hopefully include some aspects that the game is missing. For starters I believe that the Diplomacy mod (that can be located in the steam workshop) can significantly improve the game as a whole. Taleworlds will soon be releasing Mount & Blade II: Bannerlord where I have full faith that they will be able to capitalise on improving certain elements that was lacking with its predecessor and I highly recommend that if you enjoyed Mount & Blade: Warband, it should be in your best interest that you give Bannerlord a try when it eventually releases.
On that note I will end my review by saying that Mount & Blade: Warband is well worth grabbing a hold of and I wish that you have an enjoyable experience!

As most of you may know, the new Thief reboot came out not too long ago. In honor of it's release, I am ignoring it entirely, preferring to watch GhostRobo lets-play it and compare it to this, the Thief Gold Edition. Right off the bat, I nearly broke into tears. Not at how well-rendered the worlds were (not very), or how good the voice acting is (not), but because this game is the epitome of something that most modern games are apparently deathly afraid of; having a completely stealth-based game. Most games have certain stealth aspects that you can choose to integrate into your game experience, or forced stealth sequences that your character uses to get his recently stolen items back. Thief is something different, you're a wisecracking medieval pickpocket who turned to his pickpockety ways in order to live in the city that was apparently forged to have conveniently shadowed areas right next to things like guard posts and enough loose change laying around to fund my bottomless pit of desire for nice TF2 weapons. Without stealth, it's hard to beat the game legitimately, but there's something special about it, it's still better than all the Assassin's Creed games are, and ever could be. Proceed to light your torches and grab your pitchforks, Ubisoft fans.

The game is alright, it has potential to be fun, but this is ruined by how most matches play out.
It has the right mechanics to be a game about skill, but ends up being nothing more than some berserk spam fest where no one is even actually trying to do anything, it's just firing/slashing in random directions until you kill something.
I tried to enjoy this game, and want to enjoy this game, but at the same time, the seemingly pointless button mashing ruins any enjoyment the game could offer. It's hard to appreciate the game when all you get is three people rushing, one rapid-meleeing you, while two others just spam bullets.
Melee combos are ridiculously overpowered, and are part of what makes the spam so fun-killing. It ends up coming down to "guy who managed to swing first gets to do the kill combo and win", since there seems to be no way to break a melee combo once it has started.
Some classes are
superior to others. Wayne the Strider, for example, has a whip that seems to be vastly superior to any of the other melee weapons. This wouldn't be problematic if you didn't have to buy every class except for the one you chose initially. What's even more annoying, is that you're given no way to test the classes out before you're forced to pick one.
The game doesn't
to be pay to win, it's just simply not that fun. It has its moments where it can be somewhat enjoyable, but when it comes down to it, it's just a button masher, there is literally nothing to this except spamming whatever attack, or combo.
Another downside, is that you always end up playing the same map most of the time. For some reason, people don't seem to know that there are maps other than "abandonned mansion". It's as if the community made a group decision that it was the only map that should be played out of the 8 available, because who wants to avoid repetitive gameplay, right?
Another thing I strongly disliked, was the fact that game rooms seem to be temporary. You join one, win or lose, and then it just takes you right back to the lobby. So after every single match, you're going to have to play the waiting game again while you sit back and wait for the system to find your next match. This wouldn't be particularly troublesome if it weren't for the fact that it can take quite some time before you actually get into a new match.
But don't take what I've said so far as me saying I hate everything about this game. I like the fact that it offers a very competitive feel, the movement system is far more engaging than any other F2P game I've played, and it achieves the idea of fast-paced combat.
If the classes were rebalanced much better, game rooms were changed so that you can stay with the room after the match ends, and melee was improved so it's not just consisting of unstoppable combos, the game would feel much more entertaining.
Yes, I already know some predictable troll is going to fly in here with some half-minded comment such as "git gud" or something along the lines of that, so let me answer your ignorance before you post it:
I had several matches where I did good, in contrast to the matches where I didn't do so good. The problem, is that in the matches where I did good, it felt no different from the ones where I didn't do good, since it was nothing more than a matter of coming out on top of the ridiculous spam fest where eight people are flying all over the place, using unstoppable melee combos, and gun spam. That's the problem:
Being good = spammed more, not because you're actually better at the game whatsoever. There is no "getting good" at the game, there is merely "spamming harder".
For the TL;DR people, I'll include a pros and cons section:
Pros:
Has a competitive feel.
Interesting movement system.
Fast-paced combat.
Easy to learn how to play.
Seems to not be Pay to Win.
Cons:
Combat is nothing more than a spam fest.
Melee combos cannot be countered.
Classes are unbalanced.
Switching to new classes costs you in-game currency.
No way to test classes before you select one.
Community seems to have picked one map that will always be played.
With all of that said, I will continue playing the game for a little while, just to see if perhaps I was wrong, and this is all a misunderstanding of the game. But from what I've seen, I can't honestly recommend this game until improvements are made.

This review is certainly a review I should have wirtten long ago, but here we are now.
This game is brilliant, and I loved every second of this expansive game.
The design of this game (Which comes from the narritive mind of R.A Salvatore, and Oblivion's director) is an overarching theme that all life is dictated by a thread of fate when they are first created or born; and the protagonist cheating fate and forging a fate of his own that affects the fate of all.
The concept is one I've really not seen before in a video game narritive, and it definitely soothes my ache for strong philosophy and writing in video games.
The story seems to lack a bit though.. You do meet a few characters througout the story, but they feel more like pieces on a Chess board than breathing individual (Besides one you meet towards the end of the game's second act), but I enjoyed their presences when they were around.
The art is great, I love all of it. It evokes many different vibes, and the environments are lovingly crafted, despite the way each area on the map is segmented out, giving a weird map design in an otherwise fluid game world. Klurikon will forever stand in my brain as a testiment to how much focus a narritive design can have on the impact to the world around the player, while still delivering tight gameplay and fantastic visuals.
The gameplay of Amalur is very reminiscent of the Fable series, giving open variety to the player, and rewarding the player for switching up their moveset and exploring the way to game works. In combat, the player may have two weapons equipped at a time, free to select either with the press of a button; while magic spells are always available to use, and can be selected via the keyboard, while the UI shows any macro'd spells. Fighting enemies offers the players points towards their fate bar, which builds up and allows the player to trance into a state where they can unleash their true awesome power and deliver satisfying finishers to enemies for extra exp, which is a fun treat to watch and revieve; performing well in fights (eg. not taking damage, varying up attack combos) will earn the player more points for the bar.
The DLC is a whole review in itself, as it offers dozens of hours of fresh, new content, so I'll leave this review concise enough. Amalur is a grandly underrated game (I presume due to lack of marketing during its release) and deserves full attention of the gaming audience, please give it a chance to play, you won't be let down-- Look at my face, would I lie?

Samorost 2 has astonishing art style and fun puzzle/adventure mechanics, but it is too short even for the budget price range.
Amanita Design, in a sense, is a one–trick pony company that makes surreal, textless, and speechless point ‘n’ click puzzle games. Luckily, said trick is a seemingly endless imagination, reflected in each of their products; Samorost 2 (the sequel to their first game which is
) being no exception.
This incredibly short room-by-room type point ‘n’ click game has an almost childishly simple story: the protagonist’s dog gets kidnapped, and he travels to another asteroid to save his pet. But Samorost 2 isn’t really about the plot; the real content is the creativity. There is more of it present in the alien landscapes (and all the little details they are filled with) than in many large-budget AAA titles. And Samorost 2 manages to present it all under an hour, leading to a really concentrated experience. Sure, it has its price too, but if you like games a little more on the artistic side, then Amanita delivers yet again.

Samorost 2 is pretty cool. People will go on and on about it, out-snobbing each other with cries of BURRR THIS IS A FLASH GAME IT SHOULD HAVE BEEN ON NEWGROUNDS, REAL GAMES FOR HARDCORE GAMERS ONLY PLEASE!!!!, but ignore them. They're dumb.
I love the way Amanita Design makes their games - a lot of love clearly went into the worldbuilding. You're a little man in his PJs exploring floating mushrooms that have been uprooted from the ground and left in space! Your spaceship is made out of a discarded can of weenies! There's a sewage tank and the water stains look like a pastoral farmscape! So many little beautiful details that are worth the price of admission alone.
I'm not so much a fan of the puzzle-solving. Most of the puzzles are fine and are nice little breaks from the art, but sometimes they are a bit of a pain when trying to decipher context clues in a small Flash window. (FYI, this game was released ten years ago and it holds up well, though it's hard to see things sometimes.) Sometimes, there's areas that you need to click on that weren't clickable before and the game doesn't bother to tell you whether or not they're activated. It's not a perfect system, but it's fine.
Samorost 2 is uneven but overall fine. If you want something with more difficulty, check out their games Machinarium and Botanicula. There will be a sequel for this one coming out very soon, too.

The first Torchlight, while being an indie tribute to the original Diablo, still managed to feel like its own game. By taking place in a single stratified dungeon, it has a very arcadey feel, with an emphasis on making you feel powerful and useful right from the start. There was enough variety in the weapons and enemies to keep you interested, but with a small enough scope to allow for ever-refined runs down to the depths. The retirement system meant you could roll your own legacy, complete with an ever-improving heirloom weapon or armour, adding notch to your lineage every night if you played hard and fast. It was lonely, with no multiplayer, but user-created mods that streamlined things and an ever-faithful mutating pet could suffice.
In contrast, Torchlight II feels too self-aware of its positioning as “the alternative to Diablo III”. It’s too aware of its status of being the David to Diablo III’s Goliath, thus aiming to “beat” Diablo III directly in two areas it knows the competition has trouble: features and pricing. That said, Torchlight II may sacrifice too much of its own style in an attempt to ensure a certain laundry list of features. It feels like Runic fell into the trap of thinking that people appreciated Torchlight for being “the little Diablo”, and so focused too much on making sure Torchlight II hit all those Diablo II notes. Even so, while it may not be a unique medley, there’s no denying Runic plays the tune effortlessly.
Some elements of Runic’s own thinking on the genre does shine through, like the refined pet system. The idea of having a pet that fights with you, and is well-trained enough to handle selling your junk in town, isn’t new. You can find the system wholesale in WildTangent’s Fate, which precedes Torchlight by almost half a decade. It’s no surprise though, since Fate was designed by the same person who went on to design Torchlight. For the sequel, your pet has learned a new trick: reading a shopping list. You can specify up to four consumables, like Town Portal scrolls and Mana Potions, that the pet should bring back from town if you send it off to sell the junk you packed in its trunk. It’s a small thing, but small things add up over time.
Four new character classes replace the original three, and each has its own “system” bar that fills up when damaging enemies.. The Engineer uses heavy steampunk-themed weapons, which get powered up when your bar is full. The Berserker uses animal-themed special powers and super-punchy-fist action, and gets all-critical-hits for a while when their bar is full. The Embermage casts spells and gets 12 seconds to cast spells free of charge when their special bar is full. Lastly, the Outlander uses ranged weapons and tribal magic, getting improved dodge and critical chance when their bar fills up. All classes can use all weapon types, for the most part, though you will find some items with class-restricting affixes.
Where Torchlight took place in, well, the town of Torchlight, the sequel starts by destroying that town, not just symbolically. The cute and vapid plot (one of the three original classes from the first game goes nuts, powers up and starts sucking the life-force from very-important guardian animals) acts as barely-sufficient scaffolding to support your reason for going from place to place. Not that we need a reason: the world is made of loot. The game spans across four acts, following the overly conventional structure of grassy-mountains, desert, foresty-swamp and <removed for spoilers>. New Game Plus replaces the Retirement system, letting you restart the game with the same character and stats as when you finished, but with ever-increasing monster difficulty. You also gain access to a Mapworks vendor that lets you buy level-specific randomly-generated maps (an excellent idea that Path of Exile also implements), giving you endless replayability, in theory.

The myth of Rise of the Triad
Before the next-gen consoles and the achievements era there was chaos.
Mouse cursor didn't even exist at that time.
Chaos was a black screen filled with white text.
Some call it DOS.
DOS gave birth to five young FPS:
Wolfenstein, Doom, Rise of the Triad, Duke Nukem and Shadow Warrior.
The first child was made of rooms and corridors.
The second added stairs, elevators and hordes.
The fourth added environment interactions in modern setting.
The fifth merged China and Japan as one culture.
What about the third child?
He was the strangest of all five.
He was made of floating platforms, deadly traps and trampolines.
As time passes the five FPS had to struggle against their successors and competitors.
All of them met a different fate.
Wolfenstein made to the modern era and set a new order.
Doom is waiting for the resurrection of evil to spread hell on earth.
Duke Nukem couldn't stand the 3 dimensional realms forever.
Shadow Warrior made to the modern era as he picked the lucky fortune cookie.
What about the third child?
Time has been cruel with Rise of the Triad.
Death took him in a gibs fest while he was begging for his life.
And thus he never made to the modern era.
