Rise of the Triad is a rarity.  A game that so faithfully updates it's original counterpart and manages to keep just about everything the way it was, and should be.  This is very much a shooter rooted in 90's logic and design, it's stronger for it, and I applaud the developers for it.
Basically the idea is you have weapons, and your objective is to blow up everything.  The combat is solid and extremely fast, you're practically encouraged to take damage so long as the damage you're dealing is greater.  Weapons include most everything from the original, including the Firebomb, MP40 & dual pistols, Split Missile, some new ones too and are heavily geared torwards explosives (this is a good thing).  Your base weapons have infinite ammo and don't need to be reloaded.  Your health doesn't regenerate automatically, you have to eat food, which you can cook by firing a rocket at before doing so.
As with the original, there's some platforming to be had.  And as with the original, it can be mildly frustrating, though at the time of writing a quick save has been patched in making this issue much much less annoying.  You'll jump on bounce platforms, check every wall for secret areas, collect coins to boost your score, avoid spinny blades and fireballs and sometimes become God.  Or a dog.  Sometimes you question the validity of the power up's you acquire.  It doesn't make sense, but it doesn't need to, and that's why it makes sense.
There's a story, though it's just an excuse to blow up not-so-vaguely Nazi cult members.  The entire single player should last you over 10 hours if you do even a little hunting for secrets, and more if you want to find everything.  It's also replayable with other charcters, though the game doesn't change at all.  But when it's this much fun, it's worth replaying anyway, and there's always another secret to be found.  There's also a multiplayer mode a-la the original title (which was quite fun), though this review is based solely on the single player.

Stealth has always been an interesting genre. One where you rely on sneaking around to get to the objective rather than going in guns (Or swords) blazing. And I will have you know that Thief as a series is one of the best first-person stealth games on the market. Gold is an expansion of Thief:  The Dark Project, and I recommend getting this one as it adds more levels and enemy types. The medieval/steampunk setting really immerses you, and lets you feel like you're actually a thief delving into the depths of a manor, or any of the other levels you're placed in. The gameplay is fantastic, although you might want to change up your key bindings as they're a bit...odd...You also get a map, although it's a bit rudimentary it still does the job fairly well.
Now, I do have two major issues with the game, and those are the combat and overall level design. The combat is clunky and cumbersome, which isn't an issue in earlier levels, since killing people isn't your main goal, and you'll often try to use your Blackjack to knock them unconcious, but then you get further in the game where it's absolutely necessary, and then it becomse an issue. The level design is twisty and mazelike, and the map won't really do you much justice when you try to crawl around caverns that twist around like a coked up Etch-A-Sketch.
Overall, it's an excellent game for being an immersive first-person stealth game, but still suffers with clunky combat and sometimes poor level design.

If you are into stealth games, Thief is for you.

Simply amazing. Pioneered the stealth genre. I beat the game on hard but had to turn the difficulty down to normal starting on the last few missions due to a few frustrating bits.
Great storyline, amazing cutscenes, funny voice acting, and good gameplay come together in one big heap of awesomeness, but near the end the game seems to focus too much on the supernatural. The second game has much less zombies and such in it.
I recommend it greatly for anyone who is curious about buying it.

Note: This game can be very troubling to play on modern systems. It's ideal that you download a fan-patch known as T-Fix before playing, as it will fix several issues, including limited resolution options and missing cutscenes. The patch also allows you to download some enhanced texture packs among other things, but they are optional.
Pros
+Game should run well on any modern computer, but you'll probably need TFix to ease several issues.
+Plays like a true stealth game, with emphasis on staying out of sight and excellent light and sound mechanics that work perfectly with this genre.
+Voice acting is superb, and the dialouge is witty as well.
+Non-linear levels allow you to take on missions as you choose, and enhance replay value.
Cons
-The game actually holds up quite well, but the style of the cutscenes are laughably dated. Thankfully you can skip them.
Overall
As the first 3D stealth game (it was released a few months before Metal Gear Solid), it's easy to see why it made such an impact in the genre. The focus on staying in the dark and moving silently, while also discouraging but not preventing combat, is just perfect for a game like this. I got it for free on Amazon thanks to a contest for the recent reboot of this series, but I'd say it's well worth the current price here on Steam.

So here comes my 'old fart story': I remember, when a friend told me about this "new game" and after school he showed me the demo he got from a magazine. I never played a single demo level so many times and i couldn't wait to get the full game. Long story short, it was a great game back then!

I'm know, that not every one can play 'slow games' like Thief, so if you're a shooter-loving action-junkie, you probably won't get happy. This game is about waiting in dark corners, sneaking around and being patient.
The atmosphere is the best part of the game, so when you play the game while watching TV or browse internet-porn, you won't have much fun either (well, depends what porns you find). But if you have the right setup (dark room & headphones) and the right attitude, you can enjoy one of the best games of all time (and probably the best 'stealth game ever').

Simply astounding. I'd give it a 10/10 if you were to include all the fervent community, and the mods the game could offer. Even without the mods and helpful community, I'd give the game a 9/10 for the fun, realistic fighting and nation-building process. I also highly applaud its customability for character growth - the sky is the limit (with mods of course).
So first of all let me split the game down into several aspects for rating.
1) Story - N/A
First of all, the story is very limited. Besides the beginning quests which is set the same for all beginners, the game story changes along with your actions. You could literally make yourself a king or play as a merchant and try gaining the most out of trading (I highly recommend a trading mod for you to make the best out of this playstyle.) There are so many different paths you can take and no set ending besides going to camp and see for yourself how you fared. As for that ending, I'd give it almost no marks for the effort but remember the fact it's simply there for score rating, not for the story.
2) Mods - 10/10
This is the heart of the game. There are so many mods out there to test, and so much more you can get out of the game once you start downloading those mods. I simply cannot applaud the mod community any more than this.
3) Gameplay - 8/10
The gameplay is fun and addictive but the logistic process, finding the guildmaster or village elders can get a bit tedious. The mods and possibly future updates may remedy the repetitive process but until then I'll give the gameplay a 8/10. Of course with some mods, I'd give it a 9/10 :D
Don't forget that there are a wide variety of weapon/ army tactics and composition to choose from when fighting and that leveling the character can heavily sway whether the battle will be in your favor or not. Diplomacy is in dire need of mods, as the vanilla game simply is... simple. Diplomacy mod solves all that :)
4) Sound - 7/10
Meh. The sound is suitable for the game but I'd say that it's just alright. It's nothing too amazing and sometimes the shouting sounds can get pretty annoying. The sword sounds especially... hitting the enemy more than 100 times and hearing the same sound can get pretty boring/ annoying - at least for me it was.
With that I conclude my review! Hope the review helps and feel free to comment!

Mount&Blade: Warband is a sandbox game where you make your own story. Its a game where you play as a chracter who's origins you can choose that is living in a fictional medieval realm controlled by 6 factions. The factions are the Kingdom of Swadia (Knights), Kingdom of Nords (Vikings), Khergit Khanate (Mongols), Sarranid Sultinate (Saracens), Kingdom of Vaegirs (Eastern Europeans), And Kingdom of Rhodoks (Italian States). In the game you decide which land of these factions you go to after the origin selection but choose wisely since each faction has a different way to be handeled.
The gameplay of Mount&Blade Warband is fun and engaging, the combat is fun and based on how good you are at fighting (Note that how good you are is not the same with as stats) and the archery is based on how good are you at aiming (Note that the damage you deal on archery and combat is based on your stats but the way you play is based on your skill). Horse riding is fine for the most part but can be a bit clunky in combat. However the gameplay can be repetative at some parts like for example the traveling on the main map. The traveling can take a while and can easily cause boredom and when you're chasing routing enemies or herding cattle can cause frustration at times. Combat can also be tiring but you can just send your men to fight without you but if you are gonna fight with them prepare for the amount of enemies you'll face since it can be pretty ridiculous and mind numing.
The game can look pretty bland and just meh since you're mostly spending your time on the main map itself. There isn't really much to look at in cities, towns, and castles other than npcs walking into walls. There are not much glitches on the game and there are only a few bugs so there isn't much to worry about.
There is so much to talk about that I can't cover it all on one single review but I will say this, it is a very fun and immersive experience and it does have a ton of replayability. Overall I recommend this game, a worthwhile game for sandbox players and medieval genre fans.

I would like to begin by stating that Mount & Blade: Warband is a truly marvellous game, Mount & Blade: Warband is a Role-Playing game which has many elements of strategy involved, it is set in the Medieval period in the discordant land of Calradia where six opposing monarchs are striving for the lordship of all of Calradia. Each monarch rules a faction  and have numerous vassals to support their claim to the throne of Calradia.
The names of these factions are as follows: (Nords, Khergit Khanate, Vaegirs, Sarranids Sultanate, Rhodoks and Swadians.) These factions have their own unique units and cultures which took inspiration from certain countries during the medieval period. However as the protaganist of the game you will ultimately become the king of all of Calradia but there are a multitude of paths that you can take before ascending to the throne, for example you could be a merchant, bandit, knight etc. before doing so. You will find that there will be many oppurtunities in the game that can turn out to be profitable for you or could potentially lead to your downfall.
As you can see I have already invested a number of hours into Mount & Blade: Warband due to the vast replayability that this game has to offer, furthermore the DLC developed by Taleworlds such as Viking Conquest and Napoleonic Wars and mods made by the community provides the game with a fresh experience so that you never grow tired of some features that the native module has to offer.
Personally I was dissapointed by some aspects that I felt the base game could improve in, such as the very repetitive nature of the quests given to you, the lack of battle formations, the inability to execute lords (Klargus) and the game lacking some immersion, the game could have had more interactions between the NPC's and your character and you should be able to do more things than raid villages and caravans or slaying bandits on the world map, although as I have already said, the DLC's and mods made by the community can provide fresh experiences and can hopefully include some aspects that the game is missing. For starters I believe that the Diplomacy mod (that can be located in the steam workshop) can significantly improve the game as a whole. Taleworlds will soon be releasing Mount & Blade II: Bannerlord where I have full faith that they will be able to capitalise on improving certain elements that was lacking with its predecessor and I highly recommend that if you enjoyed Mount & Blade: Warband, it should be in your best interest that you give Bannerlord a try when it eventually releases.
On that note I will end my review by saying that Mount & Blade: Warband is well worth grabbing a hold of and I wish that you have an enjoyable experience!

The Sims is a "people simulator", which puts you in control of a neighborhood, dictating the personal lives of the residents one household at a time.  It is, I believe, the best-selling game series of all time, despite being a niche market.  It is an awkward game to explain from a gaming standpoint, as design Will Wright found when he pitched the series in the 90's.
The Sims 3 makes a number of changes that in hindsight seem so obvious and address issues in the previous versions.  Some examples:
*Aging is now optional and adjustable.  You have the option of turning sim aging off (like The Sims 1), or having it on (like The SIms 2), and you can change the length of each age.
*Story progression, also optional.  Now the neighbors who are not actively being played will carry on their lives without your input.  They will age, marry, have children, get jobs, and other things on their own.
*Moodlets replace the previous method of tying emotional state directly to needs.  Now situations dictate emotions (and needs are just one trigger of moodlets).  This has a lot of great advantages, because it takes the emphasis off gaming the needs stats and onto the character's interactions.
*Personalities expand on the previous aspiration system, with each sim gaining a number of personality traits that determine moodlets, learning, abilities, and many other aspects of their lives.
*Interactions between all of these systems make interesting results.  You can watch a lifelong feud between a Good personality-sim and an Evil personality-sim unfold, where their mood drops just be being around each other.
One strange decision, however, is locking the focus on a single household.  Previously, you could freely switch families during a session, but while this is still possible, the game makes it a little awkward.  Sims 3 is designed for you to focus on a single house for most of the game.
The worst thing about this game is DLC and microtransation creep.  The Sims 2 had a lot of expansions, and experimented with an online store eventually, but The Sims 3 truly went all out.  There are endless expansions, stuff packs, and an online story for buying clothes and objects.  I am not even sure it is possible to own the complete content of The Sims 3.  On the other hand, the variety of extra content allows you to customize the game to your liking.  You don't have to play Supernatural or get Katy Perry stuff if you would rather have Pets and 80's nostalgia.
Personally, with the addition of some mods (like Overwatch and Story Progression), I consider this the most interesting version of The Sims, especially if you are interested in the neighborhood story.  Just remember DLC creep is optional...

This game totally reminds me of the original Deus Ex, which is a good thing. I can't remember having this much fun with a singleplayer game since Skyrim.
Pros:
Graphics: The graphics are amazing - seriously, they set the bar for what is possible with high-end hardware. Even if you have a top-of-the-line PC, don't expect to run this game at it's highest (Ultra) settings. This game is built for the future.
Gameplay: Like I said, this game reminds me of the original Deus Ex in a good way. The gameplay is very similar to the original, with nice additions like the cover system and the augmentation management tool. The game gives you choices in a multitude of ways - such as dialog choices, aug choices (to enable certain augs, you need to permanently disable other augs), and a wide variety of choice in how you approach missions and situations. Supposedly you can play through the entire game without killing anybody, which would obviously rely on using stealth a lot. However, I find that the gunplay is too fun not to use occasionally, so I take advantage of that when I think it's the best approach.
Cons:
Bugs: This game is buggy as♥♥♥♥♥♥ there's no way around it. Even with an above-average PC and the latest drivers, the game crashes for me about once every hour or so. A patch came out to fix some of the crashes, but they really need to shore this up before the game is playable for a lot of people. If you decide to play even if you're getting game crashes, make sure you quick save often (default is F5 to quick save and F9 to quick load).
Overall, a great game and I strongly recommend giving it a try. Maybe wait a week or two and see if they fix the crashes or AMD/Nvidia come out with a driver update to fix the crashing.

This game is being metabombed because of Square Enix's shady DLC model. Essentially, the minor DLC (like the Assault Pack or the Praxis Kits) are one time use only. You access your inventory in game, and you transfer the item from the storage tab into your inventory. If you lose the save it's gone, and if you start a new game the content is gone.
I wish to separate the review of the physical, final product from the DLC/Store content which, IMO, is optional and not required in any way whatsoever. Yes, the model is shady and deplorable behavior by Square Enix, however, the actual game itself is a very good and enjoyable experience.
If you love the franchise but are hesitant about the DLC model, purchase the game and avoid the store entirely. Square Enix (if they're smart) differentiates between micro-transaction sales and physical/digital game copy sales. Vote with your wallet against the store and not the game.

For starters, my PC is extremely powerful, so your mileage may vary. Under the hood I have 2 980 Tis, an i7 4970k processor, and 32 gbs of RAM. It's probably overkill for this game, because I experienced no major issues and maintained a solid FPS of 60 with most settings maxed. There were some dips here and there but they were brief, and it never went below 40 fps.
The mouse sensitivity is a little high (my mouse's inherent DPI is set to 800) so you're gonna want to reduce it quite a bit in-game. Some users have reported Mouse Acceleration, however I experienced no such thing.
Hint: Disabled MSAA and go with Temporal AA. I believe MSAA is disabled by default when you first start the game.
Besides that there's nothing really to say. For a console -> PC port this is a pretty smooth experience. My favorite bit is that for users with Chroma keyboards, the game has inherent settings built in for your keyboard colors. Loading screens have the keyboard doing a cycled wave of gold color. Very nice touch.
As far as story goes, it's relatively uninspired and very 'safe.' You assume the role of Adam Jensen again, 2 years after the events of Human Revolution. The golden age of human augmentation has come to an abrupt halt in light of the 'Aug Incident,' when millions of augs (augmented humans) went rampant and killed naturals (humans without augs). Mankind Divided's backdrop essentially captures the growing tension between augs and naturals. This is reflected in the environment where you'll see augs getting bullied by zealous police.
You essentially run around trying to stop an Augmentation Right's Group from committing a major terrorist attack. It's a fairly standard story, but the biggest issue is that it sort of just ends suddenly after a relatively anti-climactic boss fight. It gives credence to Jim Sterling's original report from January that detailed the possibility that the bean counting suits/upper management at Square Enix HQ had requested the game be spliced up into several parts.
This becomes massively transparent during the game where they hint at certain locations, specifically Tai Yong Medical corporation which has a laboratory in San Francisco.
Finally, the game only has a single hub this time around (Prague), however the city is massive and very well-detailed. There are a lot of apartments/open interiors that you may enter and explore for items and loot. The sheer openness of the city also allows for the side-quests to have a more open nature to them (i.e. you can use the environment of the city to achieve objectives differently). You'll still visit various areas like a Ghetto on the outskirts of prague called Golem City, a place where augs are deported to. You'll also visit the Swiss Alps *very* briefly for a quest.
I find the gameplay to be a step above Human Revolution. The cover to cover mechanic has been improved greatly and is far more fluid than before. Gunplay, stealth, etc, all feel very satisfying. There are a few new augments that have been added, but for the most part you don't really need them. You can easily complete the game using the tried and true augments.
There's a new crafting system which lets you create your own items such as Mine templates, biocells (your energy source for augments), and multi-tools (yes they've returned). Multi-tools are my personal favorite because they allow you to quickly hack through computers/keypads when you're in a hurry and need to sneak by a guard patrol. Definitely a great addition to the game.
There are a few choices you can make in the game, however they aren't that impactful. The last mission, for example, had you choose between
The strange thing about that segment is that I was able to save all the parties involved, so my choice ended up not being all that important. It could have also been the order in which I chose to do it.
Lastly, the alternative routes/sneaky gameplay we've all come to admire in the Deus Ex franchise is intact in Mankind Divided. There are tons of routes/methods to completing a particular objective. I also recommend that player's get the CASIE augment very early on. It will help them out in a lot of situations.

The one thing that stood out to me with this game was how much better the user interface was. Everything is a lot more seamless, and icons/notifications are much more reactive/contextual to the player's actions. A huge step up from Human Revolution.
The big thing Human Revolution players will notice going into Mankind Divided is the major shift in tone and color. Human Revolution had a black/gold filter which helped establish one thing: The augment renaissance (gold). Mankind Divided has mostly dialed back the color palette and gone with more natural colors. I feel that this was largely done to serve as a visual cue to the player that the renaissance era of augments was over - and it most certainly was.
The gold/black filter does return, surprisingly enough, during the very last mission (which takes place at night). This is also another reason why the Gold/Black filter worked so well in Human Revolution. The game took place mostly at night, and so you had a natural build up of yellows/golds from street lights constrasted against the black night sky.

Mankind Divided is a *good* game. There are still some areas that can be improved, but as a sequel to Human Revolution and a continuation of Adam Jensen's story arc, I have to say that I am overall very pleased with it. If you can look past the DLC model and look at the game itself, I know for a fact that you'll probably enjoy it as much as I did.

Holdfast: Nations At War is an early access game with a lot of potential. The game feels like a graphically superior, albeit functionally inferior (for now) version of Mount & Blade: Napoleonic Wars.
Pros
- Great naval battles
- Pretty good graphics (In comparison to Napoleonic Wars at least)
- Fairly good gunplay
- Excellent community
Cons
- The melee system at this stage of the game is quite frankly, horrible. It needs serious work and I'm hopeful that being an early access game the issue will be fixed. For now, hitboxes are completely broken and melee is almost always determined by luck or internet connection.
- Sound design could use some work
- Some slight server lag issues
Overall I would recommend the game but just keep in mind that it isn't flawless and still has a lot of work to be done to make it into the game that many of us want it to be. If you can deal with a few issues then go ahead and buy it to support the devs in building upon what is a promising foundation of a game.

A blast from the past of PC FPS games, including all the previous glitches and annoances, but overall, a decent game.

There's a lot of firefights, but there are also a lot of avoiding obsticals and making perfect timed jumps.   It never gets to the point where it's too ridiculous to get past, if you keep trying you can beat the more difficult parts.   Ammo on your primary guns is unlimited, the only weapons that are limited are the rocket launches and other various weapons that you can pick up randomly throughout the game.  The graphics are decent, but by no means are amazing or stunning.   I like the gameplay, has a very retroish PC FPS feeling.   It is very unfortunate that the game does not have co-op multiplayer.
The problem I have with this game, is they have also brought back oldschool FPS PC gaming problems.   Sometimes when I use the quicksave and reload it, the game crashes.   Somehow the game corrupts its own quick save files randomly, no big deal though, you can still restart at the beginning of the level.   The framerate will randomly glitch and drop on you, but it’s not game breaking, and it doesn’t happen often.
Overall this game is definitely worth what they are asking for it.  Anyone who likes the oldschool days of FPS shooters should definitely pick this title up.

If you're wondering what this game plays like, it's essentially a space sim with large battles. Add in RPG, 4x, and roster management elements (Darkest Dungeon). In fact, Civilization has a lot in common with this game, despite M&B not being a "pure stretegy" game.
Combat feels clunky in the beginning, but once you watch some videos and understand the mechanics, there is a very high skill ceiling. Combat is also essentially optional in the singleplayer campaign with so many soldiers to fight for you. While graphics feel dated, they hold up well and mods improve them. Many mechanics are deceptively simple; a dynamic world economy controls prices and prosperity in towns.
Mods, while not part of the base game, are much more than reskins; they add hours of gameplay and depth. The mods in the Workshop are probably only 1/6 of the total available mod content on other websites. Some are Game of Thrones conversions that incorporate well-known storylines and add new locations and items.
Possible caveats:
While there is a wealth of things to do, the game ultimately drives you towards conquering the entire map, which can feel limiting. Conquering everyone is naturally grindy, as well. Mods can alleviate this by adding a lot more variety and depth.

Given that this game came out in the same time frame as Skyrim, causing a cannibilization in sales, I think the base game and story is better than that of Skyrim. That being said, mods put Skyrim leagues above this game.
Aside from that, KO:A is an open world RPG where you can choose most of your own fate and change the fate of those around you based on your decisions. The world in this game is laden with fate and those who can read the strings of fate. You are an abnormality that bends fate to your own will and even use it as a weapon itself.
The game has 3 different combat styles that can greatly differ depending on how you play your character.
-The first is a warrior, the obvious and probably the main combat style for humans. You can go in with a heavy weapon, such as a greatsword for powerful slow swinging attacks. A warhammer to bash your enemies in with brutal force. Finally a longsword for closing the gaps and decent combos against your enemies.
-The second is the mage, and personally my favorite playstyle. The weapons here dont matter as much except to augment the damage of your skills. They consist of short range staffs, medium range chakrams, and long range staves. At higher levels you can summon a rain of fire, a lightning storm, or a condensed blizzard to take out your enemies.
-The last playstyle is that of an assassin. Their weapon set consists of daggers, faeblades, and bows. Short, medium, and long range respectively. The assassin deals mainly with bleeds and poison, causing damage over time and time to set up cunning traps to finish them off.
Each of these paths get their own destinies (unrelated to the storyline) and buffs.
My main complaints with the game is the massive amount of gold fodder for either a house, upgrading your pack, or repairing weapons.
-I also have a problem how this game also tries to copy Diablo a little bit, though does it a bit poorly. As such you have sets in the game that rarely show up, and by the time you get anything more than one piece of the set, you've already out leveled it to the point where the set bonus won't bring it to par. Easily fixed by a shared inventory between characters, but not going to happen.
-Some of the skills and playstyles don't feel viable for progressing either. Though you can become an alchemist or blacksmith, you would spend an immense amount of time trying to progress by taking these paths.
All in all, I think this is a really good game, even after 4 years if it releasing, and I still come back to playing it time and time again, not even always on PC. I would suggest this game for anyone who enjoys open world RPGs.

I really want to like this game. I really, really, really want to like this game.
But.. I can't.
It's got varied and unique game types. This game has not only the standard CTF and Team Deathmatch modes, it also offers a Horde mode, a RACING mode, and a "Lava Survival" mode where you scurry and climb to the very top of a map while keeping your opponents from doing the same, whether that is by shooting the ground out from under them, or shooting them and temporarily turning them into snowmen.
You can create your own maps, weapons, or skins with the built in editor. You can make maps in Minecraft and import them! You can do literally anything with this game. You can even place helicopters in random parts of your map!
However... you won't WANT to do anything with this game. The shooting is very clunky, it's serviceable but not something you'll crave and want to come back to. When you die, you get shuffled to a killscreen with no notification. You are often killed instantly with ZERO feedback on what or who killed you 99% of the time. You hear no gunshot or explosion and just instantly get kicked to the kill cam to watch your opponent and see where he was for two seconds. Then you spawn and hope that doesn't happen again.
The driving mechanics are also very poorly done, and take quite some time to get the hang of- and even then, they're not something you want to use often.
For all the hate Ace of Spades gets, at least it makes shooting fun. This game falls flat on the very basics and doesn't do anything very well, outside of letting you make some great maps. Then again, Minecraft serves that purpose much better.
I'm not going to recommend anyone buy this. Watch some gameplay on YouTube, get a feel for how bad the game was crafted [lol.] At the same time, I'm always going to come back and try to give it another chance. I love the idea and even though I know it's not going to improve, I still have some dumb blind hope that I'll actually have fun with this someday.

This game is being metabombed because of Square Enix's shady DLC model. Essentially, the minor DLC (like the Assault Pack or the Praxis Kits) are one time use only. You access your inventory in game, and you transfer the item from the storage tab into your inventory. If you lose the save it's gone, and if you start a new game the content is gone.
I wish to separate the review of the physical, final product from the DLC/Store content which, IMO, is optional and not required in any way whatsoever. Yes, the model is shady and deplorable behavior by Square Enix, however, the actual game itself is a very good and enjoyable experience.
If you love the franchise but are hesitant about the DLC model, purchase the game and avoid the store entirely. Square Enix (if they're smart) differentiates between micro-transaction sales and physical/digital game copy sales. Vote with your wallet against the store and not the game.

For starters, my PC is extremely powerful, so your mileage may vary. Under the hood I have 2 980 Tis, an i7 4970k processor, and 32 gbs of RAM. It's probably overkill for this game, because I experienced no major issues and maintained a solid FPS of 60 with most settings maxed. There were some dips here and there but they were brief, and it never went below 40 fps.
The mouse sensitivity is a little high (my mouse's inherent DPI is set to 800) so you're gonna want to reduce it quite a bit in-game. Some users have reported Mouse Acceleration, however I experienced no such thing.
Hint: Disabled MSAA and go with Temporal AA. I believe MSAA is disabled by default when you first start the game.
Besides that there's nothing really to say. For a console -> PC port this is a pretty smooth experience. My favorite bit is that for users with Chroma keyboards, the game has inherent settings built in for your keyboard colors. Loading screens have the keyboard doing a cycled wave of gold color. Very nice touch.
As far as story goes, it's relatively uninspired and very 'safe.' You assume the role of Adam Jensen again, 2 years after the events of Human Revolution. The golden age of human augmentation has come to an abrupt halt in light of the 'Aug Incident,' when millions of augs (augmented humans) went rampant and killed naturals (humans without augs). Mankind Divided's backdrop essentially captures the growing tension between augs and naturals. This is reflected in the environment where you'll see augs getting bullied by zealous police.
You essentially run around trying to stop an Augmentation Right's Group from committing a major terrorist attack. It's a fairly standard story, but the biggest issue is that it sort of just ends suddenly after a relatively anti-climactic boss fight. It gives credence to Jim Sterling's original report from January that detailed the possibility that the bean counting suits/upper management at Square Enix HQ had requested the game be spliced up into several parts.
This becomes massively transparent during the game where they hint at certain locations, specifically Tai Yong Medical corporation which has a laboratory in San Francisco.
Finally, the game only has a single hub this time around (Prague), however the city is massive and very well-detailed. There are a lot of apartments/open interiors that you may enter and explore for items and loot. The sheer openness of the city also allows for the side-quests to have a more open nature to them (i.e. you can use the environment of the city to achieve objectives differently). You'll still visit various areas like a Ghetto on the outskirts of prague called Golem City, a place where augs are deported to. You'll also visit the Swiss Alps *very* briefly for a quest.
I find the gameplay to be a step above Human Revolution. The cover to cover mechanic has been improved greatly and is far more fluid than before. Gunplay, stealth, etc, all feel very satisfying. There are a few new augments that have been added, but for the most part you don't really need them. You can easily complete the game using the tried and true augments.
There's a new crafting system which lets you create your own items such as Mine templates, biocells (your energy source for augments), and multi-tools (yes they've returned). Multi-tools are my personal favorite because they allow you to quickly hack through computers/keypads when you're in a hurry and need to sneak by a guard patrol. Definitely a great addition to the game.
There are a few choices you can make in the game, however they aren't that impactful. The last mission, for example, had you choose between
The strange thing about that segment is that I was able to save all the parties involved, so my choice ended up not being all that important. It could have also been the order in which I chose to do it.
Lastly, the alternative routes/sneaky gameplay we've all come to admire in the Deus Ex franchise is intact in Mankind Divided. There are tons of routes/methods to completing a particular objective. I also recommend that player's get the CASIE augment very early on. It will help them out in a lot of situations.

The one thing that stood out to me with this game was how much better the user interface was. Everything is a lot more seamless, and icons/notifications are much more reactive/contextual to the player's actions. A huge step up from Human Revolution.
The big thing Human Revolution players will notice going into Mankind Divided is the major shift in tone and color. Human Revolution had a black/gold filter which helped establish one thing: The augment renaissance (gold). Mankind Divided has mostly dialed back the color palette and gone with more natural colors. I feel that this was largely done to serve as a visual cue to the player that the renaissance era of augments was over - and it most certainly was.
The gold/black filter does return, surprisingly enough, during the very last mission (which takes place at night). This is also another reason why the Gold/Black filter worked so well in Human Revolution. The game took place mostly at night, and so you had a natural build up of yellows/golds from street lights constrasted against the black night sky.

Mankind Divided is a *good* game. There are still some areas that can be improved, but as a sequel to Human Revolution and a continuation of Adam Jensen's story arc, I have to say that I am overall very pleased with it. If you can look past the DLC model and look at the game itself, I know for a fact that you'll probably enjoy it as much as I did.

This is a new re-write of this review; up to date with the "full release" of the game. Keep in mind I've had this since it greenlighted last year.
The good news is that the playable characters are now much closer to their original appearance; that is to say, team RWBY actually look like team RWBY now. They're just a hair away from being back to their original 1:1 to the show, so there's that. The faces are vastly improved from the god-awful Forever Fall update models.
Speaking of Forever Fall, those levels are buggy as all hell. I've got an above-average computer; I play most games on their highest settings with steady fps, so the fact that Forever Fall stutters pretty noticeably makes me think it's the game and not my comp. But whatever, it's playable. Ugly and un-fun, but playable.
Weiss is my favorite in-game and in-show, so I'm also glad they removed a lot of her stupid "grunting" sounds she used to make while attacking. It was dumb, but it's gone now.
The combat is okay, gameplay overall is rather bland and very, very repetitive. I will say that it's pretty fun to play this along with loud music while you're intoxicated, so if you're a RWBY fan and you're looking for a game to♥♥♥♥♥♥away ~2 hours and a blunt with, this is okay. Not great, not even really good, just okay. This is "meh" material at its most mediocre.
Or it WAS okay, but I wouldn't recommend this at it's current price. I bought it for $15 back in EA, and I've gotten quite a few hours out of it so I don't feel jibbed, but I wouldn't pay $25. Wait for a sale.

I became a PC gamer because of the beauty of the open platform, and to get the best experience out of my games; not to be told from a company what I can and can't do with the games I purchase. I love Grand theft Auto V, but I will not support a company no more if they continue these anti consumer practices. Rockstar is gonna learn the hard way you can't control us PC gamers.

First of all, my recommendation of the game is based purely on the fact that I love the series and I think as fans we should support this game to see it reach its full potential, much like the show itself has. Also I will admit that some issues I have may be chalked up to playing the game on a laptop, and may not be shared by other players.
Okay, so...
*First, the game takes FOREVER to properly load. Often I have a window popping up stating that the program isn't responding at all. The screen goes black, then white, then the window pops up, then my desktop pops back up and the game icon has disappeared, then FINALLY Ruby's voice and the Rooster Teeth logo pops up. It's quite annoying when I just want to play the game.
*The character models look like cheap facsimiles of the actual characters from the show. This is perplexing after reading earlier reviews that state the characters looked exactly like their show counterparts, which is what I would have expected.
*On the character models, their movement animations need work. They are far from fluid, if anything they seem laggy. And this is on the single player mode(more on that later). The jumping animation looks to be two or three frames total, where the running and attacking animations seem rushed and missing quite a few frames. Fleshing these out might make for a more visually appealing experience. Also, jumping should be a little higher than the slight hop that we're given. Just to make it a bit more useful.
*Expanding the upgrade tree will definitely help the game, as it is there's little to actually invest points in that would really be useful. I found the level 5 survivor upgrade and the extra ultimate pool to be the only things worth upgrading.
*The HUD is a little bland, to be honest. I remember playing an alpha of the game as a RT sponsor and the HUD there was much better. Moving the Aura and Ultimate gauge to the upper left will be helpful, as you don't have to look out of your way to see your own stats.
*I would say more game modes are sorely needed, but this is early access. I fully expect them to come anyway. Horde mode will be a nice addition when fully implemented, but another kind of challenge mode would also be nice. Maybe a Vytal Tournament mode, where you fight against other students or huntsman/huntresses?
*For single player, I would strongly recommend working in AI teammates. As it was for me, playing just as Ruby or Yang, that first set of waves of Grimm took me way too many tries. This isn't Dark Souls, it's RWBY. This also allows for team banter as you explore the environment, which is one thing I'd expect in a game about the titular team.
*More playable characters is a necessity, I feel. I mean, I love Team RWBY, but I'd also love to play as Pyrrha or Nora. If villains were considered, I'd pay extra just to play as Neo.
*MORE COLLECTIBLES. MORE INCENTIVE TO EXPLORE.
*This one is more than likely because of my laptop and/or internet connection, but multiplayer was practically unplayable for me. Lag on lag on lag. I think the game dropped to 2 or 3 frames per second. Again, could just be me. Take this one with a grain of salt, unless other people are complaining of it as well.
*FOR THE LOVE OF ALL THAT IS HOLY, PUT IN A LOCK ON FEATURE.
All of that aside, this game does have potential. The combat is fun and engaging, it reminds me of the Arkham games and Dynasty Warriors. It's incredibly unpolished and in need of some work, but that's the point of early access. I've certainly spent 20 bucks on worse things. I want to see this game grow and reach the potential it has, so if Rooster Teeth is taking our suggestions, these are mine. I'll be keeping an eye on the game going forward.

Being a PC game that's the better half of two decades old, my immediate first impression of Thief was that it was very old and very dated. Graphically speaking, it's nothing an N64 couldn't handle, sound-wise, it feels like someone opened a can of stock "swoosh" sound effects, and after playing it only for a few minutes, I found myself very disappointed indeed. It seemed very bare-bones from the tutorial. There's not even a run button, and the controls are laid out pretty awkwardly. Overall it's hard to jump right in, but then I started to break the surface tension and I realized that underneat the surface of the water was... was a metaphor I'm putting way too much effort into.
As it happens, a lot of what makes Thief old is what makes it good. I think this is best exemplified in the map system, chiefly because it's actually a freaking map. Most games don't give you maps nowadays, they give you radars and blip points and arrows and "go-here-if-you-want-to-win"-type things. It makes everything feel very soulless; Thief manages to get around this by giving you the bare minimum. It's pretty neat how this is actually how you would imagine Garrett would put a map together. The game gives you the tools to progression, and you have to interpret them. You never quite know what's going to be around the corner. It's a much better approach than "oh, please, chauffer me to the nearest mundane objective so I can move into your next playground and do the same thing all over again." Cough, Hitman Absolution, cough.
The amount of effort that has gone into the levels is very nice; it's easy to immerse yourself into the world. You're given a few details and have to fill in the pieces. Sure, it's dated, but at the end of the day it's a hell of a lot better than almost every stealth game released since... since 1971. Yes, I dare say this game is better than Tennis for Two. Couple that with a fantastically snarky protagonist and a nifty steampunk setting and you're left with a stealth game done the way it should be. This game makes Hitman Absolution cry. Get it.

If you are considering trying a stealth game, I would highly recommend any of the original Thief games. The series is credited with being one of the most influential upon the stealth game genre, and rightly so.
Unlike most first person games, Thief doesn't give you powerful weapons or superhuman abilities. You feel
. Seeing a guard frightens you; your heart skips a beat when you hear footsteps behind a closed door. And this tension - the knowledge that making a mistake can alert others to your presence or even get you killed - is precisely the appeal of the game. Don't think you can just overpower the guards and carry on, either. You may be able to kill one guard without dying, but you'll probably take a lot of damage in the process, and there's no health regeneration. But, good lord - pulling off a successful heist without being detected is
The level design is fantastic. The environments range from city streets to ancient ruins to haunted chapels to demonic realms. Seriously. And most levels are very large, so you won't be left hungry for places to explore. You don't have a compass, marker or radar to help you navigate, so you will have to rely on a map and your ordination skills. Some may disagree with me, but I feel this adds immersion that is absent from most modern titles. You need to look around and "get a feel" for an area - as you would in the real world when going somewhere for the first time. Learning the patrol routes of guards is vital to avoiding them, and you need to factor in environmental elements such as lighting, noisy floors, obstacles, water and more when planning your route.
To survive this harsh world, you have a wide variety of tools at your disposal (think of a larcenous form of Link, only better). You have a blackjack to knock enemies out without killing them, and a short sword for... well, you can guess. Lockpicks can be used to, err, pick locks, but the process takes time - time in which a guard may happen upon your cloaked figure hunched over the chest or door handle. The bow can shoot arrows of which there are many different types: broadheads for shooting things in the head, water arrows for extinguishing fire, rope arrows that function like a grappling hook for reaching high areas...
There are few criticisms I can make of this game. The graphics are dated, so if that really bothers you then you may wish to pass up on this title. I personally have no issue with this. Sometimes the player character (Garrett) can have difficulty traversing poor terrain geometry, with results that are more irritating than entertaining. Some game mechanics are inconsistent and may cause confusion for new players if they don't go out of their way to learn them thoroughly. For instance, fire and gas arrows travel in a straight line or some reason, whereas all other arrows follow a parabolic trajectory (affected by gravity). That said, none of these spoiled the experience for me - they were just occasionally a little annoying. And lastly, some levels involve the undead (yes, there are zombies...), which cannot be killed like normal guards. If you are not prepared to just run from your enemies, then these levels can become walls until you are skilled or lucky enough to overpower them. I'm just saying - this is a game about sneaking, not killing.
To summarise, Thief is an excellent introduction to the stealth game genre (if you can overlook the dated graphics). Its mechanics are well-balanced and interesting, and its open level design allows you to approach a problem in many different ways. There are plenty of secrets to find, and the varied environments are always refreshing. The lack of information in the form of objective markers or a radar forces the player to pay attention - listening is as important as, if not more than, looking - and with this comes incredible immersion. Or course, some players may be put off by this if they lack the patience to plan their approach to a situation, and sneaking past hordes of the undead isn't as fun as it sounds. But if you can step back from modern action games, if you can try different things when your attempts to sneak past enemies keeps failing, then you will find this game immensely enjoyable (and get a real adrenaline kick when things work out perfectly!) Thief is a game of sneaking and planning, and if you can do these then you find much enjoyment.
Just play it. It's quite tough, but you will like it.

An absolute classic.
Thief: The Dark Project was one of the first games which spawned the stealth genre as we know it today, along with Metal Gear Solid and Tenchu, and still holds its place as among the best games the genre has ever produced. Thief: Gold is effectively the "Game of the Year" edition which includes two extra maps (which admittedly are among the weaker ones in the games). In the game, you play as Garret, a master thief who contains a jewel which notes his visibility at all times, and you use it and your other skills (specialty arrows and especially listening skills) to sneak your way through levels pilfering everything along the way. It is played from a first-person perspective, so there's no means to be able to see around corners, which leads to a claustrophobic experience and requires patience to move forwards, listening carefully for what might be ahead.
I poured an enormous number of hours into this game and its sequel when I was younger (prior to Steam), and had replayed them relatively recently - while the graphics have certainly aged, the atmosphere and gameplay have not, and they're well worth checking out. The mod community has put out a wise variety of patches to help those on modern systems play teh games, and the sequel has an entire new "sequel" campaign that was made for it.
I cannot recommend this game enough.

It simply amazes me in this day an age, how people manage to screw up a simple reboot. You already have a fantastic, well respected and loved title, which that lone puts you 50% of the way to your goal, all you need to do now is to include what made that title good, and improve on what wasn't so good. A very simple concept.
However, Rise of the Triad misses this mark by a country mile, and for some reason the development team decided to follow the exact opposite of the formula I listed above. Allow me to explain...
Rise of the Triad was one of those game released on PC in the early 90s, when the home computer field discovered it wasn't going to suffer the same ♥♥♥♥♥♥ inspection as Consoles like Sega and Nintendo were getting over their subject material. It came along the same vein as Blood, Doom 2, and a host of clones such as Dark Forces, when FPS was the name of the game in PC titles. Having an adjustable violence setting was RotT's selling point, saying it was fit for play by children on one end, and chew your enemies into hamburger on the other. But what set it apart from the other titles of the time, was it's bizarre game modes, weapons, and power ups. Made my Apogee who was already worth it's weight in gold by that time, it got a dedicated following while still remaining a cult title for years. The game play was mostly solid, though it did lend itself to a lot of gimmicks like floating platforms and trampolines that shot you around the level which sometimes didn't work as well as it could. However, it made up for this with a menagerie of strange ways to dispatch your foes, including a "God Mode" that didn't just make you invincible, but enabled you to smite people with a touch.
The reboot manages to remake this title, with absolutely none of the charm of the original, and compounds the broken gimmicks of the first, even adding a few new ones of it's own.
For starters, this games graphical requirements are outrageous. On par with Painkiller Hell and Damnation, this game uses an insane amount of PC power for a game that really doesn't need it. The backgrounds are rather dull, and the character models aren't anything to write home about, so I'm befuddled at the disregard for any kind of resource streamlining. This game also uses motion blur that does more to make you sea sick than enhance game play by any means, and until recently wasn't possible to toggle off.
Secondly, the dialog, flavor text, descriptions, and spoken parts are horribly dated. Riddled with the worst in 90's humor, the game gives you the feeling they went back to 1996 and drafted the dialog writers of Duke Nukem 3D. "All around bad♥♥♥♥♥" is not a clever description of a character in 2014.The enemies resemble WWII German solders and Occupied Berlin guards, once again reinforcing the idea that it's okay to kill in unspeakable ways, so long as the people resemble Germans.
Lastly, you will die.... a lot. Not because the game is actually difficult, but because the the aiming mechanic for the enemies is hopelessly broken. I am conflicted which way to go with this review.
The fighting is great, the online is great. In terms of compeditive Tekken play this is one of the best experiences yet...
But that all comes at the cost of EVERYTHING else that we've come to love about Tekken over the years.
The Story mode is pretty good... it's kind of like an interactive movie inturrupted with fights. I actually really enjoyed the bombastic experience there.
Everything else is a ♥♥♥♥♥how however.
Charachter customization is really generic, and almost all the items are universal (and ugly).
Treasure Battle is incessantly grindy to even unlock the phoned in customization items. As you unlock more and more stuff you start winning fight money more often than unlocking the last remaining objects.
(and objects are unlocked completely at random)
Fight money itself is entirely worthless, unless you have tekken bowl. It's incredibly easy to obtain, and there's not much to spend it on.
The DLC is really dissapointing as well... Basically you get tekken bowl... with no online mode and no custom costumes... and like 2 bikinis, only 1 of which looks good.
Even practice mode is a♥♥♥♥♥♥show with a lot of really poorly described moves in the moveslist, and an extremely clunky interface (especially if you are using a fight-stick)
Whatever you do, don't buy the season's pass or the delux edition. All there is to this game is the compeditive play and local play.
On top of everything else, a number of fan-favorite charachters have been removed and their replacements are questionable at best.
I.e. Lee Wulong is mysteriously absent... but Panda and Kuma are now split into 2 different charachters... with virtually identical moveslists.
Mokujin is gone entirely with no equivalent replacement
The list goes on, it's not worth nitpicking here.
One thing I really have to complain about relates to the actual customization system used here. On top of limited (& mostly shared objects) to choose from... objects are equiped in very rigid categories, many of which are incompatible.
For example:
Steve has over-sized boxing gloves as a customization object. But choosing this means he can't wear a shirt, since there is no "hands" category. Oversized boxing gloves w/ no shirt is the only option you have. On top of this, full body costumes like the Fundoshi (actually the only full body costume for Male charachters) is incompatible with the gloves etc.
There are many issues like this... such as hats. Want custom hair color? Well you can't wear a hat then.
I almost want to give a thumbs down for the bad customization is my point. It's really bad. Generally there's only a few decent outfits you can make (excluding 'alternate costumes' which you can buy with fight money after grinding to unlock their individual parts), and there's very little besides 'alternate costumes' that's unique to any charachter.
Customization parts for Kuma and Panda are virtually nonexistant
As I said... I have incredibly mixed feelings about this title.
Pros:
Compeditive play is as the best it has ever been
Cons:
Compeditive play is about all there is to this game
Missing fan-favorite fighters
Lackluster charachter customization
Unlocking customization parts is a ♥♥♥♥ING NIGHTMARE
etc.
etc.
etc.
Basically you should only buy this if you are a serious Tekken player. You aren't going to have much fun single player or casual.

is a puzzle and exploration game that's rough around the edges, but worth it for the journey.
The player takes control of the eponymous brothers on an adventure to save their ailing father from his illness. There's a linear path to follow to reach the goal, but from that path is the occasional branch that allows the player to interact with the brothers' world. There are benches that dot the landscape, allowing the player to view the scenery, and perhaps grab a screenshot.
It's no wonder. The art style, and fantastical events, lend to the feeling of a fable being brought to life. This is aided by the strange and new sights the brothers encounter, and the dangers they face. That's not to say only the young could appreciate this game; beneath its colorful and wondrous surface reside themes of grief, loss, death, struggle, and fear.
The control scheme is simple, and it needs to be. It's no misnomer that both characters are controlled at once; the older brother is maneuvered on one side, and the little brother on the other. Therein lies much of the challenge of the game, as puzzles and progression blockers will often require the player to divide their attention between the two concurrently. One can play with mouse and keyboard, but the game was designed with the controller in mind (as the game page explicitly recommends).
The sound design works in the game's favor. The people in the world speak in a “Simlish” style language, which actually lines up with the rest of the game's fantasy feel. Music kicks in at just the right moments at vibrant quality, and the ambiance plays unobtrusively with a quiet melody when not otherwise engaged.
Not all of the game is a grand adventure, though.
really could have used more polish, and it actually felt, at times, like the game didn't want to be finished. This shows when one of the characters jitters or does Cirque du Soleil-worthy mid-air stunts before teleporting themselves to the surface the player's jumped to. Physics checks often get confused with moving parts, meaning the player can
the gap between two objects, but can't pass through it. Three bugs in particular are worthy of note. The first where a grab cue never manifested. Another where a bridge triggered as being secure, but still had the physics of being in motion. Both required a quit to the main menu to rectify. Finally, a moment in which the game glitched the characters into a building they'd yet to enter, queued the next cutscene, and then check-pointed in the midst of it, rendering the current checkpoint useless, and requiring a restart of that particular chapter over again.
The camera is a fickle mistress. At times, it's a great guide, gently nudging the player in the direction that's navigable. At others, it will swing so that something is between the player's line of site and the brothers, or zoom so close the correct path seems absent. This problem is lessened by the brothers getting colored outlines through solid objects, but it can still be murky if the player is near something hazardous.
All told, I recommend
. It may not be spotless, but if you're looking for an emotional, charming narrative with some simple, but fairly involved puzzles, this is certainly worth your time.

Mortal Kombat X on PC during launch was a mess! This game at one point had the most negative reviews I've seen due to a craptacular port. Overtime the game got better with updates, but it still left a stench of mediocrity. As someone who purchased the game at launch, and plowed through the game as much as I could at the time I could never recommend the game.
After a couple of a months later NetherRealm Studios had said they weren't going to continue updating the PC version of the game, and it left a really bad taste in MK community. We were all pretty salty, and to be honest I still believe we had every right to be as upset as we were. The game still wasn't that great of a port, and in our eyes we believed that the PC Port was abandoned.
Come recently a little after Injustice 2 was announced the community of MKX were teased of MKXL to be released onto PC. Months after being teased we were given a Beta, and it provided us new hope! Finally, after months of waiting NetherRealm returned to their senses, and we were given the update that both the Playstation 4 and Xbox One had for what seemed like a lifetime!
We finally have what we've been pleaing to receive - Mortal Kombat XL! Surprisingly, it's the best PC Port that Warner Bros. has had to offer! Could the optimization be better? Absolutely! But, for what this community has gone through, we'll take baby steps from Warner Bros. and NetherRealm to get the game functioning to the best of its abilities.
Mortal Kombat XL is a huge balance patch essentially, and it fixes some of the characters, settings, and best of all the netcode! You're actually able to play the game without much lag. The servers are incredible, and most of the time you don't have to wait for a match.
Can I possibly recommend this game at it's current state? Absolutely! I'm hoping the PC community returns back to game as it had been dead for quite some time. I don't remember combos, the bread and butter, and who I mained in the game. Overtime I'll get back into my groove, but until then - you should ALL get the game! Who knows? This might lead to Injustice 2 to come onto PC?

We will start this review by focusing on the Land Combat portion of Holdfast, and as you will discover, my opinion is about this game is about as Jekyll and Hyde as the game's opinion of itself is.
So...land combat...what can be said except...yuck.
Everything else is either dumbed down or non-functioning here. Of course we still have no cavalry due to this phase in development, but Artillery is no longer a team effort to man, and the cannons are just static objects randomly placed around the battlefield (Perhaps this will change). Everything from movement to shooting to ESPECIALLY melee feels clunky.
Melee is about next to useless, I prefer War of Rights melee at this point, and it's literally just a place holder. I think Holdfast's melee irritates me MORE, because it FEELS like a finished melee system that just doesn't vaguely work, whereas War of Rights feels like a place holder, but it's a place holder that WORKS so you sort of ignore it.
Going back to War of Rights, I think it's fair to spend the rest of the review comparing War of Rights to Holdfast, as both games are in Alpha and both games are representing the same type of warfare.
Holdfast is essentially (SOMEHOW) an arcadey representation of  blackpowder warfare, however it suffers from trying to do too much. There are a slew of units to select from, but what they do and how they function aren't clearly laid out. You have everything from line infantry to freaking carpenters...some of the units feel different, but most just feel like the same same with different clothes.  The game looks pretty, but doesn't offer anything more than it's predecessor. In fact, the most I can ever see Holdfast being is a prettier version of Napoleonic Wars for Mount and Blade II, with about 1/2 the enjoyment...because now you had to spent $20 on a graphics update...EA pulls that♥♥♥♥♥♥ it's highway robbery, but someone plops that infront of the NW community, and they are gods...I said it once, and I will say it again:
"If you are on the outside looking in, take all positive reviews from the community with a grain of salt. If someone developed a Napoleonic ASCII game, the NW community would have 100 regiments reserved for it in 24 hours, and already be calling it GOTY"
But when compared to War of Rights, this game does not hold up, at least to me. War of Rights feels like it has more heart into it. Everything has a rhyme or reason, from how the characters move, to how a certain animation works. It's obviously more realistic, in everything from how it looks to how it plays. War of Rights is the Black Powder era's ARMA, to Holdfast's Call of Duty.  If itwas just the land combat, I would want a refund....but...a saviour rolls in....
And it's name is Naval Warfare!
And here is where the review does a full 180, naval warfare in this game is a hoot! It's like a LESS arcadey Blackwake. You have multiple ship types to crew with multiple types of weapons, again, the roles make little sense, and some of them don't work, but unlike land combat, you just don't care because the whole process is so goddamned fun.
I think Holdfast would do better to just ignore anything that doesn't have a ship in it. And this seriously goes back to the concept of a game trying to do too many things at once....I am not saying that to be a smartass, I am saying, the land combat is so underwhelming and bland and just...terrible, but the naval combat is so good, that at this point if they decided to entirely scrap the land combat portion of the game, and focus on the naval combat, it might very well be one of the most entertaining games I have ever played.
But again, the land battles are just an albatross hanging around this game's neck.
So in summary:
Do I recommend it? No, not yet. As much as I want to because of Naval Warfare badassery, I can honestly say I am a little disappointed I spent $20 on the early access of this game. If you are outside of the NW community, and not instantly going into convulsive fits because I didn't suggest you run out and grab this now, just wait. It might be okay eventually, but really...it's marketing to a niche, it knows it will have that niche no matter what, so don't expect it to do anything too spectacular.

People need to understand that we pay for early access so devs recieve money to fund their game- that is the entire point of early access. It's good to know that they're using the money well, and I hope to see their dev team expand.
On to the review. This game is pretty much the same as NW-Warband with the addition of enjoyable naval battles, naval sieges, better graphics and character animations. That isn't a bad thing, as Napoleonic Wars was perfect in its' own way, it's great to see a game that was left barren by the community be revived in Holdfast. I rejoined a regiment I left almost 3 years ago, and have been addicted to it since release.
The problem is; this game will not survive under nostalgia. I seriously do hope that they can add far more than their planned tornuments, maybe in the far future, a coop campaign to play in all of Napoleons battles with your regiment and to fight against large AI armies could be a promising change of pace for those who don't always want a loose multiplayer experience and might want a fun campaign in their with characters. And should Holdfast be stuck in the Napoleonic wars? I don't think so, why not move this into multiple eras and fronts. The War of 1812, the American Revolution, the American Civil War, the 7 years war and so on. I'm sure once mods are enabled, people will attempt these anyway- but why not include them into the base game? Of course, this is all far out of the minds of the devs who are just trying to build upon the base game. Though I hope they read this and consider the massive possibilities of creating a huge game that people will come back to for years. I would not want to see this game fade like NW.
Anyway, this is just my first review. Once the devs move this into beta, I'll make a final opinion on it. I recommend this ONLY IF you are willing to push through expected bugs from an early access game. These guys aren't AAA, they are a small team and have done a great job so far and are already active in fixing bugs. Buy at your own risk. If you aren't an NW player, then you may feel less inclined to play this until it has more content.

This was a gamechanger, in my opinion. Elements from the original Thief would be incorporated in countless games over the coming years. To this day, this title, to me, is one of the most influential games of all time.
The plot is unique but takes a few missions to set up. Most of the graphics are on par for the year - nothing special with the exception of the lighting. The game heavily focuses on environments - the light around you, the floors you walk on, the noise of the actions you make. Sound is beautiful in this game - surround sound is a MUST so look into OpenAL or fixes for Creative Alchemy if you need to. Combat is straight forward. The gameplay itself, played as its meant to be played, is strictly about avoiding conflict and remaining undetected. When combat is mandatory, it's usually against nonsentient creatures (undead, magical creatures, etc). Overall, I can recommend this game to -anyone-. It is difficult at times, but it is one of the greatest games of all time.

First, I must assure you that this review is completely free of nostalgia. I never played Thief: Gold (or Thief 2, for that matter) before 2014, and was far too young to play and understand video games when The Dark Project was released. I must also note that I patched the game with TFix, as without it I would be playing a 640x480 600% speed mess designed for a computer from the late 90s. I also installed a texture/lighting mod called HDmod, which was not neccessary but did vastly improve the graphics from their dated, fugly appearance.
With that out of the way, I have been wholly impressed with my first few hours of play. The movement feels surprisingly good (after assigning WASD controls, of course), and the bow and arrow feels realistic (though the arrow flies slowly). The melee weapons aren't perfect, but fit their roles nicley. The sword combat is deep but slow (fine, since combat is discouraged) and the blackjack has a limited range and requires you to stand up. It's slightly awkward to use, but it's satisfying to knock out an unaware guard. The level design so far (on level 2 currently) is perfectly balanced in terms of being difficult to navigate but not so much that you get stumped for hours on end. I like how it presents you with stealth situations that have no apparent solution, challenging you to think of your own clever work-around. The animated cutscenes look surprisingly good, and the story has me curious, especially about the Keepers.
I definitely reccomend it so far. I will update this review as I progress through the game.
EDIT (3/30/2014, 14 hours in): Level design is a bit inconsistent. The "Assassins" mission was an absolute joy to play through, giving you a surprisingly large chunk of the city to sneak through in addition to Ramirez's well-designed mansion. I am unfortunately hitting a bit of a rough patch in the "Guild" mission, which started off great but quickly degraded into possibly the most convoluted labyrinth I've ever seen in a video game. Perhaps the new missions introduced with the Gold edtion should have been optional, or just side missions. The story feels both vague and simplistic, with a little bit of backstory on the Hammerites and Keepers between chronicles of Garret's unrelated (as of now) thieving exploits. I sense it's going to pick up soon, though. Still loving the gameplay, of course. Can't wait to finish Guild and (hopefully) get something a bit easier to navigate!
EDIT (4/11/2015, 30 hours): It should be said that this game has a ridiculous amount of content.There is a good amount of variety as well. Levels with human guards showcase the superb stealth gameplay. Levels with monsters/undead focus are weird, but encourage the player to take an action-stealth approach that is very satisfying. Story has picked up nicely, some very interesting characters have showed up and each mission has a purpose and cool backstory. Despite my 30 hours of game time, I am only a bit more than halfway through the game. Even if I never finish, It's been a fun ride and I'm glad this game hooked me into the phenomenal Thief series.

I really wanted to like this game, and I kind of did. Kind of.. I have fallen in love with story driven games that tries to tell an engaging story over the past years, and games like To The Moon, the Telltale Games, and Life is Strange top my list. I checked this game out after looking some recomendation sections for different other games. I was amazed by the critics given by some highly trustworthy people, like Totalbiscut, and decided to buy the game.
First of, the visuals are incredible. They try to use a cartoonish style in the game, and they succeed. I really liked the touch that they add benches in front of different landmarks that you can sit on to give you an amazing view of the wonderful landscape. They nailed it.
The story, which is why I buy games like this (the visuals don't need to be great, hence To The Moon being on my top list) and Brothers tries very hard to bond us with the two brothers. The characters are speaking in an unknown language (as far as I know) and we can therefore not understand what they are saying, except for their names. What this does to the game is to make it very hard for the developers to give us a deep fundament for how we see our two brothers. They succeed in making some scenes where for example the older brother helps out an old man, while the younger teases him. This shows us how each of the characters behave, and how the older brother have responsibility over the younger. Furhter than that, I feel like the game would have greatly favored voiceacting in a common language. The ending is decent, I myself can very easily cry over both movies and video games, bu I did not cry in Brothers. There was a couple of scenes where I got emotional, but they did not bond me enough to burst out in tears. (SPOILERS!!!)
. (SPOILERS!!!)
The gameplay in this game is utterly awful and boring. You control both brothers via a controller, and after some getting use to it becomes relatively manageable. The game consist of the same "puzzles" over and over again, and they are very simple to do. Jumping and releasing buttons is what you will mostly do, and give your brother boosts to reach a ladder. There was times where I wanted to quit playing because of how boring it was. The visuals do however help to minimize the damage dealt by the awful gameplay. I will however say that the boss battles, if you want to call them that, are actually quite fun to do, but even here the gameplay falls a little short.
All in all, the game was pretty enjoyable, however, (like to the moon) I will not be playing this one again.
