Brutal Legend is a game from an older time before people really knew how to make games well, at least that's what it feels like.  The gameplay in the game is split between a million and one different ways.  There are hack and slash portions, car races, boss battles reminiscent of zelda, car battles, open world exploration, and-- I kid you not-- a large section of the game randomly changes to Real Time Strategy half way through.  This list isn't even comprehensive.
It has no idea what it wants to be, and it doesn't have to focus to make any individual sections very good.  Despite that, it is a fun game.  There is clearly a lot of love put into it, and ADHD on a crack pipe isn't the worst design when all the portions are acceptable, and you always have the excitement of not knowing what is coming next.
There is a strong metal musical aesthetic that the game keeps to, and it ammounts to being extremely creative.  This is coupled with an extremely large liscneced soundtrack to match the theme.  The game feels cohsive in a very creative way outside of the gameplay.  It just doesn't work, the look, feel, and sound are very unique and not somethingn I think I've ever seen before.
The downsides are inherent in the game design.  The further you get, the more frustrating some of the modes are.   The game isn't built to a Real Time Strategy game, but the final battle is a riduclous campagin of building units, capturing and building on zones, and it's taxing beyond the tools they give you.  This feeling pops up again and again like in combat; it isn't well put together.
Overall though, the positives outway the negatives.  A lot of love wnet into this game, so many things are incorporated that you rarely see, and it is ambitious.  It is by no means a perfect game or even a must play, but people looking for something different with a bit of an older feel to it will get a lot out of this game.

Singleplayer: Rise of the Triad is and old school FPS, which means that you will see a lot of fast movement and frantic combat, and it is ROCK HARD. the main problem with the combat is the weapons. The seventh installment of Tekken is the ultimate realization of the series' endlessly deep and rewarding mechanics, but like many recent fighting games, it lacks the content and polish necessary to make a major impact with both noobs and veterans alike.
Tekken 7's mechanics have been slightly streamlined compared to past titles, and although streamlined has become a dirty word to those familiar with fighting games, they haven't been changed at the cost of depth. For example, holding back on the ground now initiates a safe back roll (although still punishable). In the same vein, some new characters have very simple playstyles and inputs that cater to new players, though your favorite Mishima is still just a few hand cramps away. Harada and his goons have really struck a chord offering more game to inexperienced players without anything feeling braindead or overpowered. The new screw system which replaces bound, is simple to understand and helps balance the cast. Additionally, the powercrush system opens up even more depth. Armored moves add a whole new layer of depth in the neutral, and choosing to sacrifice rage for a rage art or super allows a player to make explosive decisions in the clutch. The new slow motion-camera zoom that activates when a player has low health and nearly gets hit makes for unbelievably hype moments, showcasing the complicated three dimensional hitboxes, and clenching anuses worldwide as spectators watch in horror.
With so many amazing improvements to Tekken's gameplay, it's unfortunate how lacking the game is in all other departments compared to previous titles. The particle effects and textures look great in the UE engine, but the dull drab design of the stages (no footprints in the snow?) do them no justice. The netcode isn't bad, although the matchmaking system is quite a barebones mess. There's also an uninteresting and short story mode, strange roster decisions with lots of core characters missing, and a completely garbage customization mode that may as well not exist. Typically, these things aren't to be expected in a fighting game, but when older installments have all of these features and more, it's hard to ignore.
I would absolutely recommend this game to veterans of the series, or anyone looking to challenge themselves. Just understand that if you don't get into difficult online fighting games, you might not get your $60 worth.

Mount & Blade Warband is one of the best strategy - action games I have ever played! I love playing and it maybe is an old game but it never loses its value! I recommend it to people who want massive action on huge battles with huge rpg aspects.

The Good:
Graphics, Music, System, Voice Acting. The quality of presentation overall is incredibly impressive and definitely looks to stay through time. Some CGs seem to have different resolution though and perhaps look poorer than the sprites, so some attention should be paid to that.
EDIT: I forgot to mention the Voice Acting before, but it is top notch Japanese VA. This caters to anime lovers and people who read original Japanese VNs because we personally prefer English text with Japanese VA on a Japanese product. And this one's great!
The Just-Ok:
Characters, Larger Picture. This is obviously a 'starter' route where it seems like the second worst of the worst case scenario (the worst case will be their failure to reveal the truth naturally) has happened. There are probably 3 or 4 more routes to go through before we can achieve the true route, so I'm willing to give it the benefit of the doubt for now. Characters are the same - they're cool, but there's too little screen time to judge exactly how cool they are.
The Bad:
Story, Plot, Possible Unsavory Price Model. On its own, this route is terrible because it doesn't give much insight to almost all of the characters introduced at all. You don't even get to know Reina too much because it has been crisis after crisis from the beginning to the end and the fact is, crisis is not the best way to get to know each other better. Moreover, there are some obviously 'stiched' together parts where it could've been written better, but for the sake of getting to the important bits were carried over quickly.
And of course, the Price Model. If you're going to do 1 release per route, some buyers who didn't kickstart it from the beginning will be very unhappy. It's already priced at $15 after all.
Conclusion:
A gorgeous looking visual novel with the potential to become a shorter, but just as epic version of say, the Baldr Sky Dive series. I'm looking forward to be surprised in a good way.

RWBY: Grimm Eclipse follows closely to the fighting style of the anime series and is a great little pickup for any RWBY fan.
I realize the game is still in early release but these are my thoughts on the game as of now:
Pros:
Great graphics and attention to the game world's detail.
Fast paced action-oriented game that runs very smoothly.
Skill tree as you level up that allows you to choose your own style.
Co-op that allows you play with up to 3 other players and/or friends.
Point system that allows you to compete with said 3 other players and/or friends.
Random hidden  artifacts that you can add to Beacon's collection.
Cons:
Rather repetitive after a few playthroughs.
Skill grinding which can get rather dull, can take a while to unlock.
No level selection, of which there are only 3 levels anyway.
Very little teamwork besides a "MASH YOUR E BUTTON" team attack.
Level 10 cap, but sometimes you don't even hit it, especially multiplayer
Can't adjust game difficulty.
You can't keep track of the artifacts you've found. D:
I'm really hoping that they add on more team-oriented features or difficulty tuning but the game is pretty fun in itself. The game has extremely high potential and I look forward to the polished version of RWBY: Grimm Eclipse
Edit: It would also be cool if they made each of the 4 more unique towards their respective roles. They currently all have their own attributes but they're not super distinct imo.

Overall I cannot recommend this game.  If you can get it on sale for < $3 and feel like spending $3, go for it, but you're only going to get ~3 hrs out of the game.
There is no dialogue in this game.  Everything in the story is driven by what you see on the screen and the body language of the characters.  Because of this, the ending made absolutely no logical sense to me.  Maybe it was the fact that I played the entire game through 3 separate gaming sessions, the first one starting in January, and the last 2 in June.  The whole "no dialogue" thing may impress the foo-foo artsy fartsy types that somehow derive intense emotions for a game in just 3 hours of playing, but that's not me.  So when I finished the game my response was not "OMG teh feels!"  It was more of "Well that was dumb."
The game mechanics itself (played on an xbox360 wired controller) were interesting.  You control 2 brothers, one with each joystick on the controller and using the right and left trigger buttons to help each other complete tasks that require 2 people.  The puzzles used to progress through the game are quite simple.  That whole experience was enjoyable, but it felt like as soon as I started enjoying the experience it was over (remember, just 3 hrs to complete the game).  The visual landscape of the game is impressive and definitely screenshot worthy.
All in all I can't say I had a bad experience playing this game, but I just can't justify telling someone else to purchase it for more than $3, because honestly, the replayability is zero.

Brothers - A Tale of Two Sons is a beautiful game with unique controls. The story is heartbreaking, but endearing; the scenery is breathtakingly beautiful, and there are loads of secret things to find in your exploration of the world.
The game has but one goal which is to get a cure for the brothers' sick father. On the way, you must solve simple puzzles to traverse the land.
This is where the unique control system comes in to play. Brothers is a single player game with two playable characters. Instead of switching back and forth between them however, you control both of them at the same time. Getting your left hand to work with your right hand is not always an easy task and it's here where the game mechanics shine.
As I mentioned before, the graphics are gorgeous and you'll find yourself pausing several times throughout the game just to enjoy the view.
I whole heartedly recommend this game. Even though it's short, it is worth every penny of the full price.
This is a very sentimental experience.  I love games like this that tug at your heartstrings a bit and tell a good story.  The enviroments were also very well done.

Brothers: A Tale of Two Sons is a co-op game in single player mode in which you control two brothers at once. I saw this a perfect opportunity for my 8 y.o. little sister who wanted to play "serious games" like this so I gave her the control of the right thumbstick of the controller. Naturally, we were screaming at each other within the first 15 minutes.
The puzzles are not that hard, if you are playing alone the challenge comes from coordinating both of your fingers. I had someone else so it wasn't a big deal for me (she just sometimes tend to wander a bit and do her own thing). Also, the puzzles were never boring, the obstacles are pretty varied so there was always something to enjoy.
So there we are, pretending to be the two protagonists in the game who must find the magic pool of water to heal their father. We enjoyed the scenery and the music, thanked the trolls, laughed at goats, and gradually enjoyed working with another for real. We were both engrossed as the story progressed. Consequently, the yelling and the pointing of fingers stopped. The two siblings in the game, like us, had to rely on each other, despite not being equal in terms of strength or skill. It was a very obvious lesson but nonetheless it’s still something always forgotten by most people.
The main theme of this game is about
. It was extra special for me because I shared the experience with another family member.
If you have a sibling or not, or a family, I still recommend this game. It has this quality that makes it impossible to put down.
Overall:
Gameplay and visuals are good, and the story is sweet, captivating, and moving. If you are being economical though, buy it during a sale. With its short length it’s just like going to the movies, except this one is much better than watching a movie.

I have just finished the game for the first time. And after seeing all the negative reviews based solely on the micro transactions or performance issues, I decided it was only fair to give this game an actual review. Something I rarely do but in this case I feel compelled to because of all the negative reviews about a game that is outstanding in my opinion.
First please note that the micro transactions are
. Stuff you can get freely and easy in game. The only time you'd buy them is if you wanted a shortcut. They do not affect game play and are 100% optional. Don't like them? Don't buy because you do not need them and not playing the game because they exist is plain stupid because you are missing out on what I think will be game of the year or a very close contender.

This game is well optimised, if you have decent hardware you wont have any problems. I currently run a i7 5930k @ 4.5 ghz and sli GTX 980s. Playing at 1440p with everything at max settings and I mean everything I average 70-80 frames. Rarely very rarely in fact did I see sub 60fps. Of course if your rig isn't so new you will have to adjust your settings. But please do remember to get the latest drivers for your GPU as I fear many people seeing bad fps haven't bothered to upgrade their drivers.
Graphically this game is stunning if you have the computer to play it on ultra you're eyes will be well looked after.
People have had issues with crashes which I believe can be fixed quite easy, I only crashed once during 29 hours of game play. So I'd go on to assume they are actually quite rare and are only affecting certain hardware/software setups instead of just being caused by bad programming on the Dev's part.
The game play is fantastic in short, If you're a fan of previous Deus Ex games then you will love this game. They took all the good stuff Human Revolution and built on it. Slight changes like right click to ADS instead of middle mouse button etc all subtle little improvements and some major ones. One major addition is the new Augs which are great fun to play with, my personally favourite is the nanoblade.
The missions are well thought out and if you wanna complete all the side missions then you need to explore the city. You are not spoon fed like most modern games, Whilst exploring you never know what you're going to come across or what you might find, It could be a mission or it could be a useful item like a praxis kit. This for me makes exploring rewarding in which most games never really do. The amount of intriguing mini stories you can find just by exploring is amazing.
The environments are packed without so much to find and do, you can lose hours just crawling though vents lol.
The combat is also vastly improved, I had my concerns about the AI when watching earlier videos before release but what I can say is if you play on "Give Me Deus Ex" (which is what I played on) The enemies are very perceptive. Getting spotted and shot to death was a common occurrence when trying to sneak around. Depending on how you build Adam you do not take a lot to kill. Movement and shooting also feels very smooth for a Deus Ex game which has had clunky systems in the past, This is a major thing they have definitely improved on.
Another improvement is the amount of ways you can complete you're missions, there was always multiple ways to do this in Deus Ex but Mankind Divided really pushes the boat out here. There is a lot of ways to get to where you need to go and do what you need to do. Enough to suit any play style.
Some people have always been complaining about the mouse acceleration, Now this is again a personal thing for me it felt fine but I'm used to having a very fast responsive mouse. I didn't need to adjust it but if you do. I hear its not so easy to get it where you like it.
Game play 10/10 for me

I wont say too much here because I do not wish to ruin it for people but what I will say is I fully enjoyed the story, It is your typical Deus Ex story that keeps you glued to your screen though out. Full of surprises twists and turns. The side missions also have very detailed stories which keep them interesting and non repetitive.
One criticism I have with the story is its length, I just feel there is more to be told and for Deus Ex, Mankind Divided is a little short in my opinion. Although I didn't do 100% of the side missions only the ones I actually found. 29 hours for a Deus Ex title just feels a bit short for me and I spent a lot of time exploring too.
I hope really hope that something wasn't cut from the game to be sold as DLC, This likely isn't the case but if the DLC feels like it carries on from the game and should of been included I will be very disappointed.

I kind of want to not recommend this game....
I have a love hate relationship with Jack Black, well not really Love hate, more like Hate Hate, I'm just not a fan of his, but at the same time I liked him in Goosebumps, and I like him in this game for the most part.   He's not an awful person, I just find his persona to be a bit annoying.
At the same time I like Metal music, I'm not an uber fan, and I feel like at times this game expects you to be an uber fan of Metal music to really love this game.  Since I'm not at that level, I still enjoyed the music, but banking so much on one style of music is a pretty gutsy move.
The story feels like it almost lags in the second half of the game, what began as a really interesting and funny premise seems to be monotonous in the second half.   You go from a gorgeous landscape to well three rather dull locations.  The game switches from the action adventure feel to more RTS battles which each feel quite dull especially after you had a Zeldaesque experience.
And finally there's the gameplay.  I like Zelda, and I mostly like RTSes, Brutal Legend though found a way to make me kind of hate it's gameplay as a mix of the two.  The RTS sections aren't exactly thrilling, and the adventure parts of the game are dull.
So clearly I dislike it right?
Well the first half of the game has a lot of great moments.  While the second half really isn't as good, the first half is pretty sweet, the second half just is ok.  The gameplay as an RTS isn't annoying like many RTSes and it allows you to fight instead of just being an RTS, so it's not fully committed to RTSes, where some games are all or nothing, and the final battle is kind of cool and different.  It's not a battle you can just win, but you have to just barely survive, if you know how (and if you don't, you'll have to figure it out)
The metal in the game is awesome.  Having Ozzy Osbourne have a cameo is brilliant, so much of the music is awesome, and the story is quite metal.  In fact the entire sound and music in the game is AMAZING.  Definitely worth playing.
And as I said I'm not a huge Jack Black fan, but I liked him in this.  So that worked.  Even his over the top antics works great for when you're doing a stage slide past an enemy and grinding on a guitar.
This is a game where I recommend it with some big caveats.  If you don't like heavy metal (or just metal/rock in general)  you're going to have a bad time.  If you don't want to play an RTS (because make no question about it, this is an RTS even if it starts off as an adventure game) you're going to have a bad time.  If you want a really strong story, you're ... you get it, right?
But at the same time I'm not a huge Tim Schaeffer/Double Fine fan, and most of his games leave me a little flat.  This game really made me happy, even if it's not perfect, so I recommend it, but you really have to understand that even the demo doesn't give a good representation of the final product, and that does kind of annoy me(the bait and switch).  But if you want to see a new take on an RTS, or hear some awesome Metal music while playing a game, this is really your only option.

Im not going to talk about the single-player in this review, it's not needed. To put it bluntly if that's all your interested in then go ahead and buy it, I will assure you it will be a purchase well made.
My review is based off the online gameplay section, that many will be looking at for their long term entertainment once they are done with the single player.
'Sigh'
Where the hell do I begin...
It was not all bad. Back before even the heists is when GTA Online shined the most. It was a far more fun game to play. Sure people still killed each other as much as they do now, but back then you had nothing they didn't have, it was a far more even playing ground. Now... It's a different story.
Armed vehicles have taken the streets and have really turned the city and coutryside into the real life version of Iraq. Updates bringing in jets, helicopters, cars, boats and even bikes that are all armed to the freakin teeth with enough weapons to make the USA blush have turned the game into a free for all mess.
You have no hope of surviving if your new. You will be blown up for trying to drive your modest car out of your garage. You will be gunned down repeatedly if you even think of trying to do one of the 'online only' missions for some cash. You will be targeted for trying to do ANYTHING of any worth in the game..
Now your probably thinking "Yeah that happened back then as well".. And you would be right. Difference is back then you could fight back, even if you were a noob and just starting out. Now... How do you fight back against bulletproof vehicles that standard weapons cant do bugger all against, or vehicles that can take multiple rockets. How do you counter a flying bike that can missile you from the sky without you even knowing it was there before it was too late. How do you counter a freaking space cannon that can shoot anywhere on the damn map and destroy anything in 1 hit.
This is not exclusive to vehicles either, even weapons have had their dials turned up to 11. Snipers can now be equipped with explosive rounds, able to destroy vehicles in 1 shot. Just to give an example...
So how do you fight back?
The answer to that is 'acquire that gear as well'...
Ok... be prepared for the absolute ♥♥♥♥ loads of grinding you will need to do to get said gear. With vehicles costing in the millions, and warehouses, bunkers, CEO buildings, hangers etc needed on top of that for even more money, prepare to sink some serious hours into the game if you hope to get anywhere. Each update adds new vehicles, each more expensive than the last...
Of course you could bypass that as well, that is why 'Sharkcards' are a thing in this game. For an outrageous, real money, price you could bypass all the grind in the game and start your way to becoming another one of the 'problems' for everyone else in the lobby, but hey as long as your enjoying yourself..right?
That's what Rockstar and Take-Two interactive want you do to. That's why the game is how it is. That's why everything is so damn expensive, and the ways to get money are so long and boring and overall not worth the time investment. They want you to buy those overpriced cards... again... and again... and again...
Back then it was not an issue, you didn't need money really. Everything was reasonably priced and could be acquired through steady gameplay. You never felt the grind hitting you as hard... Now the phrase 'money is power' is too true.
I have gone on quite a bit about one topic, but there are other issues as well other than the hugely un-balanced gameplay:

Brothers: A Tale of Two Sons is a co-op game in single player mode in which you control two brothers at once. I saw this a perfect opportunity for my 8 y.o. little sister who wanted to play "serious games" like this so I gave her the control of the right thumbstick of the controller. Naturally, we were screaming at each other within the first 15 minutes.
The puzzles are not that hard, if you are playing alone the challenge comes from coordinating both of your fingers. I had someone else so it wasn't a big deal for me (she just sometimes tend to wander a bit and do her own thing). Also, the puzzles were never boring, the obstacles are pretty varied so there was always something to enjoy.
So there we are, pretending to be the two protagonists in the game who must find the magic pool of water to heal their father. We enjoyed the scenery and the music, thanked the trolls, laughed at goats, and gradually enjoyed working with another for real. We were both engrossed as the story progressed. Consequently, the yelling and the pointing of fingers stopped. The two siblings in the game, like us, had to rely on each other, despite not being equal in terms of strength or skill. It was a very obvious lesson but nonetheless it’s still something always forgotten by most people.
The main theme of this game is about
. It was extra special for me because I shared the experience with another family member.
If you have a sibling or not, or a family, I still recommend this game. It has this quality that makes it impossible to put down.
Overall:
Gameplay and visuals are good, and the story is sweet, captivating, and moving. If you are being economical though, buy it during a sale. With its short length it’s just like going to the movies, except this one is much better than watching a movie.

Thief Gold is a first-person stealth game which takes place in a surprisingly interesting world of both fantasy and technology. Walking down a street, you can find machinery running underneath of a magical lamppost. The gameplay has its ups and downs. When Thief Gold is good, it's excellent. When it's bad, however, it's frustrating. There are some really fun levels that'll have you running around a building, knocking out guards and stealing oodles of valuables. Then there are levels that task you with navigating a long series of confusing caverns, possibly filled with enemies (packed to the rafters by the end of the game), fighting the undead and monsters and wondering what went wrong.
The plot is decent enough, though it doesn't really pick up until the last quarter of the game. Thief Gold can be cut into three parts: the episodic, mostly unrelated thieving missions, the quest to collect "The Eye", and then the endgame. The first few levels I found to be rather uninteresting, but the pace picks up for a good while after, requiring you to track down a couple assassins sent to stop you, or infiltrate a mansion that seems to be built out of pure madness. One fun level in the middle has you seeking out a contact who, it turns out, has been spun up by giant spiders, and then continues along a series of caverns wherein a crazy old opera-loving hobo sings the way to find your sought-after prize in the guard-riddled opera house above.
Controls are decent enough, though there are more for movement than one may be used to in a first-person experience. Sound is well-done, but then it would have to be, as you'll be spending a lot of time listening for patroling guards and creatures. Voicework is clearly done by whatever staff they had on hand at the time, but I honestly find it somewhat endearing. Visually, the game isn't all that pretty on its own. I recommend seeking out the TFix unofficial patch, which increases resolution and improves textures, in addition to fixing a number of issues (such as videos not playing - happened to me), and adding some new key bindings if you happen to want them.
There are three difficulties. Like GoldenEye or the TimeSplitter series, higher difficulties add new objectives - some of which add to the overall plot of the game - and can change item locations or existences and throw more enemies into the mix. I finished it on Normal, and that was about as much challenge as I needed. But then, I'm not very pro at stealth.
In all, I like it. It's a great stealther. But some levels are just confusing or frustrating, especially late into the game. If nothing else, you can still goof around and pick up ghosts or abuse the game's climbing system to get out of the level.

Rating: 7/10
Overview: Third Person Action RPG
The Good:
+ Character development is really the highlight of the game. By investing skill points across three different skill trees; might, finesse and magic you can develop a play style to your liking. Depending on where you spend your skill points you can unlock passive bonuses in the form of fate cards. The good thing about this is that you can spend skill points across all three skill trees and unlock some really cool bonus perks or you can focus all your skills on a single tree and unlock another set of perks. Its a really good system because it allows for so much flexibility. While most action rpgs require you to focus on a few skills, amalur allows the option for spreading your skill points over multiple skill trees without it hurting you.
+ Combat is fun and fluid and fit the skill trees perfectly. The combat is very accessible and easy to learn right from the start. The only downside is that you can only assign skills to 4 slots on the controller making it very hard to make a build with more than 4 skills.
+ Tons of weapons and armor that make you look incredibly cool. Every type of weapon set has their own unique move set.
+ The environments are bright and colorful. Most areas feel distinct from one another.
+ For a game this size and this much content it is incredibly well polished, very few glitches or bugs to be found.
+ Although the UI is clearly designed around controller support, the UI is surprisingly well done. Accepting any side quests will automatically show every waypoint on your minimap. Finding items in the game world, you can compare, take, equip or place it directly in your junk pile without ever having to open a menu. Little things like this really help the game and provide a much smoother experience.
+ Soundtrack
The Average:
The game features a ton of content; lots of locations, dungeons to explore, side quests to tackle, characters to meet, cities to travel to etc. It is everything you would expect from a large scale RPG. The problem however is that non of this is really interesting. The dungeons are linear hallways with little to no exploration, all the character are boring and say the same things, all the Sid quests devolve into kill x number of enemies, collect x number of items, gather x number of ingredients etc... The game features so much content but very little depth. Of course this is a matter of opinion, and if you find the main story and side quests to your liking then you are going to love everything this game has to offer.
Exploration feels limited. You can not jump nor can you fall off ledges. Level design seems to be very flat.
The Field of view (FOV) is a bit to close to the character making combat a bit weird sometimes. Luckily there is a third party program that can fix this, however you should never have to use a program for an option that should be in the game.
Bosses feel under utilized, feels like wasted potential.
The Bad:
- This game is not balanced at all, even at the hardest setting you can quickly kill enemies early on. If you craft or socket any high level gear the game becomes even more broken to the point of one shot killing enemies. Completing too many side quest will cause you to over level too early on. If you want any challenge you have to purposefully hinder yourself. The lack of difficulty really hurts the game because it makes an otherwise fun combat system, trivial.
- Gold is also meaningless. You will quickly have more gold than you know what to do with, buying items/weapons is useless as you will usually find better gear just by killing or looting treasure chests.
Conclusion:
When I first heard about Kingdoms of Amalur I thought it would be one of my favorite games. I loved the idea behind the character creation, sadly everything surrounding that concept turned out to be average. I had high hopes for the game that never materialized.

This game is just more of the same, with some new features, some good and some.. VERY.. bad.
The game plays smoothly, i played from launch (literally the minute it came out on PC), and never had a single crash. Gameplay is as fun as the other Deus Ex games, and the game has nice balance of powers and together with a smooth difficulty curve ip plays out real nice.
But it is just the small things that keeps nagging me, like the fact that the game prides itself in being "stealthable".
I geared up with tranq rifle, stun gun and a silenced 10mm for good measures. I went through the whole game on hard in about 20 hrs without killing anyone.
But once again the last boss is not stealthable by any means, even though i turned all his minions against him, he was not close to being dead by the time he cleaned them up, and i have to kill him from a ventilation shaft like the biggest cheese on the planet
They say that choices matters alot in both the trailer and between the lines, but during my second playthrough where i run though totally opposite of last time, helping other people, killing EVERYONE, i still don't see much difference, the game had me paranoid that it actually mattered what i did...
Small things like unskippable opening credits every time you launch the game should not be a thing of this day and age… and W...T...F... unskippable ending credits, with hint of next game in the middle... F*** you... if you want to skip that s*** you have to forcibly close the program from desktop…
Most people rate this game as a bad one, because of the "pay to win" aspect, but in my opinion it does not get in your way, we should however all be able to agree on the fact that micro-transactions in non-free games is and will always be a major sin, and the people who made it happen WILL burn in hell once they get there.
Overall, lovely game, WAY too short, WAY too like the old games and WAY too hard to realise, that we might have to wait another 5 years for the feeling of Deus Ex again.

I'll update this as I go, but if you love Deus Ex, you'll love this game.
It's a real shame that this has been panned by a bunch of kids with pocket money PCs, as this doesn't actually run all that badly - the problem stems from people not knowing which graphical settings are intensive and which are not. But then, a PC gamer should really know what they do, so it's hard to write this off as a con. It's the fault of ill-informed gamers. The performance could be better in places, however. I cannot complain about a solid 60fps at 1440p after turning volumetric lighting to 'on' and contact hardening shadows to 'on' rather than their ultra settings.
That said, the game isn't perfect; there are microtransactions which allow you to purchase the likes of Praxis Kits, giving you an edge in the early game where you'd normally have to complete quests for them - but does that affect any normal gamer wishing to play through without paying? No, not really. The game experience hasn't been dampened in favour of them.
The story so far seems inferior to that of Human Revolution, but enough to stand on its own two feet as a Deus Ex game. The UI has been improved considerably and the gameplay feels very similar with light improvements in areas -- the new augs are great and having to disable your choice of augs in order to use them is a good way to stop the player getting too overpowered. A good decision, I think.
It's a shame that the game has been reviewed this way, in a way detrimental to the overall reception of the game when really it's the fault of gamers not knowing what to expect from their own hardware. Games deserve to be panned when they're bad, but the truth is that Deus Ex: Mankind Divided is not bad at all. In-fact, it's very, very, good. Remember next time you pan a game like this, that it may affect the next iteration in the series adversely -- or, you might not get a next game at all.
TL;DR: Pan a game when it deserves it by all means, but this game does not. It's a solid game in the series but quite a bit weaker than the original and Human Revolution. We don't talk about Invisible War.

Brutal Legend is a game from an older time before people really knew how to make games well, at least that's what it feels like.  The gameplay in the game is split between a million and one different ways.  There are hack and slash portions, car races, boss battles reminiscent of zelda, car battles, open world exploration, and-- I kid you not-- a large section of the game randomly changes to Real Time Strategy half way through.  This list isn't even comprehensive.
It has no idea what it wants to be, and it doesn't have to focus to make any individual sections very good.  Despite that, it is a fun game.  There is clearly a lot of love put into it, and ADHD on a crack pipe isn't the worst design when all the portions are acceptable, and you always have the excitement of not knowing what is coming next.
There is a strong metal musical aesthetic that the game keeps to, and it ammounts to being extremely creative.  This is coupled with an extremely large liscneced soundtrack to match the theme.  The game feels cohsive in a very creative way outside of the gameplay.  It just doesn't work, the look, feel, and sound are very unique and not somethingn I think I've ever seen before.
The downsides are inherent in the game design.  The further you get, the more frustrating some of the modes are.   The game isn't built to a Real Time Strategy game, but the final battle is a riduclous campagin of building units, capturing and building on zones, and it's taxing beyond the tools they give you.  This feeling pops up again and again like in combat; it isn't well put together.
Overall though, the positives outway the negatives.  A lot of love wnet into this game, so many things are incorporated that you rarely see, and it is ambitious.  It is by no means a perfect game or even a must play, but people looking for something different with a bit of an older feel to it will get a lot out of this game.

Do not let the screenshots fool you. They do not resemble the actual product. This game looks like a 2003 title, but plays much worse. The controls are terrible, it is not optimized graphically, and it is buggy in almost all other aspects.
The auto-save system is utterly broken. No thought was given to auto-save intuitively, forcing players to rerun long stretches of levels due to traps or otherwise unavoidable instant deaths.
The weapon system is terrible. You can only hold a single missile weapon with limited ammo at a time. Bullet weapons have unlimited ammo but feel and sound like air guns with reload animations that don't actually reload. Even Duke Nukem Forever did a better job with weapons, and that's a low bar.
This is a title designed to get into your wallet via nostalgia. It is not even worth the $15 bargain-bin price. As much as I wanted this to work, I cannot in good conscience recommend it. This game has taught me a valuable lesson. Never pre-order, and never let them play on your nostalgia.

Here's why I like this game:  There are tons of weapons with many stat variables to try out many fighting styles.  There are tons of armor with many stat variables, shields, and horses, even the food you buy for your army has a morale stat!  There is character progression (stats and abilities) and army progression\upgrades.
The story draws you in right from the beginning of the game because you have to make a few (short) choices about your character's background, which also affects your starting stats/abilities and starting armor/weapons.  Although you really choose your own path through the game, there is always a strong overlying narrative playing out around you as the kingdoms battle each other.  The game doesn't hold your hand, you have to make things happen for yourself, but there are always quests and other choices available if you simply talk to NPC's.  From kings to tavern-goers to peasants in a tiny town, talking to people will reveal choices for you to make.
I'm a huge fan of Medieval: Total War, and this game reminds me a lot of that, except you find yourself right in the middle ot the fight.  The combat system works pretty well.  It can be frustrating when you have trouble hitting people, but battle is really skill-based (as opposed to point-and-click) so it is something you can improve.
This is a huge and ambitious game, it's done well, and is full of interesting content.  One of my best finds on Steam.

Writing this while it's still in early access.
Right now, the game isn't that well-optimized. It will chug once you get a larger store if you have a crappy laptop with integrated graphics, but it will run fine if you have a regular gaming machine.
The game also isn't balanced yet -- you can get tons of gold without much effort, thought, or risk, although I did have a store wiped out by barbarians once because I wasn't paying attention.
What is good about this game is that there's a solid core to it. What made it click for me was designing a store around the different character classes. You can organize it so that one section you have armor and weapons fo rogues, another for wizards, another for warriors, and so on. That makes it easier to figure out what you need to restock while also making it look more interesting. That aspect is solid right now and will hopefully be built upon. More cosmetics and more gameplay impacts from layout and item sorting would make it more interesting to play.
The other neat thing is that you actually get to see your customers getting equipped as you improve your store stock. They start out looking generic, but they eventually grab whatever the best armor and weapons are for their class. The game does track their names and inventories, but it's kind of finicky to get the interface to show up.
Some caveats are that the game really needs more pressure on the player. Something like a debt mechanic, timed scenarios, more brutal invasions / calamities, more effects of having well-equipped customers, inventory decay, inventory weight, maintenance costs to repair objects, custom difficulty levels, or price fluctuations could improve this a lot. The UI also needs to be improved a lot -- particularly when you're carrying a lot of inventory and crafting something.
I'd recommend this if you're interested in testing it out and the concept sounds fun to you. It's a good simple game to play while listening to podcasts or lectures as it is right now.

A classic and rare edition of the game that made the Stealth Genre viable, "THIEF Gold" is the story of a man whose talent for becoming one with the shadows lands him in hot water with the law...and less pleasant forces that would use him to bring  destruction to The First City.
It holds up to the stealth games of today, blowing past them in many cases, and the level designs are still some of the most imaginative I've seen.  Its backdrop of an industrial-mediaeval civilisation beset by crime, religious fanatacism, and dark magical arts, is as enticing as it is unsettling.
Seek out the patches online for maximum visual quality; otherwise the game runs very well indeed on most advanced OS.

In 1998, Looking Glass Studios, a company that wasn't afraid to tread new ground in innovation and game design would release one of the most fascinating games of all time that would pave the way for many future titles, stealth and otherwise.
Thief is one of those games where you can lose yourself in it's atmosphere quite quickly. Doing steampunk before steampunk was cool, it throws you into this marvellous Victorian styled world of magic and technology as a character you can't help but love; Garrett.
As Garrett, you will visit mansions, underground tombs, ruins and abandoned sections of The City, risking life and limb for that final prize; unimaginable wealth.
The gameplay is solid and rewarding. Your 'Light Gem' will tell you how visible you are at any given time. Hide in the shadows and sneak past at the right time to avoid your enemies... if you want. You could kill them or knock them unconscious but that's your choice to make. Its perfectly possible to complete this game without killing or knocking anybody or anything unconscious.
The story is also very well written however the main story doesn't start until a few levels into the game so you get time to take in the world around you and see a tiny bit of it, time to master the controls and learn how to play.
Small story segments are given to you here and there that may tell you things you need to learn about your objective or the environment; two guards having a conversation, a dropped scroll or book on a bedside table. Exploration of the open-ended levels is rewarded either with loot to steal or with tiny story segments.
Speaking of loot and gear, you'll need to get exploring and collect it. The more loot you collect in one level, the more money you will have to spend on gear for the next. Gear such as Water Arrows to put out torches, Rope Arrows to climb or to find alternate entries into buildings, Flash Bombs to temporarily blind pursuers, Moss Arrows to silence your footsteps over loud surfaces or Noisemaker Arrows for a quick distraction.
The game does have it's flaws; the sometimes confusing level design can make it hard to navigate some levels, a small amount of voice-acting isn't that great, the slight overuse of the undead in places and the character models haven't aged very well but the art design, atmosphere and storytelling still hold up today as some of the best ever encountered in a game.
Mods are out there to update the graphics and textures if you want to use them. The game is very mod friendly and there are plenty of user-made fan missions out there to keep your inner taffer happy for a long time. You can also find help on setting up the game on your PC here:
It may be a little rough around the edges but it changed the way I look at games forever and not many games do that. I can't recommend this game highly enough!

So I started playing this because I like exploration and stealth, and despite it's age this game has those in spades. There are a lot of hurdles to overcome for your experience - The game must be patched to run. The cutscenes still won't display. The graphics are horrendous. The controls are awkward. The locations get a little too nonsensical. The gameplay demands a lots of quicksaves...... Do not expect to be amazed when you start playing. It won't be very fun right away.
That being said, it is a testament to just how fantastic this game is, that it can have all these drawbacks and still be a truly great game. Give it some time and a couple of missions in your reward will be, that somehow, without you realizing it, Thief started to sink into your bones.
You learn how to master the controls, and begin to feel deft at dodging from shadow to shadow. You end up feeling like you taught yourself, you actually learned during the course of the game, how to slink forward, dart out, and whisk away your prize like some kind of master. You creep around as alert as you can, and don't notice it directly, but the enormous levels, the twisting passages, the touches of detail, the remnants of notes left behind, and (most of all) the sounds of the world begin to revebrate and leave you a small piece of a large, strange world, full of secrets and powers beyond your understanding. You don't do it consciously, but you begin to fill in for the graphics. You begin to guess at the mysteries and stories of how these places came to be. There are times when the game environments and the game mechanics rudely interrupt your experience, but most of the time it is a perfect blend that draws out a far richer and more salient experience than most of the games I have ever played.
I never played the two older Thief games before this year, and although I like exploration and stealth, those are my only two biases that might affect my opinion. I highly, HIGHLY, enjoyed it. The expectations I had for this game did not coincide with my actual experience, but it more than redeemed itself by far far exceeding my expectations in other regards. I had no idea ambiance could come through so strongly with such limitations in graphics, sound, AI, and clunky controls. I also hold great respect for it for respecting my intelligence. It did not hold my hand, nor was it devilishly difficult to figure out what to do. Yeah, I wandered around lost and unsure a lot, but there was nothing that was unenjoyable about doing that. The game encourages you to do so, and there is a lot to discover (and steal) while you unlock the greater picture of the mission.  I played slowly and patiently, but I missed a lot of content and could easily play it again for a new expierience. (and probably will)
To summarize:
Gameplay started awkwardly and unfun, but became solid once you are familiar with it.
Sound is not something I care about, but was used masterfully to make this game the excellent piece of work it is.
Graphics are a pain, but the world starts to fill itself in with more than visuals before your mind.
Storyline balances out to solid after averaging out the complaints and the compliments.
The age was a detriment, I won't understate that point.  Even taking that into account, I enjoyed it immesely despite having no history or nostagia-borne fondness it to smooth over my perception.
I highly recommend this game, given that you are patient, don't care about action, do care about a game's background details, and have time to properly become involved in experiencing an entire mission at a time. You could not find a better game for stealth, exploration, atmosphere, memorableness and sheer uniqueness.

Fantastic game.
The gameplay is simple. You click the ground where you want to go, and click, right-click, or press a key to attack an enemy, depending on which attack you want to use.
There's a few activities that you can utilize these gameplay principles. All these can be done with multiple players.
-You can play through the campaign, which features quests scattered throughout the open world. You can do some of them or try to beat them all.
-You can play various maps after you have completed the campaign.
-You can run around killing things looking for loot.
-You can trade loot with other players.
-You can play numerous mod campaigns with fan-created classes (or just use original classes).
-You can do many other things introduced by mods.
The game has high replay value.
-You can start a New Game Plus (NG+) after beating it once if you choose, which makes the game harder and gives loot for your higher level.
-You can start a new character altogether and make a different build, creating new experience every time.
-You can play with mods, which makes things new again.
Compared to its competitors, namely Diablo III, Torchlight II takes the cake.
-T2 is moddable, D3 is not.
-T2 plays smoothly and can run offline, while D3 has a constantly delay in your clicks due to bad netcode and cannot be played offline.
-T2 feels like the developers used creativity and enjoyed making the game, whereas D3 seems uninspired and fails to live up to the expectations of the previous Diablos. T2 was largely made by people that worked on the old Diablos, which may be why it seems better.
-T2's campaign is more fun and less linear than D3's.
-T2's builds are more flexible- put the points where you want, which you can't simply do in D3. You can also use extended and mod builds from the workshop.
-T2 has cool pets, which fight for you and can run to town to buy and sell items if your pack is full.
And then much more.
It's a great game; well worth $20. If you can get it on sale for less, whether to buy it is a no-brainer.

To begin with, I'd say that Torchlight2 is not something that will suit everyone and each person will most likely get a unique experience after playing it. Therefore, some people might disagree with what I say/think about this game and those things that I consider to be good in it might sound bad for you and vice versa. Finally, let's start:
1) It is long, which gives you a good value for your money. On the other hand, it is also always about the same thing: press "LMB" and explore a bit to win. As a result, it is very easy to get bored with this game and leave it forever.
2) For those guys (like I am) who prefer to play slowly and find every secret on the level co-op in Torchlight might be way too intence since it is actually hard to explore all the corners when you're forced to go on by your friends. Therefore, I highly recommend those people to either not buy it for a multiplayer or to complete the game alone before joining friends.
3) Although the mini-bosses in this game are too easy, there is a great amount of them and they will never let you forget about them.
4) This game doesn't really care about your skills and tactics at all. If you're playing on normal and exploring at least 50% of the dungeons to get all the experience and other useful stuff, you'll most likely never meet any problems on your way.
To cut long story short, I think that Torchlight2 might be a good choice for everyone who loves spending a lot of time wandering through the game and achieving 100% completion of it.  As for the others, well, be wary of monotony.

Brutal Legend is a game from an older time before people really knew how to make games well, at least that's what it feels like.  The gameplay in the game is split between a million and one different ways.  There are hack and slash portions, car races, boss battles reminiscent of zelda, car battles, open world exploration, and-- I kid you not-- a large section of the game randomly changes to Real Time Strategy half way through.  This list isn't even comprehensive.
It has no idea what it wants to be, and it doesn't have to focus to make any individual sections very good.  Despite that, it is a fun game.  There is clearly a lot of love put into it, and ADHD on a crack pipe isn't the worst design when all the portions are acceptable, and you always have the excitement of not knowing what is coming next.
There is a strong metal musical aesthetic that the game keeps to, and it ammounts to being extremely creative.  This is coupled with an extremely large liscneced soundtrack to match the theme.  The game feels cohsive in a very creative way outside of the gameplay.  It just doesn't work, the look, feel, and sound are very unique and not somethingn I think I've ever seen before.
The downsides are inherent in the game design.  The further you get, the more frustrating some of the modes are.   The game isn't built to a Real Time Strategy game, but the final battle is a riduclous campagin of building units, capturing and building on zones, and it's taxing beyond the tools they give you.  This feeling pops up again and again like in combat; it isn't well put together.
Overall though, the positives outway the negatives.  A lot of love wnet into this game, so many things are incorporated that you rarely see, and it is ambitious.  It is by no means a perfect game or even a must play, but people looking for something different with a bit of an older feel to it will get a lot out of this game.

Im not going to talk about the single-player in this review, it's not needed. To put it bluntly if that's all your interested in then go ahead and buy it, I will assure you it will be a purchase well made.
My review is based off the online gameplay section, that many will be looking at for their long term entertainment once they are done with the single player.
'Sigh'
Where the hell do I begin...
It was not all bad. Back before even the heists is when GTA Online shined the most. It was a far more fun game to play. Sure people still killed each other as much as they do now, but back then you had nothing they didn't have, it was a far more even playing ground. Now... It's a different story.
Armed vehicles have taken the streets and have really turned the city and coutryside into the real life version of Iraq. Updates bringing in jets, helicopters, cars, boats and even bikes that are all armed to the freakin teeth with enough weapons to make the USA blush have turned the game into a free for all mess.
You have no hope of surviving if your new. You will be blown up for trying to drive your modest car out of your garage. You will be gunned down repeatedly if you even think of trying to do one of the 'online only' missions for some cash. You will be targeted for trying to do ANYTHING of any worth in the game..
Now your probably thinking "Yeah that happened back then as well".. And you would be right. Difference is back then you could fight back, even if you were a noob and just starting out. Now... How do you fight back against bulletproof vehicles that standard weapons cant do bugger all against, or vehicles that can take multiple rockets. How do you counter a flying bike that can missile you from the sky without you even knowing it was there before it was too late. How do you counter a freaking space cannon that can shoot anywhere on the damn map and destroy anything in 1 hit.
This is not exclusive to vehicles either, even weapons have had their dials turned up to 11. Snipers can now be equipped with explosive rounds, able to destroy vehicles in 1 shot. Just to give an example...
So how do you fight back?
The answer to that is 'acquire that gear as well'...
Ok... be prepared for the absolute ♥♥♥♥ loads of grinding you will need to do to get said gear. With vehicles costing in the millions, and warehouses, bunkers, CEO buildings, hangers etc needed on top of that for even more money, prepare to sink some serious hours into the game if you hope to get anywhere. Each update adds new vehicles, each more expensive than the last...
Of course you could bypass that as well, that is why 'Sharkcards' are a thing in this game. For an outrageous, real money, price you could bypass all the grind in the game and start your way to becoming another one of the 'problems' for everyone else in the lobby, but hey as long as your enjoying yourself..right?
That's what Rockstar and Take-Two interactive want you do to. That's why the game is how it is. That's why everything is so damn expensive, and the ways to get money are so long and boring and overall not worth the time investment. They want you to buy those overpriced cards... again... and again... and again...
Back then it was not an issue, you didn't need money really. Everything was reasonably priced and could be acquired through steady gameplay. You never felt the grind hitting you as hard... Now the phrase 'money is power' is too true.
I have gone on quite a bit about one topic, but there are other issues as well other than the hugely un-balanced gameplay:
-Hacking is rampant - Literally every lobby you are in. Cheaters spawning themselves in money, or dropping it on some innocent player, putting them at risk of being out right banned for having false money on their accounts. Teleporting players all over the map, blowing up their cars and shipments. Crashing the server all together... Need I go on?
-P2P can result in horrible load times and poor performance. I can not forgive this one, Rockstar has enough damn money to host dedicated servers. It would improve the experience by miles, and may help deal with the hacking problem as well.
-Cancerous community. Every game has this to some degree so I won't comment any further on it, just felt like it should be mentioned anyway.
-Crashes and bugs. Some have been around for a long time, still left unfixed to this day.
I won't say anymore. If you think this is your type of game then go right ahead, I won't think any less of you. All I ask is you think about it before purchasing...

First of all - The microtransactions:
They do exist. Do they hamper the experience? No. The game shells out more than enough praxis kits to get through the game VERY comfortably, so sorry it just isn't the case that they would harm the game in any way.
To the actual GAME:
It has a very well made atmosphere that actually does grip you and pull you in, there are some odd performance issues but it never crashed on me (maybe luck) and the few issues there are didn't bother me personally while playing, on my specs with a 970 I was around 80 fps constantly.
Positives:
True to the core gameplay, stealth and routes are very nicely laid and planned out, augs provide significant improvements to your chosen gameplay style, as they should.
The story is very engaging and I especially liked the side quests, many of which start as random diaries lying around in the city.
Overall the story is well written, dialogue well executed and there just isn't much to scoff at in regards to the story that the game presents, even the side quests.
Solid AI (for the most part).
Negatives:
As with most games in recent memory, massive sequel bait ending, especially the second ending cutscene with possible hints to a complete 180 in the percieved story.
Performance issues for some people, I know about people that can't get the game to even run above 30fps.
Sometimes the AI will act a bit random and seemingly get suspicious of your body odour 50m away.
A few of the augs feel completely redundant, especially the two nonlethal ones that I don't get the point of having (game gives you plenty of ammo for your nonlethal weaponry).
The social enhancer is OP yet again as it was in HR, makes too many critical things trivial.
Bottom line:
8.5/10 An excellent game, not perfect,  not the be-all end-all but a valid sequel to HR and the franchise as a whole. In my opinion.
If you are a big fan of the franchise buy now, if not wait 'till it goes on sale but a deffinite must play for any cyberpunk fan.
I put in around 20 hours and I consider myself a very quick player, this is with all the sidequests and whole main quest line (a friend of mine is 16 hours in with maybe 20% completion but he is literally exploring every inch of the city).

On the other hand, the combat is SO GOOD. Admittedly, their archery doesn't make a lot of sense(THATS NOT HOW QUIVER WORK) but it is still really fun. Thief is probably one of those games that gets overlooked. It's a shame because this is probably one of the most memorable, unique, gaming experiences. In 1998, the Dark Engine was ahead of its time. Modern games today would rival Thief with its unique and sprawling levels, its interesting story, and wholly unique gameplay. Being able to truly be free in choice to handle mission objects is fresh, even by today's standards. Sound is an important factor. Dropping in on conversations can lead useful clues. The game boasts some really terrific audio. As good as the audio is the gameplay is where it really shines.
I will never forget the first nerve-racking moment where an alerted guard begins sweeping the room, looking for me as I, the player hunch in the shadows praying he doesn't find me. You do have access variety of weapons and gadgets and  your arsenal gives a multiple means to accomplish goals but combat is largely a risky venture. You are a thief, not a warrior. These sort of experiences seem incredibly rare in modern games.
In summy, for the cheap price, you are getting an amazing gameplay experience. If you find yourself wanting more, you'll find a fantastic community of dedicated Thief fans over on Thief theCircle. Fans are still creating Fan Missions, and hell, there is even a full blown expansion for Thief 2. Get this game, you won't be disappointed.

Right I have noticed a pattern in alot of the other reviews that seem to be focusing on the fact the DLC content can be used once and there are microtransactions, let me put down both of these issues (Not completely but I can explain it a bit). Microtransactions in single player, yes its a wierd thing to happen but its optional, the game gives you a good amount of upgrades and credits if you explore making the microtransactions low priority. If you complete the game you get a thing called New game + which starts a new game while saving all your augments, items, credits etc. So you only need to use the DLC once since it will be carried over and some of the DLC can be used in multiple saves such as the elite combat rifle.
Now onto the actual gameplay, it recycles alot of functions from Deus Ex Human Revolution its predecessor, this isnt a bad thing as it keeps the gameplay familier, however some of it has been improved such as the gunplay and takedown mechanics and the hud is alot less cluttered, the energy system has also been improved for convenience. It recycles all the familier augments from human revolution and without doing spoilers the new augmentations and its system forces you to balance and focus your build which is really new and refreshing. The side quests are actually useful in this game as they give you better items and give you a proper view of prague and whats going on behind the scenes, such as crimes, poverty etc. Straight to the point though the story is quite good and relativly easy to follow and im limiting what I say in order to prevent spoilers. You can non lethally take down everybody now including bosses which is really nice. However upon gaining the CASIE augment the social persuasion is just too easy, in Human revolution you had to experiment with a choice and see how they react, now you just see which personality flashes the most and choose the response matching that. It has got the classic choose how you want to play feel where you can be a walking tank, non lethal stealth or assassin and Jenson + other characters react to these choices. I have already completed a non lethal stealth runthrough and I am now starting the tank run, however the new game + isnt something I would advice for a new run as you can feel incredibly overpowered at the start since all your stuff is retained.
I did experience some crashes at first although these have been patched along with a few bugs.
Overall this game is effectively a new and improved version of Human Revolution with a better story, sidequests, gameplay and augments to make it refreshing to play. Hell I even found Jenson a lot less like a robot and more of a person since his facial expression actually changed now and he would make movements and acknowlage what others were saying, however loading times are a bit long in my opinions with only a few animations to keep you occupied.
I would really recommend this game for someone who wants a new experience, or a veteren of the Deus Ex series as it shows really good promise aslong as the devs keep patching known issues.

Guess I'll do my own little review after finishing the game. Before I do that I should say that I haven't played the original deus ex, but I did play human revolution (like finished it 3 days ago). Anyways, to start off I think Deus Ex Mankind Divided is a good game. I just finished (am now waiting for the after-credit scene) and while I do agree that the ending was way too abrupt, I guess it might be setting up for DLC or another sequel (If it's DLC then I'll be disgusted, but whatever).
STORY:
As I just mentioned and as you might have read elsewhere, the ending of Deus Ex Mankind Divided is pretty damn abrupt. You're just getting to the really juicy and secretive part when it stops. That's however the only gripe I have with the story. I just finished Human Revolution too and don't understand how people can praise the story of Human Revolution and then say that the one in Mankind Divided was bad. The story of HR wasn't better than this one in my opinion besides the ending and even then the ending of HR wasn't all that great either :P. So long story short: good story with a sadly abrupt ending.
GAMEPLAY:
The gameplay is honestly better than in HR and anybody saying otherwise has to be lying. From controls to levels to augments, everything is better. The controls feel more fluid and I don't understand what people are complaining about (though I did play stealthily, so maybe it's the gunfights?). I've seen people complaining about mouse acceleration, but didn't notice a thing myself. summed up: the controls are fine (I am using a mouse and keyboard by the way). The levels are 18,446,744,073,709,551,616 times, better known as infinitely, better. The levels have been made way bigger and now have a ton more ways to be navigated. Instead of that one vent that you know leads to where you need to go, you'll be debating whether you should take vent nr. 1, nr. 2 , gas infested crawlspace 3, 'shocking' room 4, ... . The one gripe people have however is that you only have one hub city, Prague, which makes everything seem smaller even though it's just as big, if not bigger, as the hub cities in HR. I have to admit that it's true. You don't feel like Columbus anymore going around the world. The pure amount of detail and interaction put into Prague makes up for it in my opinion though. From the daily aug harrasment to the drug dealer that lives on the first floor of your apartement complex. The thirdimprovement is the augs. I really love the new augs that you can choose from and think they're a nice addition. There's not a lot to say about it besides that. To end this part of the review I'll address another thing that some reviews I read complained about. Some people seem to think that the 'augism' (racism against augs) has been badly done in the game and feels fake or something (I really don't understand what they're complaining about). I'll just say that I've actually gotten♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥at some of the 'officers' (♥♥♥♥ing♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ and have thought about giving up my pacifist playthrough just for them. Try taking a 'naturals only' train...
GRAPHICS:
I guess there must be something wrong with my eyes. I've seen countless people complain about the graphics, even comparing them to those of the console peasants! This review is for everybody who, unlike most of the negative reviewers in this thread, don't give a flying ♥♥♥♥ with what other people do with their money.  Seriously people?  "Not Recommended" because there are micro transactions?  I'm so sick of the "gaming" community crying about micro-transactions, or any other way for studios to make profit.  Game prices have not gone up in nearly 30 YEARS.  Go check SNES game prices when they were new.  NBA Jam was $80 at Toys R Us when it came out.  That's equal to $133 at today's rates.  Game prices have become exponentially more expensive to make as the market has grown, and yet the prices have gone DOWN because volume has increased.  And yet, entitled pieces of♥♥♥♥♥♥come in here and try and shame developers for trying to make up for a revenue gap by selling single player perks for $4.  If somebody wants to skip the leveling up system and pay for Praxis kits, WHO CARES?  Why are you going to write a negative review for the game because of what Timmy wants to spend his allowance on?
Here's a real game review:
Deus Ex: Mankind Divided - Overall score 8.5/10
Graphics: 9/10
Simply put the game looks amazing.  The lip sync animations are a little clunky and some of the character animations are a little funky but overall I've found myself spending most of my short time in this game exploring every nook and cranny.
Sound: 8/10
The levels are a little off at points i.e. the voices of people around you are louder than the machine gun in your hands that you are shooting.  But overall the soundtrack is really enjoyable and the ambient sound is really immersive.  NPC dialogue is plentiful and pretty interesting to eavesdrop on.  Melee and take down sound effects are super satisfying.
Controls: 8/10
The only thing that I really gotta knock is the mouse acceleration.  I had to turn it to 0 in order to even play the game, but once I had it set to 0 it felt fine.  Should be an easy hot fix.  Beyond that the control scheme is not typical and takes a little getting used to with the odd cover system but once you get it down it feels fine.
Gameplay: 9/10
They did an excellent job at making you able to control the way you approach levels.  Just in the first few missions I could already identify that there were several ways to achieve your objective.  The replay factor is definitely there.  Add on top of that the simple and fast quick save/load feature and you have yourself so many opportunities to experiment.
Now let's address the♥♥♥♥♥♥talk:
Micro transactions - Seriously?  You're going to NOT recommend this amazing title because they decided they needed another form of revenue?  It's a single player game people.  Why do you care what others do with their $4?  Back when I was a kid my neighbor bought a Game Genie.  We spent hours messing with games and seeing how we could break them.  Today he'd be burnt at the stake.  I could care less if you decide to spend an extra $20 on praxis kits.  Honestly, you're downgrading your experience if you do though because leveling up is part of the challenge of this game.  There is absolutely NO reason why optional micro transactions for a single player experience should affect the overall rating of this game.  None.  If you factor that in, ♥♥♥♥ you.
DLC - Ok, so people are supposedly♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥off about "one time use" DLC.  Maybe if they took two seconds to read what the DLC was they wouldn't have spent their money.  From what I've seen it consists of character skins, weapons skins, and things like extra praxis kits and health stims.  Some morons out there are literally complaining about praxis kits being one time use.  What the ♥♥♥♥ did you expect?  You expected to get an unlimited use praxis kit so you can max level in the first 30 seconds of the game?  So let me get this straight... the community here on Steam DOESN'T like the fact that you can pay for praxis kits in your personal, single player game.  At the same time they also DON'T like the fact that the praxis kit they paid for by pre-ordering isn't unlimited use...  SM♥♥♥♥inH.
Technical issues - NEVER, I repeat, NEVER in the history of PC gaming has 100% hardware compatibility been achieved.  My parents bought me Star Wars: Dark Forces when I was a kid and it crashed our Gateway PC so many times.  The polygon and kotaku articles about Deus Ex's technical issues are seriously so minor they are not worth the pixels they are displayed on.  This Polygon article:
cite TWO Steam reviews as their source material for Deus Ex being "Kind of a Mess".  Seriously?  If I spent two minutes on Twitter I could find two people to complain about anything.  That does not make a news article.  On top of that the technical issues they address are the mouse acceleration I mentioned above, and a few minor crashing issues which the developers have already publicly addressed.  Queue the Reddit hive mind hate-wagon to♥♥♥♥♥♥talk and drive this game in to the ground.
Deus Ex: Mankind Divided has met and surpassed what Human Revolution was.  If you liked that game then this is a must buy.  If you have technical issues, do what every PC player has had to do several times and troubleshoot.  If you don't reach two hours of in game time Steam will refund you.  What is there to lose?

If you are reading reviews for this game, please ignore all these complaints about microtransactions that are clogging the review section, it's not like they are required, or you HAVE to purchase them.
now on to my actual thoughts about the game so far.
These are my pros for Deus Ex:MD:
- Patches, fixing misc issues every 2-3 days
- The game looks gorgeous.

- The populated areas feel alive with the amount of npcs chatting and/or going about their daily business.
- Prauge is filled to the brim with places to explore, and lootable items are all over the place.
- The gameplay is great, fairly similar to Human Revolution, with some improvements.
- The story is satisfactory (excluding the ending, see cons), and most of the side quests are interesting.
- The new Breach mode is pretty entertaining and seems to have a decent amount of content, which is great for it just being a side-game.
Cons:
- Deus Ex: MD could run a bit better, as of now I get around 50fps on an i5-2500 @3.3ghz cpu, GTX 960 2gig gpu, and 8 gigs of ram, while on medium settings. However I find it highly likely that the game will get some kind of optimization patch soon.
- Only one 'hub' zone.
- The ending was kind of disappointing, and felt almost unfinished.
______________________________________________________________
If you are someone who's willing to overlook microtransactions (which honestly, don't have any affect on the game if you don't use them.), and you are a fan of the Deus Ex series, then this game is for you.

First of all, I'd like to say that if I ever have a "Are video games art?" discussion with someone, I will bring this game up as a prime example of a video game that is undoubtedly a piece of art.
The basic premise of the game is that you control two characters at once, and use this mechanic to solve the puzzles that the game throws your way.  These range from climbing, to operating mechanical devices, to a good variety of more interesting puzzles.  The game is about 2.5 - 3.5 hours long, depending on how long it takes you, but the puzzles are all fairly straight-forward.
The art style is one of the prettiest I've seen in a game, managing to look like a moving oil painting.  The story, while very simplistic, is conveyed very well, even though there no intelligible dialogue, just vocalizations from the characters.
I played it with a keyboard, and just by judging by how it's clearly an Xbox port, I can only assume it plays much better with a controller.  (EDIT: I originally played this without an anti-ghosting keyboard so the controls were kind of messy to work with.  If you don't have a mechanical keyboard, I'd recommend using a controller, but it IS doable on a standard rubber dome keyboard, just clunky).  It was fairly well optimized - didn't have any crashes, and only had two or three frame drops throughout my play time.
Overall, I'd recommend this game if you enjoy this type of thing - a mostly slow-paced, quite easy but very beautiful and touching puzzle game.
