Incredibly bitter-sweet experience. For a game that I spent years waiting for, I can only say that I both enjoyed it immensely but at the same time feel a strange weight of disappointment. It wasn’t a game I hyped either, I was just excited to play another Deus Ex, and I guess that’s what we got, in fact we got even more of a Deus Ex than HR gave to us in some aspects.
It’s astonishing. Like, absolutely fantastic. I love exploring tightknit, well-layered game worlds, and boy does this game have an amazing world to explore. So many hidden routes, paths and shortcuts to get you from A to B to C. You can go over it, you can go under it, you can go around it and you can go through it. It’s like a toy-box, so much fun to be had exploring Prague and finding your way around the various other levels in the game. To me, this is what Deus Ex is all about, being presented with an objective and having so many pathways to use to achieve that objective.
I really liked the art-style of HR (sans yellow-filter) and the aesthetic it presented. To me, Human Revolution was a perfect representation of just what our society is going to be like in the future, it’s never too unbelievable. Another key part of what Deus Ex is to me, the dystopian cyberpunk jet-setting adventure, and uncovering conspiracies in a near-future world. Also, triangles.
I loved Jensen, I think everyone did. Elias does his job and does it well with Adam. In this game, we get more to Adam’s character, there are events that change him from what he was in HR to the man/machine we have now. Not only that, there’s now a mystery, a conspiracy, which Adam must solve about himself.
The game got slated in critics’ reviews for this, and in my entire time playing I could never understand why. When you move around the world, completing main-quests, side-quests, reading e-mails and pocket secretaries, you find yourself very immersed in the world. It’s believable that augs (augmented citizens) are a victim of prejudice and hatred in this world due to the climactic event that occurred in Human Revolution, The Aug Incident or The Incident.
Soundtrack.
Another stellar album of music from Michael McCann, my personal favourite track being the background music in TF29. There is even more brilliance to the music in Mankind Divided than HR, especially in the conversation challenges that now work off musical cues, kinda' like L.A. Noire.
It’s hard to define this, since the level-design is such an absolutely large part of the Gameplay, but for the sake of this review I’m going to talk about combat systems.
It’s alright. In my first playthrough, I played stealth non-lethal, and it’s obvious that this is the optimal gameplay style, the style that the developers designed their game around. All the hidden pathways and vantage spots point towards this being the best way to play the game, and I had a hell of a lot of fun playing this way, it was a blast. In terms of weapons, I only used two, the Stun Gun and the Tranq Rifle. I didn’t use any augmentations for combat, but I used stealth-orientated augmentations for moving around the levels. Mostly, my time was spent knocking people out with takedowns/stuns/tranqs and dragging them out of sight of other guards. It reminded me of Metal Gear Solid.
But then I played guns-blazing combat on my second playthrough, and it’s meh. It’s much improved over the gunplay from HR, but it’s still nothing special. It has interesting mechanics such as switching out ammo types to deal with certain enemies, but eventually that just becomes a chore and you end up stocking up on one ammo type and using that all the time regardless of whom you are fighting, whether it’s turrets, drones or armoured police. Lethal takedowns, for whatever reason, make noise whereas non-lethal takedowns do not, so when I’m trying to stealth my way into a good spot to wreak havoc I still end up just knocking people out as opposed to killing them, an utterly bizarre design choice from Eidos.
There’s no boss battles anymore, which I guess is a lot more like the original Deus Ex, but I thoroughly enjoyed the ones in Human Revolution (Director’s Cut) and it was a shame to see them go, there’s a grand total of 1 in the game and he can be dealt with the same way you deal with some other previously-before seen enemies.
It’s weird. Incredibly akin to Resident Evil Revelations’ Raid mode, you go through series of repetitive challenge rooms/levels doing certain things a certain way to finish the level. Once you finish you get a currency, XP for your avatar and sometimes booster packs. Booster packs work like card packs in say a game like (strange example) Plants vs. Zombies 2: Garden Warfare, you open ‘em up and you get stuff, that stuff plays into the game. The stuff you get in Breach can be a few things that are ranked by a rarity scale labelled D, C, B, A and S, with S being the highest rank naturally. You can get weapons, ammo, attachments etc. You can also acquire modifiers that you can apply to a level to make it easier or harder which results in a higher score at the end. There’s also speedrun challenges and score challenges with targets for every level.
I like this sort of stuff but I know it’s not for everyone, it requires a lot of repetitive grind to get the best scores a hit those targets.
What a mess. Microtransactions, augmentations locked behind pre-order bonus DLC (Also available to purchase on the Steam Store. ™) General AAA ♥♥♥♥ery that knocks the majority of gamers sick to their stomach.
Oh boy.
What happened?
I adored the story in Human Revolution. I know it wasn’t anything super-special, but I loved the idea of Adam following a thread that just got longer and longer, unravelling even more plots and conspiracies that led him to Panchea. Jetsetting, spy-thriller action. It was brilliant.
I feel like they tried to do that here, but something has gone wrong, terribly wrong. Either the game just wasn’t finished, or they’ve split it in half so we have to shell out another fourty quid next year, or whenever the next damned part is going to release.
I had a lot of fun playing it, but for the love of god do not think too hard about the story or the narrative, it’s just not worth your time.

Final Review:
Graphics: These are pretty great to be honest.  I turned some stuff down to ensure I had a 60+ frame rate but it is a great looking game.  The textures are nice for the most part and even with some turned down I am hit by the occasional "wow" moment when the perfect confluence of light and shapes hit my eye.
Control: These are solid but I do have some complaints.  They changed how cover works.  In the last game you could stake out a situation and move around keeping an eye on the bad guys.  They changed it so now you have to look at the area you are moving to making you take your eyes of the baddies.  This has lead to more than one instance of me running out of cover because in a lot of ways it still feels like DXHR.  They also changed certain things and you are stuck with them. In DXHR you would right click for cover and middle mouse for iron sights.  You can edit your controls but it won't let you change the middle mouse click from an Aug activation. Meaning you cannot set up the control for more of the stealth only gameplay I like so much.  All in all, having to learn a new control scheme is not ruining my fun in the game.
My one complaint here is the fidgety ledge grab system.  I sometimes struggle to get Jensen to do what I need him to do.  Sometimes he grabs a ledge and sometimes he doesn't.  This comes with the fidgety jump enhancement.  You hold the space bar to get him to jump higher, which means he will sometimes unintentionally grab a ledge.  They actually fixed my initial double jump feel complaint.  Now when you hold the jump you are just sent on a steady upward climb to the apex of your jump.
Gameplay: This is mostly the same as the last.  Each area has a plethora of ways to access it.  I sometime go into a situation the hard way and have a much more poor outcome only to find I missed a much better way of approach if only I had been paying more attention.  You can also still approach the game multiple ways.  Stealth is always an option, but you can also go in guns blazing.  You are still offered a nice expansive aug tree to pick how you want to play.  You play stealth and switch to guns blazing, bad idea.  You are very squishy so just deciding you are going to start shooting everyone is a bad idea.  But the right augs will turn you into a terminator, which is the way I imagine people want a game like this to be, a character that is highly customizable.  Hacking is the same but a bit more attractive interface.  Hard at first, but no matter how you spin it, at level 4 and 5, it's hard.  They had a very good use of the same hub area at different times.  They felt very different and new because you had different obstacles in your way at different times, it made the world feel very good.
Story:  I don't feel like it just ended when it was just getting going, I have seen this criticism many times.  The game feels complete with me, there are 2 boss encounters in the game, one of which is an optional sidequest.  These are open, you are free to do them how you want, I was able to do both in a non-lethal fashion.  It was very fun.  I think it's a bit of a writing faux pas that they ended it like they did.  If they had simply avoided the opening cinematic with the Illuminati speaking, they wouldn't have run into a problem since you don't see them for the rest of the game.  I feel they simply gave the player too much data at the beginning and then they don't address it except in a few conversations.   It's a writing error to give the player more data than the character you play as has in the game.  It tends to feel very frustrating as a player/viewer/reader.  They could have even kept the mid end credits scene and it would have been fine because that is an appropriate time to let the player know more is happening.
Bugs:  At the time of this review most of the bugs had been fixed.  The only one I ran into now is a strange waypoint situation where sometimes the waypoint doesn't update.  I only just discovered this in the last area of the game (which I beat last night).  I think it's the result of an update though, because I do think I experienced it once just prior to that.  Nothing major, you just keep going and it will update, but it can get a bit confusing in reference to more open areas.
Overall: This game is still very good.  I enjoy it thoroughly for what it is.  I have some complaints about the UI, such as the new energy level display mechanic is better looking but not nearly as telling as the last one.  I definitely have to suggest this game at this point if you like the previous game as much as a lot of people did.  I have seen some complaints about the Microtransactions, but it's the same as what EA did with Deadspace.  Optional if you wanted it, not at all necessary.  The load times were a bit ridiculous at first, but they are loading an entire area of prague with all it's hidden corridors, people and events.  Once you load into a section or prague there is no loading what so ever.  Load times also change depending on the size of the area you are going to.  Smaller areas load pretty quick, as do save loads into the same area you are already in.  But it really is long when switching areas.  They fill this with kind of neat world flavor with some videos that play as Jensen rides the train with other people, or walks through subway tunnels when the train is shut down.  Total playtime at the time of this was 29 legitimate play hours.

Brothers - A Tale of Two Sons is a simplistic, yet provoking game in which you play as two brothers (simultaneously) on a quest to rescue their father from an unknown ailment. The story, character backgrounds and even your mission are shrouded in an unknown (probably gibberish) language, forcing you to rely on what the character's body language and surroundings are telling you. While it may seem difficult at first, the game does a marvelous job of keeping you on track and never feeling truly lost. It's a delicate balance that the game does quite well. I never felt lost, scrambling for what to do next.
Without delving too much into the plot (for fear of giving away any spoilers), the story is straight forward, but very powerful. As the game progressed, I couldn't help but feel connected to the brothers, their family and the cast of characters you meet along the way. Without language, you're not so much being told what is happening, but experiencing it first hand, which was a treat.
Visually, the game is filled with eye candy. The environments are beautiful and change drastically as you progress, letting you see a plethora of sights - from charming villages to the aftermath of a war zone. It's as visually appealing as it is thought provoking. Overall, the game is enjoyable, albeit short. If you enjoy puzzle games with some emotional storytelling, I would highly recommend this game to you.
Overall, the pros heavily outweigh a few cons in my opinion. This one easily goes into my games recommendation list. It's a pleasure from start to finish, but remember to bring a a few tissues with you just in case.

Heroes and Generals is a WWII-themed multiplayer shooter. It claims to be a MMO, which is partially true. It features a lot of  popular MMO systems, such as teired gear and long grinds. It does not, however, support many players on a single map. The maximum amount of players, per match, is barely 42, at most. Usually, however, it maxes out at 36. These aren't small, DoD/DoI-style maps, (that don't feel crowded, even at max players,) but huge, open maps, easily over kilometers in size.
Heroes and Generals simply isn't a competitive game. There are too many issues, be them with balance, visuals, sound or hitreg, (all of which I will cover in greater depth later,) to make it a fair, well-rounded game.
When you begin playing this game, it is exciting and enjoyable, as everybody is new, like you, and learning the ropes. Everybody has the same weapons and equipment, so the balance issues aren't apparent. Then, just when it starts getting fun, they dump you into 'Gold Matchmaking'. Think of it as being akin to 'Global Elite' in CSGO. Unlike CSGO, though, you don't get placed into skill groups based upon skill, you get placed in them based upon your lifetime score.
Once it hits 12K, you are locked into Gold Matchmaking, with no option of returning. You are trapped with every other player in the game. This ranges from the newest players in Gold Matchmaking, to the best, brightest and longest-playing players in the game. It becomes a slaughterfest, as you get dominated again and again by higher-teir weapons and players that greatly outmatch your own skill level. The game becomes unfun and tedious
.
Your starter rifle is in no way ineffective, but it requires modifications to become truly competitive. Modifications that you have to grind for, and then buy. The most effective modifications are at the end of the weapon's 'ribbon', and aren't cheap. You can easily grind for hours to unlock them, then get stopped because you still haven't grinded enough money for 'em.
This game is riddled with sound issues. The game's netcode drops gunshot sounds like an old man with parkinsons and a broken piggybank. A lot of the time, you won't hear the gunshot, only the bullet as it whizzes past/kills you (You can't even use the sound of the passing bullet to find the shooter). The game's poor muzzle-flash code goes hand-in-hand with this, with the guns sometimes neglecting to show that a player has fired 'em.
Hitreg is random in H&G. Sometimes it works fine, sometimes it is horrid. The easiest way to demonstrate this is to show you the end of a video where a tank shoots at a plane, viewable at this
(I advise turning down the audio, though)
Three shells, that visually detonated on the aircraft, dealt no damage whatsoever. The game simply decided that, even though they hit, they didn't hit. This applies to all forms of combat, but is most obvious when tankers shoot at pilots, as some of their shots simply decide not to hit.
The graphics in the game are another issue. There are bushes everywhere, and after a certain distance the game will render them as being completely opaque. This means that, if anybody is hiding behind them, you cannot phyically see them. They can still shoot you through them, however. This makes camping an extremely powerful tactic, one that, if pulled off right, can net a lot of easy kills and change the tide of a match. I'd be fine with this, if it wasn't for this garbage bush-rendering logic, and the utter♥♥♥♥♥♥♥sound system.
Weapon balance is a difficult topic to describe in this game, as weapons are teir-based. The game follows a simple 'later gear = better gear' system. The early SMGs, Pistols and LMGs are worse than their late-teir counterparts, with the exception of the MG42, which was greatly over-nerfed. Usually, the only reason to use early-teir gear is that they cost less to repair, but Pistols cost more the lower-teir they are. That's right, the
the pistol is, the
(I will cover Repair Costs later.)
Balance in this game isn't based upon overall statistics, but the statistics of the teir group. Teir-2 SMGs are balanced against other Teir-2 SMGs, while being better than their Teir-1 counterparts.
Tanks also work like this. The higher teir the tank, the better it is. If you know what you are doing, you can skip half the tanks in the game, because there is simply no reason to buy them. I have skipped the T28, M4A1 Sherman, T34/76, Pz3, Pz4, Pz38(t), Bt7, T38, SU76, Jumbo Sherman, KV85, Pz2C and M3Lee, simply because they are not worth using. I haven't bought the Tiger 2, simply because the Tiger 1 does it's job almost as well, without costing me 800cr each time I spawn it. (It also looks more iconic, lol.)
You have to pay repair costs on your equipment in H&G. Every bullet you fire, car you spawn or grenade you toss comes out of your wallet. Some of these costs are cheap, like 0.1cr per shot for your basic rifle. Others, however, cost a lot. A fully modded BA rifle costs about 40cr per shot. Anti-Tank Weapons are very expensive, but also slightly imbalanced. The German/SU AT grenades cost 190 per throw, while the US AT grenade costs 380. You will need, on average, 3 to kill a tank. Your reward for this will be, at max, 330cr.
The game is designed to encourage you to use real money in every way possible, and hinder your fun if you choose to play for free. The Veteran Membership that paying players can get is borderline OP anyway, as it allows you to carry a fourth weapon and a second combat badge. A fourth weapon in a loadout isn't that much, but a second badge can be the difference between winning a gunfight and losing it.
An example badge is Heavyset, which, at it's highest level, reduces all incoming damage (even falling) by 15%. This prevents fully modded BA rifles from OHKing you, but also means that a lot of other guns become less effective. Unmodded BA rifles will require
bodyshots to kill a target with heavyset gold, resulting in a minumum Time To Kill (TTK) of 3.4 seconds. This, once again, comes down to the pitiful balance logic that Reto have designed for the game.
There are numerous little issues and poor design decisions that plague this game, but I won't go into much detail as I have already made this review into a poorly-organised Wall of Text. Instead, I will now end the review with a few extra words and a TL;DR.

Heroes and Generals is a frustrating, poorly coded mess of a game. While playable, it is in no way well balanced or competitive. I encourage everybody to try the early stages of the game, as it is good fun, albeit with long queue times. However, I cannot recommend this game after you hit Gold Matchmaking, due to how frustrating and un-fun it is.
My personal score? 2/5. Not good enough.

I'm afraid this franchise might fall into disarray like so many before it because of this silly new fad of making half♥♥♥♥♥♥♥content and then selling it, that DLC and microtransactions have so easily allowed these days.
Yes. Ultimately, it's a good game. I give it 8/10

You can disable each individual HUD piece in the menu
If you liked Warband: Napoleonic Era you should like this. It has some ups but it also has its downs due to early access nature. The game is lacking a lot of content that it needs to be a full game and some features like melee combat need significant work. I was hesitant to purchase because its early access but it was worth the 20 dollars. If you're not familar with Warband then I recommend doing some research before purchasing the game.
There are only two playerable factions which are France, and Britain. Both factions use the same class list. Theres an array of voice commands to use and they're spoken in native languages. There is currently no cavalry. There are unique units for the naval maps in marines, sailors, etc...
Each class has a set loadout but the games arsenal is limited. Weapons include muskets, musketoons, rifles, pistols, swords, pikes. There are also cannons that anyone can load and fire with ammo that lies in boxs. You can play drummers, fifers, etc... or a flag bearer to boost the reloading and accuracy of the men around you. The mucisians have an array of songs they can play. If you stand next to a fellow mucisian when you go to the song list and choose the highlighted song to play in sequence.
Shooting mechanics are pretty good. I hit targets easily up to 20m and struggle beyond 50m. Though I did see one player get a shot from 200m away! Cannons fairly easy to use. Theres round ball shot and also chain shot on naval maps that rips their sails apart. Ships can be sunk.
The melee needs significant work. Theres a large delay when attacking and blocking. The key layout doesn't help either so you'll want to change that right away.
I'm not sure how many maps in total but I want to say around a dozen considering theres multiple maps for 4 game mods.
Theres a good amount of team work. My first game had me lining up in front of an officer at spawn and we headed out in a proper line formation however it all falls apart as soon as you get to combat. There's also VOIP. I haven't had any problems with people being rude but only a few people use it and only at the start and end of the match.

Really good considering its early access and this game is made by three people that self funded this game, I personally think they deserve some slack. Many systems are already great, the graphics are really good. Main things that need work is the melee, because it is a bit clunky. Also needs some optimization, but that is coming. I definitely don't regret my purchase.

Rage Drive is an amazing function to the game.
Slowmotion is one of the best features they decided to add, it adds tension during the fight and really does the job.
Some iconic, great characters from previous games are excluded entirely (Such as Bruce Irwin), and there seem to be no plans to add them in the future either.
Rage Art is a letdown function to the game in my opinion. Unfortunately, there is no option to disable the usage of it in a match.
DLCs are a joke, don't bother with the season pass.
Customization used to be a lot better. In TTT2, it had not only a larger variety of customs, but also decals which were an amazing decorative function.
In addition to fewer customs and the complete absence of decals, Tekken 7's customization is an extreme downgrade from its TTT2 counterpart.
you actually can't put head accessories with a custom hair. The hair automatically reverts to the basic hair the character has.
I highly recommend the game, the standard version, that is. The PC version is amazing and does not fail expectations.

CONS:

This is, perhaps, my first long fantasy RPG experience, outside of Baten Kaitos and FF titles. It's definitely got a lot of lore/story/in-game history, and some fun line choices, but it does get a little repetitive and long-drawn, and the fights get easier as you level up. Even if you change difficulty part way through to hard, the monsters retain their easiness. I didn't die even once, which is a first for me in a game. No real romance or S/O options, though you do get maybe one in the main game, and two in the Dead Kel DLC, and they don't seem to be gender-limited. I've only played through once, though.
There's a LOT to do in this game, especially if you like doing sidequests. Unfortunately, the studio went down, and several people have posted issues with bugs (the only one I had was a resolution/screen one that got fixed tinkering around in the settings), and I only had one side quest glitch out on me because I approached from the wrong side. It's open world, though, so I guess that was bound to happen at some point.
This game's got a lot of beautiful scenery though, and has had quite a few humorous lines, so it's not hardcore serious, and it's especially funny watching some of the bodies fly around when they die.
The game's definitely got a lot of story to it, yet I wouldn't exactly call it story-rich, since I went more than halfway thru the game without noticing events lining up, or understanding things as part of an over-arching arc with the main questline, and the main quest itself is a little lacking of interest imo, but I did enjoy learning what the loose ends were at the very end.
Since I've not yet played any of the other major fantasy A-RPGs, I can't vouch for how it fares up to stuff like Dragon Age and TES, but I can say that it's definitely worth trying. You get at least 2 free hours to explore and do whatever in the demo, which is a pretty good indication of what you'll get to experience in the rest of the video game. Or you'll find out if you can run it or not.
If you get it on sale that's an even better deal, but if you can get all the DLC + base game for $20 or less, that's worth the length and adventure in my book.

If you get this game in a bundle or for <$2, it's just about worth the 30-45 minutes it takes to play it.  There are 12 scenarios, each of which have 5 mostly static scenes that you can rotate around in 3D and then put in sequential order.  When you do, it shows them to you again in order and you go to the next.  If you get it wrong (once I switched two scenes), it shows you which ones were right so you can fix the rest.  That's it, you're done, back to the menu.
Someone went to a lot of trouble to make these cute 3D scenes in the Unreal engine.  They are charming, and a few illustrate interesting potential stories that you can imagine going on, but two or three seem totally throw-away, such as one with harvesting on a farm and one with a goal in a soccer game.
It's kind of clever, but not really worth paying money for, and it's very easy and short with no replay value at all.  Sorry.

I'm reccomending it but only if you liked what you saw in the trailer, because it's pretty much what you're going to get, and you don't mind dealing with questionable gameplay. Basicly here's what you get: a couple of good ideas, great voice acting, decent humor and outdated and medicore gameplay.
The good idea seems to come from it trying to blend RTS, strangely in the vein of Blitzkrieg (of all games), with a traditional 3rd person action adventure game with a tad of a spectle fighter. The problem here is that the game plays a lot like a previous previous gen game (I mean it) - like a PS1 or a PS2 game, and even then there are plenty of PS2 era games that have better controls than Brütal Legend, like GTA: San Andreas. But the title it really reminds me the most is Conquer's Bad Fur Day from the N64, and as much as I like Conquer's you won't hear me praise it's gameplay, because it has aged poorly.
And that's where BL fails, it woks, the mechanics work, but they don't work too well, everything is a bit wonky. But sometimes this is a virtue: the driving stages where the player has to defend the bus end up working well, because all the player has to do is drive normally but pressing the shooting button. The art design also deserved a better engine, and if there's a game that would beneffit in the future from a remake, it'd be this one, because the only thing that looks rendered as intented are the cartoony characters, but the environments are rather poor with a lot of pop-ins and low density.
Now I'm giving this game a pass on the gameplay because it's functional, you can finish the game, something that can't be said for other games. But beware that it will be only the story that pushes you forward to finish it.
Another great idea comes from using lights in the distance to signal the objective, it allows you to appreciate the scenery instead of being focused on a compass on the side of the screen. However the sceneary because of the engine is a bit confusing and too similar, and the lack of clearly defined roads and signs also make driving less pleasant than it should be.
The performance is also lackluster, I pretty much get around the same frame-rate running on my desktop and my laptop with rotten rocks for graphics, and the game always struggles to stay at 60 or feel fluid at 60 fps because of this. The sidequests are fairly pointless, they give you points to spend in upgrades but you don't really need those upgrades, and they're all very repetitive.

A startling concoction of strategy and "hack'n'slash" gameplay, Mount & Blade: Warband presents a fresh atmosphere of adventure to the RPG community. A game that truly immerses it's player in its own world, Mount & Blade: Warband is capable of delivering a myriad of dynamic and altogether gripping playthroughs. Any who enter the legendary world of Calradia and lay stake in it's war-torn realms will be forever engrossed in the sense of adventure, danger, pride and fantasy that exists around every corner in this game. Be it from the deserts of the Sarranid Sultanate to the cold taiga of the Kingdom of the Vaegirs, Mount & Blade: Warband offers unique landscapes and play styles for it's community, and for those who cannot find comfort in the game's native setting - fear not. There is a plethora of stunning, hard-worked mods that will allow for better immersion and even total conversions of the game.
When you pay $19.99 for Mount & Blade: Warband, you are not just paying for another lackluster adventure game. You are paying for the experience of a lifetime. You are paying to become the greatest adventurer ever seen in Calradia, the most skilled warrior in any of the realms' armies, the military commander with the greatest for strategy, and even the Emperor of all Calradia.
These playthroughs are just a few of the options presented in Mount & Blade: Warband. So, what are you waiting for? Get your sword, saddle up, and add this baby to your cart.

Amazing level design.  The levels are labyrinthine and ingenious.  Some individual levels in this (The Sword, to name just one) are some of the most interesting I've ever played.  Likewise, there are no quest markers and you are usually only given a crudely drawn map (if even that) to find your way around, which is a refreshing change of pace compared to newer games.  The result is that while this is billed as a "stealth" game (and it definitely is) I'd say the biggest element of gameplay is navigating your way around huge levels and solving various puzzles.  This could very well suck, but luckily the levels themselves are well designed enough to keep things interesting.
Unfortunately the game stumbles somewhat (and begins to show its age) when you run into the combat segments.  I'm still not entirely sure why the designers thought this game needed zombies as it works perfectly fine as just a stealth/exploration game.  But luckily this is (mostly) not enough to ruin a great game.

The single player lives up to the high standards of previous GTA titles. The online portion however has gotten gradually worse with increasingly overpriced and trivial content. I don't have a issue with micro transactions generally but when a car can cost £40 of real money it's gone too far. We've had no meaningful story or map updates in almost 4 years. A lot of the new DLCs are not only expensive but just reskinned versions of other DLCs with a few very minor differences in gameplay. Since the VIP update Rockstar seem to have taken to strategy of forcing player to do missions in public sessions and rewarding players for destroying other peoples cargo creating a very toxic environment. A lot of the business style gameplay is very dull usually involving driving to one end of the map picking up supplies and the same for resupply missions. Don't get me wrong there are decent elements to GTA online like the track creator, cars and heists being a few but considering within just 1 year we got 2 huge single player DLCs with new characters missions and cars in GTA IV it just feels like Rockstar/TakeTwo are getting greedy with GTA Online.
I would not recommend this game on PC if you plan on using mods because the company have gotten greedy trying to get players to only play the official online to get more shark card sales. Especailly when a lot of the mods they are banning are single player only.

Currently very tired and boasting an absolutely miniscule playtime, but I feel this product of love deserves a thought or two.  If only as a first impression and one perhaps lacking in quality or accuracy; I may revise later as time permits.  My early access review as of April 24, 2016.
Unlike other games, Grimm Eclipse knows what it wants to be: a fast paced hack and slash, and has its mechanics and control systems are built to accomodate it.  The quick dodging, hit combo'ing, and ranged attacks allow for a fast and fun Devil May Cry-like experience in an anime/RWBY setting as you dash amongst enemies, keeping your combo climbing ever higher in what makes to be a pleasantly fluid experience.
At the current moment, the huntresses also feel rather delicate; a small number of swipes from lesser enemies and single attacks from heavier ones pack a wallop; this helps encourage dodging and quick thinking.
While I tend to stay away from MOBAs, I felt like the leveling system worked quite well in a hack and slash system.  Distributing my points inbetween fights allowed me to take stock and adapt to changing situations by dynamically distributing my skill points accordingly.  However, this leads us to a con in the future.
An absolutely necessary component of any hack and slash.  WASD simply cannot compare to the full angular freedom of motion an analog stick can bring to the table, and an appreciated coding job from the devs.
While expected, it's greatly appreciated that when playing multiplayer solo, you are not expected to take on a 4-man team's worth of enemies.  As people join, the enemies become more aggressive and more numerous, making a 4-man melee quite hectic and adding incentive to stacking parties.
I'll be the first to admit that while I find the universe of RWBY very interesting, the plot somewhat eludes me; not from a high level of complexity, but simply because my memory is awful.  However, from playing ingame campaign missions, there seems to be little significance to what the characters are doing besides "guard this" or "explore that" with little payoff during or afterwards.  "Why am I a student here?"  "What will dropping this bomb do?  I thought we were trying to escape somehow."  "What are the Grimm?"
It is one thing to be immersed in the universe, and another to be taken on a sightseeing tour.  And while it may be argued that one should be familiar with the plot of the animated series before coming into the game, I still stand that the game should stand on its own to a degree.
To address this, there needs to be more thought put into the missions themselves: what are the characters doing?  Why are they here?  What implications will there be from killing Grimm in one location versus another?  As of now, they play like Left 4 Dead missions.  A rush from point A to B in different locations.
Truthfully, this has always been a thing in the english dub of RWBY, so much so that it has unfortunately become a defining character of the series.  I speak no jest when I say that some of the voice acting is absolutely cringeworthy, at least ingame.  If you're able to put up with it and simply have some hack and slash fun, all the power to you.  Devs, check out the Japanese Dub for RWBY if you want to learn to make good voiceovers.
The combat system borrows a page from the Arkham Asylum style of combat with being able to counter most enemy attacks.  However, the camera will frequently hide an impending attack from view and even when it doesn't, it is sometimes unclear what an enemy is about to do.  Some attacks are announced by counter signals, other attacks by a strange clam-like signal (of which I am still unclear), and other attacks are announced by unsignaled enemy animations, such as hunching into a ball.  I had to learn all of this from sheer trial and error.
The lack of consistency combined with the uncooperative camera can make for a frustrating experience at times, an issue that could be fixed with some work on the camera, a simplification of enemy telegraphing, or a tutorial to teach players what to look out for.
In personal experience, a key trait of the hack-and-slash is that the fostering of a large variety of fighting styles; a look at Dynasty Warriors and Devil May Cry will prove that much.  In Grimm Eclipse however, most of the huntresses play similarly, and while their perks can add effects to their attacks, they tend serve as buffs instead of a split in fighting styles.  As a result, combat is slightly different with each build but not so much as to support an interesting range of styles and tactical options.
Many options are also unnecessarily locked behind some pretty hefty grindwalls that often involve doing a certain thing a certain number of times, which will make combat feel even more repetitive for new players, the audience for whom retention is the most important.
Finally, experience gained is mostly player-only apart from artifacts and (I believe) +25xp dust orbs.  This can lead to an unhealthy party experience as players fan out to claim enemy spawn areas instead of helping allies in order to claim the most experience or to hit the elusive level 10.
If the game is going to draw a page from MOBA leveling, let it be from Heroes of the Storm where players all share the same level and contribute to each other's leveling.  I feel that the cooperative experience can be benefited in that way.
A couple of minor points that become greater problems when combined with the ones above:
As I was still having a blast racking up combos, but once you achieve a certain level of strength, it becomes possible to eliminate some enemies with a single combo every time.  While this quickly becomes unsustainable against large crowds, it makes most non-boss 1v1 fights nothing more than an chore and a reminder to the general lack of diverse, interesting fighting styles.
Also, when brought down to critical health, it rarely takes more than a second of respite to fully regenerate it all again.  While this may make gameplay too easy for some, when coupled with the camera issues and unclear enemy telegraphing above, this makes for a lot of getting hit, and a lot of running around waiting for health to regenerate.  This breaks the action and can get tedious, while also making death rather difficult.
Deserved a mention for those buying in early, but hey.  It's early access.
Quite a few of the cons listed above can truly be forgiven for now as the game is still in early access, and still very much looks/plays like a game in early access.  There is an incredible list of things that need fleshing out: the story, the combat, the UI, the characters, the leveling, etc etc.  However, it is clear that the devs know what they want to do and the audience that they're trying to deliver to.
I'd recommend the buy if you're a fan of the RWBY series, Monty Oum's work, or an anime fan in general.  Those that enjoy hack and slash games will also be in for a treat.

Anything written here is subject to change as the game is updated.
Shoppe Keep is a "sim" of sorts where you take on the role of a shoppekeeper starting out in an empty two-room shoppe. Over the days you take small profits earned and invest them back into the shoppe in the form of new displays, room expansions, and of course purchasing new inventory. Unfortunately, it's not an incredibly deep game as of yet. There is a system of crafting that is rather convoluted and will require a guide if you want to actually make an item rather than waste money. There is also a champion in your shoppe whom you can send out on quests resulting in either new (potentially rare) items to sell, or a KO and a waste of your investment.
The soundtrack is good, if a bit samey (you'll be hearing the same few pieces several times per play session), and the game has a sense of humor to it. There are definitely aspects that need to be fleshed out further (and I suspect they will be as the game is developed). Additionally, there are some quality of life updates that would go a long way to make the game more enjoyable (e.g. an ability to sort your inventory).
Due note that there have been some major bugs during development. The devs have shown that they're on top of getting things fixed as soon as they can, but you will still possible experience points where the game is very frustrating to play due to bugs. Shoppe Keep is quite clearly an example of a game much earlier in development than some others that have been bade available for Early Access.
All that said, this is a fantastic concept, and thus far shows really strong promise. It's very much playable as-is, and can be very engrossing if you let it get there. It's not particularly deep as of yet, but it's definitely deep enough to get your money's worth.

Sadly, remake of RotT is low budget curiosity.
It looks like developers couldnt reach goals they made for themselves, couldn't say if beacuse of the budget or lack of experience with engines the were working on.
RotT looks 'not bad', sometimes okay, but it's maximum that can be said about graphics. Enemy models are boring and there's less than ten of them, I guess. They're moving like glitched robots, and die just the same. Animations are not strong side of this game. Far from it. Most of levels are boring hallways, made from same templates
When it comes to mechanics, it have it's moments, but rarely. Blowing things and enemies up is fun, weird powerups are great, and few level desings are satisfactory. But jumping sections are frustrating because of not the best desing.
On the bright side is atmosphere of trashy action movie/comic. On this field game is fully aware of itself and is making it main advantage. Some powerups and are sensationally absurd, and main characters quotes are sometimes really fun.

Nice way to clear my FPS palete after slowly working my way through Dishonored.  ROTT is fundamentally an arcade run-and-gun type game that is great for mindless fun.
The game enforces the run-and-gun style with a couple features.  Frequent death via traps take the sting out of dying.  Missles weapons are essentially use-it-or-lose-it, without which I'd be unable to abandon my ammo-hoarding ways.  The character movement speed is quite fast compared to a game like Dishonored or Bioshock, and maybe even slightly faster than Unreal Tournament.
The negatives are the occasional game glitches like getting stuck and the occasional overly-elaborate acrobatic puzzle stages.  But these are minior annoyances.  Loving this version even better than the original.

I had at one point refused to purchase this game due to the lack of quicksaves. Now, however, the developers have chosen to reverse that decision, and the result is brilliant indeed. This game is ten times what the original was, especially due to the advent of jumping controls. The multiplayer is where the game really shines, however marred it is by the utter uselessness of any weapon that isn't magical or a rocket launcher. The Dog Mode and the game's penchant for throwing the eyeballs and gore of slain and gibbed enemies on your screen in uproarious fashion are particularly humorous.
If you're looking for a good old-school multiplayer arena shooter with a modern flair, look no further.

This game really captures the feel of the old school 90s shooters.
They really hit a home run redoing this game.  The game is actually hard!  I was just about to give up hope that Halo and more modern games which funnel you through the game (so you don't get stuck) had left dificult gaming as a lost art.
They did mimic some of the levels from the orriginal game which is awesome, but the game is not a secret finding fest like the old one was unfortunately.

I'm saying this as someone who had never played the original. It's not a horrible game really but I can't wrap my head around the jumping. Every character plays drastically different which is nice but it's hard to find a balance. The shooting portion of the game is sweet, good kills even if the weapons are repitative, really has that cheesey 90's feel to it. If you're easily frustrated by a very touchy jumping mechanic (fps platforming in general) I would recommend a pass on this one.

When I heard Rise of the Triade was getting a redo I was fairly skeptical but after viewing footage and seeing the progress I preordered the game, however after hearing about it's serious game breaking issues when it was finally let out I waited.  Five months from the initial release of this game and it still has some fairly serious problems, even basic bugs are still in this game.  The level geometry is unpolished and at times sharp; during heavy fighting or boss fights you will also be fighting the level as well.  You will constantly get stuck up on objects that either are not there or are simply toe high obstacles that even the most basic old school game would just allow you to walk over and I am not even joking, in some cases it gets bad.  Only about an hour or 2 into my initial play through my game looses its ability to quick load, for no reason, and looses it for an entire level and a half.  The reason this is a big issue is because the checkpoint system in this game, while functions, does not help when the player is forced to deal with the broken gameplay and "puzzles".  When you are forced to restart an entire area because you can't load from your quick save (attempting to do so outright froze and crashed the program) sections of levels become very Very frustrating.  I have to mention this, as of this writing the achievements still do not work 100%, beating the game net’s you maybe half of what you’re supposed to get, Yet there have been patches dedicated to fixing this and other issues, which makes me wonder.
The game is trying far too hard to try and be "old school" but it fails pretty hard; some basic designs do make it in sure but over all it was far from enjoyable or memorable.  The so called puzzles are nothing but jump pads, and again this is where the game falls flat, your character floats around, not too much but just enough to skip clear across objects that you should have been able to land on.  Other times you'll jump clear over the very small floating islands only to fall to your death and be insulted by the game.  One section in particular will cause you a great deal of frustration, this so called "puzzle" was a small room of jump pads, this room took me around a 45 minutes to an hour to finally get the finicky player movement and poor controls to work before I could pass just that one section.
Boss fights, this game sure has something along the lines of boss fights, just nothing like they used to be or should have been.  Some boss fights are simple or just outlast and outshoot all but one has multiple forms to them so be prepared to fight the same enemy again 2 or 3 times.  All of them are extremely unforgiving even on medium; some are only beaten by pure Luck or a series of coincidences that brought you to a victory rather then skill or learning a pattern.  The final boss can almost only be beaten by using basically a "magic pixel" an area where the boss can't hit you; otherwise the arena and the actual boss are just completely unbeatable.
I had a lot of hope for this game and to its credit the first hour or two were fun, however after a while and about 30 quick loads later it soon became clear that this was not the remake I was hoping for, nor was it close to the original.  The comedy, honestly I could not see it, not taking this game serious in any way I found the comedy forced and dry, it lacked the charm of the original in some ways, that and the jokes have already been done before.  Sorry but an achievement to watch the credits is always an automatic point deduction, especially when the credits are almost thirty minutes LONG!
I will give the game a few things to its credit, one, the music, very good, it gets you in the mood and you have the option to turn off the remastered music and play the game with the original music, cool idea.  Second the game looks great, for the most part, there were some really dull and low resolution textures, however the effects and environments looked great, though I think that’s more thanks to the Unreal Engine more then the game developers to be fair.
Unless you as a player are the most die hard Quake 3 Arena or Serious Sam fan I would stay away from this remake, while it does some things well, the over all package was not very enjoyable.  Keep in mind my time spent playing, I will say that 40% of that time was spent redoing boss fights and jump puzzles.  If you must buy this game wait for a 50 or more percent off sale.

I personally rate the original ROTT as a classic (better than Doom and Duke Nukem IMO) and this is a good remake.  They've kept to the same ideas and the devs have taken Lee Jackson's original epic midi and turned it into a heavy metal soundtrack! It suits the game a treat and is absolutely brilliant.  The only negative is that it is slightly hefty on system requirements at higher gfx settings and there are bits that cause a bit of framelag even with a decent rig, but I am being picky.  I would highly recommend it at the price and would rate it as the best first person shooter of 2013 in my humble opinion.  A must have for any FPS enthusiast - 9/10

DAY 1 REVIEW
When I first got it..I was unsure, I hesitated watching the timer slowly tick toward the 2hr non refundable deadline.
Initial issues...first game I click on....black screen back to the main game menu.
WHAT?!.. This happened 3 times. I was getting mad. So like an adult I went to the community hub and found out from a dev post that the number of players ingame is incorrect for servers and that the black screen is caused by the server being full. They just havent added a "server full" text yet. Ok so I am less mad now..black screen for a second means server is full and to keep clicking join or find a different one.
(UPDATE) Black screen fixed, in under 24hrs, If you buy this game now, you will not experience it.
Get in first game, 126 players playing, gunfire all around me, I fire 1 shot just testing stuff out and now i cant reload..... I keep stabbing the air..well WTF? check game controls X is melee mode, i press x...this is does not do anything..i then press every button on my keyboard, my man starts shouting crouching jumping stabbing wildly at passerbys as if I am possesed. Even now, if I use a bayonet, i can not fire my gun again. others can...so its a bug..i swapped to a different class..flag bearer!.... Now I just scream and stand there during a enemy charge while my team gets their bayonetts ready. I feel I am helping. I can stab with my flag, pull out a sword, or a pistol.
(UPDATE: Bayonet is working for some of my classes now)
So there I am, standing with a flag, huge target..and what do I hear?..drums! ...a flute?...I look behind me, and marching up next to me is a band! I join their ranks with my flag...others start to join, marching inline formation across a battlefield. Cannon fire flies over my head, I keep the flag high, the drummer keeps drumming, the line keeps marching into the center of the fray. The man infront of me falls, had he not been there my flag holding career would have ended. More drop around me, we return fire, smoke billowing from every musket hazing the battlefield. We exhange vollleys for 2 minutes when someone screams charge! with baoyonnets fixed (expect for me ofcourse) Our line charges. Me out infront, flag held high for all to see as we push forward past all our allied units and collide with the enemy. this is when the melee comes into play and god is it awful. the tragedy wasnt the lives lost that day for England...it was how they were lost during the melee portion. It still haunts me.
My review is getting long, aside from the line battles there are ships battles that are absoluetly fun! and costal battles where ships try to take a fort (havent played one yet)  Its almost two games..the ship battles are MUST play though Nothing like 120 players spread out on 8 or more ships in various sizes battling it out.Full control, you got a captian that steers, crew man who fire cannons and load them, royal marines who find off boarding parties..yes you can board enemy ships. ..point of my story is..this game has some serious bugs, and needs a good bit of work. But theres alot of games out there like that, and i tend to have an amazing time in them anyway.
A dev was in game playing on the same server, I looked at their profile, they have 1,440hrs logged into mount and blade. You can tell they care, you can tell they want to play with us, and hey it just launched, the Melee needs improvement and they know this, they are literally playing it with us. So yes, support these guys, its still loads of fun, just dont take it too serious when those lines collide just yet. I see lots of potential and I do not regret my purchase.
UPDATE: Melee has gotten better, server is more fluid, melee seems quicker and i feel i have more control.
UPDATE Severs can now handle 150 players, and it is expected to keep going up.

The game was overhyped and realistically so. People who hyped this game up were either the people who are self advertising their own game and company that they worked with, or people who were told it would be good and just listened to them because they have nothing else to look forwards to in a community.
This game was released in Alpha, yes. People usually expect Alpha games to be broken and have a lot of bugs, or be poorly optimized because of course... It's ALPHA. However, this goes beyond the line of Alpha. It's not even a technical test version. It was in comparison to how early EA's Battlefront was released except that was playable. To be fair, EA is a major company and this game was not made by a big company, but I would expect a smaller company to make better decisions than EA. Hell, even better than Ubisoft.
The main part of this game is suppose to be shooting and melee, however, those are both terrible. Most of the budget most likely went into advertising this game to overhype it. The animations are unpolished, the jumping makes it seem like they have a turtle poking it's head out their♥♥♥♥♥ and the melee is like people who have casts on each arm poking each other with sticks. The melee is poor and it's more like a dancing simulator with the occasional sparks from the metal hitting and someone dying, but most of the time you'd end up being shot mid-melee.
The shooting is pretty poor when it comes to the differents with rifles and muskets. There seems to be no difference in accurracy or reticle size to them as well as not being able to block with a rifle.
The riflemen especially have it worse since they have to pull out their sabre to fight and even then, the lag between the changing of weapons is pretty damn poor.
This is one of those games that may not even leave Alpha, and if it does, then I commend the devs for it, but this is not acceptable for an Alpha game.

Ok, I have a few things to say. But this is a pretty fun game, i cant wait to see whats to come. That said, this isnt fully what i wanted in a RWBY game. The ideal rwby game for me would be a game in which you get to create your character, choose attire, design your own weapons, and go through the games campaign in a 4 person coop, if they made it an mmo itd just be cheating the players for a variety of reasons, first and foremost being mmos literally HAVE to have some form of either "pay to win" or "pay to vanity", Its how they thrive. Id much rather it be like Borderlands than SWTOR or LOTRO. for a better multiplayer experience it would also be really neat to include a tournement mode. Like they had in the actual show, with teams competing against eachother. Imagine that, you grab your friends with your sick character thats asthetically pleasing and your mad weapons and all that. (Adding armour would just sorta ruin the clothing, youd want to keep as close to the show as possible) and face off against other teams. This is my ideal RWBY game.
Now onto THIS game. Dont get my words twisted, this game is very fun, 4 players, 4 characters. The characters of the show, Ruby, Weiss, Blake and Yang, pretty standard stuff. You go through a few short levels with fellow players (or by your self), and as the game advertises, you hack and slash your way through them. You gain XP and upgrade abilities, and there are a few bonuses that actually really made me wanna strive to get them, for example whenever you are defending an objective against literal waves of enemies, at the end of each wave one player will recieve a MVP XP bonus of 50 points, and i really wanted to get that as much as possible. Now I have a few problems with the game, In the game there are side paths to pick up artifacts (The chess pieces from S1), but not every side path has a chess piece, or even a crate, some just have nothing, and Im fine with having misleading paths to make it a challange, but it looked as if you could keep going, but if you tried to continue down your path by say... Jumping up a hill, youd end up looking through the map. What im saying is some of the hitboxes for walls can be a bit ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥. I also encountered a glitch in which a laggy player joined my game and one of my players just couldnt move at all. no controls responded, pressing esc didnt fix it, waiting didnt fix it, and alt tabbing didnt fix it. A serious problem in quick match games. Another problem is that theres no way of knowing which characters have already been chosen by your other team mates once you join, and the game allows for multiple of the same character. So i joined a team of 3 weiss's... as weiss. and they were all attacking the same enemy. But over all, this game is above average and well worth the price, but not over $20, Its a work in progress, yet it has tonnes of potential, even now id consider it a very fun and enjoyable game.
TL;DR pretty good, 8/10, but not an ideal game concept for the RWBY universe.

“A good RPG has four aspects – exploration, narrative, advancement and then combat. And it turns out the first three things – people have been doing a pretty good job with them. But the combat, we really just haven’t been asking enough of ourselves with that and haven’t really known what an alternative would be. So we decided; the world needs an RPG with good immersive combat.” - Ken Rolston, Amalur’s Design Director (Click Online interview)
Kingdoms of Amalur did deliver on that promise. Originally planned as an innovative MMORPG, the game eventually came out as a single-player experience. Many of the flaws are actually the remains of the former structure, like the roughly 200 hours long playtime, simplified quests and vast amount of lore. The classic aspects of the rpg genre mentioned above are all flawed in KoA, but the forth one, which is considered to be meaningless considering the quality of combat systems seen in games like the Elder Scrolls and Gothic series. Something that is definitely got better in the third installment of the Witcher franchise, but still not as enjoyable as it was in Amalur or Dragon's Dogma for example. How important really is combat in a game with a strong narrative, a huge explorable world and a good progression system?
For my part, the latest rpgs which I really enjoyed are KoA and DD:DA on the pc, which are two games with great combat and weaker story and overall world cohesion. But in these cases it is enough, because these games are much more fun in the end.
One of the older examples from the era of the Infinity games (Baldur's Gate, Icewind Dale, Planescape Torment) is Temple of Elemental Evil which similarly had a good tactical combat system while its "classical rpg" aspects were less developed. It is considered a less successful game partly due to this weakness.
In the end it really depends on who the player is, what he/she seeks in these games. Thrilling action with decent progression, exploration and lore, or the more hardcore "wall-of-text" style games with immersive worlds and interesting narrative which usually needs a little bit extra imagination to fill the holes. Therefore I definitely recommend KoA to everyone looking for a fun game with great combat.

It's pretty good. Each playthrough is different. Managing a commercial empire becomes difficult as you have to really consider supply and demand. The game has such a breadth and depth that it's hard to comprehend. It's entirely possible to go through the game peacefully, to only ever defend yourself and instead engage in purely commercial ventures. It's possible to be a bandit, or a mercenary captain, or become vassaled to a king. Eventually, you're able to become a king yourself, or to rebel against one of the current rulers and place a claimant on the throne.
There are certain patterns however. Swadia, being in the middle and surrounded on all sides, usually is defeated quickly. Typically only incredible luck or the intervention of the player can save them. Cities produce the same things in all playthroughs- that is to say, Suno produces certain things in abundance (supply) and requires other things (demand.) This is the same with other cities, which all produce a variety of goods. This should be taken into consideration when making commercial ventures.
Now for the actually good stuff. The horse combat is good. By this, I mean it's very good. It make sense. It's not a gimmick and horses aren't stupidly OP. There are ways to combat them (spears, or massed pikes) which the AI don't usually take advantage of. The archery is pretty good, and the melee combat is also good. It takes time to learn the intricacies of directional blocking, feints, and that stupid angling and yawing ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t people perform in multiplayer. I remember Jedi Knight: Jedi Academy had that sort of nonsense. This kills the Camel. But don't let that stop you, the game itself is great. There's no story, of course, but that's fine. Who needs a story? You're here for good gameplay, to make your own story, to forge your own, um, thingy.
There are a couple problems. The graphics are a bit bleh, but if you want a good game, graphics aren't king. Some of the community are a bit weird, though I suppose you get that anywhere. If you desire xXxHISTORICAL_ACCURACYxXx in the year of OUR LORD 1257 (AD) then you'll be sorely disappointed. There's russians, vikings, plate-armored knights, saracens, hill-folk, and horsefuc- I mean MONGOLS. All of these factions exist in the same time frame, despite in reality being separated by centuries.  You'll notice that none of these things are actually bad. None of these "problems" make the game less playable.
D'you know why?
Because this game is good, and it's weird that there's this sort of game, and that this particular game is actually really good.
Also, Bannerlord is never coming out. All hail Warband.

As one of the first 3D stealth games, Thief Gold does a surprising number of things really well, even after only 5 missions. Dynamic lighting combines with an amazing stereo sound (get a headset) to create an intuitive atmosphere, where you're sneaking from shadow to cover, nicking things and conking guards on the head. Levels are huge, exploration is huge (no invisible walls), and the tools/arrows you have are large and varied. Top it up with a spooky, tense soundtrack and you have a real gem.
It's not all great: graphics are ofc 1998, enemy AI isn't perfect (enemies don't notice patrolling guards go missing or torches going out), the Steam version doesn't show cutscenes (which is what Youtube's for), you backtrack a bunch, item menu is a bit clunky, but all these minor setbacks don't stop it from being a great game. It takes a while to get into, but if you love nicking someone's bag of coins before whacking him on the head, it's well worth $10.

If you are a fan of the Diablo series you will find a lot to like in Torchlight.
Torchlight II is a fast-paced isometric hack-and-slash action/RPG hybrid - just like Diablo. However, although it is technically a "Diablo clone" it may be unfair to label it as a copy since Torchlight was created by two of the original members of Blizzard North who created the first Diablo. It can therefore be considered to be a spiritual successor, and in some ways it is more true to the original Diablo than the subsequent sequals.
History aside, Torchlight is a great game in its own right. It improves on the genre in a few notable ways: the addition of the pet is the most noticable. Although it may seem like a pretty small addition, it makes a big difference in the pace of the gameplay. You can send your pet to sell loot and pick up neccesary items from town for you, without having to take a break from dungeon delving to teleport to town. This means less time for inventory management, and more time for murder. Not having to repair your gear, also, I feel speeds the game up and focuses on what makes Diablo enjoyable in the first place.
I enjoyed Diablo III, but Torchlight is diverging from the Diablo series in some new and interetesting ways, and I hope that some of the gameplay innovations will be incorporated into future version of Diablo. If you enjoy hack and slash RPGs, I would recommend that you pick up a copy.

I've played the original Gunz as well as this current iteration. The community seems to be stuck in the past about the prior game's mechanics, and they continue to judge this game purely based on that. Since this game is still in the early access stage, people seem more expectant and hopeful on what may come rather than what the game currently is. For those that are trying to come to this game in hopes of finding a spiritual successor of Gunz: the Duel, the only thing this game has for you is the namesake and empty nostalgia. For those that are just finding a game to play, the game barely matches up to any other free to play out there, and truly earns its early access categorization.
Here are a few simple facts, this game was released nearly a year ago in Korea and it did not do so well there. Even after being re-released in 3 different regions (Taiwan/Malaysia, UK, US) the game looks and feels like it is still in the alpha stage. There is very little content, and the majority of the game is of low quality, subpar coding and this comes with limited hosting and servers. While there are some interesting aspects, the mechanics are being changed back and forth as Maiet is still on the fence on how they want their game to play. Even more so, for all of its hopes of trying to create a game with freedom of movement, it is outshown by many other games that feature any use of parkour. The previous game was not perfect, but it did allow you to play however you wished and gave you so much freedom that it became a technical brawl fest with a heavy learning curve.
Everything from the horrible AI, the dated textures, and the subpar user interface is barely a notch above the original, and that game had its International release in 2005. So for this game to receive an recommendation, they will need a major overhaul in the entire design of the game, as well as an increase of content.

I'm reccomending it but only if you liked what you saw in the trailer, because it's pretty much what you're going to get, and you don't mind dealing with questionable gameplay. Basicly here's what you get: a couple of good ideas, great voice acting, decent humor and outdated and medicore gameplay.
The good idea seems to come from it trying to blend RTS, strangely in the vein of Blitzkrieg (of all games), with a traditional 3rd person action adventure game with a tad of a spectle fighter. The problem here is that the game plays a lot like a previous previous gen game (I mean it) - like a PS1 or a PS2 game, and even then there are plenty of PS2 era games that have better controls than Brütal Legend, like GTA: San Andreas. But the title it really reminds me the most is Conquer's Bad Fur Day from the N64, and as much as I like Conquer's you won't hear me praise it's gameplay, because it has aged poorly.
And that's where BL fails, it woks, the mechanics work, but they don't work too well, everything is a bit wonky. But sometimes this is a virtue: the driving stages where the player has to defend the bus end up working well, because all the player has to do is drive normally but pressing the shooting button. The art design also deserved a better engine, and if there's a game that would beneffit in the future from a remake, it'd be this one, because the only thing that looks rendered as intented are the cartoony characters, but the environments are rather poor with a lot of pop-ins and low density.
Now I'm giving this game a pass on the gameplay because it's functional, you can finish the game, something that can't be said for other games. But beware that it will be only the story that pushes you forward to finish it.
Another great idea comes from using lights in the distance to signal the objective, it allows you to appreciate the scenery instead of being focused on a compass on the side of the screen. However the sceneary because of the engine is a bit confusing and too similar, and the lack of clearly defined roads and signs also make driving less pleasant than it should be.
The performance is also lackluster, I pretty much get around the same frame-rate running on my desktop and my laptop with rotten rocks for graphics, and the game always struggles to stay at 60 or feel fluid at 60 fps because of this. The sidequests are fairly pointless, they give you points to spend in upgrades but you don't really need those upgrades, and they're all very repetitive.
The voice cast is really nice from Jack Black, Jennifer Hale, Ozzy Osbourne and other metal personalities, and also including Tim Curry. who doesn't get enough lines IMHO. The story is fairly flashy and very by the books, no surprises to be had here, it's competent but nothing new. The only thing I'll complain here is that I don't get where the decision to base the obvious red herring villan on David Bowie came from. There's also a moment here and there that feels a bit rushed, but nothing major.

Back in college, I got my roommates addicted to Dominion. We played the first four expansions, then years later when the digital version came out, we've been able to play with all of them (except Adventures, as of this writing). It was a rare game that had the perfect balance of strategy, tactics, and randomness to promote table talk and interaction among players. It's an excellent game to play with friends.
With Puzzle Strike, the deckbuilding format is evolved to be more competative and aggressive, with its fascinating Crash Gem mechanic making the game feel more like a bar fight then "multi-player solitaire" as some of Dominion's detractors call it. I wouldn't go so far as to say its better than Dominion, but it definitely has a strong, competative feel that makes it exciting in ways Dominion never was.
If you like Dominion or other deckbuilders, this is an excellent game. If you are new to the genre, I'd start with Ascension or Dominion to get a feel for if that style of game is right for you. This game does have a little more of a learning curve compared to those games, and plays a bit different from other deck builders, but it is well worth the time it takes to master it.

The Good:
-The story is truly heartwrenching, and well told.
-Character building. There as numerous instances in Brothers where the distinct personalities of the two brothers shine. One is courteous, while the other is rambunctious, and all of this is masterfully communicated to the player nonverbally.
The Bad:
- The control scheme. The developers created a truly unique and innovative control scheme for Brothers, and as a positive, this feature enhanced many of the puzzles because it was not only about what to do on screen, but how to manipulate the controller to achieve the desired goal. However, the inherent awkwardness of the controls consistently pulled me out of the experience during my playthrough. This hindered the game for me, because it divested me from the driving element of Brothers - the story.
-The game’s grim tone did not match the whimsy of the aesthetic.
-On the surface Brothers is a story-driven puzzler. However, for the most part, the puzzles require absolutely no thought to get through. With such an innovative control scheme, it seems odd that the puzzles glaringly lacked imagination.
Final Verdict:
As stated, the story is well told; although, it is obvious from the start that tragedy awaits you at the conclusion of the story, and in order to reach the end, you have to wade through unimaginative puzzles and grapple with awkward controls. Afterward, there is nothing which will compel you to play Brothers a second time through. Thus, I do not recommend Brothers. I know that this review is in the minority, and so I’ll say to the interested, buy this on sale. Otherwise, you might come out of it with buyer’s remorse.

Tuesday, 23th August. I couldn't wait to play the game. I made special preparation for it even, not including the pre-load of course. I got myself some KFC chicken wings and some cola, which I would pour into my coca-cola glass I got from McDonalds as a bonus.
The clock hits 7PM, I still can't play the game, it says that it is not ready to be played yet. I decide to brush it off and wait a few minutes, perhaps slight delay. Sure enough, five minutes later I can start the process of unlocking the game, which took me about an hour on my HDD due to Steam doing very long unpacking/downloading process, which was caused by DLCs not being part of pre-load. The lack of pre-loaded DLC defeats the purpose of pre-loading. Sure enough I untick the DLCs in Steam game properties which sped up the process.
I can finally launch it. When I do, I see this game launcher pop up, as if I was playing games made ten years ago. I proudly crank up the graphical settings to the maximum for my fairly up to date rig (R9 390, i5 6600k, 16GB RAM). I press the launch button.
The intros start showing up, which are not skip-able after a very quick discovery.
Game crashes. It crashes proudly at the same point every time - AMD intro.
I brush it off again and go ahead and tweak the graphical options and display settings through the launcher (now I see why they have a launcher). It still crashes. There is no way I am verifying the whole game on this slow HDD, so I tried other things. Everything was up to date, different game launch settings. Eventually I gave up and tried verifying game files through Steam. After Steam had finished doing that, it was downloading 8GB of files. That's a joke to people who have DSL connections or worse. Luckily download speed is not a problem for me.
This time the game launches without a problem. Progress.
I started the campaign. Game crashes at the introduction videos.
*sigh*
I tinker around the graphical settings, maybe the subtitles are to blame. Nothing solved the crashes.
I decide to re-download the whole game, I freed up space on my SSD to download it there, so I could avoid any technical or performance issues. Voila, it ♥♥♥♥ing worked. I recommended this solution to fellow people on Reddit, but this seems to have worked only for me. People were reporting same identical consistent crashes as I had.
At this point the KFC was cold and I had drunk half of the cola I had. I spent three hours getting this game running without any patches installed because those were not released yet.
25 game hours later, I have finished the game. The game ended abruptly. Before that, game was zooming into this TV which had news broadcast running as per usual, re-capping the recent events. It kept zooming and zooming into the TV, and the news kept going and going. I was thinking the cut scene would continue when the news would end, but it didn't. Once I had enough I pressed a button to skip the cut scene. The game ended there.
Other than the crap ending for a story that will continue through upcoming DLCs, here is issues that should have been solved by a triple AAA company (and mind you, the game had gone gold one month before the release): mouse acceleration, crashes, performance issues for a game that doesn't even look graphically demanding, "Unmark All" prompt not going ever away (how do you not notice this during testing?), weird running animation when running up or down the stairs, some UI is misaligned (i.e. when navigating elevator menu).
My PC configuration isn't even that complicated or out of ordinary to have this many problems.
Let's not forget this game is protected by Denuvo, otherwise I would have pirated the hell out of it. You would think they would be fine with just Denuvo to get everyone to pay for their game, but turns out they need to pump more money with DLCs (and possibly story DLCs) and single-player mode micro-transactions.
I was heavily invested in this game's world, I liked exploring it, this world is beautiful. But the story ending abruptly feels like the same as when a porn video ends too early — it was just getting started on the good part.
