This iteration of Deus Ex is certainly good, though a bit lacking in a few areas compared to the previous game:
Pros:
+ Interesting cities, detailed environments, and overall presentation
+ Typical deep and engaging Deus Ex type of story
+ Lots of areas to explore, with multiple approaches to completing objetives
+ Excellent voice acting
+ You can do stealth, full on assault, or all points in between
+ New types of augs to enhance gameplay
+ Lots of things to hack (terminals, alarms, garage doors, etc
Cons:
- Very minor issues with hacking - sometimes the labels for nodes get in the way of being able to click on them; I've had trouble with having to get out of a hacked alarm pad because it wouldn't let me select the option to disable it, but going back in takes care of that
- There is so much to look at that sometimes everything seems visually overwhelming
- Dragging unconscious/dead bodies seem to get caught on doors, furniture, etc a lot
- There seems to be a short delay from when you hit the grenade button and when Jensen actually throws it
- Some of the maps areas and navigation points are a bit confusing at first
- Navigating the menus, upgrades, etc is pretty confusing until you get used to it
- Charging players to literally buy ammo, etc with real world money seems like a really odd design mechanic to me.  You can get everything you need just by playing the game, so don't waste your money.
- Lip sync issues during dialog areas are usually pretty off.  Hard to accept since Half Life 2 got it right 12 years ago.
Also, I've had zero performance issues on a i5 4.3 GHZ with a GTX 980.  However, I am not playing the game maxed out but settings are generally high/custom.  Very very rarely do I see any stuttering, etc.
I also don't care about multiplayer, nor did I buy the DLC, so I cannot comment on either of those aspects.
Bottom line:
This game is defintiely a worthy sequel to the previous game.  However, I didn't think the story was quite as engaging as the previous game's was.  While I like the fact that you have multiple ways to solve situations, the fact that there is always a vent conveniently nearby seems a little silly after a while.   Still, I can't fault the game makers for trying to give you options.
I wasn't completely blown away in the end and I certainly need a good break before trying some of the other story options.  But it definitely held my interest and I had fun with it for sure.

By the time the game boots, you'll feel like you've jumped straight back into the golden days of 2006 as EA prompts you to create some account with them in glorious 1024x768 default resolution. You'll navigate treacherous options menus the likes of which have never even heard the words "PC Port" before. You'll set the game difficulty to 'hard' and wonder if it makes a lick of a difference as you sleep through the tutorial. Your screen will whizz around in every direction at the barest nudging of the mouse!
-cue gory introduction cutscene to earn your M ESRB rating-
Behold! Graphics as 2004 intended them to- err, hold on a sec. Graphics as 2012 intended them to look! Your eyes will water and gleam with delight as upon your screen plays out visuals the likes of which early World of Warcraft could only aspire to possess (and probably achieved by Burning Crusade, I don't know, uncle Nax never got hooked on that WoW stuff, no siree). Your soft, gooey, colorful character springs out of a mound of corpses like some necrotic phoenix, ready to bop, slash, level, traverse custcene wheels (thanks, Mass Effect), and slog through menus as the RPG gods intended. Your Oblivion-playing friends are gonna be so jealous!
From simply turning your camera to navigating your inventory (and I get the feeling you'll be doing both of these things a lot), everything is designed with a controller in mind. Wanna grab that loot on the ground? F to interact, but left click 'take all' or no dice. Pop open your inventory with the I key, then click around to get to your gear submenus. Wanna don that sword? Better left click then push enter, or right click and choose 'equip.' Just clicking stuff won't do, that's too complicated!
Walk with me now, back, back. We'll step into an era with invisible walls and tight corridors, to keep the player engaged and never you mind that wooden slope that clips into the rocks and which is inexplicably uncrossable. You'll pull a lever which dumps a corpse into an incinerator, which will then thump endlessly in there until you walk away. Why's it there? Immersion! Will you see something like this again? Nope!
Walk with me, walk further back. Further back? Yes, brave reader, we're braving the nineties and before! From the first few glimpses of action, we are beset by features etched far into the history of games and television alike!
Stock sounds!
Marvel, as the giant rats you encounter make -that one pig squealing sound- that you've heard a thousand times before! Behold, as the magic IEDs the immortal elves plant on some pillars explode with -that explosion sound- that you've heard from 1994 Doom's rocket launcher! Truly, we are living in the future.
We go any further back, and Uncle Naxza's gonna have to get unborn, so we'll stop here.
To put it simply, Amalur looks and acts dated from the word 'go.' It's an obvious, poorly-done PC port of a game made combining just about every generic RPG gameplay element of the past ten years, taking strong inspiration from modern MMOs and Bethesda titles. Areas are linear (even after you get out of the tutorial location) and lack any immediate distinction. You are pretty much 'the chosen one' living out your power fantasy of ripping up bandits and glorks and whatever else as you walk from idle NPC to idle NPC, waiting with punctuation marks above their heads for some brave hero to solve whatever ailment. The enemy AI is trifling (take four guys that stare at you and bob around while one of them winds up an attack, or bum rush the guy ahead of you while he makes threatening gestures for eight seconds), which makes even 'hard' difficulty feel like 'laughable' difficulty if you've ever played an RPG before.
And then there's the stock sounds. Call me a stickler for soundwork (and the music seems okay, if you excuse the predictably percussive battle drum music), but I lose faith in a title very quickly when it starts using stock sounds. I don't know, it's lazy. We've heard these sounds before, and if you're trying to make something new, or different, or stand out, using sounds that we've all heard before isn't the way to do it! I'm sure soundwork is expensive, and you don't need unique sounds for every facet of a game, but I don't know, maybe the sounds that don't feature in every cheap action flick/TV drama.
Harsh? Yeah. Premature? Maybe a little, I only have an hour and a half playtime at this point. First impression? Strongly made. Not good.
Buy the game? No. Buy the game on sale? Maybe if you're out of other RPGs to play (is that possible?) or you've never really played a third person RPG before.

Despite the company going bankrupt after the launch of this game, this is actually a really solid, involved, RPG.  I downloaded it years ago and finally decided to give it a shot, and I'm glad I did.
+Pros
-Immense character customization
-Incredible variety of equipment
-Fleshed-out, interesting characters
-TONS of side quests
-Innovative, easy to learn/difficult to master combat
-A huge, expansive, living world
-Lots of lore and background into the world
-Interesting, forward-moving story
-Crafting/alchemy
-Solid DLC
-Good enemy variety
Cons:
-Level cap of 40, which I hit at about 3/4 of the way through the game
-It gets EASY towards the end.  The final boss was hilariously simple to beat.
-Silent protagonist.
-Occasional camera issues
-A few bugged quests
As a completionist, doing all side quests, I beat the entire game in about 70 hours.  If you are a fantasy RPG fan, you should check this game out when it's on sale.

This review is for RoTT v1.3 from someone that played the game at launch.
Quick-saving makes the game much more fun. Being able to save whenever you want instead of having to rely only on wonky checkpoints makes the game more fun and relaxing because you can lose a lot less because of ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t design, such as the combat in E2L2. Instead of constantly worrying that some dumb trap will suddenly murder you when you haven’t had a checkpoint in a while, you can quicksave, and if you die soon after, you haven’t really lost anything. It makes the trap and platforming sections a lot more tolerable because one mistake won’t send you back about ¼ into the level.
However, the quicksaving doesn't excuse idiotic decisions in the game, such as the awful platforming, inconsistent way it handles how jump pads work, and the bosses. Quicksave is akin to a band-aid to bad design decisions; it doesn’t get rid of ROTT’s problems; it makes them much more bearable. The only problem it really gets rid of is the bad checkpointing, but that was a pretty big problem at launch.
Another issue is that quicksaves don’t work on bosses. I can understand why, but it’s frustrating that the most annoying part of the game, the bosses, have to be done in one go. I would’ve loved it if I could’ve saved when dealing with the bullet sponges that are NME and El Oscuro because it would save me a ton of time when the bosses would inevitably pull a ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t move and kill me right before I finished them off.
I’ve noticed that the quicksaves can be buggy at times. One map, E4L4, is unwinnable if you place a key, quicksave, and quickload. I’ve also seen enemies respawn after a quicksave, which is a bit annoying if you like to backtrack. Most of them aren’t a big deal, but you should be careful just in case.
I have no idea how MP is now because I felt it was pretty♥♥♥♥♥♥even before the Firebomb spam murdered any chance of MP being played beyond a skeleton hardcore group. It seems they’re putting more effort developing the MP and trying to cultivate an MP community instead of fixing SP mode, which seems to have more potential than a bunch of hArDkOrE gamers trying to relive the glory days of UT99 and Quake 1/2/3 with a busted MP mode.
I can’t say anything about any sort of optimizations since the game ran at max settings with no problems at launch. I’ve heard that the game still has some pretty big optimization problems from others, so it looks like the devs haven’t managed to fix it yet.
The modding tools seem nice, but right now the community seems to be more interested in rehashes of maps from old FPS games instead of making new stuff.There’s a lot of potential in the game, but remakes from maps from your favorite FPS games when you were a kid is not the way to do it.
The new patches make ROTT a lot more fun. Quicksaving doesn’t fix the bad level design, awful platforming, and the obnoxious bosses, but it does make the game more fun and relaxing when you don’t have to rely on poorly-spaced checkpoints when going through a bad level. Thanks to quicksaving, I feel that ROTT is a worthy purchase for anyone that likes old school FPS games, even if you’ve never played the original. There’s still several problems that probably won't be fixed, but quick saving is a good enough band-aid that it’ll make it easier to stomach them.

Ok, for starters I really do enjoy this game.
The Good:
1. Each of the classes seem viable from my experience, and I really did enjoy experimenting with each of them.
2. The loot system is quite extensive and finding the really good stuff quite uncommon.  Thankfully there is a shared stash for when you find rare items suitable for another class.
3. The difficulty selection is good.  The easier difficulties were not much of a challenge, but Elite difficulty I found exceedingly difficult.  It's too bad you cannot change the difficulty mid game.
4. Skills only need a level requirement.  No pre-requisite skills needed!  I always hated having to waste points in a skill I will never use just to get to the one I want.
5. No "immune" creatures on the higher difficulties.  Sure they have higher resistances, but you can still whittle them down.  I found this rather annoying in Diable II.
The Bad:
1. The story is quite forgettable.  One thing I loved in Diablo II was the cut scenes, but the ones in this game I find myself just clicking through to get back to the action.  Similarly, the characters you run across are little more than services they provide.
2. Respec is available, but only the last 3 skills taken.  Therefore you still can end up locked in a build.  With mod type work, full respecs are possible, but this should be an option within the game.
3. A few of the skills just don't seem all that useful, or don't seem to work well.  I ran into this problem with other AARPGs as well, so I guess this was expected.  There are still plenty of options available, and I still havn't tried them all.
Overall, I found this to be a surprisingly good game with plenty to do in it.  I believe this to be a good value for the asking price.

The Sims started out as a fairly simple franchise that rewarded player choice and experimentation, had a distinct air of optimism and innocence, and a far more neutral, natural tone. Most importantly, perhaps, the game was a satire of consumerist mores, which it managed to parody and embrace in equal measure. As time has gone by, the series has become increasingly loud, obnoxious, manipulative, and (ironically) the embodiment of the consumerism it initially played upon. With each iteration, I've found the game more and more hollow. The last significant entry I can recall was likely The Sims 2 on the PS2, which allowed direct player control of your sim, alongside the traditional list based control scheme. This was never implemented again, and I always thought that was a pity since it completely changed up the flow and tone of the game.
The biggest downfall of The Sims is that it's failed to mature with it's initial player base; the teens who once played these games are now hitting thirty, at the very least, and the game in no way reflects the reality of life, or the character of real, living and breathing locales. Everything feels like a forced smile, masking a deeper cynicism that I find, frankly, repugnant and unwelcome in my gaming life. Even if you choose to play the game dark, the aesthetic and soundtrack choices betray a deliberate attempt to keep everything upbeat; even death is treated with levity, and birth is a necessity rather than a philosophical choice. The Sims will never really be more than it currently is, and footage of the fourth major installment unfortunately confirms my belief that the franchise has no desire to do anything new, innovative, or meaningful in it's life cycle.
This franchise wants your money, and that is all. And it'll be the best fairweather friend you ever had, so long as it has access to your wallet.

If this game didn't have deep systemic problems, more of the reviewers recommending it would be playing it.  But the matchmaking is dead, and that speaks volumes.
Here are some reasons why:
Random banks skew matchups far too drastically. It's a shame, because when this game works, in a fair matchup, it can be glorious.
This game either needs a chip drafting stage before the game starts (adding to gameplay length, unfortunately), or it needs to let you see the random bank and then pick your character (this is how the remaining fans currently run tournaments).
Also, the power level spread on the characters is far to wide. There are barely a handful of tournament-viable characters.
There are ample technical glitches, but the UI is totally slick.  This IS the best way to play Puzzle Strike, from an interface perspective.
In light of the game's issues, not a lot of people play it, so good luck finding opponents.
The interface feels a bit lacking in some areas but Puzzle Strike is still a very enjoyable, easy to learn game with tons of depth.

As a fan of the tabletop game, I'm really happy with how this turned out. It translates well as a video board game as there's no setup, no need for randomizer apps, etc. Moreover, it lets me play when the mood strikes me rather than trying to get people over to play.
The Shadows expansion looks like fun - I'll buy the DLC later on, and will easily be buying the physical version later as well. Well done, very enjoyable, and I've already bought five more copies to gift to friends :)

Puzzle Strike is a video game adaptation of a board game that's an adaptation of a video game called Super Puzzle Fighter. Yes, that weird Street Fighter spin-off game that plays like Tetris, but isn't quite Tetris. So how does it work? This game is actually a deck-builder similar to games like Dominion. Unlike most deck-builder, this one has a lot more interaction between players and the ultimate goal is to defeat your opponent by crashing Gems into your opponent's gem pile (similiar to filling up your screen in Tetris or Super Puzzle Fighter). The game is also a bit assymetric compared to other deck-builder games in which each player selects a character. Each character has 3 special ability "chips" (cards) that makes them different from other characters changing up how a person plays the game and the strategy they employ. There is more to the game but this, like Yomi, is easy to learn but challenging to master. The PC adaptation is solid, and I think it plays better than the physical boardgame counter-part due to everything being automated.
For more information, check out Watch It Played's Puzzle Strike Guide:

Another tabletop adaption makes it's way to my channel this week, and it comes from the minds behind the old Puzzle Fighter HD. The mechanics are solid as the game is known for it's deck building elements, but can that do enough despite an interface that's lacking in several areas? Will the chips fall into place in terms of the multiplayer and the challenge that it gives? Will you go all in on aggro, or will stay back and build up your resources? Will I ask more silly questions in the description of the video? Come find out!

It's nice that there's a virtual version of the famous tabletop game, and the strategy element here has a core RPS element to it, but it's much more complicated then that. Granted, I wish the interface was a lot better: it's servicable, but it shows its browser based routes and some elements of it are particularly ugly. However, I found it to work a lot better then it's browser based counterpart, as online matches were easy to find with no connectivity issues that I could see. If you can stand that, there's a fun core game experience here that will keep your attention in the multiplayer seen, as the different characters do play reasonably different despite only having differences in the character chips. Good deck building mechanics that punish being too aggressive and not thinking about your next move, while giving you reasons to not just horde buying chips.  It's fun, I just wish it was better in the end, but you can find out via the browser based version if the game is right for you (if it works).

Looks like each player starts with the same 7 chips (cards), plus three character-specific special move chips.  At the beginning of your turn an ante gem is added to your pool.  At the end of your turn you buy a chip from a custom or random bank that is shared by all players.  Use the chips you buy to keep your gem pool the lowest and then KO someone else at 10+.  I'm having fun with the 4-player AI battles.  Thanks for the Linux version!
Very nice PC version of a fantastic boardgame.  The interface is easy to use, and as a plus, the game comes with puzzles to test your Puzzle Strike skills.

KoA is a very unique kind of game with an interesting story for its development. We can partially blame our boy Lincoln Chafee (failed 2016 Democratic Presidential candidate. It was his first day) for us never seeing the MMO this franchise was set to be. Anybody can Google the story, or point out the parallels between other games.
PROS:
- This game has a really expansive story. You can't hit the game for leaving a lot to be desired in backstory as this game was solely a test game with the higher hopes of expanding the narative into a MMO.
- The Crafting system is pretty solid. I have never really done Alchemy, but Smithing and Gem Crafting is pretty slick.
- The Combat is fun, engaging, and requires a small amount of skill.
- I liked the talent and skill trees. Though, some might not. It reminds me of WoW back before this 3 choices every 15 levels business.
- Fully Voiced (Hero Exlcuded). Ralof from Skyrim's voice actor does a lot of voices.
CONS:
- If you actually pick up and do all the quests in areas, you will cap out on level just about 75% of the way through the game. Very bad level pacing.
- Not enough gear sets in the game. It's basically material teired (Leather, Studded Leather, etc.), and then effects can be added through Smithing and Gems.
- Glitches out the wazzou. In the House of Ballads quest line if you loot a second set of the special quest armor, one is removed at turn in; one is permanently bound to your character taking up inventory slots. Forever. My end game char has them now.
- The combat IS fun, but horribly repetitive. In the case of my Finesse character its rolling and stabbing. End game I just killed everything with a bow because it required much less work. I don't really care for most of the combo moves. They typically end up setting you up to be attacked, and the damage output was hardly worth it. So I would have to count exactly how many clicks most of the time to avoid using a combo that is too slow.
- With the proper time put into Smithing, your gear is insanely powerful. You hardly take damage even from Boss' mega attacks. Also smithing is obselete after you cap out 75% of the way through the main storyline... so, I hope you really dig your armor's look.
- The game NEVER SEEMS TO END. I am a completionist. I like to do everything I can. But damn... its just drags on and on, and maybe this is made worse by no new gear, skills, or anything since you capped out a LONG time ago. I beat this game on sheer willpower alone, and it was a friggin' chore. They just keep giving you quests, and the end is never the end. I, seriously, had to quadruple check that the bad guy I was chasing the whole game was really, truly the end of the game.
Despite the Cons to Pros, I recommend this game. Its fun, engrossing, requires quick reflexes, combat is smooth as silk. The female models are stacked (if you're into that). Most of the game's problems could be fixed with a single patch (if the devs could have afforded to keep the lights on). The glithes I ran across were mostly inventory stealers or quest related. This game copied WoW and, maybe, The Witcher/Fable. BIG TIME! This game had Garissons in the Expansion pack long before WoW added them, just saying. It's just a badass game. It IS way too long and drawn out. Especially when you can't become anymore powerful shortly after the fight with the Balor. I loved this game so much I bought it for PC, when I had previously purchased it for XBox 360. Get the game, but don't expect perfection. For a one-and-done game developer, they made a much better game than some big name companies put out everyday.
All I can say is this game is just amazing.

**If you have a Wacom tablet, disconnect all components before launching this game**
Windows interprets your tablet as a touchscreen device and starts the related Windows service which causes Reckoning to crash every 15 minutes or so.
Once upon a time, Fable and Skyrim had a brief love affair resulting in this game. If you enjoyed those two games, you will enjoy Reckoning. So go get 'em. If you have not played one or both, continue for further explanation.
Reckoning is an open world RPG with an expansive-but-not-too-expansive map. There aren't limits on what you can explore or when, but progression of main and side quests will bring you to each area of the map as you go along. There are set paths so no jumping off stuff. I mean, not that you could. There is no jumping.
There are three classes--warrior, rogue, and sorcerer--all of which can be made a hybrid with another. Combat is fun and the animations are beautiful. You can have a primary and secondary weapon which allows for mixed combat style. And if, after spending several hours as a rogue, you realize you'd rather be playing as a warrior, you can change your weapons, class, and skills at any point in the game without having to earn new skill points.
The story line is pretty good. There's a mess of lore and dialogue to be had if you're into that. I myself never found the story compelling enough to make it through an NPC conversation without skipping dialogue. But that could be because all the dialogue is subtitled.
If you like crafting, there's plenty of it--blacksmithing and forging, alchemy, enhancement crafting. You can gather reagents and collect materials while you explore.
The inventory system is honestly the worst thing about the game. It's an unmitigated disaster--cumbersome, vaguely organized chaos. But I lived.
At 48 hours, I've played through once without touching the DLCs and have less than half of the achievements. I've got at least one more play-through in me and a few more hours to spend in my current. So for $10, I'd say it was worth it.

Rise of the Triad is a marvellous reboot which keeps everything intact from the original DOS game which I have only been able to play in small sessions in thanks to source ports. It's a marevelous hectic first person shooter where the idea is to shoot everything that moves and everything that explodes just for kicks with minimal-sense plot, without any of that rechargable health nonsense, just good old health pick ups and armour. The game is split into Episodes like old FPS'es on a map screen and each episode includes a challenging boss.
The game begins like a Wolfenstien title, but soon delves into elements of Indiana Jones style traps and tricks, such as rising spikes in floors and rotating blades and the all too familiar jumping puzzles thanks to the levitating and moving platforms found around levels, not to mention the bounce pads. One false move and you are DEAD.
Along the way collectable coins are found to improve your score and different power-ups or power-downs can be found. Including 'God Mode' which makes you an omniprescent, yawning invincible God with energy balls which vaporise people into the air, 'Dog Mode' which makes you invincible but knee height, perfect for mauling enemies in succession, 'Shroom Mode' which makes everything a dizzy, drug addled haze and a power-down which makes you bounce like a pinball in rooms when coliding with objects. These can be found commonly or in found secrets through holes in walls or seeming inaccesable areas.
The first thing that makes RoTT different is the unlimited ammo in pistols, (even dual weilding) and the basic machine gun, which you have to find early on in the level or from dead corpses one by one. You can also carry one type of heavy weapon which basically come in different guises of explosive rocket launchers but the weapon picked up becomes the active weapon, a slot is included for further mystical and damn right stupid weapons such as Excalibat. Melee is possible with a simple stabbing action which takes care of close encounters when armed with a weapon not ideal for short range shooting.
Going back to the original release of this game I would of called it frustrating due to the lack of quicksave and only supporting checkpoints at certain parts in the level, but soon this was patched in and made the game a wholly lot more playable, with quickloads being listed as a penalty in finishing a level to the stat screen and online scoreboards.
The soundtrack is excellent with great remakes of some of the old tunes from the original Rise of the Triad but composed as full rock melodies with guitars and percussion and really fits in with each level, some of the sound effects in the game are oldschool but appropriate. The dialogue in the game is quite cheesy hmour such as the briefing screens before choosing each level and each playable character has their own catchphrases.
Because the game is made by a small team and this being their first commercial project, some bugs can occur especially around quicksaving like keys disapearing and rooms with said key in locked out due to completing them which can only be remedied with a checkpoint load as set by the game.
Overall, except for these few issues a very amusing game in more than one way. Can only hope Interceptor tackle more games and maybe be allowed to make the Duke Nukem 3D remake after all, bet Gearbox are kicking theirselves.

If you've read any of the other reviews you've obviously seen that people hate microtransactions.  I agree that putting mircotransactions in a full retail price AAA game is a bad step for gaming; however, I don't want to tarnish the hard work of the developers who made this game by solely focusing on that.  Let's face it, these nickle and dime dlc/microtransactions are dictated by the publishers, not the develeopers.  The progammers and design artists get paid the same regardless of how many praxis kits you buy.  It's just a shame that cooperate greed has taken such a strong hold on gaming.  Moving on...
Pros:
Level Design:  Some of the series' best in my opinion.  The improved verticality along with multiple pathways to nearly any objective really add a sense intention to every encouter.  I love spending an hour gathering keycodes and passwords to gain access to an area just to find a vent duct that would have bypassed all of that had I been looking closer.  Prague feels more open than many of the previous games, so exploration is a blast and it's really up to the player how they want to proceed.
Side Quests:  I've honestly only completed 1 main mission so far and I'm 10 hours in.  The side quests are some of the best I've seen, and the attention to detail that is put into the entire city really adds to the feeling that this is a real place.  Each apartment and datapad refernces people and places that exist and that have their own stories that intertwine with the world around them.  This game feels catered to the meticulous playthrough gamers who search out every little detail, and in this game that type of gamer is very rewarded.
Combat:  While it's certainly not up to Bungie's standards, the gunplay is much improved from HR and feels like a solid way to play the game in and of itself now, rather than relying heavily on augs like I did in HR.  The new augs expand upon HR's formula by allowing you to further cater to a certain playstyle with focused abilities.
Music:  If you enjoyed the techno-blend from HR you'll feel right at home here.
Graphics:  It's an attractive game visuallly, and certainly an improvement over HR.  Performance wise I'm not sure that the visuals of the Ultra settings justify the performance hit, but outside of MSAA I'm running it maxed out on a 980 Ti at 2560x1440 and I average 50 fps which is perfectly fine for my performance standards.  No crashes or glitches to date.
Cons:
AI:  While on missions the AI feels solid enough to make getting from point A to point B semi-challenging, but while exploring around Prague it seems to fall apart and hurts what is otherwise a very immersive world.  For example, I'm playing on the hardest difficulty available for the first playthrough, so when I kill everyone in my apartment complex I expect some reprocussions unless I'm very careful.
Yet, using a silenced weapon in the middlee of a crowd will do little more than make the local residents panic, but no police attention.  Going loud and proud will draw the attention of the police but the flying drones can't even enter the apartment complex's courtyard and the foot patrols don't search beyond the courtyard access points unless you bait them.  I shot everyone, including the police and all I had to do to get away was walk up a flight of stairs.  If you're not directly where you were last seen they don't really search for you anywhere else.  They also have no long term memory.
I shot 3 police officers and 2 drones and once the search was over I just strolled back out into the streets free and clear.  For a game that so heavily leans on the futurstic vision of cybernetics, AI, cyber-crime, etc I would hope that with all of these technological advances they would be able to identify an unapologetic mass murder.
The AI isn't a deal breaker by any means, it just feels "off" from the rest of the world especially after I got my hand slapped early on for stealing credit chips in front of the weapons dealer who owned them.  He even had some clever dialogue specific to that action before he and his thugs started shooting me.  After that I was expecting and pretty detailed system of consequences from the game, but it's just not there....Sorry for the lengthy rant, but it's really my only true gripe with the game itself.

TL;DR
Another decent addition, aspirations are a nice touch and the sounds are really top notch but the microtransactions and 'holding back for more money' feel leaves a bad taste in the mouth. Plus, it can be a little glitchy at time.
Would just about recommend to buy. - 7/10
GRAPHICS
Putting into account when the game came out, the graphics are your standard 'good'. You can get a feel for the cartoony graphics and your Sims look like living beings in the create-a-sim. However, when you get to the real world, things start to come apart a little. There are definitely some rendering issues here and there, particulary when your Sim enters and exits taxis which they take around town now. Rather jaring. Buildings sometimes take a while to jump into focus as well but that might just be my PC. The animation hasn't moved on massively either (bar a few pleasent editions), which is dissapointing. Everything does it's job though and the textures look surfice a nothing really spectacular here or wowing, but it does the job - 7/10.
GAMEPLAY
Alot of your staple sim catagories are here: your create-a-sim, create-a-house, create-a-neighbourhood, etc. In these respects, the rule of thumb is we'll give you more, at the expense of less because we want to slap a microtransaction/DLCs ontop to bleed your money. The create-a-sim (where this rule applies the greatest) features a great deal more colour options, with the option to even change the shoulder colours and use ANY texture in the game as part of the costume (can make for some interesting results)... but at the expense of less clothes because we want to charge you for those. Oh and we'll charge you for the breast and chest enhancers to (via it's inclusion in certain DLC). Create-a-neightbourhood? We'll give you the freedom to build any lot you want... on certain spaces (which is a shame really). We'll also charge you for extra maps (which would be fine but the game only includes I believe 2 maps might even be 1) via DLC. Create-a-house, thankfully, isn't as bad. There are microtransactions for extra items, but the game does provide a number of items and item variations although this is not anything particulary groundbreaking. The inclusion of several upper and lower areas for any structure you build is an excellent edition, as well as tools to fill an entire room's wallpaper/floor in a certain way, saving you time.
Real world game play is your standard Sim affair but now with a number of extra parameters to flick on and off like how long you live in 'sim days' which are highly variable and you can even adjust the amount of time your sim spends in each area. There's also a few unique and interesting objects to interact with and you can set people to move in/out in real time, so there's lots of little tweaks to play around with. However, aspirations is the real meat in this game compared to the Sims 2. Filling aspirartions gives your sims boosts to happiness and bonus points to spend on stuff, with a massive boost if you manage to fill their life aspiration (selected at create-a-sim from a limited no. of options). The small micro-managing of what 4 aspirations you want (your sim gets new aspirations at regular times and when you add an aspiration or 'promise' it) adds a nice little dynamic to the game and surprisingly doesn't jar your day-to-day medelling. Some of the aspirations are a little superficial like 'buy a T.V.' but things like kiss such and such or go on an amazing date are always interesting to furfil and give some direction to the game, with the flexibility to ignore if you prefer.
Overall, it's pretty good - same old stuff (nothing too wrong with being puppet master) but the aspirations are a well needed spice. Some more seasoning would have been nice though. - 8/10.
SOUND
The sounds are where this game excels for me. The new build-a-home music tracks are delightfully calming yet inspiring melodies that take their time for you, just like the time it takes to build some of the monstrous projects that can occur. The usual pops and clicks are present and pleasent with the added quior like AHHHHHHHH whenever an aspiration is completed, which is a joviel touch. Even the new sim radio tunes are on the right side of silly. Sometimes, it does all get a bit samey and annoying - perhaps some more variation in tunes between the neighbourhood, create-a-sim and create-a-house thing wouldn't have gone astray, but mostly good news here. - 9/10.
FEELZ
Ah, The Sims. There's alot to like about the Sims franchise in general. The concept of creating this person that you can manipulate at will imbeds the player with a great sense of power. It is something that has been strong amogest all the Sims games. This powerful feeling still lingures, although some of the magic is starting to fade away. Not only is this the 3rd game in a row like this but also what feels like the 1,000,000th edition to this game. It's suffers from a classic (and somewhat severe) case of 'franchise fatigue' as I like to call it whereby the company tries to bleed every last penny out an initially successful game rather than come up with a new idea by tweaking and perfecting. Doesn't mean the game is bad as per se but it feels like it could be so much more and probably would be if the company wasn't to busy trying to hold back on ideas. Here we see DLC varation in it's most hideous form and, worse still microtransactions, which are pretty much the gaming equivilant of a sin in paid games. This is a proper game, I expect proper standards right from when I put the money on the table and it's a great shame when the company holds back.
Basically, it really does feel like you are being ripped off big time but what you do get fed by the EA machine is pleasent enough to taste... even if it is a little familiar. - 7/10.
ADDITIONAL:
- The initial load time is horrid, especially with all the DLCs. Hell, they even patched it with a mini-game it's that bad. It's as bad as Dues Ex Machina.
- The game glitches out more than it should but nothing that won't stop gameplay all together... it's just a bit much, even for an open-world.

I purchased the Early Access about mid-Feb.  I agree with the statements then that the controls were a little clunky and there were definitely some bugs to work out.  I haven't had a chance to sit down and play in a little bit, but I was having a RWBY withdrawal and thought I'd play for a little bit today.  I read through the updates and checked it out.  Controls and combos have greatly improved.  It is very smooth and flows nicely, and that's with a keyboard and mouse setup.  I haven't tested with a controller yet, so I cannot say anything on that.  I also tested out the "Play-Offline" as well.  It's a nice touch since sometimes you just feel like playing on your own.  Either because you don't want to deal with people, no one is on, or just to practice, it's nice that the Offline play is there.  The combat system itself is better with blocking from the Grimm as well as being able to counter the Grimm attacks.  Before, you were only able to dodge the attacks if you timed it correctly. Before, you had the 3 abilities set to corresponding keys (1-3) and had to build up your points by combos and you could only have 3 points until you upgraded to the 5 points and each ability costed a certain amount of points based on if you have upgraded or not.  Now, you are given different abilities (again this is for keyboard and mouse.  I haven't used a controller yet) set to different buttons on the mouse as well as a few on the keyboard. Overall, I think this game is a fun play through and will be a great game once it is finished.  Progress being made with the controls and such have been in a positive direction and seems the people working the game have been listening. This game is honestly disappointing.
You see it does a LOT of different things and they all feel "meh" at their absolute best.
There's hack and slash combat and it feels super stiff and button mashy.
There's driving but the driving very odd to say the least.
There's world exploration and it's one of the strongest aspects of the game, very creative but only the first island actually feels open world, the 2nd and 3rd island are an absolute joke in terms of exploration, it's just 1 road that loops around and the mountains everywhere make it really a stretch in calling it open world.
The ending realy just comes out of nowhere which highlights how the game was far too ambitious for it's own good, honestly just tried too much at the same time.
The side quests are repetitive aswell (they evens start repeating the same cutscenes)
And why would all of this be so mediocre?
Because of the RTS portion of the game, you can really tell that the RTS part of the game was where the biggest bulk of development went into, there's a TON of different creatures, abilities, "tag-team" abilities and it still managed to be a mediocre, because of the camera angle, you see, it never leaves the third person perspective so it makes micromanaging your army stupid clunky, just picture something like a total war game if the RTS parts always followed the general point of view, it's not hard to completely forget/leave units behind which in turn drags on battles.
And because it's an rts at heart and they really pushed it, your character becomes weak af by the end of the game easily being oneshotted (doesnt matter you resurect for free, highlighting how meaningless you are in how you affect the battle by the end) and every lategame enemy is a massive damage spunge, you will struggle really hard if you decide to take down 1 single enemy on your own, it dragged the whole game down.
And thats why i say it's disapoiting, because it had a lot of potential if they had just focused on the other 2 aspects, hack and slash, and open world gameplay, with a Heavy Metal setting, i'm not a heavy metal listener and i still found it very enjoyable to explore the world(at least the little that there is to explore), and i really enjoyed some of the more calm Heavy Metal tracks.
With that said i still recommend it, specially in summer sale, although i can't really blame you if you give up on the game by the end, know this, the best part of the game is the first island, beyond that point the game becomes a drag (but story wise it develops really quickly into a abrupt end), I will say the 2nd and 3rd island are incredible visually, super diverse.
So glad I picked this game up on sale...  mainly because I'm probably never going to bother playing it again as the controls hate me.

(Originally written 10/13/2009)
Jack Black is one of the most entertaining and unique actors on the Hollywood scene today; he started work in the comedic band he founded alongside Kyle Gass known as Tenacious D, and his career only went up from there. This is his first videogame, and if it's any indication, he will be in high demand in the field of voice acting for many years to come.
The story of this game is a rather unique one: Eddie Riggs (voiced by Black) is the world's best roadie, best at not being seen doing what needs to be done behind the scenes. One day while preparing the stage for an extremely weak hair metal band to which he is attached, something... interesting happens, and his blood somehow gets on to an enchanted belt buckle; what follows is an extremely surrealistic experience, in which Eddie is transported to a sort of alternate universe based largely around heavy metal and the battle between it and hair metal.
Through a combination of his axe which he finds early on, the Separator, and his "axe," his guitar named Clementine, Eddie cuts a swath through his enemies, and electrocutes or immolates them due to the added magical power this new realm gives his guitar. He'll need these abilities, as well as help from several supporting characters, such as the Forge Master (played by Ozzie Osbourne), to upgrade his attacks, his weapons and his hot rod, the Deuce, and the Kill Master (played by Lemmy from Motorhead, whose last name is Kilmister), to heal his allies in combat.
Along with the action, there is a real-time-strategy element, in which you can command your units to attack or defend various targets in the completion of your missions. You may also go down into combat during these sequences, as well as take them on in multiplayer with or against several other people at once.
With the good must come the bad; but thankfully, Brutal Legend doesn't have much of that. Sometimes it's difficult to micromanage various tasks as is often the case in Real-time-strategy games, but it's not too big a deal. Also, poor Eddie can't jump! This is pretty much a glaring omission, but it's not game-breaking in the least.
The visual style of the game is based on classic heavy metal album covers, complete with grand, metallic monsters and epic, wide landscapes. The modeling of Eddie Riggs to look like Jack Black is accurate if slightly caricatured, as is that of most other characters I've seen. The soundtrack is filled with classic metal tunes, and the voice acting is some of the best I've heard in games recently.
I strongly urge you to go pick this up if you haven't already; if you're a big fan of heavy metal music, or of games in general, you will not regret it! A solid five stars!

Shoppe keep is without a doubt a fun little experience even now, worth the money it charges. However, I feel the game is plagued with features that are unecessary and confusing. Whether it's the adventurer in the back room that never seems to acomplish anything from the quests he is sent on more than wasting a tiny amount of gold, or the crafting system that requires you to either waste gold guessing recipies or just google the full list, for the purpose of having slightly diffrent stuff to grow rich and fat off of than the easy to buy, easy to sell default gear, features are everywhere and ultimately add very little to the core experience of designing a cool little shop and selling plate helmets and rubbish swords to the people of the canyon. You know what feature I think would change things for the funner? A rival shoppe. Having a monopoly means we set prices once, and only ever have to restock random stuff to grow and prosper. Competition would force you to change tactics in order to still make money day to day; undercutting the prices of your enemy and stocking what they can't (which might just justify the crafting system), which adds more to the reason why the game is worth buying. I am excited to see where this game goes, but it risks drowning in a sea of tacked on stuff that fails to answer the question "Why is this here?".

I love the Deus Ex series and I really want to enjoy this game, but my first couple hours in the game have mostly been spent tweaking video settings just trying to get a stable framerate. I have a GTX Titan and it chokes at any presets higher than High. The game looks worse than Human Revolution at these settings. (Yes, I have MSAA turned off.) I've also had to force-quit the game on more than one occasion when the inventory and conversation UIs completely disappeared on me and I couldn't progress.
Controls are clearly not optimized for keyboard and mouse. Movement and aiming is plain awkward at times to the point where it's laughable. For example, try sprinting up or down a staircase - Adam will instead very slowly slide up or down them, slower than he would if you were to run at normal speed.
Hoping Nixxes can fix these issues as I know they have a positive reputation when it comes to PC ports.
(Oh and the single-use DLC thing is dumb but I never planned on buying any of it anyways. Buyer beware if you care about that sort of thing.)

The core shooter gameplay on display here is good fun, and in many ways a terrific homage to the frantic pace of 90s action games. The graphics are gorgeous, sound design is good, enemies are well designed, and weapons are a blast to use.
It's a shame then that the game is so buggy that I cannot in good faith reccomend it. In fact, I abandoned it during the second boss fight after twice getting stuck in level geometry after the phase 2-3 change, experiencing about four crashes to desktop during reloads, and getting locked out of firing weapons after cutting out of a net. Several game-breaking bugs in the course of one boss fight is definitely past my limit. Performance is also dodgy - gorgeous, wide-open sections of the game that should crush my "lowly" HD 6970 + i7-2600k system run at a fluid 60 FPS, then looking at a flat-textured wall will bring it down to 25.
While I'm griping, I'd be remiss to not point out that there's a LOT of first-person platforming here, and this game is hardly Mirror's Edge. It's finicky and unforgiving, which may be true to the 90s spirit but it's a trope first-person shooters have abandoned with very good reason. It didn't ruin the experience for me (at least not to the extent the frequent bugs and crashing did), but if you have a low tolerance for it, be warned.

**If you have a Wacom tablet, disconnect all components before launching this game**
Windows interprets your tablet as a touchscreen device and starts the related Windows service which causes Reckoning to crash every 15 minutes or so.
Once upon a time, Fable and Skyrim had a brief love affair resulting in this game. If you enjoyed those two games, you will enjoy Reckoning. So go get 'em. If you have not played one or both, continue for further explanation.
Reckoning is an open world RPG with an expansive-but-not-too-expansive map. There aren't limits on what you can explore or when, but progression of main and side quests will bring you to each area of the map as you go along. There are set paths so no jumping off stuff. I mean, not that you could. There is no jumping.
There are three classes--warrior, rogue, and sorcerer--all of which can be made a hybrid with another. Combat is fun and the animations are beautiful. You can have a primary and secondary weapon which allows for mixed combat style. And if, after spending several hours as a rogue, you realize you'd rather be playing as a warrior, you can change your weapons, class, and skills at any point in the game without having to earn new skill points.
The story line is pretty good. There's a mess of lore and dialogue to be had if you're into that. I myself never found the story compelling enough to make it through an NPC conversation without skipping dialogue. But that could be because all the dialogue is subtitled.
If you like crafting, there's plenty of it--blacksmithing and forging, alchemy, enhancement crafting. You can gather reagents and collect materials while you explore.
The inventory system is honestly the worst thing about the game. It's an unmitigated disaster--cumbersome, vaguely organized chaos. But I lived.
At 48 hours, I've played through once without touching the DLCs and have less than half of the achievements. I've got at least one more play-through in me and a few more hours to spend in my current. So for $10, I'd say it was worth it.

As of writing this, I'm 115 hours in and am only in the first half of the last part of the story [exhausting every quest along the way], and still have both of the DLC to go through. The combat is probably the best part of this game, the fate/destiny level system pretty much serves to let you customize your style of fighting. The artwork is quite good, if mmo-ish. The story is decent. There are plenty of quests to do, parts to combine to make items you want, and houses to furnish. It's not too challenging though if that's what you look for in an RPG [my playtime is just due to me grinding as I go to get to max level so I can do the DLC at max (DLC drops and rewards scale to level as you enter iirc) before ending the story].
My advice for maximum enjoyment, challenge, and actual decision making, in terms of gear, is to avoid getting gold through excessive gem combination farming and to not be tempted to save-scum when salvaging gear for crafting parts. Also, try to finish everything in an area before moving on because regions level lock to the first time you enter it and thus you can cripple your progression if you just run willy-nilly and locking the first regions to level 2 or something [despite it being open world].
For the power gamers: gem combo farm like hell for 30 mins after like the first four regions and you'll never need money again. And save scum like hell when salvaging to get those +damage parts for crafting when they're available, because crafted items are the most OP stuff in this game.
TL;DR - Excellent Combat, good skill set customization, good art style, ok story, plenty to do, not the most challenging, crafting is op, gem combo farming is op, region level lock shenanigans possibly spoiling the open world and ability to level up fast element for some people

Extremely fun at times, but ruined by a couple of major issues. Too many flaws for me to recommend.
- Unreliable gambling shop for acquiring upgraded weapons. Under no circumstances should you be required to wait an entire day to attempt to gamble for a weapon with unreasonable odds. Even when maximizing your odds you are unlkely to get a weapon, you can only buy crystals in bulk and hope for the best. If MAIET wants to turn G2 into a cash cow, could they at least make it consistent? Put the blues at 3.99, yellows at 14.99. The people who got lucky from the shop or have hundreds of dollars to waste love it, but nobody else does.
- Bad netcode. Zero attempt at lag compensation. You need to aim where they will likely be by the time your ping reaches the host, rather than aim where the enemies actually are.
- Even worse host & matchmaking system. MAIET is intent on keeping it P2P either because they're unwilling to fund a revamp or they don't realize just how ridiculous P2P is for the region the game is on.
- Lack of progression/direction. Weapon stats are hard to compare, and many of the bars are extremely misleading. Having to datamine to get the actual stats for comparison is unacceptable. Convert the bars to numbers, make the differences between weapons more noticeable and less clearcut as to which one is best for use, and do something to further weapon upgrade progression beyond "Get the green gear, then gamble for a couple days straight and hope you get lucky for the next tier of weapons". Make it so you can buy the blues for gold or USD, or achievements where if you get a certain number of kills with the green weapon, you get the blue version of it, and so on with the yellow version.
- The list goes on. Rena & Max are extremely strong in certain ways but terrible in most others. You need to pay for the other classes. No duel mode. Some cases of bad map design. Almost nobody prefers Time Assault. No custom games. No server browser. Ad nauseum. You get the idea. The game seems to have been released too early.
Don't let my ranting confuse anyone, I love the basic premise of GunZ. The combat, the classes, the campaign, etc. There are a lot of things about this game that MAIET did correctly, I just wish they'd done the
of it correctly.

Essentially a single-player RPG with the contents of a MMO-rpg (expect the social aspect)
Some of the games artwork can at times be appealing, but personally I prefer a somewhat more toned down and realistic style. In this game, the characters have overly sized hands and weapons etc all showered with all the brightest colours the designers could think of.
The game consist of a few faction quest lines, which at times can be interesting, but all too often quest are "go to certain point, fetch/kill, and return). Real choicemaking is non-existent.
The main story line is bland and generic, even with the "10 000 years" of background history the develpoers brag about. Magic elves, technical dwarfes, in-between humans... .  The lack of good voiceacting only contributes to the game's inability to immerse, with probably as few as 10 voice-actors trying to the best of their ability to voice all characters in the game.
The combat-system is quite nice. Quite easy, but a lot of ways for the player to adapt underway to the way they want to play. And unlike more classic RPGs all character developments can be changed for a small fee, so that the player don't have to think ahead. Nice, for some... . Almost all ingame quest-rewards and looting is scaled it seems, so the player seldom experience any sense of joy or positive surprise when overcoming obstacles. Many enemies are scaled too it seems.
Personally I had to stop playing this game after encountering a game-breaking bug (Her righteous fury-quest), of which there is no official fix to 4 years after release (due to the developers bankruptcy, I guess). Therefore I could not fully explore the main idea of this game - fate. I find the idea of fate troubling on a logical level, and the game as far as I played it, did only contribute to this with all its logical fallacies.
Nice enough game if you are looking for mind-numbing, button-mashing action-rpg, with little need for investment on the player's part. Stay clear (even on sale), if you are looking for immersion, challenge and a sense of accomplishment.
This game will suck the marrow out of your bones if you are a true RPG fan.

Below are some PROS, CONS and TIPS. Further below are some further thoughts.
PROS:
Heaps of content for your money, loads of activities, missions, races etc.
Combat, Driving, Pedestrians all the things that make a GTA game awesome.
Character customization including weapons, clothing and accessories (they cost a lot of money though).
The Heists are fun and interesting the first few times, the cutscenes can get annoying though.
Cool and unique game modes.
Free DLC
Can grown weed and cook meth
CONS:
Take two tried to remove singleplayer mod support, not cool they should be able to work how to stop cheaters without trying to do DCMA takedowns (or whatever its called).
Loading, so much loading its crazy.
Some missions and heists send you driving across the entire ♥♥♥♥ing map, its alot of driving to do.
Everything is really expensive and making money takes alot of time (mainly because of all the loading). Even clothes and jackets etc cost thousands of $$.
Lack of control over the mission and setup lobbies, you cant just do a bunch of setup missions and then do the heist. After EVERY setup you load back into freemode (if its got a lot of players this takes a ton of time).
Missions work a little differently you can choose from a selected bunch of missions on the lobby voting screen however they took away the ability to 'replay' the last mission so you cant just grind the same mission over to make money.
Lack of options when doing missions, you can make playlists for jobs/missions but you cant include the coop (standard) missions in the playlist? Why the hell not? Because you would make too much money too easily.
When you're a new player it can be tough in freemode with all the other higher level players around.
Some instances of cheating, personally I've only seen it a handful of times i just find a new session straight away.
TIPS:
-Play with friends: more friends = more money making potential, join a crew as well (im yet to do this though lol).
-Get the Kuruma: (you need a garage first i think) The best purchase you could probably ever make is the Armoured Kuruma ($500,000), you can solo missions on hard difficulty, i would say this was the most worthwhile purchase i have ever made.
-Passive Mode: Press M and then press the Up arrow key and press enter to choose to go into passive mode, you cant use weapons or fists but noone can kill you and you can go do things like get armor, change clothes get a haircut without being killed.
-The micro SMG: This is probably the second most worthwhile purchase I've made, once you get the ability to go off radar (unlocks at Level 40)  you can call Lester and then roll up on someone and fill them full of bullets and zoom away.
-Go off radar: You can use it to ambush others and to run away when you're outgunned.
-Get an Apartment/Penthouse: that enables you to do the Heists. I spent hours deciding on what apartment to get, (i got Richards Majestic 51) you should really do your research before purchasing an apartment. Think about what you want to get out of the location and what other jobs/activites that you regularly do are nearby? Where is the nearest Helipad? Is is near the CEO/Biker office/clubhouse? What garages are nearby? Is it easy to get home if someone is chasing you?
-Get a place out of town: When you can afford it buy a cheap garage or house out in the country, the city is very chaotic, lots of players have their homes there and it can be a pain to always start in the mayhem.
-Buy a fast aircraft: When you have the money buy a fast air transport, the Buzzard is a good choice, any personal vehicle can almost always be called for missions and freemode.
-Check the warstock website for discounts: I got the Savage attack helicopter (the Russian HIND gunship) for 1.4 million on special.
-Watch the minimap: Press the Z key a bunch of times to zoom out on the minimap, you should always have one eye on the minimap in freemode.
-Only buy a few guns: And clothes etc. If you buy an item of clothing you cannot get rid of it and things can end up clogging your clothes/weapon menu. Guns can be dropped with F9 or F10 but it when you load back into the game you have all your weapons again.
-Get the homing launcher: Aircraft are extremely vulnerable to homing rockets, usually one missile is all it takes and the pilot gets little warning and has a short time to eject (especially the savage, its slow and it takes ages to eject out).
-Macros: If you can do it setup macros for putting on armor and changes clothes etc, they are usually several menus deep. I have a logitech keyboard (G105) it has 6 macros keys and software to record macros, its so easy to record a macro in game. I have macros for putting on armor, going into passive mode, change masks, calling people (Lester,Mechanic,Peagsus). Nothing is more frustrating than trying to run away from someone and struggling with the menu to put on armor.
-Eat Snacks: Press M and go down to where it says 'action' change it to eat snack, then you can press Capslock to eat and regain your health. You can spam it while in cover (press Q) or in your vehicle.
-Go into passive mode: Before Heisting with randoms go into passive mode, at the end of a setup mission or heist you all load into free mode right next to eachother! Anyone can and WILL shoot you in the back.
-Save your money: Save save save, everything costs, even a ♥♥♥♥♥♥ gray jacket in the clothes store costs like $20,000. Sometimes its best to hold off any purchases.
The main problem with online is the amount of loading and the lack of control over your lobby and settings. If a player leave your setup/heist mission you get dropped back to freemode and another f**king loading screen. If you fail a mission more than four times it drops you back into freemode and another f**king loading screen. Sometimes after missions or setup/heists end you end up hanging on the loading screen for ages. The game drops everyone back to freemode after a successful setup mission and you need to load into freemode then load back into the setup lobby, its too much, way too much loading. Sometimes the game drops you and your friends into different freemode lobbies, meaning you all need load into another lobby again. The peer to peer networking means that if one friend is far away from you (especially with a poor connection) they can possibly drop out of the game and yep back into a loading screen.
Recent updates mean you can't replay a mission you just did, you cant choose what mission you want (aside from the first time and then only whats displayed), items in the game cost so much money and its difficult to grind out money when you have so many loading screens, it feels almost deliberate. They've made money harder to make so you will buy the shark cards. I don't have an issue with shark cards really, they are funding all the free DLC which is great but seriously the balance isn't right.
As for the gameplay when its all running smoothly its a ton of fun, some of the missions make you drive a long way but other than that the game is awesome. With this game you really need to be making an effort to always be making money doing missions,setups/heists, biker\CEO jobs etc. Sure you can roam in freemode stuffing about, its great fun but focus on making money and things become much better.

Came back to this game after a break for 1 year, still has same issues.
Farming :             Enemy team will stop pushing on last point and farm/spawnkill to get money/XP

Online abuse:      Due to the frustrations of the game design (see poor teamwork) and lack of
consequences (you can vote, but unlikely followed up)
Poor Teamwork : This imo is one of the reasons why the game community is so abusive to each
other. Not because of humans nature, but because of poor gameplay
mechanics, not rewarding teamplay over kills.
Poor UI:               UI does not tell you enough about whats going on in the world, and where the
team needs to focus, leading to noobs and experianced players not cordinating
Grind:                  The grind is super heavy (to be expected of a free to play) and will take+1000hrs
to get good gear, and then upgrade weapons. Even when you do get the good
guns, the cost of "maintaining them" often exceeds money earned, meaning you
have to downgrade your weapons just to stop bleeding money. This grind also
leads good players to start farming/camping in order to get XP/$, pushing
more players to tilt, throw games and become abusive.
V.I.P:                   You have to pay to become V.I.P using in game currency (or spend real money)
and is about the only way to make good in game money (so spend money to
make money) However, they do offer this for free either on special holidays,
rewards, but I see it as a way of "giving them a taste" like a good drug dealer.
Generals:           This is the complete waste of time strategy mode, where rewards are as pointless
as movie remakes, like the mummy 2017
Airplanes:           Being able to pilot some cool WWII planes is a great idea, but combine them in
this game, you will get farmed and get to star in your very own "how to be killed
without being able to do something about it" movie montage. There are AA nests,
but they are so weak, lacking in numbers, and put in the most stupid spots, they
struggle to cover or protect your team. This seems like a conscious decision to
keep pilots happy over everyone else. You could "git gud" flying planes, but you
soon realise the grind and games where you wont be decimated and farmed are
so rare, most give up.
Some of the points I have rasied could be pointed at the game being a free to play, and they have to make money, but I think they need to find a balance, to attract new players, and keep us old hands coming back for more. The number of players are down, and with stiff competition, lack addressing the games flaws, they will either attempt top fix things, or squeeze tighter to make that bottom line.

text:
Mortal Kombat X
Developer: NetherRealm Studios, High Voltage Software
Publisher: Warner Bros. Interactive Entertainment
Introduction
==========
Since 1992 when the first Mortal Kombat was released, we've seen many entries in the iconic fighting franchise. Despite it's name, Mortal Kombat X is the 21st Mortal Kombat game to see release, but it is the 10th installment of the main storyline. Featuring some new characters, mainly the children of some of the more well-known characters, Mortal Kombat X picks up 2 years after Mortal Kombat 2011 (commonly referred to as MK9) left off. Shao Khan has been defeated, but Shinnok has returned to once again threaten Earthrealm. Just to name a few of the new characters-- Kotal Khan, D'Vorah, Erron Black, Jung Jin, Cassie Cage, Takeda Takahashi, Jacqui Briggs, and Ferra/Torr. A lot of the older characters return, but with new looks. Scorpion, Sub-Zero, Raiden and more are all here. Other characters such as Kabal, Sindel, and Stryker make an appearance as well.
Gameplay
==========
MKX retains most of the features that we've come to expect from the series, with the addition of a couple of new ones. The game plays out similarly to Injustice: Gods Among Us. You'll have a cutscene, followed by a slight transition to the in-game engine where kombatants say a line or two to each other, then you have the fight. Once the fight concludes, the winner says a one-liner, then the game transitions back to cutscenes. Story Mode plays out entirely like this, and it works very well. It's *almost* seemless, but those with a good eye will see the exact moment of transition.
Returning from Injustice are the stage interactions. Scattered throughout each stage are objects you can use to your advantage, that range from dealing damage or making an escape. There was literally one stage where you can pick up and old woman in the background and chuck her at your opponent! These interactions do a lot of damage, but seemed to have been scaled back a bit due to how abused they were in Injustice.
There are a variety of game modes, spanning singleplayer and multiplayer. Let's go over singleplayer initially. First and foremost is the Story mode. In this mode you go through several chapters, each one dedicated to a specific character who you'll use to progress through battles that advance the story. Story Mode took me approximately 4-5 hours to complete. While short, it's really fun. Next, we have the Towers, which is like the classic ladder arcade mode. There are 3 towers initially, each with a different number of opponents. There's Single Fight, where you just choose your character and an opponent and just duke it out. Next is Test Your Luck, where you face off against the AI with random modifiers. Lastly, there is a Training Mode where you are free to practice with any character you choose on any stage, with various settings for your AI opponent. They can fight back or just stand there as you practice combos.
Multiplayer has a few different modes, the most notably of which is the Ranked Ladder. Participating in these allows you to climb the ranking ladder to number 1. There is also the returning King of the Hill mode from Injustice. Lastly there are Tower Battles where you face other players. I didn't play multiplayer very much, as that's not my thing typically, but what I did play ran satisfactorily. There was a small bit of lag but it did not impede my enjoyment and was easy to adapt to. This may or may not be a dealbreaker for some players.
One of the new features added with MKX are tokens. There are 2 types of tokens: Skip Fight and Easy Fatality. Skip Fight allows you to do just that: skip any fight that you choose, as long as it's in Story Mode. Use these when you happen to get stuck versus a certain opponent. When used, the game acts as if you had won the battle. The Easy Fatality Token allow you to execute Fatalities with an easy button press. Both tokens are earned by unlocking them in the Krypt, which is also a returning feature.
Another new feature is the addition of Fighter Variations. These are sort of like different styles, and each kombatant has 3 of them. Each variation gives access to certain abilities which help define the playstyle of the character. For example, Scorpion has a Shirai Ryu style, which gives him access to dual-swords, and he also has Hellfire, which gives him access to demonic hellfire powers.
Lastly, MKX features a Faction War. When you start the game you are able to choose between 5 Factions. Upon joining one, simply playing the game (in any mode) earns you Faction Points. At the end of every Faction War, the winner is chosen and all members of the winning Faction are rewarded.
Graphics
==========
MKX looks just as good as its previous installment. Everything is rendered in great detail, and as a staple of every Mortal Kombat game...there is a LOT of blood! It wouldn't be Mortal Kombat without it. Mortal Kombat is known for its amount of violence and graphic brutality. Nothing has really changed since the last game, and that's a good thing. Some character have new designs or reskins, such as Sub-Zero, Johnny Cage, and even Raiden. The biggest difference I noticed was that of Johnny Cage. He looks almost like a whole new character with the same name, but it's still the same arrogant Johnny some of you love.
Sound and Music
==========
Every character is fully voiced and each stage has it's own music. The music for the most part is largely ignored because of the action on-screen, but for the type of game this is, it works. There really isn't too much to say here, and for that I apologize.
Performance
==========
The biggest complaint that most people will have with this game is the following: some parts of the game are 60 FPS, while some parts are capped at 30 FPS. While this isn't an issue for me at all, it will definitely be a dealbreaker for some.
The game has full controller support and it played flawlessly with my Logitech F310. I never tried the keyboard and mouse controls, but I can't imagine them being any better than a controller! There are also a lot of audio and video options, such as resolution, refresh rate, fullscreen/windowed, etc.
I experienced no lag (except the tad in multiplayer), no stuttering, no screen tearing or anything of that nature. The game ran very well for my specifications (found on my profile).
Final Thoughts
==========
A worthy entry into the franchise, Mortal Kombat X is a fun, bloody fighting game that is sure to please fans of the franchise. It apparently had its issues on release, but I did not see any major problems while I played. If you are a fan, you owe it to yourself to get this installment. Ready? FIGHT!

This is a great MK game! The online connectivity is ok. I didn't have any trouble with the matchmaking, although I did get a bit of slow down on one occasion during each of my games (didn't stop me from getting my♥♥♥♥♥whipped). There's tonnes of challenges both 'on the disc' and set daily via online updates, as well as a story mode similar to MK9, and a number of variations on the classic tower mode. The game looks utterly fantastic as well, and is heads and shoulders about MK9 in terms of graphical fidelity.
However, and of course there's a however because GAMES THESE DAYS, there are a few issues. Firstly, whilst gameplay is 60fps all cutscenes, X-ray scenes and fatality scenes are 30fps, which is both jarring, and utterly baffling. Scratch that, it's utter ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥. I felt much better about it when I realised it wasn't my framerate dropping but it was built into the game, but it's still ridiculous that you cut from silky smooth 60fps during a fight, to performing an X-Ray move at half that, before the game skips back to 60 when the fight resumes. Why. WHY? 60fps was good enough for MK9, why not this one? And I swear to god if someone says 'it's cinematic' I'm gonna explode. What does that word mean? Because I'm pretty sure I don't notice films skipping frames, yet here with a side-by-side comparison built into the game it's hard not to miss, and harder not to be dumbfounded by the decision. Secondly, there is some ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t costly DLC skins and characters. More insultingly, the characters are visible but blacked out on the character selection screen, taunting you with their presence. On top of that, you fight some of the DLC characters in game, which is an even more egregious way of dangling the carrot in front of you.
BUT, apart from these annoying design choices/business practices, the game is a great MK game. The fatalities are more brutal than ever, the loading screens are negligible, the different play styles for the characters open up a whole new world of personalisation for the players, and there is still a fair amount of unlockable content that one can gain access to through gameplay. I especially love that some of the fatalities are hidden, so you have to hop on the internet to find out what the codes are, or unlock them in game. It's not quite the same as having to buy a magazine or ask your friends, but the sentiment is there, and it feels much more like the kind of arcade MK experience that most fans of the originals remember so fondly.
I wasn't sure about this game for months, but apparently it's a lot better now that it used to be in terms of technical integrity, and I'm just loving playing it.
