EARLY ACCESS REVIEW:
Roosterteeth really started off this game with a Yang, it would be Weiss to get this game now while its still on Early Access before the price Rose. While the game only has 2 hours worth of contents so far, the developer have always added Neo contents to the game. This game plays better with friends although matchmaking isnt so difficult as the sever is always Qrowded with players. I gotta HAND it to RT, this game is worth every Penny.
POST-RELEASE REVIEW:
Okay, so after getting to play the game on its fully-released form, I have a lot to say about this game. As a huge fan of the show and one out of many people who wants RWBY game, I find this game to be a huge disappointment and it fails to meet many people's expectation during the Early Access. First thing first, the game barely has sufficient content to justify its price tag and if you played the early access you've pretty much experienced everything this game has to offer. The combat system although seems intuitive and fun at first, they get really repetitive later on and the combo pretty much boils down to simple button mashing. The mission design revolves either on wave-based combat or simple escort mission. And perhaps the most disappointing thing about this game is that it lacks the interactivity between characters which is essential for a RWBY game, yes the character occasionally talks and give comments throughout the course of the game but they don't interact with each other (at least good thing is that they keep the original voice actors for every single characters). Buy this game only if you're a fan of the show and wants to get more of RWBY or if you have friends who plays the same game (seriously don't play this game alone, it's much worse). If you don't even watch the show or if you're expecting the gameplay of a good hack-and-slash games such Metal Gear Rising or Bayonetta, I can't recommend this game for you.
PROS:
-Original Voice Actors
-Some familliar elements from the show
-It isn't that bad when you play it with friends
-PUNS <3
CONS:
-Barebone contents
-Repetitive combat
-Combo boils down to simple button-mashing
-Environment feels empty
-Feels more like a Musou-type game rather than hack and slash game
-Lack of tutorial
-Team RWBY doesn't interact with each other
-Additional characters (Possibly Team JNPR) as paid DLC
RT, if you're hearing this I have to say that the development for the game felt rushed and if you're making other RWBY game in the future (which we hope you do) please make this game as a lesson to set a higher standard for RWBY game, because we as fans still want a RWBY game done right. I know you don't have the budget to realize a AAA quality but there's still a lot of things you can make better even with such a resource. This is not the RWBY game we deserve and certainly not the one we needs right now.

- The price of the base game is a lot cheaper than it used to be
- Plenty of building tools to keep you creating awesome things
- Extensive character customization
Cons:
- Microtransactions, Simpoints are terribly overpriced
- Game crashes sometimes, mostly due to a memory error
- Sim interaction can sometimes be glitchy and everything will come to a standstill in-game
- Forced to pay real world money for some necessary items
- Expensive DLC packs that make your wallet cry
TL;DR: If you like Simulation games, you'll like this. The base game is great on its own, but if you want to explore what else this game has to offer, prepare to pay an absolute ♥♥♥♥♥on of money, and expect some lag. Overall, would recommend.

This is the next game in the modern Deus Ex games. It builds upon the foundation that Human Revolution laid several years ago, but adds some more customization (weapons and Jensen himself) and more fleshed out gameplay.
Experimental modifications/abilities such as short range dashes, impervious armor, and long range non-lethal takedowns (among other things) must be balanced with other modifications.
The gameplay itself is cover-based first person shooting, with exploration and conversation dialog interactions.
The only blemish I would say is the performance. The game performs well - many reviewers are playing the game with insane MSAA x2 or x4 enabled. Disable MSAA, take down Volumetric Lighting down to ON, Screenspace Reflections to On/High, and Contact Hard Shadows to On/High. Very little visual change, but you gain 20-30 FPS on average.
The performance issues Steam users are having are a bit blown out of proportion. Tweak the game slightly and you'll get the performance you're looking for.

Kingdoms of Amalur: Reckoning came out at a bad time. It was only about 3 months after Skyrim launched and most western RPGs now had a new king to contend with. This game fell under the radar and the studio closed even, which is unfortunate as this is a great game.
Penned by R.A. Salvatore the world of Amalur is familiar enough for a traditional western RPG player but different enough in it's storytelling to be just compelling enough to keep on playing. Everything is fully voice acted and quite well at that. I personally didn't find myself falling in love with any characters in particular but the story is only one part of this game.
One of the other great parts of this game (and in my opinion the main reason to pick it up and play) is the combat. The combat is fast, interesting, and requires a decent amount of strategy. The easiest game to compare it to in terms of combat is God of War. You'll be building combos, countering, and dodging your way to victory with a wide variety of weapons that almost all play differently. Fortunately you can handle two different weapon sets at a time allowing for a significant amount of customization that let's you create a character that fits your play style.
Visually, the game is decent. There isn't much in the way of lush foliage like in The Witcher 3 but the color palette is vibrant and on an artistic level the game shines, even if it's not necessarily a technical marvel. Armor and weapons look especially cool even if many modern visual effects aren't present.
In terms of getting all the achievements keep in mind that this is an open world RPG. This means very few missable achievements (although there are a few so check a guide beforehand) and several story related achievements. There were some kill grinds which are always fun in addition to semi-collectible achievements. I would also recommend the DLC if you don't mind forking out extra dough. If you can get them on sale even better. You'll also need them to 100% the game on Steam.
Overall, Kingdoms of Amalur: Reckoning is a great western RPG that unfortunately fell under the radar. It's a shame more people didn't play this game because it tells a pretty good story, has some of the best western RPG combat around, and looks pretty good from an artistic point of view. I highly recommend picking this one up especially if you consider yourself an RPG fan.

(Originally written 10/13/2009)
Jack Black is one of the most entertaining and unique actors on the Hollywood scene today; he started work in the comedic band he founded alongside Kyle Gass known as Tenacious D, and his career only went up from there. This is his first videogame, and if it's any indication, he will be in high demand in the field of voice acting for many years to come.
The story of this game is a rather unique one: Eddie Riggs (voiced by Black) is the world's best roadie, best at not being seen doing what needs to be done behind the scenes. One day while preparing the stage for an extremely weak hair metal band to which he is attached, something... interesting happens, and his blood somehow gets on to an enchanted belt buckle; what follows is an extremely surrealistic experience, in which Eddie is transported to a sort of alternate universe based largely around heavy metal and the battle between it and hair metal.
Through a combination of his axe which he finds early on, the Separator, and his "axe," his guitar named Clementine, Eddie cuts a swath through his enemies, and electrocutes or immolates them due to the added magical power this new realm gives his guitar. He'll need these abilities, as well as help from several supporting characters, such as the Forge Master (played by Ozzie Osbourne), to upgrade his attacks, his weapons and his hot rod, the Deuce, and the Kill Master (played by Lemmy from Motorhead, whose last name is Kilmister), to heal his allies in combat.
Along with the action, there is a real-time-strategy element, in which you can command your units to attack or defend various targets in the completion of your missions. You may also go down into combat during these sequences, as well as take them on in multiplayer with or against several other people at once.
With the good must come the bad; but thankfully, Brutal Legend doesn't have much of that. Sometimes it's difficult to micromanage various tasks as is often the case in Real-time-strategy games, but it's not too big a deal. Also, poor Eddie can't jump! This is pretty much a glaring omission, but it's not game-breaking in the least.
The visual style of the game is based on classic heavy metal album covers, complete with grand, metallic monsters and epic, wide landscapes. The modeling of Eddie Riggs to look like Jack Black is accurate if slightly caricatured, as is that of most other characters I've seen. The soundtrack is filled with classic metal tunes, and the voice acting is some of the best I've heard in games recently.
I strongly urge you to go pick this up if you haven't already; if you're a big fan of heavy metal music, or of games in general, you will not regret it! A solid five stars!

I'd be remiss if I didn't write a review for one of my absolute favorite games. Now this is an older game so it's not going to blow you away, but I still to this day play it at least once a year (if not more). I've been playing it on Bigfish but since I use Steam 99% of the time, I'm glad the game moved over here.
The Hidden Expeditions are another group of HOG games that range from mediocre to fantastic. Steam is actually missing quite a few of my favorites but with the slew of hidden object games appearing everyday, I would bet we'll see them at some point.
Hidden Expedition: Amazon is all about the HO scenes. That's what the game is comprised of, with a smattering of puzzles here and there. The story is mostly told by reading journal pages, one on each scene, written by a kooky old man who is searching for the lost Beetle Temple.
And now I'll tell you why I myself love this game. A large portion of the enjoyment is the music. It's just beautiful and I never tire of listening to it. Also, Beetles! I find beetles fascinating. In every HO scene (except for the very first one) there are 5 beetles to find which charge up your hint bar. I always find the journal page and all 5 beetles before searching for the other items. I also always read the journal pages (though I probably have them memorized by now) because they are quite amusing. The combo of lovely music, a beetle theme, lots and lots of HO scenes, and a story that makes me smile - it's great.
I can certainly say this isn't for everyone. Obviously look elsewhere if you don't enjoy hidden object games. It's also not super easy and not super hard - definitely for the casual gamer. (Well, some of the items and beetles are very sneakily hidden but you'll find them eventually :p). But I really had to write a review because this game is dear to my heart.

Hidden Expedition is one of these series that were famous at the previous era of hidden objects games. It means that while you have a story, you're just going from list of items to list of items. Here, you're still an adventurer but you're in South America, as the title is suggesting.
And when you're thinking about this era, it means lots of items in the scene, with some being well hidden without forgetting a number of hints instead of it being resplenished. You can also get more of them by finding insects (5 of them are hidden but not at the same place). It means also random list as every playthrough is different. And generally, that era was also setting high scores.
While I'm more inclined to play the new generation of HO, that are mixing adventure, puzzles and HO scenes, I must say that I still have good moments with the old generation. However, for those that never played them before, it may appear as boring as hell. The graphics are correct, like the soundtrack, but I must admit that you're quickly fed up of the lists after a moment, even me that played Mystery P.I. or the other Hidden Expedition in retail.
Despite that, it's like retro-gaming or playing an old Doom, you enjoy these memories of another era. Or it's nice to know where the genre comes from. Anyway, while I admit that 10 euros is maybe a little too much for the game now - and that you may never see a discount, the game is still worthy. And thanks to Tristetea for the gift too else I wouldn't have played that entry that is missing in my retail collection :D.

A review should be about a game, and how a game plays. A review should not be about tertiary or trivial concerns individual to the player. A review should tell people if a game is worth buying: nothing more, nothing less.
Mankind Divided is well worth buying for any fan of the previous Deus Ex game, Human Revolution. It takes the gameplay of the original and enhances it with many tweaks. Using the cover-to-cover sneak system feels like I'm playing a game of XCOM, and really allows me to think more critically about my surroundings. The variety of new augs, along with the returning ones, offer plenty of options for navigating Mankind Divided's world (I particularly enjoy how they even give the player a bounty of Praxis towards the beginning, allowing for them to specialize from the get-go). Every stronghold has several weakpoints, but they are for the player to discover.
The soundtrack is definitely a lot more emotive than HR's, which only had occasions of brilliance (such as in Zhao's penthouse). The graphics look beautiful and, contrary to what everyone has been saying, the game actually runs remarkably well on non-maxed settings. I'm on a laptop that reasonably should not be able to run this game, and I can do a solid 30fps with some dips. And this is before any performance patches which will inevitably come.
Mankind Divided is a great game, taking HR and enhancing it. Don't be blinded by nonsensical, almost unjustifiable rage.

I beat the game on 8/25/2016 at around 2 AM. There will be spoilers in this review.
I'll start spoiler free.
The gameplay of DX:MD is good; it's pretty much a copy/paste of the gunplay and stealth from DX:HR with a bit more polish. If you liked the mechanics from the first prequel, you will like the mechanics from the second. However, playing it on PC can be a bit of a chore with the way menus work. The UI for every single menu is sluggish and, frankly, laggy. Every item has a drop down list, but those drop down lists are fade ins from left clicks instead of instantly appearing on a right click. Actions that are important to gameplay share the same key, which can get in the way of perfect stealth. I had to reload multiple times trying to do very specific maneuvers involving moving bodies because my quest menu would open up. The overclock mechanic is also a pretty useless tack-on.
The content of the game is deceitful at first; when you're in the first throes of the game you're immersed in side quests and possibilities. Completing those side quests is fulfilling, and exploration feels fairly rewarding if not a little dry. However, whenever you venture to the new "areas" (despite them not being full-on hubs), exploration takes a drop off and rewards start to get repetitive.
Let's get onto spoilers.
Starting with the characters, none of them leave a lasting impression. The one person that felt like they had a unique personality is a terrorist leader, and doesn't get very much screen time. The characters you have direct interaction with don't exactly stand out, including the ever-so excentric Koller. Your boss is a run of the mill old, battle-jaded Call of Duty commander; your competition in your unit is your normal hardass soldier (The two combined may as well be Price and Soap) who doesn't like you; your pilot is a boring guy who survived the Incident and pretends to be racist. While they give Miller, your boss, a decent back story and a good time uncovering it, you never have the opportunity to expand on it. He exits the game in a fairly dry way, and the decision you make as to how he does that exit has no payoff. Also, forgive me if I don't remember the names of the characters, as they simply weren't important or impactful enough to remember them. Marchenko, the main villain, is basically just Barret with a more solemn attitude.
Down to story. Square Enix and Eidos hide their hand for the entire game, and proceed to fold. They feed you a story where Jensen is uncovering his mysterious year in a coma, and they never give you a true conclusion. They make an attempt at developing a story around the Illuminati, and then never have you meet one of them as the player (Technically, you meet one of them if you sit through the UNSKIPPABLE CREDITS). They set up a reunion with Megan Reed, and never knock it down. They mention Pritchard, but never do anything with him. The story is based on teasing things that you want, and then never giving you any of it.
By the time you're running around the Reception Hall, trying your best not to be even spotted by the enemy while taking them out in a crowded area a la Hitman, you're feeling like the game is about to start actually telling you the story. You go in to fight the first real boss of the game, and you win it. And that's where the game ends.
I can't suggest anyone buy this game in its current state; I don't really care about microtransacs that don't do anything (Well, I do, but I can't stop it). But I do care about being given a half, or even a third, of a game. It's been obviously sectioned off for DLC to make the Season Pass a good buy, but make the game itself a bad one.
Wait for the GOTY.

While everything I say is going to feel negative, I have it a thumbs up because overal I enjoyed my time with it.  Still consider everything I say before putting down your hard earned money (or steam wallet) on this game though.
Mortal Kombat X, like most modern fighting games, is an example of DLC exploitation, although not to the extent as something like Dead or Alive.  Several costumes and characters that would normally be unlocked through the games "Krypt" system instead are available through DLC.  There is even a $20 DLC to unlock everything in the krypt, which amounts to some concept art, finishing moves (fatalities and brutalities).  and tokens to allow you to skip fights and easily perform finishing moves.  I won't rant about the DLC, but I will say that I wish it wasn't there, and that everything was unlockable in the game.
As a game, it feels like a huge step back from Mortal Kombat (9).  The roster has shunk quite a bit, and many characters such as Rain, Kabal, Baraka, Jade, Sriker, etc. are left out for no reason.  Worse yet, you can fight against them in story mode or occasionally in Invasion boss fights, so there is no reason they couldn't be included in game.  While there are quite a few new characters, they don't feel all that different from characters already on the roster.  Cassie Cage, for example, feels like Johny Cage with a gun.  The different varients only add a few new special moves and combo variations, and most of them end up being useless in a fight.  Also, you can only select one in the beginning, which feels like a step back from Deadly Alliance when you could change them on the fly during a fight.  Finally, the balance in the game is really bad, and the on-line community knows it.  Nine times out of ten, people will pick Scorpion, who always seems to be quicker then every wake up attack.  If you try to use anyone else, you will be lucky to get any offense in without spamming ranged attacks.
As a port, the game is much MUCH better than Mortal Kombat (9).  It feels like the developers (or whoever ported the game to PC) knew what they were doing this time.  The only issue I have seen is odd frame skipping during the character endings, but they are in no way a game breaking problem.  You can still watch them and get the full experience, even if they do look a bit jittery.
I'll end with this, even though the game is a bit of a dissapointment for me, I still enjoyed it.  If you like the Mortal Kombat series, you will like this game.  If you are new or looking for a good on-line community though, stay away.

This game is often compared to Skyrim, for a reason. Both present a huge, open fantasy world with hundreds of quest which can be taken in no particular order. This is, however, where any similarities with Skyrim end.
Kingdoms of Amalur: Reckoning has stunning and very colorful visuals that had me hooked in an instant. I pay a LOT of attention to scenarios in RPGs, and Amalur probably has the most beautiful I've ever seen. The forests, ruins and towns really give you the impression of a world full of things to explore.
That being said, there are a bunch of things that feel "off" in this game. The gameplay is just fine: not brilliant but not bad either. It is not a challenging game and most of the time I just found easier to hack and slash my way to victory than to use spells or rogue abilites. The way your casting is interrupted by literally any attack is really annoying and counterintuitive. The most powerful AoE spells take a long time to cast, and should be more useful against several enemies, but chances of being interrupted are huge and therefore said spells become useless. Like I said, the melee strategy was the most efficient by far for me, which is a little underwhelming since I really like using magic.
Another problem with Amalur: questing. 90% of quests will reward you with gold and experience. The quests have some cool stories and lore behing them, but being rewarded with the same things over and over agains becomes tiresome, especially considering you won't need that amuch gold.
There's also no reason NOT to use the "fast travel" ability, which makes exploring the world less interesting as well. You won't get cool random events like in Skyrim, ever. 90% of the experience you get comes from quests as well, so fighting monsters is not a reason to backtrack ON FOOT (because there are no mounts).
To be honest I think Amalur should have inspired itself in Skyrim even more. Maybe it didn't had the budget to do so, I don't know. I highly recommend this game for anyone who is crazy about fantasy and cool scenarios (like me), but be mindful that most of it's problems are glaringly obvious for players who are used to play lots of RPG games. That being said, Amalur does provide a satisfying experience under its own limitations.

An extremely fun game. There is the occasional camera issue and the absence of a jumping ability does give the game the feeling that it's lacking something, especially when you can't jump off cliffs unless you're standing on a specific location. Some of the locations can also feel generic and some of the enemies attacks just feel like they're hacking away at your health, which can ruin any sense of strategy.
All of those are minor flaws, though. The biggest flaw of the game is when you're fighting multiple enemies at once. You'll be hacking away at an enemy, then another enemy will injure you and you'll automatically lock onto that new enemy. This can get frustrating when you're facing off with a boss and they summon a swarm of monsters. You're character will keep getting hit, hack at that enemy, get hit again, turn around and hack at that enemy, then get hit again and hack at that enemy. This can cause the fight to last forever because you're not locked on to one enemy long enough to actually kill them.
This may seem like a lot of complaints, but I've gotta admit that I still really like the game. The story is interesting, with a deep lore, and you can usually either work around or suffer through the enemy locking problem. The bottom line is that, despite its flaws, this game is very entertaining.

I've been playing fighting games competitively for over a decade now. I started as a Street Fighter player, then got into the NRS games like MK9 and Injustice when I used to travel to tournaments, and now I've transitioned into being a Tekken player. To put this short - Tekken 7 is one of the greatest fighting games I've ever played.
It is a tough game to learn but it constantly rewarding. It demands a lot from the player just to get the basics down. For one, there is no traditional tutorial in the game. While that may be unforgiving to new players there are plenty of resources out there to learn the game with from the Tekken Zaibatsu forums to all of the youtube content creators helping educate players. Also an incredible perk of the PC version is having access to the frame bot which can help you learn character frame data. However even if you're a veteran of fighting games you'll quickly learn that Tekken is a different beast altogether.
Tekken 7 is a game of movement mastery. In order to really play the game well at all you have to learn how to properly move in the 3d space. This game allows you to cancel movements with other move inputs. This allows you to cancel things like backdashing and sidestepping so that you can create whiffed attacks from the opponent that you can punish. Creating space, conditioning, whiff punishing, and juggles make up the majority of the gameplay in any given match.
Fighting mechanics aside Tekken 7 is a beautiful game to look at with great presentation touches like the slow-mo that occurs towards the end of a round when two players' attacks are about to meet at the same time, giving you a moment of hype as you witness whether or attack hits and kills or if you are the one who is KO'd. It also includes a fair amount of detail options to tinker with and in my experience runs fine at 1080p med-high settings on a gtx 1050ti.
I don't dwell on the content outside of the versus fighting much but there is a decent story mode that wraps up the Mishima saga pretty well. There are also little character chapters that give you some background information, one match against a rival, and a goofy cutscene. There is an arcade mode but there are no character endings as it looks like those assets where impliment in the character chapters. I kinda wish they would've just scrapped the chapters and gave us arcade mode endings but once you've seen them that's as much as you're going to get out of them. There is also a special boss battle versus Akuma that is extremely challenging and will probably be your last achievement/trophy to go after.
There is a good training mode that'll let you practice movement, combos, and recreating any situation you'd like to practice against. Treasure battles serve as a constant single player goal to unlock all the customization items in the game since it takes over 2000 battles to unlock everything. As mentioned you can customize all the characters in the roster with different outfits, hairstyles, colors, effects, ect. I really like the addition of New Japan Pro Wrestling clothing and outfits for the characters, especially the Rainmaker Okada outfit for King which actually changes his Rage Art into the finishing move of the current IWGP Heavyweight champion. There's also UI customizations for the health bars and player profile.
For online play the game highly encourages you to play ranked move as it allows you to play against opponents you've matched with as much as you two want and gives a visible indicator of your progress as a player. Unfortunately player matches suffer from the lack of an instant rematch option unlike ranked so you'll be going to character select after every game.
A breakdown of Tekken 7 as a package doesn't do the game justice since there are other fighting games out there with more single player content and tools to learn the game, but the pure fighting in T7 I feel outmatches all the other games. Combos are fun to execute and every punch, kick, launcher, and counter-hit feels powerful. It's always fun to play and is a game I'm going to be playing for a long time to get good at.
If you're looking for a fighting game that you can invest yourself into for the long haul, Tekken 7 is the game for you. If you're a more casual fighting game player that just wants to play by yourself against the computer and not against other people then I'd look to Netherrealm or Ark Systemworks games to fill that need. That aside, this is easily the best tekken game since Tekken 5 maybe even as far back as Tekken 3 and I can't recommend it enough for people who love fight. A review should be about a game, and how a game plays. A review should not be about tertiary or trivial concerns individual to the player. A review should tell people if a game is worth buying: nothing more, nothing less.
Mankind Divided is well worth buying for any fan of the previous Deus Ex game, Human Revolution. It takes the gameplay of the original and enhances it with many tweaks. Using the cover-to-cover sneak system feels like I'm playing a game of XCOM, and really allows me to think more critically about my surroundings. The variety of new augs, along with the returning ones, offer plenty of options for navigating Mankind Divided's world (I particularly enjoy how they even give the player a bounty of Praxis towards the beginning, allowing for them to specialize from the get-go). Every stronghold has several weakpoints, but they are for the player to discover.
The soundtrack is definitely a lot more emotive than HR's, which only had occasions of brilliance (such as in Zhao's penthouse). The graphics look beautiful and, contrary to what everyone has been saying, the game actually runs remarkably well on non-maxed settings. I'm on a laptop that reasonably should not be able to run this game, and I can do a solid 30fps with some dips. And this is before any performance patches which will inevitably come.
Mankind Divided is a great game, taking HR and enhancing it. Don't be blinded by nonsensical, almost unjustifiable rage.

I beat the game on 8/25/2016 at around 2 AM. There will be spoilers in this review.
I'll start spoiler free.
The gameplay of DX:MD is good; it's pretty much a copy/paste of the gunplay and stealth from DX:HR with a bit more polish. If you liked the mechanics from the first prequel, you will like the mechanics from the second. However, playing it on PC can be a bit of a chore with the way menus work. The UI for every single menu is sluggish and, frankly, laggy. Every item has a drop down list, but those drop down lists are fade ins from left clicks instead of instantly appearing on a right click. Actions that are important to gameplay share the same key, which can get in the way of perfect stealth. I had to reload multiple times trying to do very specific maneuvers involving moving bodies because my quest menu would open up. The overclock mechanic is also a pretty useless tack-on.
The content of the game is deceitful at first; when you're in the first throes of the game you're immersed in side quests and possibilities. Completing those side quests is fulfilling, and exploration feels fairly rewarding if not a little dry. However, whenever you venture to the new "areas" (despite them not being full-on hubs), exploration takes a drop off and rewards start to get repetitive.
Let's get onto spoilers.
Starting with the characters, none of them leave a lasting impression. The one person that felt like they had a unique personality is a terrorist leader, and doesn't get very much screen time. The characters you have direct interaction with don't exactly stand out, including the ever-so excentric Koller. Your boss is a run of the mill old, battle-jaded Call of Duty commander; your competition in your unit is your normal hardass soldier (The two combined may as well be Price and Soap) who doesn't like you; your pilot is a boring guy who survived the Incident and pretends to be racist. While they give Miller, your boss, a decent back story and a good time uncovering it, you never have the opportunity to expand on it. He exits the game in a fairly dry way, and the decision you make as to how he does that exit has no payoff. Also, forgive me if I don't remember the names of the characters, as they simply weren't important or impactful enough to remember them. Marchenko, the main villain, is basically just Barret with a more solemn attitude.
Down to story. Square Enix and Eidos hide their hand for the entire game, and proceed to fold. They feed you a story where Jensen is uncovering his mysterious year in a coma, and they never give you a true conclusion. They make an attempt at developing a story around the Illuminati, and then never have you meet one of them as the player (Technically, you meet one of them if you sit through the UNSKIPPABLE CREDITS). They set up a reunion with Megan Reed, and never knock it down. They mention Pritchard, but never do anything with him. The story is based on teasing things that you want, and then never giving you any of it.
By the time you're running around the Reception Hall, trying your best not to be even spotted by the enemy while taking them out in a crowded area a la Hitman, you're feeling like the game is about to start actually telling you the story. You go in to fight the first real boss of the game, and you win it. And that's where the game ends.
I can't suggest anyone buy this game in its current state; I don't really care about microtransacs that don't do anything (Well, I do, but I can't stop it). But I do care about being given a half, or even a third, of a game. It's been obviously sectioned off for DLC to make the Season Pass a good buy, but make the game itself a bad one.
Wait for the GOTY.

Summary of points about the game:
Optimization: game runs great, solid 60 on highest settings on a 980,i7 build. complaints I've seen usually come from people who havent updated drivers or are running AMD (IRONY) builds.
I suffered from one crash which occured at the end of a game upon returning to the main menu post credits. it doesnt seem to be some sort of unfixable bug and it didn't really hurt my experience (as i had finished playing for the day).
Gameplay: fixed from HR, the control sceme takes a little getting used to at the start but becomes second nature very quickly, combat is very fluid, as is stealth. Social was my favourite new feature; i really felt like I had augments assisting a touchy conversation
I only ever had one issue at the final battle of the game, where if you get hit by a certain munition, you get unbelievably jarrring screen shake. this was a minor complaint however.
Story: fantastic. it felt like a true Deus ex experience, the story was rich and the characters felt real. you get to interact with a lot of dynamics and you actually feel like your decisions have a butterfly effect now. 10/10 for me.
sound and music: never a huge focus for me, however I have nothing to complain about other than the splash screens ignoring system volume
Animations: this was my only real significant criticism of the game. the characters faces are extremely diverse, and the amount of time and effort the artists put into animating them and making them look real really paid off. you feel like you're talking to a human with their own facial ticks and eye movements.
sadly some of teh focus was lost on the rest of the body: at times characters walk around or make stiff gestures that Kinda detracted me from the conversation. these are characters who you can't really pay off the "because they have robot arms" argument, because they're not augs (such as Miller). I feel that there should have been a bit more detail given to the animation of characters during conversation, to ensure that conversation felt as smooth as the rest of the game did.
Breach mode: Its fun, but can wear out quick. my bias is that I loved the premise of games such as coded arms where people would hack using virtual reality. for any other person it really is just an online challenge mode with a mobile-style equipment system (which is quite generous at that). it has some fun little puzzles however, which made me enjoy myself for quite a while. ultimately my only complaint is that the story, tutorials and dialogue is slow and gets in the way of a mode that is designed around fast intuitive gameplay, with things we're essentially already meant to know.
I strongly recommend this game. (the 60 dollar version)

Solarix is a Deus Ex clone, or at least is trying to be one really hard, and fails miserably. Sneaking past a guard, when the only available option is blocked off by an invisible wall, opening doors with a digital tool impossible not be successful, trying to stay hidden from the guards, or just trying to find an access card somewere. Somewhere. Because you haven't really the slightest idea, where to look, or how to get there. There's nothing that indicates, or at least hints where to go, or look. No map, or an option to get a hint for the location. You just look for it. That's it. That's the game. You look for an item, use it on a specific door, then go and look for another thing, while trying the impossible to avoid the guards.

AI can work two ways. Not work at all, all reacting to every little step you make, even, when crouching.

I've been playing fighting games competitively for over a decade now. I started as a Street Fighter player, then got into the NRS games like MK9 and Injustice when I used to travel to tournaments, and now I've transitioned into being a Tekken player. To put this short - Tekken 7 is one of the greatest fighting games I've ever played.
It is a tough game to learn but it constantly rewarding. It demands a lot from the player just to get the basics down. For one, there is no traditional tutorial in the game. While that may be unforgiving to new players there are plenty of resources out there to learn the game with from the Tekken Zaibatsu forums to all of the youtube content creators helping educate players. Also an incredible perk of the PC version is having access to the frame bot which can help you learn character frame data. However even if you're a veteran of fighting games you'll quickly learn that Tekken is a different beast altogether.
Tekken 7 is a game of movement mastery. In order to really play the game well at all you have to learn how to properly move in the 3d space. This game allows you to cancel movements with other move inputs. This allows you to cancel things like backdashing and sidestepping so that you can create whiffed attacks from the opponent that you can punish. Creating space, conditioning, whiff punishing, and juggles make up the majority of the gameplay in any given match.
Fighting mechanics aside Tekken 7 is a beautiful game to look at with great presentation touches like the slow-mo that occurs towards the end of a round when two players' attacks are about to meet at the same time, giving you a moment of hype as you witness whether or attack hits and kills or if you are the one who is KO'd. It also includes a fair amount of detail options to tinker with and in my experience runs fine at 1080p med-high settings on a gtx 1050ti.
I don't dwell on the content outside of the versus fighting much but there is a decent story mode that wraps up the Mishima saga pretty well. There are also little character chapters that give you some background information, one match against a rival, and a goofy cutscene. There is an arcade mode but there are no character endings as it looks like those assets where impliment in the character chapters. I kinda wish they would've just scrapped the chapters and gave us arcade mode endings but once you've seen them that's as much as you're going to get out of them. There is also a special boss battle versus Akuma that is extremely challenging and will probably be your last achievement/trophy to go after.
There is a good training mode that'll let you practice movement, combos, and recreating any situation you'd like to practice against. Treasure battles serve as a constant single player goal to unlock all the customization items in the game since it takes over 2000 battles to unlock everything. As mentioned you can customize all the characters in the roster with different outfits, hairstyles, colors, effects, ect. I really like the addition of New Japan Pro Wrestling clothing and outfits for the characters, especially the Rainmaker Okada outfit for King which actually changes his Rage Art into the finishing move of the current IWGP Heavyweight champion. There's also UI customizations for the health bars and player profile.
For online play the game highly encourages you to play ranked move as it allows you to play against opponents you've matched with as much as you two want and gives a visible indicator of your progress as a player. Unfortunately player matches suffer from the lack of an instant rematch option unlike ranked so you'll be going to character select after every game.
A breakdown of Tekken 7 as a package doesn't do the game justice since there are other fighting games out there with more single player content and tools to learn the game, but the pure fighting in T7 I feel outmatches all the other games. Combos are fun to execute and every punch, kick, launcher, and counter-hit feels powerful. It's always fun to play and is a game I'm going to be playing for a long time to get good at.
If you're looking for a fighting game that you can invest yourself into for the long haul, Tekken 7 is the game for you. If you're a more casual fighting game player that just wants to play by yourself against the computer and not against other people then I'd look to Netherrealm or Ark Systemworks games to fill that need. That aside, this is easily the best tekken game since Tekken 5 maybe even as far back as Tekken 3 and I can't recommend it enough for people who love fight. The King of Iron Fist is back and better than ever.

An Alpha survival game with litterally nothing to do.
First off you can only craft 36 items, those being mostly for building a base. No options to actually build any tools to gather resources with (like an axe to chop trees with). Couldn't find any wood lying around. An hour of game play, no wood what so ever.
Crafting is very time sonsuming. Resources are very scarce. The only resources you can gather are the ones lying around on the surface, no mining what so ever. There's text above the resoucres to show what it is, so that means you'll not be able to chop the trees.
Second off, your guide Brad shows up in the middle of the night and tells you to follow him (1st game), except you can't see squat, so natuarally you can't follow him.
You don't actually mine anything, all resources are lying around on the surface.
There's no mini map, so you don't know where you're at. It's easy to get lost.
You get a drone, but the commands for it don't work, so it's completely useless. Also once the drone command window opens, you can't ever close it again. since it uses the same keys as your inventory.
I just wandered around until I starved to death.
I tried a second game, thinking I missed something. Brad never showed up, found the ruins, well, that's all it is, it just ruins, empty ruined buildings, nothing else. Also found the survivor camp (by accident), was told to talk to someone who wasn't even there. Otherwise the survivor camp is useless.
You can't even make a torch, so you have to use the resource gathering tool you start out with for light, it's very annoying.
The only danger you have in the game is starving to death.
Eventually I just got bored and quit. This game isn't even worth 10 bucks.

I played this when it first came out, and it reinvisioned my music playlist.
So I decided to get it again on sale, because why not, and realized how great and how much this game actually is. It's certainly not for everybody, but you definitely do not need to be into hard metal to like it, as long as you don't dislike it. It does have it's flaws (samey side quests, a simple story, basic combat), but it is above all else fun.
The game offers two types of combat - normal hack-and-slash and tower defence battles. The first is action-packed, the second adds a layer of strategy. But they go well surprisingly well, and the second mode is never boring so long as you know what you're doing. You'll find yourself ripping out gutiar solos on the battlefield one moment and organizing waves of headbangers the next moment.
As for sound and music, this game has one of the best soundtracks I've ever heard in a video game. Dozens upon dozens of songs ranging from soft rock, hard metal, and even hair bands. And it nods to all of them, with characters that humorously reflect the different genres
. The variety is surprising, and I've fallen in love with a lot of songs and styles I would have never discovered otherwise. Speaking of sound - Jack Black's voice acting is hilarious and adds tremendously to the game's great dialogue.
Honestly, it hasn't aged too badly either. I was wary about playing it again 8 years after it came out, but I found myself having an absolute ball. Double Fine's style never ceases to amaze me. If you enjoy Double Fine games or have even the slightest interest in rock, I'd highly recommend this game.

I think that I have enough hours on my account that i can give a review of this game. Heroes and generals is a great game for casual play. It is fun, easy to pick up, and has lots of playability. However, there is  only ugly part of this game that prevents it from being popular, the massive grid. This has been a problem that has been adressed many times in the past but there really havent been that many significant changes to it. The first 4 or 5 ranks are easy becaus starter equipment is easy the obtain. But, as soon as you hit Gold matchmaking, the balance is thrown off. Players with high end equipment out class lower ranks who just moved up and that is the worst part. I can only hope that in the Future that Reto Moto, the company that makes heroes and generals, recognizes this problem and fixes it as soon as possible. Overall here are my final thoughts:
Pros:
-free to play
-lots of content
-graphics are decent
-Diversity in styles of play
-Great with friends
Cons:
-The grind for high end equipment
-minor unbalancing with weapons
-high priced skins, vehicles, etc.

that left a bad taste in my mouth. The science fiction and horror labels of the game pulled me in, but after playing the game a few times, I cannot give a recommendation.
First, I'll say that the setting, narrative, and atmosphere are well done. The voice acting is surprisingly phenomenal! There's no cutscenes or anything, the whole story is told from radio transmissions, voice memos etc, but it's still really impressive. All of the voice actors do a fantastic job, and the story itself is well written, with memorable characters and motives. They also nailed the industrial space setting. It's a great fit for the atmosphere of the game.
But everything else? Oh man. The gameplay is so clunky and bad. It forces you to take a "stealth" approach most of the time because the pistol (the single gun you carry for most of the game) is weak as♥♥♥♥♥♥ The A.I. is absolutely abysmal and they have incredibly ugly animations. (They'll run up to you and hit you, and the only thing that moves is their upper body around their torso. It's really uncomfortable to watch.) The "hacking" consists of selecting a tool and holding a button down. While the atmosphere at times is spooky for sure, there's no actual good scares or moments that got my heart racing. Movement can be really frustrating, especially when exploring some of the levels, due to clipping. The save system is outdated. A whole chapter in the middle is just poorly optimzed and tanked my FPS. There were other glitches and bugs through my playthroughs as well.
I'd have to give this a final score of 4.0/10. It's a decent experience, definitely not the worst thing I've ever played but it is really rough. I will say, the developers are really nice on the forums by interacting with the players, getting feedback, updating the game etc. Two of the achievements were bugged for me and a lot of other players and they patched it, among other things. . They really want this to succeed, and it's clear that they're passionate about what they do. Hopefully one day they do hit it big with a game that has a strong story like
, but also carries the weight on the gameplay front. If you're interested in
, I'd get it on a sale.

No major character revamps this time, a first in a new Tekken game. Also no Mokujin.
Queuing got worse after the update.
Very polished and well balanced for the most part; no lag on a good internet connection. No input lag either on offline. If anything it reads inputs too well.
Most moves have more oomph to them now, and the new systems integrated are a welcome addition; save for the unbalanced rage drives.. Because it is a boon to some (instant startup, damage on block, heavy block jail), but a bane to other characters (if not unuseable at all and heavily punishable 90% of the time).
The Slow motion K.O. is really, really, cool at very tense moments.
Rage drives are ok I guess, but they get boring fast.
Tailspin is a more balanced way of incorporating bound, and really makes players learn how to properly gauge frames and practice dashing. Movement overall is improved and is a lot more important in this game.
Certain characters are obsolete and the buffs/nerfs/new moves are spread VERY unevenly; however if you're a Mishima/Kazama player this is a great time to shine.
Speaking of the Mishimas, if you have a hard on for their story this is a great must buy. Absolutely. If you want other characters (probably your main) to be fleshed out in this supposed final installation, they probably weren't cause everyone was given a♥♥♥♥♥♥story continuation/conclusion.
If you don't like rage quitters, don't get the game. If you tend to tilt don't get the game.
There are a ton of customization options in the game per character, however it gives off a smackdown 2014 feel of not being able to go anywhere because there isn't enough there.
Auras, kis, etc look like crap, considering the great visual feedback and VFX on character moves. Seriously, was customization tacked on as a last minute thing..
DLC's aren't great so far.
Main problem is that unless you aim to get really good, and you set a high bar for yourself, there is almost no progression to the game at all since unlocking customization items feel like a boring grind even on the highest difficulty... and since what items you get is random at a certain point, you might not get what you want for that character. And when you do, it's usually worse on the character (in terms of color, fitting, etc) than on the thumbnail.
Main selling point is that its Tekken on PC. I mean that's it, really. There's a lot of good players with varying levels of experience to play with, and the community isn't as toxic as most competitively focused mainstream games out there.
I love Tekken, and I played it nonstop on the arcade before (Tekken 6). Still do. But I feel very lukewarm to this game. It feels like there's less respect given to the characters themselves, and a lot of mechanical focus. The "Mishima Saga" is full of cliches I couldn't even take it seriously even if I have a huge fan boner for Akuma and Jin. It was hype, sure, but it was a lot of flash and no substance. And then everyone else was swept under a rug; barely any story for them.
It's funny that you can buy the old cutscenes and gallery arts from the previous games with ingame currency; just to remind you of how cool, charming, witty, or actually funny they used to be. (talking about you, lars ending from Tekken 6)
I'd say get it on a sale. Last time I'm getting a season pass.

I recommend this with all my heart, but bring some tissues :)

Let me start out by saying I am a huge fan of the series. I have played every single deus ex game, and really enjoyed human revolution and was very hyped to play mankind divided.
Upon seeing the mixed reviews, I was a bit dismayed and investigated further. From my perspective, it seemed most bad reviews were from people complaining about performance issues (which is totally their right to do so, and I actually agree with them giving a bad review because the game is poorly optimized for their system). All of the mixed reviews even made me consider buying the game after a couple of patches came out. But as I said, I am a major fan of the series and have a relatively good computer and decided to roll the dice and hope to not have any technical performance issues.
I have a gtx 970m i7 laptop. With all settings maxed and MSAA off, I am averaging 40-45 FPS, which is just fine IMO. The game looks absolutely stellar in my opinion. The only other game I can think of that has much detail in the environment is the witcher 3.
I am really happy I decided to buy the game now, because it is a truly great deus ex experience. If you are a fan of the series, and have a computer that is of similar specifications as mine, I highly recommend this game. The only bugs I encountered were in the introductory mission with all the tutorials (invisible walls, floating objects, clipping) and its a damn shame its poorly optimized for less high end computers because those people are missing out on something spectacular.
I hope things are patched up quickly because this game deserves better reviews than it is currently getting. That being said, I would have given the game a thumbs down if it ran poorly on my computer, the same as everybody else doing, and that is an understandable and justified thing to do.

This was probably the game i was most excited for this year, and like an idiot i pre ordered it despite swearing off pre ordering. I was expecting a roller coaster ride like with Human Revolution, however that's nowhere near what i got.
TL;DR DX:MD could easily have been game of the year material, however rediculous micro transactions and a story with no payoff make it an example of the sorry state the industry is in today
The Good:
The gameplay is FANTASTIC, leaps and bounds above human revolution. The new powers are all awesome and really satisfying to use and the environment design is some of the best ive ever seen. There are so many ways to appreach every situation and more open up as you get better powers.
The setting is also a very strong point. Instead of having two shallow hub cities they poured all their effort into Prague, and it shows. The city is dripping with charactor and really draws you into the narrative.
The graphics are good, but poor optimization hamstrings it a bit.
The bad:
Two words: MICRO TRANSACTIONS. Fo all your new powers and cool abilities there are less opportunities to upgrade them. Praxis points are fewer and father between than in Human Revolution so instead of earning the extra ones though gameplay or maybe a challenge mode you have to buy them. This is the same as with credits, why let the player work harder for their credits when you can just let them buy more. Also the weapons that come with the collectors edition can only be used ONCE, and if you start another playthough then they're gone. The suits at square enix really screwed the pooch on this one, how about we pay for them game once and then actually get the fing game.
The Ugly:
It feels like this game was being juggled by three different studios with no contact with eachother: a brilling programming team, greedy publishers, and pants on head ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ writers. The story, the cornerstone of the deus ex franchise, is pathetic. Now that's not to saw that the writing is bad or that it doesn't make sense, in fact it does a really good job of setting up a mystery and making you suspicous of both factions trying to use you. However for all the buildup and intrigue there's no playoff. The plot feels like it's been cut in half, nothing is actually resolved, and they pull the resolution to conflict between the two factions is a total cop out. When i finished i literally just stared at my screen saying, "What?" over and over again. There's no payoff, no deonstration of the effects of your limited choices, and so much is left unexplained; probably to be sold in the DLC.

This is a sprawling, epic action RPG. There are three classes to choose from, might (fighter), finesse (rogue) and sorcery (wizard). It is extremely easy to create a pure character or a hybrid. Respec'ing your character is easy and you will find yourself doing this several times, if not for anything but to be able to purchase skills from an earlier trainer. I started with a pure melee character and took him to level 36. I played around with a hybrid melee/sorcerer/rogue, but didn't have fun. In the end I settled with a powerful rogue/melee hybrid that could barrage enemies with arrows from afar and mop up with blades afterward.
Combat is a mixed bag. It is essentially a click fest like many action RPGs. Even still it is rewarding. Loot is the end game and trying to find the right equipment will keep you going. Unfortunately, as with most ARPGs by the time you get a complete set of armor you have better non-set stuff. However, sometimes the bonuses gained with a full set overrides the slight decrease in protection.
Side quests can be annoying. Many are of the FedEx variety. It can be extremely frustrating to move from place to place delivering goods, or killing X number of beasts to collect your reward. There is a fast travel system that allows you to move from location to location as long as you have been there on foot at least once. This does cut down on travel time, but these FedEx quests are tedious. Since this is likely the only time I will play, I finished the majority of side quests. I did get bugged out of two and couldn't complete them. And a couple others I didn't do early and never went back to finish them. The quest system is easy to navigate and helpful markers show up pointing the way to your next objective.
In the end, I was finally glad to get through the game. The last levels are mobs after mobs standing in your way of the final battle. I did enjoy this game and can recommend it to anyone who is looking for a good action RPG. There isn't a lot of depth in character development, but what is here is good.

(This review is relevant as of patch 1.3)
Rise of the Triad (ROTT) is a game I'd recommend solely on the basis of how wildly entertaining its fast-paced shooting is, and because of the huge nostalgia factor it will entice on old-school FPS fans (especially fans of the original ROTT). This game successfully brings back the long missed crazy action of twitch shooters. It's a completely insane frag-fest that doesn't bother with the nonsensical plots or uninteresting character development that seems to plague today's modern shooters. Here, you're thrown into a sadistic single player campaign where the only thing that matters is to blow away whatever dares move. To that end, you are fed an incredible arsenal of rocket launchers, magic weapons, and crazy power-ups. As a consequence, ROTT is very good at what it does: mass murder, plain and simple. The multiplayer is also a welcome comeback to the days of Unreal Tournament and Quake 3, and while it still suffers from a lack of modes variety (even after the content patches), it's inmensely satisfying.
With all that in mind, it must be noted that, although this game is a truly faithful remake of the classic 1995 shooter, it does suffer from some HUGE problems that might turn off more than a few players. I'll go ahead and describe in length all the issues that were big bugbears for me.
First and foremost, Rise of the Triad is extremely poorly optimized, even after the patch that was supposed to fix its performance issues. Expect constant framerate drops during the levels, even if your machine laughs in the face of the recommended system requirements. Interceptor Entertainment has promised to work around this problem and give ROTT the performance you'd expect from an Unreal 3 Engine game, but truth is, the game still doesn't work as it should.
Another big complaint I have with this game is the level design. Even though the developers promised to give this game awesome non-linear levels reminiscent of the original game, it turns out most of them are fairly linear, and, although there are lots of secret areas to explore (which is always a nice thing in a shooter), I was quite dissapointed to see that the levels in the single player campaign turned out to be "modern" in a rather bad way, that is, the linear way. Even more importantly, this game heavily abuses on platforming and jumping puzzles, which, in my personal opinion, unless done in a very moderate manner, simply do not belong in a first person shooter. I understand that a small platforming section can help vary the gameplay if paced correctly (which was often the case in the original ROTT), but, considering the extent in which they have been deployed in this game, they simply hurt the quality of some levels inmensely. It's a shame that one of the few truly non-linear levels in the game (E2L2, The Room) gave me an horribly tedious time because it consists almost exclusively of platforming. Thankfully, the developers added the option to quicksave in one of the patches, making the terrible chore of platforming a little bit more passable.
My final and most minor complaint is that, because of the fact that Rise of the Triad is so faithful to the original game, it also retains some of its problems, namely the complete uselessness of the first two weapons, which are replaced by the MP40 submachine gun right in the first level. I think the developers could have gone a bit farther and given the bullet weapons some actual use (other than being the boring spare weapons for when you are out of missile or magic stuff)
Verdict:
I want to end this review by saying that, even while I spent most of the time describing the problems of Rise of the Triad, this game was overall an enjoyable experience, that manages to just barely outlive its many issues in favor of an extremely satisfying and highly violent action. I'd definitely recommend this game to any fan of the original Rise of the Triad, and also to FPS fans in general if they are willing to cope with the problems I described, particularly the poor optimization.
The Good:
-Fast-paced, old-school ultraviolent action
-An excellent arsenal of explosive and magic weapons that set up some crazy shooting
-Very enjoyable multiplayer
The Bad:
-Extremely poorly optimized
-Fairly linear level design
-Overuse of jumping and platforming puzzles
-Bullet weapons feel uninteresting, with two of them being completely useless

I wish there were optimization options for GFX, so I could run it at a decent framerate on my duo core laptop :/
Otherwise its a decent attempt at modernization of an fps classic.

With 85% of the Steam achievements earned and near towards the end, so I nearly completed it before writing this. In ten hours give or take afk time with cooking and toilet trips...  In short this game is more frustrating than anything else, I imagine it is a broke persons "SOMA".
You get one save slot and it saves at checkpoints, when you die you might have to restart the saves actual chapter to get around complete / incomplete objective bugs not allowing you to open doors and progress. Also meaning if you die this error will loop in certain sections of the game *GRR*  > *uninstall?* > *Stay strong*. Not being able to go back and fix this where certain doors remain closed means you end up spending more time unbugging your efforts restarting which really started to kill it for me. Add this to the brutal AI that can be where your save spawns you or magnetically not allow you to escape their clutches without really leaving you at death's door, and  your left with this very hostile feeling from the game, that is more felt than its concept. You will find dying often or quitting the game is in greater amount than the jump scares if anything else.
The story was fine and the voice acting was excellent, clearly heavily inspired by things actually shown within the game's content which should be a no no, it should be conceptually strong enough to stand alone, not break its own imersion referencing other games, but I didn't make it so... Given the refernces and pictures of other games and one game title in particular, yes... it did remind me of SS in that it looks, plays, and feels rather similarly but very stripped down. The ai were unforgiving and very robotic, you learn to avoid them and when cramped and dying, to keep trying until you get around them.
Performance in certain areas is due to pushing sprites in the UDK engine past the acceptable threshold, it simply is over done in areas and on a stock I7 920 + MSI GTX 970 with 4GB of ram - its clear to me its the game that is the problem and could do with some more work to make it better.

This game reminds me of the System Shock and Thief games sort of mashed together, and that's awesome - they are two of my favorite game series.  This has all the tension and atmosphere of those games, if maybe not being as intricate or refined as they are.
The game mechanics rely heavily on stealth - you don't want to be seen or heard by your enemies, at all.  Being spotted by an enemy is very, very bad.  You will never have much in the way of weapons or ammo, so your best bet is to avoid enemies altogether, or take them out by stunning them from behind undetected.  Failing to do so results in a brutal death.  The best method I found for taking enemies out is to watch their movements in order to plan the right moment to attack - get in a dark nook, wait for your moment, follow them close while crouching, look up and zap them right at the back of their skull with the tazer.  Any other method I tried resulted in missing most of the time and being detected.
The sci-fi elements here are spot on for me - they hit all the right notes.  The level design is pretty good, conveying the sense of actual places, but come off as not being as sophisticated and clever as any of the Thief or System Shock games (secrets, alternate routes, etc.).  In fact, the levels, being generally expansive, seem to encourage exploration, but VERY rarely reward you for it.  And after mapping out the entire map you realize how generally shallow the maps feel - just not much depth to most.
The story and voice acting are pretty good.  Some of the bugs left in the game are not - like reloading a save and finding yourself stuck in level geometry, constant sound glitches, inexcusably poor framerate, etc..  Quite awhile back I posted feedback to the developers in the hopes that they might address some of the things I felt would improve the game, but they've apparently moved on to other projects.  That's very disappointing.  As is the very ♥♥♥♥♥♥ FPS I get on this 3 ghz dual-core machine.  This is an Unreal engine game - so why is it so poorly optimized?
Yes, I recommend this game for Thief and sci-fi fans, but with caveats.

I'll preface this by saying that I had very high hopes for this game, and that my level of hype for Holdfast was unbelievable for several months now. Unlike many others that reviewed the game so far, I was not a pre-alpha tester, nor did I receive the game for free.. in fact I bought three copies of the game. To begin, Holdfast: NaW has the unique advantage in that the game and the community itself are backed up by some of the most dedicated and passionate devs I've ever seen in a project. That's all I have to say on that matter. Now, on to the game.

Pros:

- Graphics/Visual effects. The game is absolutely gorgeous. Many like myself come from NW, and the graphical fidelity between these two titles is immense. Looking objectively without the NW looking glass yields the same results. The game is beautiful graphically speaking, and the art style is quite unique in nature, boasting a "different" color palette that can only be described as warm.. it works wonderfully; everything from the unit detail, explosions, death animations, to the smoke effects and terrain are superb.

- Voice acting. This one genuinely surprised me, as it's something I had no idea I would pay attention to. However, the voice acting in Holdfast is a solid performance. Anything from the huge selection of voice commands, to taunts, to battle cries and different generic yells/screams on the battlefield all add to the experiential effect that Holdfast provides to the player. I had literally zero expectations here and came away pleasantly surprised.

- Shooting. This deserves its own area for praise. One of the things I hated about NW was the terrible RNG-fest that was shooting. "Aim.. somewhere and Fire!" is no longer the case, and while some random factors come into play, shooting and marksmanship are both factors that have been smoothed out and refined to create a whole different and unique aspect for linebattles and other public events. The shooting and ballistic mechanics in Holdfast is everything I've wanted from a game like this, save for lack of proper ADS (more on this later).

- Movement. Players on the battlefield walk and move in a human fashion, rather than NW's "stickman" form and regimented manner. In Holdfast, player movement can only be described as fluid, no matter if you're an NW veteran or a newbie to the Napoleonic era.

- VOIP. Yes, it's a thing. Yes it works. Yes, it's just as lovingly cancerous as you would imagine.

- Maps. The maps in Holdfast are for the most part excellently designed. Large, open desert ruins lead into forested cabins and stone walls to create a diverse and decently balanced gameplay experience that feel unique from one encounter to another. There isn't a big copy/paste issue with regards to map design here, and it's all the better for it.

- Selection of Units. The accuracy and selection of units in-game is pretty solid, down to the correct equipment each soldier has. Whether you want to be rank-and-file, a musician, or a glorious flag bearer, you can pretty much have at it. The play styles that are supported with this system are as vast as they are unique in their own right. This is not to mention the options wehn it comes to naval warfare!

- Optimization. This is something that I've heard mixed feelings about as of today (launch day), though I find that the game is fairly well optimized. I have a decent mid-ish PC, boasting 8GB of RAM, an AMD FX-8350, and a GTX 960 4GB GPU. I can run the game at "Very High" with nearly maxed out graphics settings and I get a solid 40-60 frames, depending on what's happening on-screen. If I turn down AA and shadows for example, I gain several fps each respectively. Lower end computers may have issues at higher settings, however I see no issues being able to run this game with a potato if you are reasonable with regards to your expectations. I put this in the pro section because it's definitely pretty good in the alpha stage, but will only get better with the devs working hard on both server and graphical optimizations in the future.

- UI/HUD. The game's UI is simple and great, and the HUD is quite useful as well. Getting a kill yields a satisfying message and icon on-screen and the overall placement and implementation of the game's UI and menu system is pretty well done, if not for needing a little prettying-up down the road, though it's not at all necessary. The only main negative here I would say is the mini-map. I personally would like it done away with completely, at least for infantry.

- The community has pretty much carried over wholesale from NW and elsewhere. With that, the community is both terrible and amazing all in the same package (with a bow on top). With all the bad that comes with it, you'll be hard pressed to find a group of players who are more passionate about a game than those flooding to Holdfast at this point.

Now onto the cons:

- Melee. Simply put, melee is pretty bad. Is it game-breaking? No. Is it annoying? Definitely. The melee animations and delay are quite cheeky and can make for some hilarious non-kills. The blocking is nearly useless and I think I was able to successfully utilize the blocking mechanic once or twice, otherwise I've been spamming and spinning like mad. I won't utterly lambaste Anvil Game Studios for this like others are, because they have said time and time and time again that melee is of the utmost importance with regards to their game. It needs work, but it will get fixed and I see no point in calling out the end of the world when there is no need. Besides, it gives us all time to work on our shooting..

- Server latency/crashes. Even as I write this I know for a 100% fact that AGS is working at fixing the current launch-day server issues, but it needs to be said that the servers were not ready for the load they received today. Between lag jumps, sometimes pushing my ping from 34 to upwards of 600, to server crashes on menu actuations while in-game, the servers definitely need some work. That being said of course, this launch day was the most impactful stress-test to date and fixes are coming in due order.

- Server player count. This isn't an inherent negative, so much as a wish. We all want 200-man servers, and the devs know it. I have no doubt we will se higher server count numbers (again, AGS states as such in their development roadmap). I'll leave it at that, but the game is nowhere near boring as it is, and by the full release a few months down the road I have full faith this will be a non-issue.

- Arty/Cav.. or lack-ish thereof. In its current state, Holdfast does not have any cavalry, which is a big bummer for me personally as I love what cav brings to the table in terms of gameplay and momentum. Furthermore, artillery as it stands is very limited in it's use and deployment opportunities. This, once again, has been addressed in the dev roadmap and will be addressed but as of the writing of this review these are a couple of the things I would like to see implemented.



Holdfast is a great game. Even with my astronomical expectations, I was definitely not disappointed, and while I have some quarrel with a  few aspects of the game as of now, I understand completely that much of the issues being had this early in the game's life cycle are a result of just that. It's an alpha and I, like many others are going to look forward with a positive outlook because of this. There are indeed many things I'd like to see added. More nations - Prussia (obviously), Russia, Sweden, Spain, Austria, etc - as well as more maps and game modes, but as it stands in its alpha state, Holdfast: Nations at War is more polished and most importantly, more fun than most games twice or three-times its price (side note: $20 USD is a very reasonable price for a game like this). With all things considered, I can happily recommend you pick up Holdfast: NaW.

The Hat Man at it's core is a
clone with a few new brushes of paint for distinction. Consider this recommendation with a caveat -- only purchase if you are a fan of the Slender Man series. You play as a mother (or father) of your presumed missing institutionalized daughter. The hospital you last checked her in has not replied to your messages so naturally, you head over to investigate. The game begins with you riding up an elevator to the lobby of this hospital. To your surprise, you arrive to a desolated, dilapitated and somber hospital -- no one at the front desk, no nurses and all the doors seem locked. Graphics are nice, controls are easy -- again, Slender Man-esque. You walk up a set of stairs to a room where you find your daughter's journal. After reading it, the game
. You are transported to the
.
I would like to emphasize to qualities of the Shadow Ward that serve as divergence points from the classic Slender Man series. If you stay too long in the room that teleports you to the Shadow Ward, (i.e. collecting journal papers or just looking around) strange shadow figures will start to appear and attack you. This happens occassionally throughout the game and the way to counter it is by pointing your flash light at them. Nothing revolutionizing, but a good small detail as far as Slender Man-esque games are concerned.
. After breaking a door with an axe you enter a maze in the hospotal where your task is to collect the missing journal entries while also escaping the Hat Man. The interesting part here is that the maze is constantly randomized. There are a few checkpoints that are stable but to the routes and locations of the journal entries are entirely randomized every time you hit a checkpoint or every time you restart the area.
I think this is very ingenious and at least to my experience, something not most horror games do. I think it's a curious application of RNG that serves to disorient, displace and confuse the player. More so when you have Slender Man's cousin chasing after you. In other aspects, the story is easy to follow if you read the journal entries and the soundtrack is good as far as this niche sub-genre of games is concerned. All in all, The Hat Man: Shadow Ward is a worthy attempt at a Slender-clone. It decidedly has its faults, does not revolutionize the genre, but it also has just enough redeeming qualities to appeal to hardcore fans of the horror sub-genre.

I don’t enjoy being scared but I do enjoy creepy atmospheric games with engaging and mysterious stories. So I occasionally buy horror games in the hope of finding something like the good Silent Hill games but sometimes I end up buying games as dire as this one.
On my first attempt, right near the start I picked up the diary and immediately died. Okay so I assumed that was not what I was supposed to do. After scouring the rest of the room I found out I was supposed to pick up the diary but just the game had spawned an enemy right in my face.
Having got past that hurdle I was able to start the game properly. I’m the type of person who when they play a game they wants to explore all the game has to offer so I tend to look round the whole area before moving on. So I started methodically exploring the level and quickly got frustrated as I kept stumbling onto things to progress the game but there were so many avenues I hadn't explored. The same rooms were reused over and again so there was no way to keep track of where I had been without a map. Only at this point did I realise that the map was not fixed it just procedurally generates the map using the same handful of rooms. Upon realising this I lost any remaining interest in the game. All there was left to do was aimlessly wander through the same rooms over and again till the things you need to progress appear.
In the latter part of the game the enemies move faster and spawn closer to you. So whether you win or lose felt entirely arbitrary, depending on how the items and enemies spawn and nothing to do with the players input.
The one thing I did like was the voice actor playing your daughter, she did a good job. This then directly contrasts with the voice actor of the mother. She is so bad I honestly wasn't sure if she was a voice synthesizer at first.
All in all the only saving grace of this game is that I bought it in the sale for 19p but still I could spent that on something useful like an onion.
