This game is incredible and has elements that may appeal to any type a fighting game lover. The characters all feel balanced and unique. I imagine the game would be very fun casually as Unreal Engine 4 and the rage mechanic allow for incredible looking hit effects and stages and very satisfying to hit and satisfying to look at rage combos. There are unique soundtracks for each stage and it sounds as if they put a lot of effort into them as the production quality is top notch. You may find yourself finding a couple favorites as I have (I love solitude and infinite azure moonsiders 1st). The slow motion effect creates tension in close matches, the story mode is epic and dramatic, and there are a lot of choices for character customization. The combos in this game are its best feature in my opinion as they are so fun to learn, they aren't unnecessarily complex, and it is easy to create your own unique variations as you get more experienced with the characters. Certain combos are better for certain situations (such as wall combos and combos that leave your oponent grounded etc.) and start off on different moves so you won't get bored from practicing or performing the same combo repetitively as in other games. For the more hardcore players, as I said before, the characters all feel balanced. You may see tier lists for deathmatches with certain characters, but whichever character you choose isn't going to hinder you from beating other players of equal or lower skill level. If you put in the work on any character you will see results. Also, the skillcap in this game is very high as there is always room for improvement in learning different matchups on your character(s) of choice, efficiently using each stage to the fullest, learning when to use certain aggressive/defensive moves on certain characters, how to punish/defend against moves, etc. The ranking system is fair and for the most part except for rare occasions I've seen on reddit/youtube you will get penalized for disconnection/rage quitting. Also you rank up the fastest from fighting against players of your own rank which the system allows you to filter depending on your preference so it isn't possible to exploit the system and farm lower rank players or fluke wins against high rank players as you will rank up dramatically slower. Lastly, the connection is very good especially on PC and you can filter your matchmaking to include specific connection qualities. I love this game and I think I'm going to keep playing it for a while longer as the game is active and fun and so is the community.

I've been following Solarix and the team developing it for a while, and spoke with them on Twitter a couple of times about their influences and their goals for this game; nice people with rather lofty goals, especially when the game drops System Shock as a key source of inspiration. It took a little bit for me to pick it up, as I couldn't back them on Kickstarter and I also wanted to catch the game on sale because it was a little ambitious, and post release the feedback wasn't encouraging, to say the least. On sale, this game is well worth the price of admission, but not without its flaws.
Within the first hour of the game I found myself fairly immersed in the world of Solarix. The game is something of an amalgamation of a Giger-esque science fiction setting with stealth primarily rooted in the Thief series. I can feel notes of Dead Space in the story, as well as System Shock, but neither of these inspirations are truly borrowed from in full, and that serves to set it apart from those franchises. The game does a great job of setting up a very atmospheric and realistic world, oftentimes content with letting the player wander and see what they can see, but this is one of the aspects of the game that I feel is somewhat of a double edged sword.
When the player wanders away from mission goals, immersion begins to set in, especially in non linear games leaning on exploration. Solarix seems content to remind you that if you decide to leave an area and your minor objectives in that area have not been completed, the game reminds you aggressively with a pop up. This seems somewhat odd a problem when there are so many subtle but effective ways in the canon of game design to keep a player on task without pulling them out of the experience.
While It is fairly obvious where to go, it is difficult to follow an exact path because well lit areas more often than not serve as places to avoid, lest you get put down by a mercenary or one of the infected. Pulsetense had a huge opportunity there to add tension to these small moments, but instead I'm left feeling somewhat disappointed because the game requires you to spend your time on objectives that are vague about why they are treated with such importance. That broke the immersion quickly and unpleasantly for me in one instance when I found myself prodded to backtrack and explore two buildings that didn't necessarily serve a purpose other than to grab access cards and listen to an audiolog. Whether that series of events was important or not, I just wish I had a choice.
While I recommend playing the game for the sheer amount of effort you can see from a team that has never produced a finished title, I can only recommend this game with half of my heart. On one side, the game is beautiful to look at, even in Unreal Engine 3, and I admire the scale and ambition that Pulsetense accomplished with this title, but on the other hand, it hasn't truly brought anything new to the table to mix up the Looking Glass Studios formula, and I find that serves to lessen the impact of a title that could have been a bit better than just good; instead something much closer to remarkable.

Solarix isn't bad for a crouching sim.
Nah, just kidding. It's actually pretty bad. This has got to be one of the all-time glitchiest, bugged out, and wonky games I have ever played. The developer and publisher must have spent like zero dollars on their QA testing Oompah Loompahs for this one and it really shows. You can literally crouch your way through walls and obstacles to areas on the map that you should never be able to access or see. For example in one of the beginning outdoor areas I was able to crouch walk through a wall to see the end of the map. And that was at the beginning of the map. I encountered numerous glitches with attempting to pick up items and move them. The best glitches are the ones where you can't pick up the item and move it even though you are supposed to. Really love those. Frequently you'll get jammed or completely stuck on the edge of a pathway or obstacle. The only way to get free is to restart the level. Very annoying. Super extra special bonus glitch- I shut off the background music in the main menu and when I play the game I have background music. That's glorious.
The game describes itself as a stealth combat shooter, with a bit of choice as to how you want to tackle it. I went into it expecting something along the lines of Hitman, and boy was I wrong. There isn't much of an option other than stealth as you rarely come across any ammunition for a weapon. Instead you get to use a goofy lookin zapper that will one-shot space suit nitwits from the back of their noggin. If you are into that sort of game play style then this one is definitely for you. I found it tedious and kinda boring quickly. Oh yeah and when that one-shot to the back of the head goes wrong- and it will a good portion of the time it will also become very frustrating. Once the bad guys are alerted to your presence from a botched attack you'll be blugeoned to death like a baby seal faster than you can say baby seal.
On the positive side Solarix does have a lot of atmosphere. It's got an interesting story line and decent voice acting. The graphics are not bad, even if some folks consider them dated.
Final verdict- if you are looking for a science fiction horror game that's slow paced and you prefer to crouch sneak around the majority of the time get this on a deep discount only. Be prepared to deal with a ton of bugs as you push through each area and get yourself killed up a bunch by spacemen polluted with interstellar Ebola. Otherwise I'd skip this entirely. For reals.

This was probably the game i was most excited for this year, and like an idiot i pre ordered it despite swearing off pre ordering. I was expecting a roller coaster ride like with Human Revolution, however that's nowhere near what i got.
TL;DR DX:MD could easily have been game of the year material, however rediculous micro transactions and a story with no payoff make it an example of the sorry state the industry is in today
The Good:
The gameplay is FANTASTIC, leaps and bounds above human revolution. The new powers are all awesome and really satisfying to use and the environment design is some of the best ive ever seen. There are so many ways to appreach every situation and more open up as you get better powers.
The setting is also a very strong point. Instead of having two shallow hub cities they poured all their effort into Prague, and it shows. The city is dripping with charactor and really draws you into the narrative.
The graphics are good, but poor optimization hamstrings it a bit.
The bad:
Two words: MICRO TRANSACTIONS. Fo all your new powers and cool abilities there are less opportunities to upgrade them. Praxis points are fewer and father between than in Human Revolution so instead of earning the extra ones though gameplay or maybe a challenge mode you have to buy them. This is the same as with credits, why let the player work harder for their credits when you can just let them buy more. Also the weapons that come with the collectors edition can only be used ONCE, and if you start another playthough then they're gone. The suits at square enix really screwed the pooch on this one, how about we pay for them game once and then actually get the fing game.
The Ugly:
It feels like this game was being juggled by three different studios with no contact with eachother: a brilling programming team, greedy publishers, and pants on head ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ writers. The story, the cornerstone of the deus ex franchise, is pathetic. Now that's not to saw that the writing is bad or that it doesn't make sense, in fact it does a really good job of setting up a mystery and making you suspicous of both factions trying to use you. However for all the buildup and intrigue there's no playoff. The plot feels like it's been cut in half, nothing is actually resolved, and they pull the resolution to conflict between the two factions is a total cop out. When i finished i literally just stared at my screen saying, "What?" over and over again. There's no payoff, no deonstration of the effects of your limited choices, and so much is left unexplained; probably to be sold in the DLC.

Holdfast is a Napoleonic warfare game and it describes itself as such "Holdfast: Nations At War is an online multiplayer first and third person shooter focusing on a combination of teamwork and individual skill" So far it's living up to expectations, the game is without a doubt teamwork based, and individual skill is something you'll gradually get as you play. The The Naval combat, and coastal sieges are rather unique gamemodes that I haven't really seen in a game that is so well polished for early access. The largest complaint you'll see in reviews, or what your friends may tell you is that it's melee system is rather bad, and to give them the benefit of the doubt it isn't great, but after you get used to it, it's not as bad as you first thought it was. Also they have a roadmap for development and to quote it from the roadmap itself "Improvements are ongoing for the core mechanics of the game such as the melee and naval combat along with player count optimisations." So to put it simply. the melee isn't going to stay, truly that is the only thing that makes the game not seem great and release.
To answer the simple question "Is it worth the £15/$20" It is, it really is. Playing casually, or joining a regiment, you're going to have a great time on this game with smooth animations, great looking graphics, and a good, but also expanding combat system that makes the game even more thrilling and fun. I would rate this game a solid 7.5/10 This rating will without a doubt be a lot higher when they implement it.

Proudly endorsed by Dave's Reviews For Aging Gamers. Shoppe Keep may be early access, but it's the most interesting casual management sim I've played in a long time. It's a fairly unquie concept, and the designer has a classy sense of humor. Despite a few minor bugs which I'm sure will be resolved long before release, it's a solid game that's well worth the price. As a first generation PC gamer, my golden rule is an hour of play for every dollar spent is a solid gaming investment, and Shoppe Keep delivers.
Bugs aside here's a few cons over-30s should be aware of:
- The wife and I agree: musical score is great, but becomes a bit repetitive. Get your ELO records out.
- The character advancement needs refining, and a lack of speed controls make for long days at the shop.
- Late game is a bit dull at this point in development.
- Personally, I had a bit of difficulty figuring out which items went with which display so it could be sold, but I'm a trial by fire kind of gamer, and dove in head first. A few minutes of reseach could save you this frustration... or it could serve to motivate you like it does me.

This is a game I sincerely wish was more popular for 5 specific reasons.
1) Its a massive open world adventure. Think of a game like Skyrim or the Witcher, and just simplify it a tiny bit. No theres no intense crafting or dynamic combat, but the combat in the game is smooth and there is a very real sense of adventure. Plus, the global map is massive and (in my personal opinion) quite beautiful.
2) The story was written by R.A. Salvatore, one of the greatest fantasy writers of his time. Seriously, look up this mans work and subscribe to whatever nonsense unlimited book service Amazon is offering, because his writing is phenomenal. (Quick note: He's NOT dead, and is still writing). This is the man who brought to life figures like Drizzt Do'Urden and Gwenhyver. He writes amazing masterpieces, and he wrote a world to life in this game. The core story is deep and engaging, but the even the side stories show a love of lore and storycraft I've seen in only 2 other games, both of which are masterpieces.
3) The lore in this game is incredible. A bit of a continuation of point 2, but really the stories in this game are charming, witty, and extremely fun to enact and play through. Exploring is rewarded with a real tale to tell.
4) Interesting progression system. Not to spoil anything, but progression through the unlocks of cards is novel and highly endearing. I spent a good chunk of the game building a mage up from scratch, only to grow tired of the theme and eventually develop into a Jack-of-all-Trades role. The game rewards you for inserting yourself into the story, and taking your own progression however you'd like.
5) Definately worth the money. I like to calculate the time I spend games vs the amount of money I spent on them (and how entertained I was). This game really hits it out of the park. For the price, you'd have to find something like skyrim, or be a huge rts/strategy fan like me to beat the sheer number of time vs expense this game offers. I'm sitting around like 4 cents per hour right now, and I'm not even finished with the game yet.
TL;DR -
The game is an excellent value, and I would highly recommend it to anyone whose a fan of epic stories in a open world sandbox enviroment.

KoA:R is a game that I can play for hours and just get lost in the world.  I am an player of RPGs and I bought KoA:R on a whim when I wanted a new game to play.  The artwork was not a big seller for me.  Indeed, my initial reaction was that it was overly "cartoony" for my liking.  It grew on me and now I'm happy to see this world.
You're allowed a fair bit of character customization (beyond the normal aesthetic options).  Skill point progression is, at first, odd since you can choose a destiny card to become a fighter, sorcerer, or finesse (thief) character - or a mixture of them.  You can "respec", for a price, via the Fateweaver NPCs throughout the world.  Any character race and skill combination will, at higher levels, be totally overpowered.  It's not really possible to completely hose your character, especially since you can tweak your character at the Fateweavers.  A fighter is a melee machine, a sorcerer can use elemental spells and "magicky" stuff to devastating effect, and finesse characters are backstabby/archers of doom.
All characters can, via metagame knowledge, gain max skill points in every skill.  If you roleplay the character it might be more enjoyable than simply min/maxing, but either playstyle would work.
Although the world is open and allows you to go just about anywhere, there is a bit of "go this direction" happening.  The world is broken down in to smaller map sections and each of these sections is sort of a self-contained adventure.  You quest in the zone and move to the next.  Nothing prevents you from running three zones over and, assuming you aren't killed outright, you can "do stuff".  There is a wierd level cap for each zone that sets the level to whatever your character's level is upon initial entry.  That zone is forever capped at that level.  This can break your adventure when you come back to the zone again.  It's not something I really noticed on my first playthrough.
Like many games that offer choice, your choices are only a passing thought in the grand scheme of the world.  Some characters will recognize you for certain accomplishments or choices but overall the world remains largely unaware of your existance (apart from the NPCs involved in the the main questline).
There is a great wiki and other online resources for the game if you like to game with the references open during the journey.
Pros:
* generally open world to explore, with a few quest locked areas (especially the second-half of the game)
* nice character progression
* easy to get into and play and not overly complicated
* hard to "gimp" yourself
* nice array of side quests to guide you on your journey
* has a nice casual feel about things for relaxed play (if you enjoy that)
Cons:
* some may be put off by the graphics
* the controls took a bit of getting comfortable with
* the ability to easily reclass/respec your character may limit you on replay value
* has a nice casual feel about things for relaxed play (if you're into hardcore)
* choices in-game have only minor effect on the world
Overall rating:  8/10
* Definately worth picking up on sale, or at any price if you're a fan of RPGs

Mortal Kombat is one of those franchises I will always cherish.  That being said, the pricing model of this game is atrocious.  There are decisions I agree with - for example, offering to allow players to spend money to unlock all Krypt items.  Not everyone enjoys unlocking.  The biggest ones I disagree with are the way the characters are sold.  It's almost like the game wants to be a F2P with microtransactions, except that it's not F2P because you have to drop $60 to get in the door.  The Kombat Pack kind of sort of is like a Season Pass, except it isn't because it leaves out Goro. It's a simple and somewhat linear tower defense game. I say somewhat linear because your towers are limited to static build platforms. You can't just place a tower anywhere, it has to be on these preplaced platforms so strategically speaking it's not that difficult. The one redeeming factor is there are pilotable vehicles on each battlefield. You can either pilot a medium tank, a heavy tank, a fighter plane or a bomber plane. You may also take control of any tower so these factors make up for the linearity of the tower placements.
The one thing I didn't expect is there are boss battles, and these bosses are surprisingly fun to fight with. You got super trains, massive blimps, super tanks, and big♥♥♥♥♥laser-shooting robots. Each boss has a unique attack style and it's a new challenge each time. It's not just a simple HP ganking game, some of these bosses have tricks up their sleave which negates ganking and it's not game breaking at all. It's very fun, in-fact. Keeps it interesting.
Towers have 3 tiers of upgades which makes them more useful as you get more money. I've noticed that sometimes upgrading isn't necessary. For example, a level 2 machine gun tower is actually better than a level 3 machine gun tower because the level 3 tower has such a slow fire rate that it misses most of the time. "Sometimes" a tier 1 anti-aircraft gun is all you need. I say sometimes because a tier 1 anti-aircraft gun can take down enemy fighters and bombers within a few seconds. The only levels where I needed to upgrade to tier 2 or 3 is when there are enemy blimps, And you really only ever need one anti-air tower with the exception of two maps where they spam air units in the end (dirty tactic that almost got me).
The sound design is great but the tower gun sounds seem a little quiet. It's loud when you're beside the tower but sounds like a distant whimper when you're in the overhead view. Sounds also sometimes glitch out. A few times, my tanks made no cannon sounds or engine sounds, the tank was completely devoid of noises. Things like that and noises cutting in and out kind of breaks immersion a little bit.
Tip: Use tier 3 toxic towers near the entrance of your base in survival. Place tier 3 artillery towers and turn them towards your toxic towers. It doesn't say this in the tooltip but toxic towers slow all units including tanks. This gives your artillery towers time to reload and completely wipe the floor with them. Then it turns into a turkey shoot.
That's the gist of it, I guess. 9/10 for a single-player game. Had great fun with this one.

This game is incredible and has elements that may appeal to any type a fighting game lover. The characters all feel balanced and unique. I imagine the game would be very fun casually as Unreal Engine 4 and the rage mechanic allow for incredible looking hit effects and stages and very satisfying to hit and satisfying to look at rage combos. There are unique soundtracks for each stage and it sounds as if they put a lot of effort into them as the production quality is top notch. You may find yourself finding a couple favorites as I have (I love solitude and infinite azure moonsiders 1st). The slow motion effect creates tension in close matches, the story mode is epic and dramatic, and there are a lot of choices for character customization. The combos in this game are its best feature in my opinion as they are so fun to learn, they aren't unnecessarily complex, and it is easy to create your own unique variations as you get more experienced with the characters. Certain combos are better for certain situations (such as wall combos and combos that leave your oponent grounded etc.) and start off on different moves so you won't get bored from practicing or performing the same combo repetitively as in other games. For the more hardcore players, as I said before, the characters all feel balanced. You may see tier lists for deathmatches with certain characters, but whichever character you choose isn't going to hinder you from beating other players of equal or lower skill level. If you put in the work on any character you will see results. Also, the skillcap in this game is very high as there is always room for improvement in learning different matchups on your character(s) of choice, efficiently using each stage to the fullest, learning when to use certain aggressive/defensive moves on certain characters, how to punish/defend against moves, etc. The ranking system is fair and for the most part except for rare occasions I've seen on reddit/youtube you will get penalized for disconnection/rage quitting. Also you rank up the fastest from fighting against players of your own rank which the system allows you to filter depending on your preference so it isn't possible to exploit the system and farm lower rank players or fluke wins against high rank players as you will rank up dramatically slower. Lastly, the connection is very good especially on PC and you can filter your matchmaking to include specific connection qualities. I love this game and I think I'm going to keep playing it for a while longer as the game is active and fun and so is the community.

Solarix's strength is it's story.  It's a nicely woven tale with several layers that all come together at the end.  Interspersed throughout are a few subplots told through PDA's and email.   But it's the main story that really carries the game.  The voice acting is surprisingly good.
I also liked the massive scale of structures both on the planet and of the ship itself.  I found it fascinating, making my way around the environment, to wonder what everything was and how the colony originally operated.  Lighting was always dark and oppressive, fitting for a stealth game with horror overtones.
Gameplay was ok.  Not stellar but not bad either.  I was instantly reminded of Thief: The Dark Project.  Solarix is a stealth game and so confrontations with enemies tend to end badly and are best avoided.  I played on medium difficulty and found the game fairly easy.  The game uses checkpoint saves which are usually sufficient.  There was only one point where I wished I could have saved progress due to a tricky area.
While Solarix succeeds in many ways, its low budget production values show.  Complicated machinery constructed with different parts is often covered in a single texture (which isn't a big deal given how dark the game usually is).  AI isn't very good.  Enemies stick to the exact same patrols unless alerted.  Enemies sometimes appear to get stuck.  At least on medium difficulty detection distance is pretty forgiving.  I also got stuck (i.e. immobile) on different maps 4 times and had to reload the game to continue.
But overall I thought the journey was worth the $10 I paid.  I completed the game in about 11 hrs.  If you are looking for a solid sci-fi/stealth experience with an engrossing story, Solarix delivers.  Just don't expect AAA production values.

I would like to recommend this game, and if it is on sale, it may be a worthwhile purchase.  Unfortunately for me, as you can see by my shorter play time, the game bugged out and my save loaded with the camera sinking through the environment.  It just wasn't worth replaying the game to get back to where I was...
As far as my impressions of what I did get to play, the game OK at best. It is a novel title that if you are very hard up may prove to be fun, but there are far better games than this to play in this genre.
GRAPHICS
Graphically this game looks horribly dated, for a title that came out in 2015, it is horrendous.  Texture quality is bad and optimization isn't very good.  With a 980 ti that was hitting 39% @ 4k, I was seeing a lot of screen tear, it lessened at 1440p.  The lighting is fairly good and sets the mood, but the fire effects aren't even on par with the first half life.  It's dreadful really.  The Unreal engine is capable of so much more than what is shown here.
SOUND
Sound wise, the atmosphere is done really well, conveying the dread well.  Audiologs can be hard to hear at times, due to the overpowering ambience, but this is forgiveable.  Character noises i.e. grunts and things, are laughable at best and completely pull you from the immersion.
AI
The AI in this game is bad.  Constantly getting stuck on the environment, failing to fully investigate thrown objects that have all but bounced off of them.  Thier vision cones are terrible as well, sometimes allowing me to stand right next to them and at other times they would spot me in the dark, behind things at distances that were crazy.
CONTROLS
The controls were fluid and smooth.  I never had any problems here, except when I mapped buttons and the contextual messages didn't change.  It's a small thing, but something that bothers me.
All and all it's not a terrible game, but at this pricepoint, I say nay.

This review was written after completing the game with a full stealth/pacifist playthrough.
So, Deus EX :HR brought back a loved franchise to life, and despite its many flaws, the plot was nice, there was a bunch of side quest/exploration and the overall visuals where refreshing. (Yes, even the yellow filter)
Deus : MD was supposed to continue the story of adam jensen, and, hopefully, start tying it to the Denton's.
The game in itself takes around 15hours to complete, with all sidequests done and the full exploration missing (Scattered ebooks, breach software, etc...).
But, a good portion of that time is actually spend running back and forth in the town Hubs. That leaves the game with a medium map, cut in half, and 'instances' for all the missions.
That's not very good.
Maybe the plot is better? Well, no. Most of the plot can be deduced after about 1h into the game, and side-mission wise, i have to find a single one where the whole thing wasn't obvious/cliche.
Lore-wise? You don't learn much either. You leave the world in pretty much the same state than when you started.
It's really sad that despite all the terminals you hack to read mail / pocket secretary, you don't get to learn much, only sometimes general background to the place you are.
So, that being said, the story let's itself be played, no gaping plotholes, and the pacing is correct.
Gameplay time? I have yet to do a mass-killing playtrough, but the overall feel of the pisto/tranq gun was okay, but it didn't make me want to get into any firefight. Tried some guns at the shooting range, they felt 'meh', it's like you expect firefight to be a spray fest.
AI pathing was OK, but sometimes the cones of vision are weird, they don't seem to look 'up' most of the time.
The hacking minigames feel better in this game than in HR, and they do require some strategy if you don't want to save-scum.
The game added some new augs that look nice, but they feel completely unnecessary, you can easily finish the game with just the hacking upgrades maxed and a few 'old' upgrades.
I have yet to try the breach gameplay, so i don't know about that yet.
Bugs? A few glitches here and there, notably with grabing ledges and minimap objective locations. No game-breaking bug, a few instances of disappeared cursor (annoying when you're in terminals trying to disable cameras) and, the 'not-a-bug' massive slowdown on stairs (Adam is teaching a life lesson, don't run on stairs boyz, spam jump, it's faster)
Overall : The game isn't bad. But they tried so hard to make it a HR 2.0 that is fails so develop it's own character. I'm not very thrilled about the 'season pass' aspect to MD, especially when the current plot was not enough. (Cut content?)
So, i'd say it's an okay stealth game, a mediocre shooting game , and mediocre RPG (not many quests, poor lore). Currently, i'd say don't buy yet, let's see where the DLCs are going or get it on sale. But i'd rather recommend HR or the original Deus Ex.

Mods add offline gameplay, and takes away the potential for revenue (from SharkCards). Mortal Kombat is one of those franchises I will always cherish.  That being said, the pricing model of this game is atrocious.  There are decisions I agree with - for example, offering to allow players to spend money to unlock all Krypt items.  Not everyone enjoys unlocking.  The biggest ones I disagree with are the way the characters are sold.  It's almost like the game wants to be a F2P with microtransactions, except that it's not F2P because you have to drop $60 to get in the door.  The Kombat Pack kind of sort of is like a Season Pass, except it isn't because it leaves out Goro.  So you've gotta drop your $60 for the game, another $30 for the Kombat Pack, and on top of that you also have to buy Goro.  I'm assuming that if they release any more characters, you'll have to buy them as well.  Unacceptable business practice in my opinion.  Either make the game free to play and then nickle and dime players for specific content, or put a price sticker on all of the content that we pay up front and then give us the content.  For this reason, I am going to have to say not recommending this game.  It's a shame too, because it's otherwise a fantastic game.  But I refuse to support this kind of greed.

Solarix is a first person stealth game, desrcibed as a science fiction / horror game. This description is incorrect, as I played for two hours with no scares whatsover.
Considering that this is one of my favourite genres it takes a lot to bore me, but Solarix is mindnumbingly tedious for a stealth game. Bizarrely you move faster crouching than you do running, though if you alert an enemy it's pretty much game over on hard. Which isn't helped by some autosaves plonking you right in front of an enemy....
The stealth is too easy but also unreliable, and weapon / item  switching takes ages when playing with a gamepad. The plot seems okay though I haven't seen all that much of it - and to be honest am not that bothered about playing further.
I really enjoyed games like old school Thief/ Outlast / Alien isolation/ Penumbra / Soma, and wouldn't compare Solarix to those - it lacks atmosphere /  scares, and isn't very compelling in general.
Bear in mind though that this is only a few hours in - it may get better, but I seriously doubt it.
EDIT: Played it some more......
1) The story - crap, has a "twist" that had me in stitches it's so poor. If Ken Levine is the Stephen King of twists, then whoever wrote this is the Dean Koontz (or M Night Shamalayan if you're not familiar with one of the worst authors you could read)....I was laughing, which is not a good sign when you're trying to be dramatic....
2) The weapons (when you get some) are awful - the shotgun does less damage than the pistol, and has terrible hit detection.
3) At 70% completed I died, and the autosave happened at the exact same time - so now when I reload it instantly goes back to me being dead, and asks me to reload. Around and around it goes.....
In essence - this game is rubbish!! The fact that there's an easter egg of a computer that's playing System Shock 2 is laughable, as that game is hands down miles better than this, and whilst it's not a stealth game you would be better off buying that instead. Despite being fifteen (or so) years older it
embarrasses Solarix in every way.
Buy the real deal and not this glitchy, mediocre imitator! Which, by the way, is not scary or "horror" in the slightest!!

This game is a very beautiful and innovative title that lets you perform badass combat and kill sequences as epic as you see them in anime. The game is extremely easy to pick up, and it is rather a game of skill more than it is a "who has the better stuff" type of game. You can purchase different items if you want to using the in-game currency, and the weapons and items make a noticeable difference, but it is not even necessary. If you are going to play the campaign though I reccommend to play with other people, since it is very difficult to go solo. K style is not incorporated in this game which is fine (there was one guy able to glitch the game and unlock it but it takes like 15 minutes to do so so I don't reccommend it) and for all the people who don't know what K style is, it is a glitch in the original game where you can practically fly around the map slicing people with your melee weapon that is used by mostly hackers nowadays. Anyways, as for multiplayer, I reccommend playing the new time assault andelimination modes rather than team deathmatch because team deathmatch is a pain in the♥♥♥♥♥since there is almost always that one guy who kill everyone and you are normally paired with people who suck or have bad connection. As for the other two modes Team Elimination is awesome for when there are one team dominating the other or when there is a clutch moment pulled off by you or a teammate. Time assault adds a twist to the game as you and your team either play on offence trying to infiltrate and destroy an optimite lab or play defense trying to hold them back until time runs out. Just remember that in any game the outcome can be predicted by whose team has the most variety in the team. IOW, a team with one person of each class is probably going to win over four Silent Avengers or four Gunslingers. The reason for this is because every class has a different role in the game. In conclusion, GunZ 2: the Second Duel is a spectacular title that I reccommend to anyone who wants the perfect game that fits their demanding third person shooter needs or to anyone who wants to try something new.

W.W. II Battlefield conquest. Most intresting aspect of the game is its duality. From one side its classical FPS. Shoot at enemies, capture objectives yatta yatta yatta. Time you spend in your game and the efectivness on the battlefield is rewarded with money that you use to buy new weaponary and customizing it to your needs. You need that money to buy other classes too. Like pilots, tank operators, paratroopers or snipers. The other side is unlocked when you get the General. Then this FPS turns into a "Turn" Based Strategy. 3 Countries on the map fighting to get the major cities of the other one. They acomplish that by capturing "nodes" on the map. Each node is a battle fighted by solders in FPS mode on the battlefield. More units send by generals means more respawns and other units joining the battlefield. For example you can fight with snipers and tanks, against enemy planes. More generals sent more lives you have and more blodier the battle gets.
I recomend this game.

I started playing in the opening months of 2015 - the game was quite well balanced and apart from a few optimisation issues, enjoyable and fun.
I started playing just recently again after a year's long break, and I am greeted with an all-new GUI that doesn't work the way it should, maps that favor camping (and so making defense battles instant wins - apart from when it's the US forces - I will get to this) and most of all, no optimisation fixes.
Balance in the game has gone down the drain - the Soviets and Germans have access to better equipment than the US does - almost always causing 10 minute losses.
Tanks now don't work as they should - controls are awkward and cumbersome at their best, they use the same acceleration as any other vehicle - Civillian Truck, for example - and M18 Hellcats accelerate just as slowly as a JS-2

This is my first game recommendation. I used to play legacy RotT after it was first published. Shooting Nazis in a game with elevating platforms everywhere was a huge blast in contrast to the hallway maze games before it, although I gotta say the guards dogs always did a good job of pumping the adreniline up (Wolfenstein 3D).
This modern day rewrite of that old RotT classic really works for me. The sounds and sensations from the original are here but technically ramped up, especially the colorful fast-moving graphics. (Remember the starchy redish grays? Not here.) And the best part is the pace is still there, moving elevators and all.  Your reflexes have to be fast and continuous, almost like doing a dance - you get into a rhythm -  your movement becomes fluid and calcuating.
Having said all this, I have yet to get far in the game as a single player. I don't say this embarrassingly as the game can test your nerves and reflexes. But even playing in snippets it's a very fun FPS. I suggest you grab a copy!

Deus Ex is probably one of the last franchises where I can safely say still preserves a semblance of an engaging story, good character development, level design, and skill progression. Most games now are churned out every one or two years, Square Enix took the time to refine the game, unlike most publishers who love rushing games to meet the holiday season. The final product, while not perfect, still delivers on many levels.
Prague is an amazing and beautiful city, and will remind you of the opening city that takes place during Half Life 2. There's plenty of side quests to keep you busy, and overall with world building Eidos did a much better job here than with Detroit.
The graphics are top notch, albeit with some optimization issues they need to fix. That's ok, just turn off MSAA, switch volumetric lighting to on/off, and have contact hardening shadows to on/off as well. Nothing is perfect, give the developers a break, it's hard enough to squash bugs and design an entirely new game engine.
If you're complaining the price, you can get it on green man gaming for $45. Otherwise grab it in a steam sale, when all the optimization and remaining bugs will be fixed.
I didn't like how the game reset my skills after the prologue. I thought this mechanic was quickly getting old in video games, but also gave me a reason to spend my points on rebuilding my skill tree instead of just basking in OP augmentations.

*****SPOILER ALERT*****
The area in the sewer beyond the gate with the sentry drone during the neon drug quest.

The part in Golem City where you climb the rafters to sneak into the enemy base
Your apartment when attempting to call your old boss David Sarif
Most likely other parts of the game I have not gotten to yet.

I usually don't write alot of reviews, but in this specific case I thought I would share my opinion with the community, and that it is nessesary for people who are fans of previous deus ex games just as I am.
I am mostly going to compare Deus Ex Mankind Divided (MD) with Deus Ex Human Revolution (HR) which is the deus ex game i have played most of by far (100 hours, roughly 3 playthroughs).
Pros:
Very good textures and grapics -> I have a GTX 980 and can only play this game at high (best setting being ultra)
Extensive options menu -> Alot of options regarding gameplay and display
Hacking -> The new hacking system they've put into this game is very extensive and fun, almost like a mini-game within the game. In HR one simply had to get stealth augments for hacking and then you could hack everything in the game, here however one has to use different abilities to make sure to secure a hack, even with augmentations to help.
Cons:
Short and shallow story -> I ended up at 18 hours when I finished this game, and then I also tried to do pacifist and foxiest of the hounds achivments (not killing anyone and setting of no alarms) at the same time. The ending was kind of like a sad ending in bed with a girl saying: "what? Are you done Already?!" compared to HR, which has a very extensive and deep story that really emerges you with the world, and usually has a playthrough finishing at 30 hours, I didn't feel any connections to MD what so ever, and that the issues that were brought up as a starting point in the begining of the game, wasn't solved what so ever at the end of the game. I just didn't really feel like I accomplished anything.
In-game microtransactions -> This is not a huge deal to me since it's a singleplayer game, but it still says something about Square Enix when they put a feature like this into the game. I'm not really going to go further into this, but the fact that it's there sets a new bar of low standards for a triple A release.
Combat -> The combat is very responsive and fluent to play. I actually feel like it's a rippoff of HR, since the only thing that's different in the combat is that there is LESS weapons to choose from in MD than in HR and a few more augmentations (8). I basiclly used the same exact build as I used in HR. This in itself is not a problem really since it is a sequel, but I expected something more for the amount of money I put on this game.
Conclusion:
For the price, defenitly not worth it. Buy it at a sale at atleast 50% off or more. Compared to HR, not even worthy of being called a sequel, Especially not when looking at the story.

This review will be kept short and to the point as only one paragraph will have to do with the gameplay and story and the rest is going to be about the performance issues I'm encountering.
Th storyline for this game is very well written however as mentioned in a few reviews, the lip syncing is sub-par. The gameplay is very reminiscent of Human Revolution with some simple tweaks to improve overall experience. Atmosphere is wonderful and definately gives way to a cyberpunk theme we all have grown to love. Muic and overall sound quality is sublime.
Now then the main issues I find in the game.
Extremely long load times.
This is insanely annoying, however, I can undertand why. Though the zones may not be huge in size, there are hundreds of physics objects and tons of NPCs moving about. This brings me to the worse part.
Graphic lag
I overclocked my video card a bit for this and measured my fps before and after the overclock. No difference and yet my fps wavers inconsistently between 14 and 60 frames, this borders unplayable.
The 2 above things are my biggest beef right now.
Oh and just a heads up to any buyers, DO NOT use the spyglass/telescope in the apartment parralel to yours in prague. You will be stuck in the scope and will not be able to leave.

Hardly ever fans the die-hard fans of an old franchise will be satisfied with the new reincarnation of their beloved game.
Gladly, the reissues of the MK prove to be rather unique exception, at least for me. The MK X is a very balanced, interesting  and detailed game, that revitalizes the story of the fallen elder god Shinnok, previously described in MK 4. Though the main idea of the plot hasn't been changed, we see some new details about this new interpretation, like the fact, that the honor of dealing with this false ruler is being passed to the new generation, a concept which is criticized by some people as a "shady attempt to renew the characters list".
What do we have in the end, putting aside all the prejudices and looking at the real pros and cons?
+ Beautiful graphics.
Like, for real. Warner Bros and Nethterrealm studios have proven their graphic potence in the MK Komplete Edition, but here, they jumped far over their own heads - they made cinematics, background and character textures as real as they could get.
+ Lots of humor.
I know that the gameplay and the plotline should be interesting, but it's cool to sometimes have some fun stuff to relax. And here, we can observe plenty of it - some characters, like the Cage family are filled with sarcasm and fun, so their behaviour looks more realistic. The way Cassie curses makes me smile, really.
+ Fighting system: using surroundings.
That, for sure, is a HUGE and very cool addition to the fighting system. And certainly it adds more fun to it, especially if you through a granny toward your opponent on a marketplace. :-)
+ The new Krypt is fenomenal!
Seriosly, it's size, the number of achievements you can discover there, the fact, that you should find special elements to break through some areas (which to me is a cool mini-quest) and the creatures, randomly appearing, which I absolutely adored; in other words - it only got way better!
But don't get me wrong - though I absolutely recommend playing this game, I am not going to be a vanilla-like on its disadvantages, because there are some serious (in my humble opinion) gaps, that the developers didn't manage to fill.
- The plotline. Particularly, the end of the story.
Allthough, I like the reincarnation of it as a whole, and it was good to see some new faces, there are a few big questions to the storymakers: do you really suppose that 18 y.o. girl is capable of knocking out the super-evil-former-elder-god-now-butt-kicking-demonic-Shinnok with all his superpowers, even if that girl is a straight descendant of famous Johnny Cage and Sony Blade? That was a HUGE dissapointment to me (especially the fact, the someone as powerful and capable as Shinnok got knocked out so easily by some gal, which is ridiculous). I know that this way the developers gave path to a new generation, but...well, to me, it just occured too quickly, without any preconditions to it.
- Short story mode. And easy story mode.
And let's be honest here - that comes none close to the Komplete Edition, which had longer story mode, and was obviously harder to complete. This also dissapointed me a lot, because it literally took me 3-4 hours to complete the story mode, with all the cinematics. In Komplete Edition, it took me several days to do that.
Conclusion:
Well, all in all, it was worth playing it, and I will certainly have more fun plaing it with my friends in versus mode, but due to the couple of big disadvantages, I give this game 8 out of 10. In other words, good enough, but still there's room for improvement.

Solarix is a first person shooter/stealth game, with survival horror thrown in set in a sci-fi world. The gameplay and story is great. I like the stealth aspect, along with the hacking aspect that let's you get through doors, shut down turrets, and do hacking to help you get around. That really reminds me of the original Deus Ex, which is always great to see another game use a similar style.
The stealth aspect is very cool, I love stealth games, and the way it's done in Solarix reminds me of Manhunt. You hide in the dark, sneak up on the enemies, and use the taser on them, or you can shoot them in the back of the head with your pistol. Although wasting bullets would be ridiculous since you have limited ammo.
The graphics are great, very well done, the setting is dark, but has that sci-fi feeling to it. Fits perfectly for stealth, and even that survival horror aspect. There isn't much for music, although it's more ambient, and fits the setting, for instance, you could be sneaking around, hear a noise, look around, and see nothing, that really fits the game. The voice over work is great, although Betty annoys me, but that is the point of Betty.
The controls are easy to understand, although some might get confused that the "use" button is the spacebar, rather then "E" on the keyboard, but it shouldn't take long to get the hang of that. They are very responsive, no slowdowns, or anything like that.
Solarix is a damn good game, very fun, I put 14 hours into the game, and enjoyed every minute of it. Although I did run into some flaws, nothing real major, because I could continue the game. The first flaw, was loading a saved game, and I would fall through the world, and die, I would reload, and it would continue to do that. I did contact the developer on this, and got it figured out, the easiest way would be to restart the chapter. The other flaw, would be the game crashing a few times, but this didn't happen often, and I continued through the game. I am sure updates will, happen. If you like survival horror/stealth/first person shooter games, check out Solarix.

Pulsetense approached GameReviewsAU to have their game reviewed via the gaming platform Steam. In our opinion Solarix goes beyond our expectations and proves to be a great game. And for something so absorbing to be produced via an Indie developer is even more surprising.
The story of Solarix is inspired via a range of classic science fiction films. You play as an engineer, delightfully named Walter, who is fighting for survival after an unknown infection wipes out the population of an interstellar research station. Walter must try and contain the disease whilst battling the remnants of the hostile crew and struggling with his own fracturing mind.
Solarix does a great job using sound and music to invoke different feelings. Harrowing sounds await you just outside the first room’s door and they constantly change and follow you depending on what is nearby. Malfunctioning computers whir and buzz as it sounds like they’re struggling to boot up, creepy and atmospheric sounds stalk you as your journey through the remnants of the space station begins.
The voice acting is described by Pulsetense as being professional but I would say it sounds even more professional than most next-gen games. Good voice acting is absolutely key to engaging gamers minds and Solarix has done a brilliant job in finding their voice actors. Betty’s character is delightfully disturbing!
You can choose your own way to play. Burn through your ammunition like a crazy person, sneak around without laying a finger on the hostile opponents with the help of throwable objects to create distractions, or creep up behind enemies and stun them with your stun gun.
Personally I preferred the stun gun method but when push came to shove, the pistol (or at a later point, the shotgun) ended up playing a important part in my survival.
If Solarix is what we should be expecting to come from Indie developers, then I’m incredibly excited for the future! The textures for everything are sharp and detailed, enemy design is so imaginative and the scenery is breathtaking. When you get the chance to see your surroundings from outside you’ll be blown away by the sheer enormity and scale of each level.
As mentioned earlier, sound plays an integral role in Solarix and should definitely not be overlooked when playing this game. At times you’ll hear haunting music playing to accompany the situation in which you find yourself, and trust me, wearing headphones whilst playing is an incredible experience. If you have a super sound system then please hook your computer up and play Solarix. I’d love to know how good it sounds!
With so much to deliver, of course there are going to be a few bugs which is the only downside to Solarix.
Parts of the environment that look accessible can often be unaccommodating. The jump key almost seems a bit pointless seeing as you’re able to jump over ledges lower than a person’s ankles. However, getting rid of jump altogether would make some parts of the game unplayable which you’ll find out about as you play.
It’s quite easy to get trapped inside walls, forcing you to restart from an earlier save and sometimes when you’ve loaded up a save game you are presented with a world full of nothing. This, once again, forces you to restart from the beginning of a chapter which could prove to be even more troublesome.
I was blown away by Solarix and find it to be an incredibly exciting yet disturbing adventure. It’s been quite a while since I was creeped out this much by a game, but I’m glad Pulsetense have managed to pull it off!

I rarely write any reviews, but since I was asked so polite (By Pulsetense Games itself) - I accepted it. I can only say how I felt about the game. Sorry for any bad english, not my native language you know... :p
Solarix is a scifi horror game, made by the Pulsetense Games, and anyone who has played Systemshock 2, may notice, that these have something in common. After all Solarix was influenced by it, one of the most epic scifi-horror-adventure game. And Solarix does it well for  indie game. Not entirely the same though. No adventure game, but dark creepy atmosphere, that has some horror elements, and well written story - that sometimes leave you puzzled on what to believe. Unlike many other indie games in my opinion, that tend to be bad, this one works good. But I have to admit on the horror factor, I didn't felt scared all that much.
For me it was all about stealth: sneaking around the enemy without getting noticed. When they turn around, hack that door open and slip in undetected. Hide behind the shadows and possibly go around them. Yes, you can hide in the shadows, like in many other stealth games. I usually tend to play stealth games in a way, that I don't kill anyone. Sometimes it works in this game. In the beginning you need to sneak your way past them. You don't have any guns yet. Sadly when you do get a gun, (tazer in fact) it's better to just taze them out. Sometimes in a situation you don't have any choices. You can only knock them out if you sneak behind one and aim the tazer to it's head. That doesn't always work though. It's really about what angle you do this.
There are many infected enemies to go around, and also non infected. These non infected are people behind the mask, and they're tough. You can't really go shoot em up on them, you have to plan ahead. Guns don't pack a punch all that much, but then again I was playing this on Hard difficulty - and also it's not meant to be played like uncle Sam would. Even the infected creatures don't die easily. Some do, but some of them seem to act like indestructible. (multiple shotgun shells, and still not dead o.o) I don't mind this, although it does sometimes get on my nervous :L and they sometimes act so unpredictable. They don't always follow that usual pattern, which leaves you more alert. I literally sneaked the whole game through :D
Unlike many other indie makers, Pulsetense Games has done pretty good job. Sure there are some minor unfinished edges here and there, such as falling off the floor :< which made me replay a whole chapter once more. This only happened once, so it might not even happen again. I'm not gonna say anything about the graphical stuff, you can just check the photos for that, and make your own opinion. For me it's between decent and good. I'm not much of a graphical dude. If the game is good, that's all that matters.
I also don't want to say anything about the story, cause I don't want to spoil it to people. Let's just say that there's a computer A.I called A.M.I, and human called Betty, that are guiding you through the darkness of infested planet and spaceship. Your goal is to find the cure. Let's just say that there's more to it than that ;)
Short version: This game is for stealth fans, and for those seeking for a scifi-space-horror like game, with deep story build into it. It's not an adventure game. It's pretty much moving to point A to point B type of adventure. It took me about 10 hours to beat this game. First time playing on hard difficulty, and while recording a playthrough for it. Sadly, there's no replay value, which is really important for me :/ unless the story is unclear somehow. Maybe building achievements would help. Very tricky ones ;)
All I can say is that I liked it. Well done, even with some minor fall backs. Usually all games, especially indie games tend to have. But Solarix is still better than most of them.
If you're like me and like playing stealthy, buy it ;)
Cheers ^^

Some technical notes: The Steam page claims it uses Games for Windows Live. So far as I know, it was patched out and uses Steamworks now. The GFWL client still works though on Windows 10 for games that use it.
Unfortunately, Steam’s info that this requires an online connection for single player games is true. It seems to just sit at a black screen with a hidden error button “behind” the program if you launch it without an Internet connection.  IMO that’s unacceptable, and worth docking points for.  I’m not even sure what it’s connecting TO, just Steam?  At any rate, aside from when I deliberately disabled my network connection, I had no serious technical issues with the game that I can recall.  I ran it at 1080p on a 3.2GHz Ivy Bridge/Geforce GTX 680m/Windows 10 AE and it ran smoothly (usually about 60fps).
It remains stable even when task switching out of it-something I appreciate the ability to do in Windows games, since inevitably I need to do one thing or another with my PC while playing.  I did notice that sometimes when I task switched back there would be minor and fairly irrelevant graphical glitches-sort of like faint 3D lines rising up from some structures.  Reloading a level/going to the next level got rid of it, but it was so minor I never bothered.
Toy Soldiers is a “tower defense” game-that is basically a real time strategy game played with small-ish levels and with the player mostly building various guns/turrets of various sorts rather than directly controlling units, with enemy waves of enemies you’re trying to defend against.  Defeating enemies gives you money to buy more turrets.
Many levels have preset vehicles you can take control of to directly fight the enemy, but that’s more a move of desperation, when you don’t have the money to build the defenses you need.
Unlike some tower defense games, turrets can only be built at specific build points, and there are two different sizes of build points-the only anti-aircraft weapon in the game requires a “big” build point, as does the most powerful/longest ranged gun (which is also limited by only being able to fire in a roughly 90 degree area in the direction you initially build it-unlike every other weapon in the game, which can fire in any direction).  A lot of the challenge of the game is figuring out what combination of turrets to put where.
The levels are fairly interesting, fairly varied-particularly in the “Invasion” campaign which adds units like robots and UFOs.  Occassionally levels have boss battles-the final enemy wave is a single, gigantic, unique vehicle of some sort.  To fight those, I often needed to sell off some of my turrets and reconfigure them for the new enemy, as well as adding to their firepower with whatever vehicles the particular level allowed me to control.  Like every tower defense game I’ve played, every level allows you to let through a certain number of enemy units before you lose the game (30 in this case), but annoyingly on levels with bosses, if that vehicle gets through, you lose, even if nothing else got through. Considering you can’t save during a level, that can be a bit annoying, but never so annoying that I quit playing.
I played on the easiest of several difficulty levels, and was able to finish the entire game (unlike with many tower defense games I’ve played).  Even still most later levels were a challenge, and I think it could do with at least one easier mode.
Graphically it looks pretty nice, although I might have preferred it to be a bit LESS realistic looking-lean in to the “toy” nature of the units and battles a bit more-perhaps somewhere in between how this looks, and how those old 3DO Army Men games looked.  Also, battles that take place at night are occasionally somewhat difficult to see, necessitating that I dialed up the brightness and contrast on my monitor.  I suspect on a higher quality TV, like a VA based TV, that that would be less of an issue.  Between how realistic most of the graphics look, and how dark some levels are, the game can be slightly hard to “read” at times.  I’d have also liked a mini-map showing where enemies are currently located-and I played almost the entire game from a pulled back overhead perspective, versus the closer in, “slanted” view levels start in.  That’s mostly just nitpicking though-the game mostly looks perfectly nice and plays well.
Speaking of which-I played it entirely with an Xbox One pad, since it originated on the Xbox.  I’m not sure how well it would control with a mouse and keyboard.
Toy Soldiers isn’t a must play, and I don’t appreciate it needing always-on DRM, but it’s a pretty solid game, and worth picking up if you enjoy the genre and can buy it cheap enough that you don’t mind the DRM.

What could be a loveletter/throwback to classic FPS gaming of yesteryear instead comes off as a flawed mess.
While it sounds like the game is in better shape than it was originally, there are clearly a plethora of flaws in design and implementation.  Examples include:
* Stuck-in-geometry bugs (supposedly this used to be worse, but I just made it happen easily in the first room of level 1-2)
* Weapon switching bugs (my first time playing 1-1, weapon switching just stopped working entirely at one point)
* The knife key (Q), which seems pointless except for the net trap (and then it's not obvious that it is the only way out of these traps, unlike the original ROTT - try searching the discussion section for "net" and see how many people were confused by this)
* The belated introduction of quicksave/load, which in part seems to serve as a band-aid for some of the other issues, but also in part shows just how flawed the game is, given that traditional FPSes (such as the original ROTT...) operated entirely on a free save/load system
* The advanced graphics options are tucked in the launcher outside the game itself for some reason (unlike pretty much any FPS I've played in the last 10 years), and some of them are inaccessible if you have Windows on a high DPI setting
To be fair, I appreciate some of the throwback references to the original ROTT, and I still want to think I can get some enjoyment out of this. I haven't yet tried the multiplayer which I have a feeling will either make or break the experience overall. It is very nice to see that unlike certain overrated big-name "AAA" FPS franchises, the devs of ROTT '13 have seen fit to add multiplayer maps for free in subsequent updates.
But given the glaring flaws that have become evident within the first 30 minutes of gameplay, I can't justify paying much more than the $3 flash sale price for this game.  I'm glad I held out until then to buy it.

This is another time when the straightforward recomend/ not recommend choice is too stark.
I bought the game for a couple of quid (about $2.00) in a recent sale and I'll review it on the basis that you'll buy it at a similar price.
Firstly for that money there's a lot of game for your money.  Big open world.  Starring role for Jack Black.  Cameos from Ozzy Osbourne and Lemmy amongst others.
My music allegiance is more hair metal (Guns N' Roses, Aerosmith, Bon Jovi) who are actually the bad guys in the game (the genre, not the bands) than heavy metal so the soundtrack isn't my core music taste.  Good to have your boundaries expanded though.
I found the controls workable albeit the boss battles can be exhaustingly long - the game does give you tips if you're at stalemate for too long.
There's a not entirely obvious (okay it's on the map) place to do upgrades which are fairly essential - I just upgraded my car to machine guns at a time just before a mission that needed them.  There's a set of extra missions just below the area on your map that becomes your base that seem to be screened off by as yet uncrossable terrain.
Difficulty on "Normal" seemed okay - I'm having difficulty with an escort mission ATM however.
But there are BIG problems.
1)  The Devs have given the bad guys identical troops to your troops - just the clothes are different.  So in a battle it's really difficult to tell who are your side and who are the attackers.
2) Four years (at least) after a problem with the save game feature was noted it STILL isn't working.  There is a solution but it involves accessing the game folders and copying over a file.  I've recopied the solution into the game forum so you can find it there if you need it.
There are more minor problems too.  There's a relatively big open world but not a lot in it.  Combat is acceptable rather than inspiring.  Most of the main good guys smoke (a lot) including the main protagonist Eddie.  Smoking may look cool but being broke, smelling awful, and dying of emphysema at a young age are not.
It's one of those games where price point plays a huge part in the review.  At £30 - £40 or even higher I'd have been VERY disappointed in the game.  At £15 - £20 the games problems would have seriously irked me.  But for a couple of quid it's an awful lot of game for your money, some serious star power, an offbeat if not exactly subtle sense of humour (what do you expect from heavy metal ?) and a worthy addition to your Steam library.

Europe is at war. Emperor Napoleon of France has led bloody campaigns throughout the continent and conquered much of the mainland, but a coalition of sovereign nations is fighting back. This troubled period of history is characterised by a crass contrast between the distinctive colourful uniforms and the brutality of the actual battles raging on land and at sea. In short: A great setting for a video game. As previous mods and games such as Battlegrounds 2 and the popular Napoleonic Wars DLC for Mount and Blade: Warband have shown there is a demand for 1st/3rd-person games set in the Napoleonic era. Holdfast: Nations At War sits confidently in this niche and promises to deliver all that its spiritual predecessors did and more.
Those who played Napoleonic Wars will feel right at home when trying out Holdfast. While the game sports a sleek new engine and much prettier, up-to-date graphics, the controls and mechanics are a faithful recreation of the robust Mount and Blade gameplay. Melee combat is directional and requires sharp reflexes and precise footwork. Shooting with a variety of different, historically accurate weapons also requires skill, though not so much quickscoping as it is an understanding of ballistics. While the firearms of the early 19th century were already a tad unpredictable, there is also prominent bullet drop to take into account, making successful long range shots all the more rewarding.
There are numerous gamemodes to try out, from the standard team vs team deathmatch to assault and capture the flag. Holdfast is a class-based game, with flavours for all sorts of player-types. The perhaps biggest difference to other similar games is the introduction of a solid naval component, where both teams crew a number of different ships, from agile gunboats to mighty frigates. Each ship crew again has a set of different classes to choose from, as of course there must be a captain, marines, artillery crewmen, carpenters and even musicians for the much needed morale boost. Each ship feels like its own completely autonomous entity and being able to walk around on deck while it is moving, loading and firing each gun separately, is an immersive experience. To go even further with this, there are also combined battles with land and sea, where the one nation's navy is taking on the coastal defenses of the other, shelling forts from a distance and launching a continuous stream of landing boats to take the beach. Currently, only France and the United Kingdom are fully implemented, but more nations are surely not far.
This is a good moment to mention that Holdfast: Nations At War is in Early Access. While the game is, at the time of writing, in a very polished state, there are still bugs and oddities. However, it is in active development, with frequent updates and changes based on community feedback. Most prominently, the melee still needs some tweaking and there are also some connectivity issues, but on the larger picture, being able to play with ~120 people on the same server without lag is exciting.
Thanks to the many different gamemodes, both players preferring more casual arcade-gameplay and those looking for ingame reenactment and linebattle events will find themselves at home in Holdfast: Nations At War. Numerous regiments have already been founded by the active community and surely, many more are yet to come. This game is well worth a look for those interested in the Napoleonic period at all and naturally for returning players familiar with Mount and Blade: Warband's Napoleonic Wars DLC.

I'm going to be writing from the perspective of a four-year veteran of NW
Holdfast has taken on the lofty challenge of providing a modern successor to Mount and Blade: Napoleonic Wars. How does it measure up? Well, if you aim for the moon, you'll still land amongst the stars, right?
Right?
In its current state, Holdfast is nearly unplayable. I don't have the best computer in the world, so I won't hold it to any graphical or performance standards, except to say that the blowing grass, trees, and occasional bird swooping by obviously aren't doing anyone's GPUs any favors. The sound design manages to be even more underwhelming than NW's. I'm also disappointed that the detailed unit selection screen shown in sneek peeks is nowhere to be found, replaced by a bland unit selection list that resembles Commander Battle from NW. Let's talk about where it counts: gameplay. Here, Holdfast completely misses the mark. The shooting aspects are decent, we're not expecting too much out of our muskets. Melee, however, is a different story. We all know that this game will live or die by its competitive community, and the competitive community will live or die by the game's melee. And the melee right now. Absolutely. Sucks. The controls are clunky, unintuitive, and slow to respond. You won't be meleeing as much as you will be downspamming. It's hard to tell but it appears you cannot melee from the crouched position, and for some reason you no longer have the option to switch an unbayonetted rifle/musket to melee mode; this means you will have to switch to your side sword, which is accessed by a less-than-responsive mouse wheel action. In fact, if I could describe this entire game in two words, they would be "clunky" and "unresponsive". I can't speak to the naval combat as my game crashed within the first ten minutes, which even Warband doesn't insult me by doing.
If the developers really needed a cash injection, they should have done a Kickstarter. All I can say is that if you haven't bought the game yet, hold on to your money for now, save yourself the disappointment, and make a blood sacrifice to the god(s) of your choosing that the developers are able to save the sauce. As for now, this pizza needs to spend some more time in the oven.
Buy it if you like to be a part of community and help the devs make it the way you like it .The game is so far good. I had  a lot of fun for the 4 hours I played will play much more.

I realise this game is in Early Access and will hopefully be improved in the near future, but I am going to just point out some issues and rate the game on it's current state.
Before I begin, I just want to point out that I am a competetive-oriented player, meaning a working melee system has the highest priority for me.
--------------------------------------------------------------
Some good things about the game are:
The graphics - they are really fancy.
The Naval Combat, which is quite enjoyable actually and the ships have proper physics, which is a very good mechanic at this early point of development.
Musicians, I guess, who doesn't like musicians? And the pieces you can play are of great quality too.
Voice chat - has acceptable quality and adds to the atmosphere.
--------------------------------------------------------------
Now on to the bad things:
Just to say it, I do not mind factions or classes (like cavalry) missing at this early stage of development, however I do very much mind core mechanics of the game just lacking in quality.
Let's face it, the melee and melee animations are horrible. The melee combat is delayed, laggy and just overall unenjoyable and unplayable. It definetely needs to be reworked from the ground up and I feel like that is quite a chunk of work.
Looking back at Mount and Blade Warband (currently 1,770hrs and counting) the competetive nature and smooth melee combat is definetely what made the game so great and addicting.
--------------------------------------------------------------
My thoughts:
All in all I can say that for casual players, who are not interested into competetive gameplay, this game is fine at it's current state.
As far as more competetive players, especially from the Mount and Blade Community, are concerned, I cannot recommend this game at it's current state, as it does not fulfill the requirements for competetive gameplay.
I have to admit that the game has great potential though, now it is up to the Devs to make something out of it.
--------------------------------------------------------------
PS: To all the fanboys saying "but it's Early Access reeeeeeeeeeeeee", think about past experiences.
DayZ was early Access too and now look at it 4 years later.
Early Access does not mean the game will necessarily be improved and it is definetely no excuse for core mechanics of a game not working properly.
(If the game is updated and fixed, I will change my review.)
