I stuck with it for about 25 -26 hours. While it is a fun game I still can't recommend it for the following reasons:
1. No tutorials. Apparently this game used to have tutorials. Not since the launch.
2. You spend more time in queue than you do actually playing the game. And while in queue you are waiting for the Matchmaker to find a battle for you to join. This is the first time I encountered this type of setup. It was unnecessary and annoying. Unless you are lucky enough to find a Squad that won't dismiss you.
3. There are a few rude people in the Chat room. I was called names for no reason. They said they were joking. Another couple players ganged up on me because I mentioned that I had found a way to leave the battle accidentally. I thought it was a good discovery in case of emergencies (like when my computer started to overheat). I was called a traitor that time.
4. In Chat, you ask a question and 95% of the time you won't get an answer. You will be ignored. Happened to me & other new players.
5. I have over 500 GB on my laptop. Yet, my computer was still getting close to overheating. It is a fairly new laptop.
6. WiFi (free) is iffy for this game.
7. The game lags. Sometimes you are late to the battle.
8. I kept getting dismissed from squads by the leaders. So, this makes it hard to get into battles quickly. It doesn't matter if you follow them or not. I tried both tactics of following & trying to find another way (different direction) to attack the enemies. Nada. Nothing. Still dismissed.
9. I know that the higher you get the more points it takes to reach the next level. And the value of the points don't change, you just need more of them. Not this game. I played a few of the 'shorter battles' before I reached a certain Rank. The points didn't change. As soon as I reached this one Rank, the points were next to nothing for the same actions. Played a couple of the longer battles, got very little points. Went back to playing the shorter battles, got very little points. Yes folks, the points aren't consistent throughout the game.
So, that is my review. Whether you like it or not is up to you. If you have free WiFi or a laptop, don't get it.

If the controls were fixed this would be a great game.  In particular, if you jump and then swing your sword your character continues on its path - you cannot change direction in mid air.  This makes the game feel unresponsive and so is hard to recommend.
Jumping and combat in this game is as responsive as a blind person in a dodgeball tournament.

I absolutely adore the concept of the game. The music is wonderful, and a lot of the concepts are very easy to understand right off, so it's easy to get immersed in the game.  But you can't get too comfy, because these will break you right out of that immersion:
-Randomly-generated levels that jumble up combinations of six room types, tops, and throw enemies wherever.
-Awful physics that make landing jumps tricky, or just bug out in impossible ways that often force you to die or quit.  (Try the ice world for the worst controls of 2015.)
-A darkness system that I almost like, except your character's "light radius" is too small.  (A veil of darkness hides enemies and terrain until you get close and "discover" it, but since the game often employs vertical shafts, this usually means you don't see enemies until it's too late to avoid falling on them.)
-Limited weapon selection, plus an XP system where they get stronger the more you use them, means you don't switch weapons nearly as much as them saying "Megavania" would have you believe.
I want to love this game, and I've cleared three worlds, but I don't know if I can bear much more of issues like this.

A (ludicrous) reboot done right

The original Rise of the Triad launched on 1995 , and it was developed by Apogee Software, the same guys responsible by classics like Duke Nukem and Bio Menace.
So, after a long time on the fridge Apogee have the idea to create a new Rise of the Triad, a reboot, essentially , that captures the over the top paced of the original.
In 2011, Apogee then contacted Interceptor Entertainment to craft this game. Interceptor was working on Duke Nukem Reloaded before that, which was halted by gearbox (colonial marines, anyone?). Finally on 2012, the production of Rise of the Triad has begun. The game could be two things: a complete failure or a good game.
Being a guy that bought this game on pre-order, i have to say even with all the bugs and some performance issues on its release version, the game is fun and really captures the essence of the original. The soundtrack is AMAZING, the gameplay is FAST, the gore is over the top, and believe me, this game is hard, and will kick your ♥♥♥. The multiplayer aspect of the game is fun and even more frantic, you will spend some time here.
With its latest version, many of the bugs and issues of the original release are now gone, and the addition of quick-saves makes the game a bit easier (but you cannot save during boss battles, which is a good thing IMO). In top of that, a development kit has been implemented, and let you create your own stuff.
Bear in mind that for a game that has been made by a small studio and being its first great project, this game is a STEAL for its price and really worth your time and your money.

---Native---
Mount & Blade: Warband native is an excellent game. It offers an immersive and realistic single-player experience, along side an incredibly entertaining multi-player with fast paced death match servers and slower paced siege servers to provide a perfect experience for any kind of player. A phenomenal game with a single-player I myself have poured approximately 300 hours into. Something about invading all of Calradia with an army of highly trained Swadian Knights gave me a real objective that, unlike a lot of games, actually made me excited to complete the objective. Every feature of the single-player is well thought out and well implemented, I have yet to find a single feature that I think NEEDS improving; in the entire game I have yet to find a single issue that REQUIRES fixing as even the concerns I have about this game are minor and are certainly not game breaking, in fact a few of my concerns simply come from the perspective of newer players to the game. The few complaints I can make concerning the single-player are certainly minor but I feel that they must be mentioned to be fair and open with my reviews, the single-player is very poorly explained. The only guidance you get is at the very beginning when it explains the general concepts of a medieval society, companions are not explained at all and the vast majority of the features are left with no explanation so newer players are forced to learn by trial and error. I personally feel that this is a minor issue and overall rate the campaign as an 8/10. Multi-player is a completely different beast, however I still find myself with the same positive feelings and I am amazed by how well the rather simplistic fighting system works and flows. This is by far the greatest fighting system I have ever found, that is no exaggeration either. The ‘simple to learn, impossible to master’ system gives newer players an easy time as the 4 lanes of attack are easy to pick up and this is just the basics of combat and truth be told all you really need to know to be a competent fighter in the multi-player of native. However, later techniques and tricks like chambering and feinting can be used to give a player an edge, these tricks can take months to learn properly and allow people of a higher skill group to progress beyond the basics of melee combat. I must however be the typical “noob” and say that I do believe the 2 handed weapons need to become slightly slower as the current state of the game is either a 2 handed sword or a Bow and Arrow, I have been on servers with 30+ people with every single person there using a great sword or a bow & arrow, there is no way you can say the great sword is not over-powered when 80% of the player base use them and they can attack almost as quickly as a 1 handed sword. There we go, now call me a noob who doesn’t understand how difficult the great sword is to use and has no skill whilst I rate the multi-player experience a 7/10 due the great game-play which is slightly let down by some minor balancing issues which I think should be sorted before this experience is worthy of a 8 or a 9 out of 10.
---Napoleonic Wars---
Now this is my favourite way to play this game; 1200 hours of my life have been spent with this DLC and, whilst I am certainly not the best in the world, I have picked up on most of the things you can do in this game. I think you’d be hard pressed to find a part of this DLC I have never seen before. This DLC provides everything you could ever want from a game. Whether you’re looking for a bit of chill gaming with a few friends you can go on death match severs and use classes like the sapper or sailor to have a bit of fun, or you’re looking for a more competitive game then you can choose the battle type servers like group fighting where you will find many players who take the game seriously and will absolutely destroy you time and time again until you finally start to notice the difference as you start to climb the scoreboard and become the best on the server. Genuinely the best feeling ever, the first time you appear best on the server. 5 factions each with their own unique units, all in historically accurate uniform and still providing a whole range of play-styles with the different troop types. Riflemen for sniping enemies with extreme accuracy (as accurate as 19th century weapons get anyway) Line Infantry for holding the front-line, Light Infantry for doing the same thing as a Line Infantryman only being a better shot (Seriously why does anybody play line? Lights have the same melee stats but they can shoot better) Cavalry for annoying everybody because cav is basically the P90 in CS:GO and sappers/sailors for trolling and having fun without being top of the leader board and finally artillery for the people who want to come 1st place on the ‘Vs Bots’ servers but last place on any server that has actual players. There is a unit for everyone! This is the greatest value DLC for any game I have ever seen and I have yet to find anyone who told me they hated the game and managed to maintain their opinion after I taught them what a melee was and how to kill people. They soon became a fan. For this reason I give this DLC a 10/10 a perfect score for a perfect game!
---Has to be said---
The DLC for Mount & Blade, Napoleonic Wars is by far my favourite game/DLC of all time. The community involved with it is astounding and whilst the public servers are usually populated by the regular internet user, the community of regiments that has sprung up around this game is amazing. If you play this game you should certainly find a regiment to gain the full game experience, but please expect these players to be more serious with the game, regiments usually uphold discipline and expect their member to follow orders and be quiet during events. I have been around for a while and have tried many regiments but the one I have stuck with for the longest and have enjoyed the most has been a regiment called the 43rdQL. I have been with this community for almost 2 years and have met some of my best online friends in this regiment. Overall a great group and certainly a group to try out if you are looking into getting this game and DLC.

I really wanted to like this game, but it is possibly the most broken mess of a game I have ever played. There is a frequently occuring gamebreaking bug where the physics stop working and your character gets trapped in an invisible wall. This happened to me roughly 15 times in about an hour. I was NEVER able to complete a single stage because the game's unstability became unbearable. This is only the major problem. There are other minor bugs like enemy animations/attacks not working properly, character randomly changing directions, attack buttons sometimes stops working... Outside of bugs, the controls are abysmal. Stiff and clunky are words not strong enough to describe how bad they are. Jumping is a nightmare, which is a big problem considering its a platforming game.
If the game functioned properly, I would recommend it even with the bad controls, but the game does not function. It seems as if the game was never properly tested or even played before being released. Hopefully a bug fixing update will save this game, the potential is there. The graphics and audio are great and the game (when it works) is actually a lot of fun.

Brothers - a tale of two sons is a cinematic adventure that takes place in a living, breathing world.
Although the path you take through the game's story is a rather linear one, the places you visit and the characters you encounter make for a very detail-rich and epic experience. The art direction is superb and the game looks very beautiful from beginning to end. The characters are strong and the story touches every aspect of human life that has been important to man in all times. Grand and universal themes such as friendship, trust, fear and sadness are conveyed by telling a story that needs no specific language to be told.
The gameplay is unique in that you control two characters simultaneously and various interesting challenges are built around that concept. When I say challenges, I don't mean that the game is particularly difficult. You will very rarely reach fail states. This is good and should be that way, because the gameplay has another purpose than the classic win/fail situations often encountered in video games: The player is bound to the main characters of the story and the very special control system lets the player experience the bond between the two brothers via the player's own hands. Every aspect of interaction in the game world is based on the idea of conveying this bond. This game is unadulterated fun with all the Rock and Roll legends and is just perfectly written for Jack Black, however,  the game has some major flaws.
First and most egregious since it's an adventure game, is: The camera is complete and utter garbage. Constantly getting lost or turned around during boss fights means you have no idea if the boss did their "special move" so I can attack it at the right time. This is a fundamental problem.  I've switched to a controller from the mouse, but it's not much of an improvement. The "lock" on button is critical when playing so you can flick the camera around which of course makes you want to throw up. The game palette which understandably makes sense for the type of game it is -- is way too dark, and there is no first person hud of any kind that tells you your health, the bosses health, minimap, etc. These didn't stop me from finishing the game, but it did make the experience a chore.
The writing has always carried Tim Schaefer's games and this one is no exception. Fantastic voice acting with authentic Rock and Roll legends.
If you love JB, heavy metal, and adventure games, buy this. Just don't do it for full price.

I'm writing this review while the game is still in beta.
Let me start off with, if you liked Gunz1 and played it religiously you'll probably dislike this game.  Everything is much more "restricted" in this game.  Your choice of character design for the most part doesn't exsist.  Skills like aerial recovery(which at the time of writing doiesn't work btw) or wake-up attacks are now tied to a meter.  Instead of "styles" you're given a skill tree which you have to unlock by levels to even get were once basic skills such as aerial recovery.  Every class has a skill from the get go that is basicly an instant kill.  Lag is rampent due to the p2p structure and net code they use.  Oh and instead of their being a lobby with a selection of games you're auto matched into a game LoL style.
On the plus side the game looks nice.  Wall running is slightly more flexible than in Gunz1.  Did I mention it's prettier than the original?  Not to say that the game doesn't have any other good points, something about it is enough to give me a small hope for the future.
I've tried repeatedly to like this game as a GunZ successor since I was a fan since Ijji days but honestly I can only enjoy it knowing thinking its not a true successor.  Hopefully MAIET pulls a FF14 and polishes this game into something more rather than pull a FF13.
Edit
With the last patch update the netcode has gotten even worse increasing lag to horrid levels.  Match making is pretty unbalanced placing unranked players of low level against ranked players of max level.  And its come to my attention that gear heavily influences the flow of the game.  If you have no premium tesla gear and go up against someone who does, chances are you're gonna lose severely especially if the level difference is not in your favor.

In the short time that I've played the game there are two things that have jumped out at me.
The first is that the game has very fun, fast gameplay. The game definitely rewards skill and with great precision you can kill even the highest levelled players. The combat can be frustrating when you get completely stunlocked by another player, which is especially frustrating for a new player who does not understand the game yet and is attempting to learn the mechanics. In terms of the gameplay, this game is very good.
The second thing that I have noticed is that this game is EXTREMELY unbalanced. Although the game claims that it will match you with players of "equal level and skill", it is lying to you. At level 1, you will get matched with level 20 players that have full sets of gear and will tear you apart. This makes learning the basics of the game very difficult. It also makes the game somewhat unfair. They definitely need to fix the matchmaking in this game ASAP. It deters new players (like myself) almost immediately from wanting to play the game any further. The gameplay is great and so is the game itself, but this level of unbalance and the feeling of it being unfair from the very beginning has made me turn my decision and not recommend this game for the moment. The learning curve is too great for you to be thrown into a game full of high level players.
I hope that this gets changed soon, I see real potential in this game.

Alright, so I'm pretty torn on this. I'd been waiting a long while, debating a long while on whether I wanted to get my hands on it, because it looked quite fun and silly and right up my alley, and it's from Codemasters, but the reviewers I normally trust noted frustrating difficulty with it. Having finally picked it up for a little under $4 USD, I think I can sum up all the problems with this game in one word: "Arbitrary."
There's an arbitrary elimination mode that's horribly unbalanced and basically just means the person in first at the beginning wins. There's an arbitrary shortcut system that requires you to find a key on the track and drive through a specific gate to basically win right off the bat. There's an arbitrary random interval of time between the "3, 2, 1" and the "Go" to make boosting at the start that much harder (though honestly I found that kinda funny). There's an arbitrary damage system that slows your car down after each item that hits you, which serves only to force you to pit and to let those in the lead keep their lead. The whole freaking point of item racing is to keep it competitive, make it so that it's a constant fight for position based on skill. The gameplay mechanics routinely defeat their own purpose here. Hell, there's an item that
. How goddamn lazy is that, destroying the entire purpose? In a great deal of the career mode's races, I didn't feel any satisfaction whether I won or lost, feeling instead like I just ended up wherever the game decided.
Now, if you've read all of that and still want to give this game a try due to curiosity, sale price, a love of F1, or being charmed by the trailers,
I can recommend this to you. If you want a better racing game, you're spoiled for choice here, but Sonic and All-Stars Racing Transformed is name-dropped so often for a reason. If you just want to check this in particular out on sale, then go ahead; you'll definitely get your $4 worth.
The course design is a major, major plus here. I'm not too familiar with F1, but I know a lot of the real tracks from other racing series, and especially racing games (and especially games by Codemasters, at that!). The KERS system encourages taking your time in sharp corners, meaning that places like Monaco and the mountain roads of Japan (because come on, it's a Japan course in a racing game) get to be twisty and winding without ruining momentum. Each course is a loving, cartoonish, theme park version of its setting, be it the country entirely or just the city, and national stereotypes are played for humor, creativity, and really exciting scenes. Racing on bullet trains in Japan, leaping through the castles of Germany, and battling in the factories of the UK are grand fun. As an American, I personally found the USA course to be absolutely adorable, and love the effort they put into these. The original courses are part of the design, of course, and it's quite impressive to see familiar sweeping curves recreated in the country's landscape. I will also have to give some points for sheer awesome value of Abu Dhabi starting with a back-to-back combo of Yas Marina and Ferrari World.
The character design is your usual exaggerated cartoony look, but the animation sells it. Seeing your driver put on their helmet a random way every single time you start the race livens up the usual countdown, much like the Battlefield games having those one-in-ten-thousand reload animations. I don't know the drivers all too well, but was able to find pretty much all of the ones I've heard of. The voice acting is serviceable, and playing mostly as Kimi Räikkönen, it took a while before I realized that every driver speaks their own home language with a peppering of English. It does add a good deal to the experience to hear an international field, even if a bit exaggerated in performance.
There is a massive amount of bloat in this game, from extraneous unfun game modes to a wealth of gameplay mechanics that are never, ever explained. The key and shortcut system is never once mentioned. Boosting at the start by pressing the pedal right at "Go" is never mentioned. Boosting after a jump by hitting the gas the second you land is never mentioned. And so on, and so forth. You're gonna probably need a guide for this one.
The sense of speed honestly isn't too impressive outside of boosts. It doesn't really feel particularly like F1. It's the courses and the KERS system that really hammer home what it's based off of. All in all, it's absolutely goofy in a great way, but I mostly only recommend it to those out there that, say, would go into a game store and pick out a racing game from the bargain bin just to see what the experience is like, not for completionist's sake or out of serious hope it'll be a major timesink and investment. For the most part, I really was tempted to hit that "Not Recommended" button. But I haven't stopped playing, so I think that answers that.
EDIT (3/10/17): Having put this game down and not ever really picked it up again, only doing so briefly before uninstalling it quickly again in frustration, it just feels wrong of me to leave a positive review up. The game's charm does NOT make up for the horrific imbalance, lazy mode design, and cheap, overpowered shortcut system. It's this sort of coasting by on "good enough" that's left us with a dearth of actually decent racing titles; don't encourage this.

The game has a WW1 set-up, pitching little toy soldiers against each other in a minature 'toy battlefield'. You have to set up a variety of defences to guard your base (A toy box) from incoming enemy ranging from infantry, tank, and air units. With each kill brings a small amount of money you can spend to buy more defences, or upgrade current defences to a higher tier. The goal of each mission is the same - Allow no, or few units pass into your toy box. If a certain number of enemy pass into your toy box, then you lose.
The animations on the soldiers, and great detail on each of the levels really what makes this game special. It's a small little gem that helps pass time. It Isn't made for the hardcore gamer, but I believe It's a game anybody can try, and love.

This is a game that does great at a lot of things, and almost makes a great game out of it.  However, a few negative points spoil what this game could be, and make it what it is: a good, maybe even very good, but not excellent, game.  It has great music, a map with some actual variety in scenery, fantastic combat and the ability to change up your character midgame when you realize you want to go in a totally different direction than you thought you did.  The story is moderately compelling, there is a lot of content, and the world is fantasy while being a relatively lighthearted break from the more gritty, 'realistic' RPGs. (Which are also awesome)
So, the bad.  Amalur, you came so very close.  But you fell short in two areas, and they're big ones.  The first place it doesn't perform well is pacing.  The middle of this game is looooooooooong.  Like, I considered not finishing the game long, and I like to finish things I start.  I'm glad I didn't, because it really picks up about 60% of the way through, but it is a major fault nonetheless.
The second fault is difficulty.  Play this game on hard if you have any experience with video games.  Otherwise, once you are a quarter of the way through the game, it will get laughably easy.  It did for me, and I'm. . . not exactly awesome at it.
But neither of these problems are why this game has done so poorly.  If you're on the fence about buying this game but are wondering if it can be as good as the more positive reviews claim if you've never heard of it, this is where you'll want to listen in.  This game had horrible, and I mean horrible, timing.  It managed to launch about 3 months after Skyrim, which had kind of sucked all the air out of the room as far as RPGs go.  Deservedly so, as Skyrim is probably the better game overall, and is certainly more groundbreaking.  But this game deserved better sales than it got because of it.  Take that for what it's worth.
Overall:
Good: Fun combat, good soundtrack, decent story, interesting and detailed setting,
Bad: Pacing, my grandmother could beat this game on the default difficulty.

I quit console gaming a few years ago. I had Kingdom's of Amalur when I first got my PS3 and had been playing on and off ever since. Between the PS3 and PC version, I probably have ~200+ hours invested and just about caught in progress in relation to my console play time. The core game itself has way more content than Skyrim with all of its DLC put together. No exaggerating, you're going to get your money's worth when it comes to content.
Kingdoms of Amalur is one of those titles that suffers from the gaming industry itself and faded into obscurity under its own weight. A shame too because there was a MMORPG in the works. But enough of the meta.
Essentially, the game is a single player ARPG that draws a lot from the Fable series and does it much better in most aspects. Combat is fluid, requiring timed button presses to block/counter or generate different effects from abilities and spells. Your character growth is based on three skill trees: Might, (your warrior) Finesse, (rogue) and Sorcery. (mage) On top of those trees, you have classes that are dependant on how many points you mix or match in the three trees. You can fully invest in one tree to gain access to exclusive abilities, split two trees into a formidable skillset or even split all three and fully customize a class to your playstyle, all with different bonuses as incentive.
The story is a bit hit or miss. There's a lot of that "Chosen One" trope being overused, but the world itself is interesting enough when you get into the literature and lorestones you find along the way. You do, however get to make choices that have lasting effects withint the narrative. (or telling proclaimed by the Fae) Most of which will affect how certain NPCs react to you as the story goes on. Without saying much, consider how you go about doing things because different actions could create more desirable outcomes. At the very least, save often.
Definitely reccomending this to any Fable, Two Worlds, The Witcher, and even Elder Scroll's fans. While Kingdom's of Amalur doesn't have the depth of an Elder Scrolls and Witcher game, or the disappointment of a Fable or Two Worlds, there's a litte of something for everyone. I'd compare it to finding a nickel on the ground but finding out it's one of those rare coins that happens to be worth $500.

The Good:
Fun game to play casally against friends.
The Bad:
If you're new to Tekken and want to play competitively/online you're already six generations of games, characters and combos behind the curve. The game has a cult-like following meaning majority of the online community is well experienced in the games underlying strategies/mechanics and many of the games diverse characters.
The Tekken series is most well known for it's incredible depth and polished gameplay, not it's incredible innovations between game releases. Often times characters are recycled in one game's story to the next with marginal additions to their core combos which persist between generations. This allows players who've followed the series from it's inception to master characters incrementally as they change and inevitably return in the following games. Characters who've persisted over several generations of Tekken games now reappear for experience players to trivially re-learn. For new players, this organic way of learning and discovery isn't possible in Tekken 7.
As with many games that develop a passionate community, it's difficult to create an atmosphere that welcomes new players to the game. New players will be disappointed to find:
- Matchmaking is rarely able to find players of similar skill.
- The campaign offers little to no direction as to how a character should/can be used.
- Practice mode offers little explanation on what mechanics/tools are available for the type of training you'd like to do.
These are just a few drawbacks off the top of my head.
That being said, this experienced community is not a gated one. Tekken information is available and abundant if you'd like to invest the time and energy you can learn to play.

First review I've written for a game and it's mostly because I feel a little short changed here. Don't get me wrong the game is great and I don't even care about the microtransactions embedded into it. The thing I'm most disappointed in was the story. I felt like it could've gone so much farther and I feel like they are attempting to milk the franchise for the next episode or more DLC which is stupid. This is a good game and it could've been a great game if they'd just thought more about the story and increased the impact it had on the Deus Ex universe.
Overall I loved the game, graphics were great, controls were fine to me and even the missions didn't seem repetetive even though the location that the game is set felt a little small and same compared to the diversity from DE:HR. I was hoping this game would carry on the story of it's predeccessor nicely by giving me the answers I felt everyone who played the game deserved, but all it's done is left a sour taste in my mouth and made me doubt whether they'll make a new game just to finish the story or try and milk the franchise for all it's got.
I think the fans of this franchise deserved more from the story than we got and we're let down badly by the plot holes throughout the game as well as the questlines which have no true ending just a simple "well what do you think about it?" ending which makes me feel like there is DLC coming just to finish this questline and I hate that more. I also didn't like the fact that there are only around 11 side missions I found. They were fluffed out so they weren't one and done but still a game like this should have enough side missions to keep you satisfied and even make you forget about saving the world. Hell I just want a game where I can have a mission to do but the sidequests look so good I just get lost in doing them which is what Deus Ex had to offer.
All in all I recommend this game if it's on sale as it is a good game but for full price I say no. It had promises to all the fans from the last game and it failed to deliver and for that I would not recommend this game to anyone who is a fan of Deus Ex: Human Revolution.

In Crystal Catacombs you play an adventurer that travels to the mentioned crystal catacombs.
There you have to fight through the different parts of the dungeon in a metroidvania-like fashion.
The dungeons are procedurally generated, so every time you enter (or die) the dungeon will have another layout.
The difficulty is kind of high.

Really, I want to like this game.
Conceptually, Its got a lot of what I love in platformers and a decent atmosphere.
The soundtrack is fantastic, the sound effects suit everything well.
I can't bring myself to recommend this game though.
A lot of the other reviews complain about the jump physics; I have to agree fully.
Between the narrow shafts and corridors the game typically generates and the overly huge area of effect most of the monsters have, the jump physics will murder you more than almost anything else.
Chase AI for the bat type monsters follows too closely... to the point that in order to evade damage you have to back track several rooms to get a decent angle to attack back.
Traps in the jungle dimension amount to a single pixel thick button, which is the same color as much of the other wooden surfaces and will bring down an instant death  crushing device from the ceiling.
Noticed the first button in the hallway? going to jump over it? yeah, about that... with the way jumps work, you'll be hard pressed not to land on the next almost invisible button.
New to the game, so played it on the lowest difficulty; not sure how player/enemy health scales to difficulty level, but many simple enemies became huge obstacles due to poor placement and bad physics.
The caterpillar enemies sometimes take up 3/4 of the platforms they are on, and will lunge at you if they see you. Good luck jumping to a safe place and being able to attack. Did I mention you don't get much health or ways to replenish it?

All they look like is cubes and blobs, the main character included. Sure, this game takes some cues from Metroid and Castlevania; there's the wall-jumping, leveling up, exploration, items, etc, but there's almost no story at all, and it's more frustrating than fun. Enemies appear out of nowhere and shoot you before you can get out of the way or attack, traps kill you instantly, and most of the time you accidentally touch an enemy because of bad hitboxes. The game does NOT even save your progress until you complete a stage. There are five levels and a boss in each stage. Good luck getting that far. Poor design decision, if you ask me. If you like games that are ridiculously hard, then you might enjoy this. Otherwise, I'd say pass on it and get Valdis Story: Abyssal City instead, a much better Metroidvania by far.

Crystal Catacombs is one of my favourite style and genre of video game. It’s a random 8bit, dungeon, platformer. However, even though it’s my favourite style it saddens me that the game didn’t live up to expectations.
Before I get into the Pros and Cons here is what some people say about the game. Some say this game is difficult and that’s what makes it fun... I say there is a difference between difficult and unbalanced and it’s clearly difficult because it’s unbalanced which shouldn’t be the case. It should be difficult but balanced where the enemies and players scale properly per character level and game level which clearly isn’t the case.
But here’s what I found Positive and Negative:
Pros:
♦ Epic Concept (Random dungeons, items and different every play through makes it epic)
♦ Epic Sounds/Music
♦ Okay Graphics (I know these are old school 8bit graphics, but they could be better)
♦ Idea of Monster Cards are cool but should have more details on the cards (Cards spawn at random for killing a certain enemy to get their card. This is a cool concept that makes the game interesting as you can find out about the Monsters. However, the problem here is the cards don’t tell you anything except show a picture and a brief description. In my opinion, there should be more details on the cards like amount of health, damage and maybe a weakness?)
♦ The ability to zoom the camera in and out is really nifty
Cons:
♦ Levels and enemies don’t increase in Difficulty per level (You can be on level 1 and level 5 for example and enemies will still deal the same damage)
♦ Leveling only increases Health and MP (Doesn't seem to increase Defense which is lame as more health doesn't mean much if you still get hit the same amount of damage)
♦ Enemies are unbalanced compared to your Character. (For example your Character at level 1-3 is really weak and can’t do anything and then when you reach level 4 which gives you a skill point, if you put it in Attack your character is OP)
♦ Some really Strong units appear out of nowhere throughout levels and instantly kill you if they land a shot on you
♦ Some Biomes have enemies that blend in. For example: 90% of Pitt Monsters and Blue Batts and Worms on Ice Fortress (This is terrible as you can’t see the enemies to attack them)
♦ Deep Darkness Biome has an unkillable flying Pink Bombs that explode if touched causing you to lose a quarter health (These are annoying as they make you unable to do anything as you have to stand still to dodge them every 2 steps or so)
♦ Enemies spawn in weird places forcing you to hit them and die (This is really noticeable on The Pitt as enemies spawn on ledges just after lava, thus if you jump they push you into the lava which does a considerable amount of damage. Also enemies like to spawn in spots where you can’t dodge them so if you want to move forward you have to hit them)
♦ Weapon leveling is pointless and takes years (This is a nice feature as using a weapon gives it xp and if it levels up it becomes stronger. However, it’s way too slow and you’re far better off spending Skill Points on Attack which serves the same purpose)
♦ Gold seems pointless as shops are rare and expensive (You normally have far less gold than you need to buy something)
♦ Bosses are way too strong (They can kill you in a few shots, compared to you having to hit them numerous and you spawn in a small room with no platforms or ledges, so jumping over a reasonably large boss is hard and you are guaranteed to get hurt or die. Only way I killed one was with an item I had)
♦ Bosses don't give you anything you can't easily get in normal levels (This is lame as it makes them seem pointless)
♦ There are pointless rooms with ledges you can stand on to activate and the room lights up. (This is cool looking, but they don’t seem to do anything at all... Why put something in that doesn’t do anything?)
♦ Very repetitive (Each level is the same just different sizes until you get to a new biome or a boss level (Some levels may have a shop in them but that doesn’t really add anything new).
♦ Number of items are limited (I’ve picked up about 5 different items in 2 hours of play...)
♦ No Trading Cards (Could have updated to add some pretty awesome backgrounds, cards, badges and emoticons etc)
♦ No Global Highscores (Could have added Global Highscores for Survival mode where the person to reach the highest level was recorded etc. This would only work providing Survival is Endless, which I think it is.)
Overall, the game isn’t terrible in concept, the main problem is that it’s not very well scaled, balanced and the difficulty doesn’t seem to increase as you progress through which ruins it. Like if you can survive long enough to level your character 4 levels and get a Skill Point then from there on all you have to do is level up Attack and you’ll be fine until you get to a boss which in my opinion due to unbalancing you’ll get wrecked no matter what you do. Therefore, on a whole, with some improvement to the negatives... this game would be a pretty decent game. However, due to not being scaled, the unbalancing and the repetitiveness then I can’t recommend this (It’s fun and it’ll make you want to come back and play it... Although each time you do come back you cringe a little more at how repetitive and unbalanced it is).

Similar to Rogue Legacy, whenever you defeat a final boss (i.e. complete one of the 5 worlds), that world is marked as completed even if you later die. However, progress within a world is not saved so you do have to complete each world in one go. I think this strikes a great balance between real challene and a sense of progression. If not for this feature, I likely would have given up due to the difficulty of the game. Being able to save completed worlds really gives a nice sense of relief when you have a good run. I would definitely recommend Crystal Catacombs!

If you, like me, get a lump in the throat every time you see a well done sad scene on screen, then this game will affect you.
The decision to use an imaginary language for the dialogue works well; any emotion in the dialogue is put in by you the player instead of the voice actors, and that means a good chance of emotional impact. Also, the final scenes made me understand why the peculiar control scheme was chosen; it only adds to the emotional impact. Sadly I cannot elaborate without spoilers, but to reiterate: if you are the type to easily empathise with on-screen actors/characters, then this game will move you.
As other reviews have probably mentioned, there is not much "gameplay"; the puzzles are pretty straightforward with very little chance of player death to derail the plot. Most of the puzzle mechanics serve to cement the relationships in the game (and thereby give the ending its impact), so the only "gameplay" that exists is purely in service of the story and the characters.
The story itself is straightforward, with a barebones plot. This game is all about a relationship, the weight of the past, and an emotional ending.

Totally stunning game.

You can only move and interact with your surroundings by pressing one key for each of the brothers, nothing more. The only game mechanic present is figuring out how to get past an obstacle in the way - take that away and you've basically got a very fine movie. It can sometimes get challenging, but that's more about confusing the controls for the characters. There are occasional "combat" scenes, but they are all based around interacting with the surroundings, so they're rather easy.
The story progresses very naturally and I very often found myself just gazing at the scenery opened before me rather than moving forward. It's overall short, and if you're a student like me with limited access to finances, the €15 price tag may be a bit too high, so I recommend grabbing it on sale. But if you don't face such issues, don't wait for anything and just go buy it.

You don't have to think. The weapons are nice. The music is nice. But damn that E2L2 - damn the last secret in that E2L2 and damn these bugged achievements.  But it's ROTT after all.
I'll pass on the story because it's your organisation against the army of El Obscuro. Anyway, you can play 5 characters, each of them having different stats. For exemple, Lorelei is the faster but also the one being the most fragile while Doug is perhaps strong but slow.
You can also carry knifes, pistols, rifle gun - these have infinite ammo. But the best are the special bombs: from the firebomb (my favorite) to the basic rocket launcher, these have limited ammo, the only way to resplenish is to find the same weapon. Thanks god, you always have another type in your neighbourhood. Anyway, the weapons are powerful. And you can also use Excalibat... eeer, well, magic weapons around. Some bonus are also thrown around: from being a dog for a few seconds to a toxic mushroom without forgetting flying or god mode, you'll love that.
The enemies are usually humans, though you can have some robots at one moment and weird creatures at the end. They're easy to beat but when you're in an higher difficulty, it can be quite difficult. But the monks.... yeah, the monks.... they're too powerful. So make sure to have a powerful weapon around.
Rise of The Triad initially didn't allow you to have a quicksave. Now, you can but at the cost of some points. Indeed, you can set scores at the end of each level. You will love hunting all enemies, finding all secrets or collecting all coins (that are just there for statistics). Also, there are secret levels that are reminiscent of the original ROTT, in the early-90' graphics era.
The problem with ROTT is probably the jump and the bouncing jump. I don't know why but I have an hard time to time them. Well, it's mainly because of E2L2, aka The Room and probably I've seen enough lava through Scott's Mystical Head. Doug Wend is the worse in jump and E2L2 and E4L3 are a real pain in the♥♥♥♥♥for him.
Anyway, you can see a progress in the story: from a military base to castles and crypts, the graphics are quite good. And the soundtrack is marvelous.
On a negative note, apart E2L2, jumps and monks, the enemies can get stuck sometimes. I mean by that that they will not react unless they see you and while sometimes, distance can matter, I feel the fact that they're not pursuing you through some doors a little deconcerting.

---Native---
Mount & Blade: Warband native is an excellent game. It offers an immersive and realistic single-player experience, along side an incredibly entertaining multi-player with fast paced death match servers and slower paced siege servers to provide a perfect experience for any kind of player. A phenomenal game with a single-player I myself have poured approximately 300 hours into. Something about invading all of Calradia with an army of highly trained Swadian Knights gave me a real objective that, unlike a lot of games, actually made me excited to complete the objective. Every feature of the single-player is well thought out and well implemented, I have yet to find a single feature that I think NEEDS improving; in the entire game I have yet to find a single issue that REQUIRES fixing as even the concerns I have about this game are minor and are certainly not game breaking, in fact a few of my concerns simply come from the perspective of newer players to the game. The few complaints I can make concerning the single-player are certainly minor but I feel that they must be mentioned to be fair and open with my reviews, the single-player is very poorly explained. The only guidance you get is at the very beginning when it explains the general concepts of a medieval society, companions are not explained at all and the vast majority of the features are left with no explanation so newer players are forced to learn by trial and error. I personally feel that this is a minor issue and overall rate the campaign as an 8/10. Multi-player is a completely different beast, however I still find myself with the same positive feelings and I am amazed by how well the rather simplistic fighting system works and flows. This is by far the greatest fighting system I have ever found, that is no exaggeration either. The ‘simple to learn, impossible to master’ system gives newer players an easy time as the 4 lanes of attack are easy to pick up and this is just the basics of combat and truth be told all you really need to know to be a competent fighter in the multi-player of native. However, later techniques and tricks like chambering and feinting can be used to give a player an edge, these tricks can take months to learn properly and allow people of a higher skill group to progress beyond the basics of melee combat. I must however be the typical “noob” and say that I do believe the 2 handed weapons need to become slightly slower as the current state of the game is either a 2 handed sword or a Bow and Arrow, I have been on servers with 30+ people with every single person there using a great sword or a bow & arrow, there is no way you can say the great sword is not over-powered when 80% of the player base use them and they can attack almost as quickly as a 1 handed sword. There we go, now call me a noob who doesn’t understand how difficult the great sword is to use and has no skill whilst I rate the multi-player experience a 7/10 due the great game-play which is slightly let down by some minor balancing issues which I think should be sorted before this experience is worthy of a 8 or a 9 out of 10.
---Napoleonic Wars---
Now this is my favourite way to play this game; 1200 hours of my life have been spent with this DLC and, whilst I am certainly not the best in the world, I have picked up on most of the things you can do in this game. I think you’d be hard pressed to find a part of this DLC I have never seen before. This DLC provides everything you could ever want from a game. Whether you’re looking for a bit of chill gaming with a few friends you can go on death match severs and use classes like the sapper or sailor to have a bit of fun, or you’re looking for a more competitive game then you can choose the battle type servers like group fighting where you will find many players who take the game seriously and will absolutely destroy you time and time again until you finally start to notice the difference as you start to climb the scoreboard and become the best on the server. Genuinely the best feeling ever, the first time you appear best on the server. 5 factions each with their own unique units, all in historically accurate uniform and still providing a whole range of play-styles with the different troop types. Riflemen for sniping enemies with extreme accuracy (as accurate as 19th century weapons get anyway) Line Infantry for holding the front-line, Light Infantry for doing the same thing as a Line Infantryman only being a better shot (Seriously why does anybody play line? Lights have the same melee stats but they can shoot better) Cavalry for annoying everybody because cav is basically the P90 in CS:GO and sappers/sailors for trolling and having fun without being top of the leader board and finally artillery for the people who want to come 1st place on the ‘Vs Bots’ servers but last place on any server that has actual players. There is a unit for everyone! This is the greatest value DLC for any game I have ever seen and I have yet to find anyone who told me they hated the game and managed to maintain their opinion after I taught them what a melee was and how to kill people. They soon became a fan. For this reason I give this DLC a 10/10 a perfect score for a perfect game!
---Has to be said---

Don't let my low game hours fool you. I played this game for over 100 hours on my xbox before I wiped it.
[Slight Spoilers]
Pros:
+This game lets you play whatever build you want to do.
-> Do you want to be a Mage and surprise people by slamming them to the ground with a massive warhammer? Do you want to play a Rogue who uses Daggers for assassinations but can hold her own in normal combat by wielding a Longsword? Do you want to play a Warrior who's only goal is to destroy people in insane combos with a sword that's twice their size? If you answered yes to any of these, please keep reading.
-> Each class has a set of weapons and armour associated with it, as well as abilities. A Rogue, for example, is built on skill points invested into Finesse and uses light/medium armour that gives bonus critical hit damage. Rogue weapons are the Bow, Daggers, and Faeblades. Their abilities are varied between sustaining mana to apply poison damage to all of their weapons to raining arrows from the sky.
-> The Warrior class is built on skill points invested into Brutality and can use Longswords, Greatswords, and Hammers with the heaviest armour that improves damage resistence and blocking ability. Their abilities vary from an adrenaline surge to deal massive damage when close to death to lifting all surrounding enemies into the air and slamming them all down.
-> The Mage class is built on skill points invested into Magic and can use Staves, Septres, and Chakrams with Robes for armour that help improve mana regeneration. Their abilities can vary from chaining lighting to summoning a meteor to crash down on enemies.
+Gives the middle finger to restricted builds with the Destiny system.
-> You are not set to one way of playing the game. Just purchase a reset from a Fateweaver and suddenly, you can rebuild your character in their entirety! Go from a Mage in robes with a Staff and Septre to a hybrid Warrior/Rogue who uses a Hammer and Faeblades!
(Keep in mind that there are many abilities to each class and you can do more than one class, or even all of them at once if you wanted. When you level up, read up on everything in your abilities tab and decide how the game should work for you.)
+Super satisfying stealth gameplay.
-> Say you were spotted by a Jottun (a reverse Dwarf as I like to call them.) You can teleport through them, throw a smoke bomb down, jump on their back from stealth, and stab their neck to oblivion only to backflip off as you watch them bleed out. It's not just the massive enemies that are satisfying to stealth kill! You can sneak up on a Bandit and in quick succession you can trip them, making them land on their back only for your character to cover their mouth and stab their chest. The sneaking mechanic itself is a little bit wonky but oh my gosh it's still amazing to assassinate half of a Tuatha scout party and have the last few left♥♥♥♥♥♥talk you only to get torn to bits by open combat; speaking of which, my next point is close to this one.
+Fluid combat system.
-> My favourite build was on my character named "Lorabella." She was a Warrior/Rogue hybrid that used a Longsword and Daggers. In the span of a minute, she can roll behind an enemy in stealth, backstab them, and immediately turn to the other enemies that spotted her afterwards. From here she can toss a smoke bomb or use an invisibility potion to get more stealth kills, or she can hold a weapon's attack (you can only equip two weapons at a time) and use the charge ability to launch herself at the nearest enemy, starting an attack combo which kills them quickly. After that, she can block with her shield at the right moment to deflect an enemy's attack and turn it into a combo to kill them quickly. I could go on and on about how many different ways you can play the same game and still be satisfied, but I will spare you from that.
+Fateshifting.
-> In a tight spot? Too many enemies and you just want to go to the next area quickly? Want to get bonus XP for doing what you already do to kill enemies? Just do it™
+Fast Travel!!!
-> Seriously who doesn't like this feature?
Some cons:
-The game can feel very repetitive.
-> Bandits, Fae, some Gnomes here and there, Jottun, Etten, Spiders, Kobolds, and so on. There's not much for diversity in enemies to face, some are just slightly different reskins of the base creature that does something different. See: Kobold Savages are Kobolds that throw their spears instead of try to poke you with them.
-> A lot of the game's quests are a variation of "go here and kill these things for me" and while the combat system is very fun, there's only so much that can be done before it feels like a chore.
-Short story.
-> Excluding the time spent running to the new locations, the Faction quests as well as the main quests feel a little short compared to the size of the world given to the player.
(Overall, I would say this game is absolutely worth buying. I haven't gotten to the DLCs yet though I do look forward to it! I hope this review helped!)

The highest, Elite difficulty, has any tech work only if you have it on manual; but that just seems more suitable for the types counting seashells and putting them in straight lines, so I skipped it.
In total there are 18 levels (12 original + 3 in DLC1 + 3 in DLC2), NG+ and a survival mode. That seemed enough for me, especially for the chump change I bought it.
Grafics do show its age, since it's Xbox 360 game and all, but they still seem rather nice-looking, in my opinion. Music was also OK but nothing too special.
Bottom line, if you want a good WW1 tower defence game, this is just for you.

An enjoyable and colorful venture in the world of avoidance and psychedelic experiences, Zero Reflex provides its audience with easy-to-comprehend gameplay and hard-to-complete levels. You are a small triangle on a circular track, in need to avoid every possible threat produced by evil-looking eye in the center of the screen. Sounds easy? Well, no it is not.
There is no game over per se, but each failure to finish the level will cause you to drop to previous one (sometimes, even more). Zero Reflex is thus a perfect game for stubborn, game-dedicated players with quick fingers and strong mental concentration. Crystal Catacombs calls itself a "retro inspired [...] love letter" and, as someone who was around to see the birth of video games, it certainly feels that way to me. This is a side-scroller from Hell, but man is it fun. The game play reminds me of a cross between Zelda II (trying jump while attacking, for example) and Commander Keen (jumping on platforms while dodging or attacking enemies, with the goal of finding a key that allows you to exit the level). The graphics are bright and, at times, feel more inspired by Atari than Nintendo (I love the jumping spider...ish...y looking thing) and the music is bass heavy and interesting enough to keep me from turning it off, as I usually do.
In terms of the difficulty level: If you're familiar with older, brutally unforgiving titles such as Hydlide or Heroes of the Lance, you'll feel right at home here. Each touch from an enemy or certain environmental features depletes your health bar, while others affect you in other ways (such as slowing your character down). Some enemies, once dead, leave behind nasty residual auras that can kill you if you're not being careful.
The controls are responsive and immediate (at least when using the keyboard, as I've not yet tried a gamepad). The most common complaint is that the jumping is slow, but I don't see it that way. Rather, the jump executes as soon as the player presses the appropriate key, but the arc in which your character falls is slow and wide, meaning you'll actually need to plan each jump and practice enough to become skilled at it. This is definitely a feature I remember seeing a lot of back in the day. Come to think of it, the PC in the original Pitfall (which this game's Jungle level reminds me of quite a bit) jumped the same way, and that's going back to the Atari 2600. Falling after missing an important jump can be incredibly frustrating, but I can't ever say it's unfair, and it's always my own fault.
The thing to remember is that Crystal Catacombs may appear to be a colorful platformer (even it's name sounds generically retro)...but it wants you dead. You need to crush your desire to burn through each level, take your time, and kill it with fire. If this kind of repetitive pain sounds like it's as much fun for you as it is for me, then grab it (especially if you can find it in a bundle or at a discount). Recommended.

Rise of the Triad is an interesting little game.
It's a blast from the past, brimming with rocket launchers, nukes and bazookas. Your character can carry bullet weapons with infinite ammo, but you also have room for one explosive and one magic weapon. These always have limited ammo, but are insanely powerful.
The game is fast-paced where combat is defined by circle-strafing enemies while blasting away at them with high explosives or cursed baseball bats. Fights will be short and your survival depends on your ability to avoid getting hit while blowing massive holes in the horde of enemies you encounter.
Bosses always come with multiple phases, so all of them could be considered puzzle bosses. Except the solution to these puzzles is to 'Use Gun on Boss'. Nevertheless, the actual fights are fun and often feature cool mechanics, like enviromental hazards you have to dodge while filling the boss with bullets and rockets.
The scenery in ROTT is also quite nice. The game looks pretty good, but it is by no means AAA-grade when it comes to textures. Still, the enviroments are all cool because they are a nice mix of classic castles, prisons and torture chambers you'd find in games like Wolfenstein mixed with a futuristic and high-tech labs and super sci-fi jump pads and moving platforms. The end result is a fun and unique setting that is unlike any other.
Rise of the Triad is old school to the max. It has a bunch of secrets in every level, doesn't have regenerating health and also features tons of platforming and traps. The platforming is by no means fun, but it isn't a problem either. Not on its own at least. In combination with the checkpoints, it can become annoying however.
Unlike older FPS titles, ROTT has no quicksave function. The game has checkpoints, usually one per area. If you die at any point before you reach the next checkpoint, you will spawn at the beginning of the level. This often means having to re-do long platforming segments.
While the platforming elements become boring due to the games over-reliance on them, they are necessary. The combat in ROTT is fun, but it simply isn't enough to carry the game. Each fights boils down to how much ammo you have in the end and how accurate you are. As such, the puzzles are 'necessary' to keep the game interesting.
In my opinion however, there are no excuses for the checkpoint system. A lot of players have said it's to make the game more diffcult and challenging, but it doesn't do either. It's just frustrating. Including it as an option would've made more sense.
ROTT also suffers from some techincal issues. It isn't well-optimized on many systems and seems to have problems with AMD cards. Since it's pretty much an indie title, this I can let slip. The developers have also stated they are hard at work on optimizing the game further.
There's a multiplayer mode too, which is just as fast-paced as the campaign if not more. It's as old school as it gets. You'll need to learn the maps, know the locations of the pick-ups and evade enemy projectiles while hitting with your own. It's fun, but difficult, as it should be.
So what's the bottom line? Rise of the Triad is a fun ride. A fun, explosive ride that's totally insane and I just wish it had fewer platforming segments and had quicksaves. If you can get past the checkpoint system and you feel you won't be bored to tears by the repetetive jump pads and platforms, give it a whirl. It's ludicruous!

Crystal Catacombs wallows in mediocrity. The gameplay is -almost- good. The jumping mechanics almost seem to work until you start trying to dodge any enemy projectile or cross any of the numerous platforming sections the game throws at you. Fighting enemies ranges from responsive to downright frustrating, and on numerous occassions I found myself inching at enemies because of their rather enormous attacks compared to my meak little blade. The randomization is pointless, all the levels feel the same in their respective dungeons. The graphics also range from terrible to stylistic and well-done. The main character would be the worst, looking more like a twig than an actual man which makes it all the more difficult to see since you rarely stand out from the lo-fi pixels.
Overall, this game is utterly forgetful. You might (and fairly so) argue that my 30 minutes or so of playtime isn't an accurate amount of time to dismiss/review a game such as this. And you would be right. But, judging from the other reviewers lack of playtime, even the positives, I can safely say there's not much staying power to this game. Go play any of the other numerous rogue-lite platformers, I'm sure you'll find one better than this game.

What to say about Rise of the Triad... first off, who likes a bit of fast-paced action? If that answer in your head (or out loud if you bothered) was a yes, perhaps read on here:
ROTT differs from a lot of the modern day FPS games that most know of in the fact that it offers the factor of intense action in its own unique sorta way. Weapons of all sorts, Powerups, Jump pads, a soundtrack whcih some would love (including myself) and even some fairly decent platforming (Platforming in an First Person Shooter?! Yes, that's right folks).
With similarities to age-old games such as Doom, Quake and more importantly Rise of the Triad's previous version, the game offers levels that though somewhat linear in fashion still offer a challenge to players. On top of the normal gameplay, you may find yourself stumbling across a hidden room with some extra secrets or even an Easter Egg thrown in by the devs. Depending on how hard they are to find, discovering one of those can be a rewarding time of sorts, speaking from my own humble opinion..
To begin with on release however, the remake did in fact have some bugs and issues (as most new games would have which is understandable), but the developers at Interceptor have been working at ROTT after its release and have managed to work out what appear to be a lot of the kinks. I've stuck with the remake since its release and have a feeling that Interceptor is making quite a good first impression to me as a game-developing group with what they've set up here. I might just keep an eye out on any other games that Interceptor works on in the future if such happens.
To sum up quite a long and drawn out reccomendation of Rise of the Triad, I'd say that the game itself can be worth your time if you're looking for something a bit different or creative... Dare I say a bit 'Ludicrous'?

Evil creatures and demons haunt the catacomb’s various lairs, which each have their own theme, and will make your life difficult. Ruthlessly difficult. Nobody has ever returned from within the catacombs to tell their tale, but if you can master this cursed place and destroy the creatures that haunt it, maybe Captain Vasil will be the first.
The developer, Super Fun Games, describes Crystal Catacombs as a “megavania”; a mix between the exploration-based action of Metroid and the relentlessly challenging platforming battles from Megaman. Having tested my mettle against its various lairs it is, most definitely, a fair analogy. The catacombs feature five different areas, which you can tackle in any order you like on normal difficulty, but all are as challenging as each other. Catacombs is reminiscent of Spelunky with its procedurally generated locations and immense difficulty, but it is more stripped back than that, with an old-school flavour that runs all the way through to its core.
After choosing the area you want to start off in you are thrust straight into the action; there’s no tutorial, so you will need to think on your feet and acclimatize to Crystal Catacombs‘ control scheme. Vasil moves with the arrow keys, and you can press the ‘A’, ‘S’ and ‘D’ keys to use items from his hotbar. Just like Samus Aran, he can do a sweet wall slide to gently glide down long passages, and he can also wall jump to propel himself upwards. I was extremely impressed with how responsive and tight movement felt, but was quickly reminded why that would be essential.
The Crystal Catacombs have a diverse and abundant wildlife, and are filled with spiders, gelatinous blobs, bats and demons, all of which are out to get you. Fortunately, Vasil is quite talented with a sword and can tear those nasty mobs a new one. Quick reactions are important and you will need to get used to each enemy’s movement patterns and attacks if you don’t want to die over and over again. You won’t last long if you just go rushing in with your sword waving, instead, if you can kite your enemy away, whilst taking a quick swipe, you will in most cases be successful. Unless that enemy can fire lasers, then you are screwed.
Combat is fast and fun and becomes even more exciting if you can find the various weapons and spells that are scattered throughout the catacombs. Using a sword is great and all but how about a bow, or a rocket launcher instead!? Successfully killing mobs and bosses rewards Vasil with experience points he can use to level up his hit points, magic points, attack and defence;  so, while it is possible to speedrun your way to the randomly placed exit, it is not advised.  It is really easy to get ahead of yourself and become cocky, blasting your way through the map at a swift pace, only to become a puddle of goop moments later. I highly advise taking things slowly and checking out all of the possible pathways open to you. If any particular passage looks too dangerous or crowded with enemies for you to make it through, it most likely is. Trust your instincts and look for another way around, otherwise you will pay a hefty price.
My only gripe with the game is its miniscule amount of graphics options. You are given the choice of a few low screen resolutions  and that’s your lot, you can’t even change to full HD. Surely it wouldn’t be too difficult to include a wider array of resolutions, at the very least?
Nonetheless, I have only begun to scratch the surface of Crystal Catacombs, here; it’s a content rich game for those with sufficient gaming skills to see it all. If you loved Spelunky or Binding of Isaac you will be well equipped for the task of conquering the catacombs. Me on the other hand, I’ve succumbed to far too many premature deaths and am in need of a lie down now.
A special shout out also needs to go to Crescent Moon Games who have been publishing some absolutely stellar titles on Steam recently. Crystal Catacombs will fit right in alongside The Deer God and Mimpi.

Disappointed to see that the jumping mechanics have not been improved from early access despite ample criticism and time before the steam launch. It's impossible to slow your character in the air. A lone captain hurtling through the recesses of space in his wooden flying ship, his captain's log scrawls across the opening screen telling of a journey for treasure and relics beyond earthly knowledge, a strange and heinous eye beckoning him to the depths of strange uncharted catacombs.
Crystal Catacombs mixes a healthy dose of fast action dungeon delving with the brutal difficulty and randomized level layouts of the roguelike genre for one addictive and challenging combination.
Running and slashing your way through the corridors of the Crystal Catacombs is an almost ethereal experience, the monstrous and otherworldly designs of the grotesque enemies, dark corridors filled with countless hazards, the welcoming pulse of neon-light lit treasure and warp gate rooms all set in motion to MidnightEpsilon's incredible nostalgia-inducing chiptune soundtrack for a total arcade bliss-out.
For those who remember the days of slamming fistfulls of quarters into arcade cabinets or scribbling down complex series of passwords to retry that one impossible part of your favorite NES game for the millionth time, the difficulty and challenge of Crystal Catacombs will be a familiar affair.
The unseen instant-deaths from crushing pillars and barrage of seemingly unavoidable and well-calculated enemy attacks will have even the most seasoned gaming vet yelling "♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t!". This is the exact the kind of spirit those of us who hold video games dear to our childhood miss these days.
The uniquely themed stages feature a consistently high challenge and although they can be tackled head on, exploring your surroundings is imperative to your success. Though you can prepare yourself with extended exploration and discovery of supplies the stage's boss cannot be defeated by means of grinding, but instead with reflexes and skill all brought out in full force.
tl;dr
It's tough. You'll give up. A lot. But it's that ridiculous difficulty, that seemingly unsurpassable moment in an old arcade game that had us returning to it so many times throughout our lives and that's the same kind of yearning I get to go back and play Crystal Catacombs, as hard as it may seem.

This game lives up only to the bare minimum of what it promises.
-It's a Roguelike: Yeah, it's random. You can explore the vast levels... but why? There's only two important things per level: The Treasure Chest room, containing the level's one unique item (which is usually a one-use special attack or potion, in my experience), and the key, which you need to progress to the next level. Aside from that, there are scant few other chests, all of which seem to contain money, which you'll NEED to use at the rarely appearing shops, because enemies only drop money one coin at a time, and never drop things a lot.
-It's a Megavania style game: Yeah, it's got the level template of 'big sprawling level you need platforming to get through'. But god, everything about this aspect of the game is poorly done. The controls are stiff and slow. Wall-jumping is extremely finicky. There's no incentive to explore, or any sort of map progression. The 'Warp' system is nearly entirely wasted. The enemies are hard to see against the rough, grainy backgrounds, and deal way too much damage to fit in with the game's unforgiving starting stats and low drop rate of any sort of healing.
It has possibly the strangest jump physics I've ever seen: When you jump, you're 'set' in an arc, but not how you'd expect. You can still turn around in mid-air, but you retain your speed, now moving in the opposite direction! So if you jump, and then want to fall STRAIGHT DOWN, have fun turning around repeatedly in order to land steadily. And don't even get me started on the ice level. Picture this: you're standing still. And you want to jump straight up. You press the button... and instead, you jump in an arc, right into the enemy you're fighting. It's a complete mess.
While it is better than it used to be, it is still unacceptable to call this a 'complete' game. I expected better.

My initial review was negative because I found one game mechanic in particular very frustrating (thieving). Just to explain this a little - NPC's will try to steal things from your shop sometimes, just by picking it up and running outside. You can't go outside yourself, and some counters are placed very nearby the entrance so it takes around 1-2 seconds for a thief to run off. The frequency of the thieves made some scenarios thoroughly miserable.
You can unlock skills by playing the game which cut down on thievery and even allow for a rechargable magic barrier which will make thievery almost none existant. This made me wonder what the point of thievery was in the first place. It was a mechanic that gave me 3 hours of annoyance and frustration that has now been nullified completely.
I don't want to wipe thievery from the game, I just want it to be fun!
I still can't recommend the game at the moment, because of the issues like;
1) Many scenario's are "Sell 10 X and 20 Y". The frequency of sales is low and the things you'd expect to help, don't. For example, when you have lots of money in the scenario and decide to sell everything for 1% of the original price, there's no Black Friday rush. It's just the same - long and drawn out. The Developer has said that there are some mechanics behind the pricing but it's not readily apparent to me. It's obvious when you've priced something too high, but there's never a low enough price to get the( effect you want.)
2) There's no progression in My Shoppe. There are scenarios to play that unlock new items but there's nothing to spend your gold on. It just feels pointless.
3) Barbarian attacks are every five minutes, and can be almost as annoying as thievery. Especially when you consider that your sword does AOE damage and if you accidentally break a counter in a Scenario, you can't replace it. That means that you might not have space to sell 10 of X and 20 of Y. That means that the two hours you already played are wasted.
The latest update wasn't really what I wanted to see. A small customization of your own character. I think they're dabbling with frequency rate of barbarians and things like that too.
Maybe I'm expecting too much for a low priced game? I mean it's basically a steal. It's just that I have always wanted to play a game like this, but with more rpg elements and progression/expansion and I would love to see My Shoppe become that.

Welcome to Sweep Simulator 2015! After setting up shoppe in a little quaint town, you soon find out that everyone is Pigpen from Peanuts. As you follow around every customer walking into your store, you try to sweep away all the grime left behind because it ruins the appeal of your shoppe. To no avail, the dirt never stops and neither does the sweeping you will have to do.... (Thanks to the devs for reducing the dirt intake of customers, so the tale above is just a horrible memory.)
:POSITIVE ASPECTS:
-Animation that isn't too complex, but complements the style of the game.
-3 skill trees to level up your shoppe, deliver time, and prices.
-Customers stealing and barbarians attacking keeps you on your toes.
-Can strike down all who oppose you or look at you wrong!
-Customers actually pick up or wear the items they buy.
-More variation than most game's npcs (add hooded rogue like characters maybe?).
-Multiple types of swords, spells, brooms, and hammers to buy as you progress.
-Mideveal/Fantasy style of the game is wonderful.
-2 game modes. Scenarios (Story line) and My shoppe (manage your own shoppe with no rules!).
-Building and customizing your shoppe is very flexible in terms of how you can place shelves, tables, counters, etc.
-You can see your character's legs when you look down and realize why you became a shoppe keeper.
-Mice appear when your shoppe is really dirty (not very positive, but a cool feature).
-You can finally walk around outside your shoppe and pursue thieves.
-Day and night cycles.
-Sombreros
-ONLY 7 DOLLARS!!!
:NEGATIVE ASPECTS:
-Sword combat is a little clunky. May hit/kill an innocent or damage/destroy a table next to you while stabbing a barbarian infront of you.
-Npcs are a little stupid and get caught on things like shelving units, tables, each other, and decide to do a moonwalk at times. (Please make Billie Jean play when NPCs moonwalk. Jk.)
-No Steam trading cards
-No Steam Workshop (Srsly guys, would be the bomb.)
:COMMENTS:
Charming game with so much potential. Can't wait to see how this game progresses over time. Of corse I will be playing often and checking out all the new updates. 9/10.
